descriptions.en: New Year's Day on January 1 opens the Gregorian calendar year and is a public holiday in most countries. The date was fixed as the start of the year by the Romans in 153 BCE and kept when Pope Gregory XIII reformed the calendar in 1582. People spend it recovering from the night before, visiting family, making resolutions, and keeping customs for good luck, from lentils in Italy to a first dip in icy water in the Netherlands.

Cuba marks January 1 as both New Year's Day and the Triumph of the Revolution, the day in 1959 when the dictator Fulgencio Batista fled the country. Rebel columns under Che Guevara and Camilo Cienfuegos entered Havana in the following days, and Fidel Castro arrived in the capital on January 8 after a victory march across the island. The anniversary is a national holiday, marked with official ceremonies, speeches and family celebrations combining the revolution and the new year.

New Year in Switzerland begins with fireworks over Lake Zurich and Lake Geneva and church bells ringing in the year at midnight. In Appenzell Ausserrhoden, the Silvesterchläuse, men in enormous headdresses and costumes of bark, moss or bells, go from farm to farm yodelling to wish neighbours a good year, both on December 31 and on January 13, New Year by the old Julian calendar. In many cantons January 2, Berchtoldstag, is also a holiday, spent visiting family and playing traditional games.

Sudan's Independence Day on January 1 marks 1956, when the country ended joint British and Egyptian rule, known as the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium, which had lasted since 1899. On the morning of independence, Prime Minister Ismail al-Azhari raised the new flag over the palace in Khartoum, and Sudan became the largest country in Africa at the time. The anniversary is a national holiday, observed with official ceremonies and gatherings in Sudan and among Sudanese communities abroad.

World Braille Day on January 4 is the birthday of Louis Braille, born in France in 1809, who lost his sight as a child after an accident in his father's workshop. As a teenager at a school for blind children in Paris, he developed a reading and writing system of raised dots, arranged in cells of six, that can be read by touch. The UN first observed the day in 2019, and it highlights braille's role in education, independence and equal access to information.

Spaghetti Day on January 4 celebrates one of the world's most popular pasta shapes, whose name comes from the Italian spago, meaning string. Dried pasta was being made in southern Italy and Sicily by the Middle Ages, and spaghetti spread worldwide with Italian emigrants in the 19th and 20th centuries. The day is an excuse to cook a classic such as spaghetti alla carbonara, aglio e olio or al pomodoro, and to share it at the table.

slogans.en: Twirl It. Slurp It. Love It.

descriptions.en: Epiphany on January 6, also called the Feast of the Three Kings, commemorates the visit of the Magi to the infant Jesus. In Germany it is a public holiday in Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria and Saxony-Anhalt. Around this date children dressed as the Three Kings go from door to door as Sternsinger, star singers, collecting money for children's charities and chalking a blessing such as 20*C+M+B+27 above the door.

Iraqi Army Day on January 6 marks the founding of the Iraqi army in 1921, when its first unit, the Musa al-Kadhim Battalion, was formed in Baghdad under the British Mandate. The army has played a central role in the country's turbulent modern history, through coups, wars and the fight against the Islamic State group. The day is a public holiday, marked with military parades, ceremonies honouring those who died in service and flags across the country.

Yennayer, the Amazigh (Berber) New Year, is celebrated around January 12 and opens the year of the old agricultural calendar of North Africa. By a modern convention the Amazigh years are counted from 950 BCE, when the Berber king Sheshonq I took the throne of Egypt. It has been a public holiday in Algeria since 2018 and in Morocco since 2024, and families mark it with a couscous of seven vegetables, dried fruits and nuts, and wishes for a good harvest.

slogans.en: A new year, rooted in older soil.

descriptions.en: International Rubber Ducky Day on January 13 celebrates the yellow bath toy that has floated in tubs for generations. Rubber toys became possible after the vulcanisation of rubber in the 19th century, and the classic floating duck spread with mass-produced plastics in the 20th. Its fame grew further when Ernie sang Rubber Duckie on Sesame Street in 1970, and today rubber ducks appear in charity duck races, collections and even in programming, where explaining a problem to a duck helps find the bug.

Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, has been an official public holiday in Morocco since 2024, after King Mohammed VI announced the decision in 2023. It opens the year of the old North African agricultural calendar, counted by modern convention from 950 BCE, and is celebrated around January 13 and 14. Amazigh families mark it with a shared meal such as couscous with seven vegetables or a dish with a hidden date stone that brings luck to whoever finds it, along with music and wishes for a good harvest.

Arbor Day in Jordan on January 15 opens the winter planting season, when the rains make it possible for young trees to take root. Schools, municipalities, the army and volunteer groups plant seedlings of native species such as oak, pine and carob on hillsides and in parks. In one of the world's most water-scarce countries, where forests cover only a small fraction of the land, every surviving tree helps hold soil, shade towns and slow the spread of desert.

Winnie the Pooh Day on January 18 marks the birthday of A. A. Milne, born in London in 1882, who created the honey-loving bear. Milne based the stories on his son Christopher Robin and his toys, and the first book, Winnie-the-Pooh, appeared in 1926 with illustrations by E. H. Shepard. The name came from Winnie, a real black bear at London Zoo, and fans mark the day by reading the books, playing Poohsticks from a bridge or sharing a little something with honey.

slogans.en: A day without a friend is like a pot without a single drop of honey.

descriptions.en: Popcorn Day on January 19 celebrates one of the oldest snacks in the Americas: archaeologists have found popped maize thousands of years old in Peru and Mexico. A kernel pops because the water inside turns to steam and bursts the hard hull, turning the starch inside into a white foam. Popcorn became inseparable from cinemas in the 1930s, and it can be a wholesome whole-grain snack when it is not drowned in butter and salt.

The International Day of Education on January 24 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in December 2018 and first celebrated in 2019. It highlights education as a human right and as the foundation for peace, gender equality and development, at a time when roughly 250 million children and young people are out of school. UNESCO leads the day with a theme each year, and schools, universities and governments use it to push for quality learning for everyone.

slogans.en: Education is a right, not a privilege.

descriptions.en: National Peanut Butter Day on January 24 celebrates a spread that is a staple in American kitchens and loved far beyond. Peanuts were grown in South America thousands of years ago, and in North America the Canadian chemist Marcellus Gilmore Edson patented a peanut paste in 1884; the agricultural scientist George Washington Carver later championed the peanut, though he did not invent peanut butter. It is rich in protein and healthy fats, and people mark the day with sandwiches, cookies, satay sauce or a spoonful straight from the jar.

slogans.en: Smooth or Crunchy — Just Love Peanut Butter!

descriptions.en: January 25 is a national holiday in Egypt that joins two anniversaries. Police Day recalls January 25, 1952, when Egyptian police in Ismailia refused to surrender their station to British forces and dozens were killed in the fighting that followed, and on the same date in 2011 the protests that began in Cairo's Tahrir Square launched the revolution. The day is marked with official ceremonies honouring the police and the fallen, and with memories of the 2011 uprising.

Australia Day on January 26 is the country's official national day. It marks the arrival of the First Fleet of British ships at Sydney Cove in Port Jackson in 1788, when Captain Arthur Phillip raised the British flag and founded the colony of New South Wales. Australians celebrate with citizenship ceremonies, community barbecues, fireworks and the national honours, while many Indigenous Australians mark it as a day of mourning, often called Invasion Day or Survival Day, and debate about the date continues.

Republic Day on January 26 celebrates the day in 1950 when the Constitution of India came into force and the country became a republic. The date was chosen because on January 26, 1930, the Indian National Congress had declared Purna Swaraj, the goal of complete independence from British rule. In New Delhi the President takes the salute at a grand parade along Kartavya Path, with military units, state tableaux and folk dancers, and a foreign leader usually attends as chief guest.

International Holocaust Remembrance Day on January 27 was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2005 and first observed in 2006, on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz-Birkenau. It honours the six million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, and the millions of other victims of Nazi persecution, including Roma, disabled people and political prisoners. Governments, schools and museums mark the day with ceremonies, survivor testimonies, candle lighting and lessons that warn against antisemitism, hatred and denial.

Data Privacy Day on January 28 marks the date in 1981 when the Council of Europe opened Convention 108 for signature, the first binding international treaty on protecting personal data. Europe observes it as Data Protection Day, and the United States, Canada and other countries took it up as Data Privacy Day. Companies, schools and regulators use the day to remind people to check app permissions, use strong passwords and two-factor login, and think before sharing personal information online.

National Hot Chocolate Day on January 31 celebrates one of winter's most comforting drinks. Chocolate was first drunk by the peoples of Mesoamerica as a bitter, often spiced beverage, and it became the sweet, creamy drink known today after it reached Europe, helped in 1828 by Coenraad van Houten's press, which made cocoa powder easy to mix. People mark the day by making a mug from scratch with real chocolate, topping it with whipped cream or marshmallows, or trying a regional version such as thick Spanish chocolate with churros.

slogans.en: Warm Your Soul with Every Sip

descriptions.en: World Hijab Day on February 1 was started in 2013 by Nazma Khan, a Bangladeshi-born New Yorker who wore a headscarf and faced prejudice for it after the September 11 attacks. It invites women of every faith and background to try wearing a hijab for a day, as a way to understand the experience of Muslim women who wear it. Supporters share photos and stories online and hold events at schools and universities, while others use the day to debate women's freedom to choose whether to cover or not.

Hala Febrayer, Arabic for Hello February, is Kuwait's month-long festival, built around the country's two biggest national holidays. National Day on February 25 and Liberation Day on February 26, which marks the end of the Iraqi occupation in 1991, are the high point of a month of concerts, markets, carnival parades and shopping promotions. Kuwaitis decorate cars and homes in the national colours, families crowd the seafront and the festival draws visitors from across the Gulf.

World Wetlands Day on February 2 marks the signing of the Convention on Wetlands in the Iranian city of Ramsar in 1971, one of the oldest international environmental treaties. It has been celebrated since 1997 and became an official UN international day in 2021. Marshes, peatlands, mangroves, lakes and river deltas filter water, store carbon, soften floods and shelter countless birds and fish, yet roughly a third of the world's wetlands have been lost since 1970, so the day is marked with bird-watching walks, clean-ups and campaigns to protect and restore them.

Groundhog Day on February 2 is a North American tradition in which a groundhog is said to forecast the end of winter: if it sees its shadow when it leaves its burrow, six more weeks of winter follow, and if not, spring comes early. The custom comes from German Candlemas weather lore, in which a badger or hedgehog played the role, brought to Pennsylvania by German immigrants; the town of Punxsutawney held its first official Groundhog Day in 1887. Thousands gather at Gobbler's Knob before dawn to hear Punxsutawney Phil's prediction, and the 1993 film Groundhog Day made the name a byword for living the same day over and over.

World Cancer Day on February 4 is led by the Union for International Cancer Control and dates from the Charter of Paris against Cancer, signed at a world summit in Paris on February 4, 2000. Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, yet a large share of cases can be prevented by avoiding tobacco, limiting alcohol, staying active and getting vaccinated against viruses such as HPV and hepatitis B. Hospitals, charities and governments use the day to promote screening and early diagnosis, to fight stigma and to call for fair access to treatment everywhere.

World Nutella Day on February 5 was started in 2007 by Sara Rosso, an American blogger living in Italy, as a fan celebration of the chocolate-hazelnut spread. Nutella was launched in 1964 by the Ferrero company in Alba, in Piedmont, a region famous for its hazelnuts, and grew out of an earlier gianduja paste made when cocoa was scarce after the Second World War. Fans mark the day by sharing recipes, from crêpes and cookies to a simple slice of bread with a generous spoonful.

Waitangi Day, on February 6, is New Zealand's national day and a public holiday. It marks the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, a founding document of the nation whose English and Māori versions are still discussed today. Ceremonies are held at the Treaty Grounds in Waitangi, with waka canoe displays, speeches and cultural performances, while families across the country enjoy festivals, concerts and community gatherings and reflect on the treaty's meaning.

slogans.en: He iwi tahi tātou — We are one people.

descriptions.en: National Pizza Day on 9 February celebrates one of the world's most loved foods. Pizza as we know it took shape in Naples, where flatbreads topped with tomato became everyday street food, and Italian emigrants carried it around the globe, where every country made it its own. People mark the day by sharing a pizza with friends, trying a new topping, visiting a favourite pizzeria or making the dough at home.

names.en: International Day of Women and Girls in Science

descriptions.en: The International Day of Women and Girls in Science on 11 February was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 2015. It recognises the vital role women and girls play in science and technology and calls for their full and equal access to these fields, where they are still underrepresented. UNESCO and UN Women lead the day, and schools, universities and labs hold talks, mentoring sessions and events that introduce girls to scientists and science careers.

National Foundation Day on 11 February is a Japanese public holiday marking the founding of the nation. The date follows the legend, told in Japan's oldest chronicles, that Jimmu, the first emperor, took the throne in 660 BC. The holiday was established as Kigensetsu in 1872, abolished after the Second World War and restored under its present name in 1967. The day brings ceremonies, parades and shrine visits, and many people take a quiet moment to reflect on Japan's history.

Red Hand Day, the International Day Against the Use of Child Soldiers, is held on 12 February. The date recalls the entry into force in 2002 of the UN optional protocol that bans the recruitment of children into armed conflict. Yet children are still used as fighters, messengers and porters in wars around the world. Schools and campaigners collect red handprints on paper, a symbol of saying no, and hand them to politicians as a call to protect children and help former child soldiers rebuild their lives.

slogans.en: No child should be a soldier.

descriptions.en: Darwin Day on 12 February marks the birthday of Charles Darwin, born in Shrewsbury, England, in 1809. His theory of evolution by natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species in 1859, changed how we understand the history of life on Earth. Museums, universities and science groups mark the day with lectures, exhibitions and nature walks, celebrating curiosity, careful observation and the scientific method.

World Radio Day on 13 February celebrates radio as a voice that reaches almost everyone, even where there is no internet or electricity grid. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2011, choosing the anniversary of the founding of United Nations Radio in 1946. Radio informs people in emergencies, gives communities a voice and keeps music and conversation close at hand. Stations around the world mark the day with special programmes, open studios and tributes to the people behind the microphone.

Valentine's Day on 14 February is a celebration of love. It takes its name from Saint Valentine, an early Christian martyr of Rome, and its link with romance grew in medieval Europe, where poets tied the day to courtship. Today couples exchange cards, flowers, chocolates and small gifts, share a dinner or simply set aside time for each other. In many places friends and family join in too, making it a day for every kind of affection.

Parinirvana Day, kept on 15 February by many Mahayana Buddhists and on 8 February by some, remembers the death of the Buddha. Buddhist tradition holds that he died at Kushinagar in northern India at the age of eighty, passing into final nirvana, free from the cycle of rebirth. Rather than mourning, the day invites reflection on impermanence and on one's own life. People meditate, read from the scriptures about the Buddha's last days, visit temples and remember loved ones who have died.

slogans.en: Peace in stillness, light in darkness.

descriptions.en: Random Acts of Kindness Day on 17 February encourages people to do something kind for someone else, with nothing expected in return. It might be a stranger, a neighbour, a colleague or a friend. The idea is simple: small gestures can brighten a day and often inspire the receiver to pass the kindness on. People pay for someone's coffee, leave an encouraging note, help a neighbour with shopping or spend time with someone who is lonely.

slogans.en: One Small Act. One Big Impact.

descriptions.en: The World Day of Social Justice, on February 20, is a United Nations day for fairer societies. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2007, and it was first observed in 2009. It draws attention to poverty, unemployment, exclusion and inequality between women and men, and to the idea that decent work and equal opportunity help keep peace within and between nations. Governments, unions and civil groups hold talks, publish reports and run campaigns on rights at work and fair wages.

slogans.en: Achieving Social Justice for a Fair Globalization.

descriptions.en: International Mother Language Day, on February 21, celebrates the languages we first learn to speak and the diversity of the world's tongues. UNESCO proclaimed it in 1999 and it has been observed since 2000. The date remembers 21 February 1952, when students in Dhaka were killed while demanding recognition for Bengali, and Bangladesh honours them every year. Of the world's roughly 7,000 languages, thousands are endangered, so the day is marked with readings, school events and calls for teaching children in their own language.

Founding Day, on February 22, marks the beginning of the first Saudi state in 1727, when Imam Muhammad bin Saud took up rule in Diriyah, near today's Riyadh. King Salman made it a national holiday in 2022, so the country can honour roots that reach back three centuries. Saudis mark it with traditional dress, the ardah sword dance, poetry, heritage markets and light shows, with Diriyah's old mud-brick district at the heart of the celebrations.

slogans.en: Honoring our roots, shaping our future.

descriptions.en: Estonia's Independence Day, on February 24, remembers the Manifesto to the Peoples of Estonia, proclaimed in 1918, which declared an independent Estonian republic. Independence was lost under Soviet occupation and restored in 1991, so the day honours both the founding and the long road back to freedom. It begins at sunrise with the raising of the blue, black and white flag on Tall Hermann tower in Tallinn, followed by a military parade, the president's speech and reception, and flags on homes across the country.

Kuwait National Day, on February 25, celebrates the nation and recalls the accession of Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salim Al-Sabah, the emir who led Kuwait to independence from Britain in 1961. The holiday was moved from June to the cooler month of February, and it runs straight into Liberation Day on February 26, which marks the end of the Iraqi occupation in 1991. Buildings are lit in the flag's colours, families fill the streets with flags and fireworks, and water-pistol fights break out along the coast.

slogans.en: Two days of flags, foam and fireworks.

descriptions.en: Kuwait Liberation Day marks 26 February 1991, when Kuwait was freed after seven months of Iraqi occupation. Iraq invaded in August 1990, and an international coalition drove its forces out in the Gulf War. Coming the day after National Day, it turns the end of February into an extended national celebration, with flags, fireworks, parades and cars decked out in the national colours. It is also a day of remembrance for those who were killed, imprisoned or went missing during the occupation.

Arabic Coffee Day celebrates qahwa, the lightly roasted coffee spiced with cardamom that sits at the heart of hospitality across the Arab world. In 2015 UNESCO added Arabic coffee to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity, recognising the customs around it. It is poured from a long-spouted dallah into small handleless cups, usually with dates, and offering it to a guest is a gesture of welcome before it is a drink. People mark the day by brewing it the traditional way and sharing it with family and friends.

slogans.en: The pot, the cup, the welcome.

descriptions.en: Pokémon Day on 27 February celebrates the anniversary of Pokémon Red and Green, the first Pokémon games, released in Japan on that date in 1996. What began as a pair of handheld games grew into one of the world's best-known franchises, spanning games, an animated series, films and a trading card game. Fans mark the day by playing their favourite games, trading cards and sharing memories of their first partner Pokémon. Many also tune in for the news and announcements the series traditionally releases around the date.

National Science Day is celebrated in India on 28 February, the date in 1928 when physicist C. V. Raman announced the discovery of the Raman effect. His finding, about how light changes as it scatters through a material, earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930, the first in the sciences for an Indian. The day aims to spark curiosity and spread scientific thinking. Schools, universities and research institutes mark it with science fairs, lectures, quizzes and open days at laboratories.

228 Peace Memorial Day in Taiwan commemorates the 228 Incident, which began on 28 February 1947. A dispute over contraband cigarettes in Taipei set off island-wide protests against the Kuomintang-led government, which were crushed by troops with heavy loss of life. The events led into the long period of martial law and political repression known as the White Terror, and were barely spoken of in public for decades. Today it is a public holiday, marked with memorial ceremonies, moments of silence and reflection on human rights and democracy.

Zero Discrimination Day is observed every year on 1 March to affirm everyone's right to live a full and dignified life, whoever they are. It was launched by UNAIDS, the United Nations programme on HIV and AIDS, and first marked in 2014, with a particular focus on ending the stigma faced by people living with HIV. Its symbol is the butterfly, a sign of transformation. Organisations, activists and communities use the day to challenge unfair laws and everyday prejudice, and to call for equal treatment for all.

slogans.en: End inequalities. End AIDS. End pandemics.

descriptions.en: World Compliment Day on March 1 is the world's most positive day. The idea originated in the Netherlands in 2001 and spread globally. The challenge: give at least three people a sincere, personal compliment.

St. David's Day, on 1 March, is the feast day of Saint David, or Dewi Sant, the patron saint of Wales. David was a sixth-century bishop and monk remembered for his simple, devout life, and his famous advice to 'do the little things' is still quoted today. The day is a celebration of Welsh identity: people pin daffodils or leeks to their clothes, children often dress in traditional Welsh costume, schools hold concerts and poetry contests, and parades with Welsh flags fill town centres.

International Wheelchair Day, held every year on 1 March, celebrates the freedom a wheelchair brings to the millions of people around the world who use one. Rather than focusing only on limitations, it highlights the independence, mobility and opportunities that a good wheelchair makes possible. It is also a reminder that many people who need a wheelchair still cannot get one, and that streets, buildings and transport often remain hard to access. Users share their stories, and organisations campaign for better access and inclusion.

slogans.en: Rolling through life with strength and pride.

descriptions.en: World Wildlife Day, on 3 March, celebrates the wild animals and plants that share our planet and the many ways people depend on them. The United Nations proclaimed it in 2013, choosing the date on which the CITES convention on trade in endangered species was signed in 1973. Each year has a theme, and zoos, parks, schools and conservation groups mark it with talks, films and campaigns against poaching, illegal trade and habitat loss.

slogans.en: Caring for all life on Earth.

descriptions.en: World Hearing Day, held every 3 March and led by the World Health Organization, draws attention to how hearing loss can be prevented and how ear and hearing care can reach everyone. The WHO estimates that more than 1.5 billion people live with some degree of hearing loss, much of it avoidable through safe listening, vaccination and early care. On the day, clinics offer free hearing checks, and campaigns remind people to turn down the volume and protect their ears from noise.

slogans.en: Hearing for life — don't let hearing loss limit you.

descriptions.en: Ghana Independence Day, on 6 March, marks the day in 1957 when the Gold Coast became the independent nation of Ghana, ending British colonial rule. Led by Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana was one of the first countries in sub-Saharan Africa to win its freedom, and its example inspired independence movements across the continent. The day is a national holiday, celebrated with a parade in Accra, school marches, flags, music and the red, gold and green colours everywhere.

World Day of Prayer is a worldwide movement led by Christian women of many church traditions, who meet on the same day each year for a shared service of prayer. Each year women from one country write the service, telling the stories and concerns of their own land, and congregations around the world pray with them as the day travels across the time zones. The motto is 'informed prayer, prayerful action': the day joins worship with learning about other countries and support for peace and justice.

slogans.en: Together in Prayer for a Peaceful World

descriptions.en: International Women's Day, on 8 March, celebrates women's achievements and calls for equal rights. It grew out of the labour and suffrage movements of the early 1900s: at a 1910 conference in Copenhagen, the German socialist Clara Zetkin proposed an international day for women, and the first one was held in 1911. A women's strike for 'bread and peace' in Petrograd on this date in 1917 helped fix it on 8 March, and the United Nations has marked it since 1975. Today it brings marches, talks, flowers and gifts in many countries.

World Glaucoma Day raises awareness of glaucoma, a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve and the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. It usually comes on slowly and without pain, taking side vision first, so many people do not notice it until the damage is done. Lost sight cannot be restored, but early treatment can slow or stop the disease. The day is part of World Glaucoma Week, when eye doctors and patient groups urge regular eye checks, especially for people over 40 or with a family history.

slogans.en: Beat invisible glaucoma — get your eyes checked.

descriptions.en: Pi Day celebrates π, the never-ending number that relates a circle's circumference to its diameter. It falls on March 14 because the date, written 3/14 in the American style, matches the first digits of pi, 3.14. Physicist Larry Shaw held the first celebration at San Francisco's Exploratorium in 1988, and in 2019 UNESCO made the same date the International Day of Mathematics. People mark it with pie, digit-reciting contests and maths games, and it happens to be Albert Einstein's birthday too.

The International Day of Mathematics, held every March 14, celebrates the beauty of mathematics and the part it plays in everyday life, from science and technology to art and music. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2019, choosing the date already known as Pi Day, since 3/14 echoes the first digits of pi. Schools, universities and maths clubs around the world mark it with puzzles, games, talks and activities built around a new theme each year.

names.en: International Day of Action for Rivers

descriptions.en: The International Day of Action for Rivers, held every March 14, is a day to celebrate rivers and stand up for the people and wildlife that depend on them. It grew out of a 1997 gathering in Curitiba, Brazil, where communities affected by large dams called for a shared day of protest and protection. Today people mark it with river clean-ups, walks along the banks, and campaigns for clean water and free-flowing rivers.

World Consumer Rights Day, held every March 15, is a day to raise awareness of consumers' rights and to push for fair, safe and honest markets. The date recalls March 15, 1962, when US President John F. Kennedy became the first world leader to set out consumer rights in an address to Congress. Each year Consumers International chooses a theme, and consumer groups, regulators and businesses around the world mark the day with campaigns, events and advice for shoppers.

World Speech Day, held every March 15, celebrates the power of the spoken word to share ideas, inspire people and bring communities together. It reminds us that speaking up, whether in a classroom, a town square or online, is one of the oldest ways people change minds and the world around them. Schools, clubs and community groups mark the day with speeches, debates, storytelling and open-mic events where anyone can take the floor.

slogans.en: Speak up, speak out, change the world.

descriptions.en: St. Patrick's Day on March 17 honours Saint Patrick, the fifth-century missionary who became Ireland's patron saint, on the traditional date of his death. It began as a religious feast day and remains a public holiday in Ireland, where many people still go to Mass. Legend says Patrick used the three-leaved shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity, so shamrocks and green are everywhere. Today it is a worldwide celebration of Irish culture, with parades, Irish music and dancing, and landmarks lit up in green.

slogans.en: Everybody's Irish on St. Patrick's Day.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Happiness, on March 20, reminds us that happiness and well-being are basic human goals. The United Nations General Assembly declared it in 2012, at the initiative of Bhutan, the country famous for measuring progress by Gross National Happiness rather than income alone. It was first held in 2013. The World Happiness Report, which ranks countries by how satisfied their people are with life, is usually published around this date, and people mark the day with small acts of kindness and time with the people they love.

World Sparrow Day, held on 20 March, draws attention to the house sparrow and other common birds that live alongside us. It began in 2010, started by the Nature Forever Society in India, after people noticed that sparrows were vanishing from many towns and cities. Modern buildings with no nooks for nesting, fewer insects and less greenery have all made city life harder for them. People mark the day by putting up nest boxes, leaving out water and grain, and planting native shrubs.

World Oral Health Day, held every year on 20 March, reminds us that a healthy mouth is part of a healthy body. It is led by the FDI World Dental Federation, which brings dental associations from around the world together behind one shared campaign. Gum disease and tooth decay are among the most common health problems on earth, yet most of them can be prevented. Dentists, schools and health services mark the day with free check-ups, brushing lessons for children and reminders to cut back on sugar.

World Storytelling Day celebrates the art of telling stories out loud, the oldest way people have shared knowledge, memory and imagination. It began in Sweden in the early 1990s and spread to storytellers around the world, and it is held on the March equinox. Each year a shared theme links events in many countries. Libraries, schools, theatres and storytelling clubs host sessions where tellers of all ages share folk tales, legends and personal stories, often in several languages at once.

slogans.en: Every Story Deserves to Be Heard

descriptions.en: French Language Day (March 20) is celebrated on the anniversary of the creation of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie. It promotes the French language and Francophone cultures worldwide. French is spoken by 300 million people.

Tunisia Independence Day, on March 20, marks the day in 1956 when Tunisia became independent from France, ending a French protectorate that had begun in 1881. Habib Bourguiba, who led the national movement, became the country's first president the following year. The day is a public holiday across Tunisia. Red and white flags fill the streets, official ceremonies are held, and families gather in Tunis along Avenue Habib Bourguiba and in towns nationwide to celebrate with music and fireworks.

slogans.en: Seventy-five years ended in a single signature.

descriptions.en: World Poetry Day, on March 21, celebrates poetry as one of the oldest ways people have found to put feeling, memory and identity into words. UNESCO declared the day in 1999 to support the reading, writing and teaching of poetry, and to give a voice to languages that are at risk of disappearing. Poetry crosses borders and generations, from oral epics to verses shared on a phone. People mark the day with public readings, festivals and school events, or simply by reading a favourite poem aloud or sharing one with a friend.

slogans.en: Poetry: the art of being human.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Forests, held every year on 21 March, celebrates forests of every kind and the life they support. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2012, and it was first marked in 2013. Forests clean the air, protect soil and water, shelter most land-dwelling species and provide food, wood and income for hundreds of millions of people. Each year has its own theme, and countries mark the day with tree-planting drives, school activities and campaigns against deforestation.

slogans.en: Forests and sustainable production and consumption.

descriptions.en: World Down Syndrome Day, held every year on March 21, speaks up for the rights, inclusion and well-being of people with Down syndrome. The date was chosen on purpose: Down syndrome comes from a third copy of chromosome 21, so the 21st day of the third month stands for it. The United Nations has observed the day officially since 2012. Many people wear brightly coloured, mismatched socks to start conversations, while schools, families and support groups hold events that celebrate what people with Down syndrome bring to their communities.

The International Day of Nowruz, on March 21, honours Nowruz, the new year festival that greets spring at the vernal equinox. Its roots go back thousands of years in Iran and the wider Persian cultural world, and today it is celebrated by many millions of people from the Balkans and Türkiye to Central Asia. The United Nations recognised the day in 2010, after UNESCO listed Nowruz as intangible cultural heritage. Families clean their homes, visit relatives, share festive meals and leap over small bonfires; in Iran they also set a haft-sin table of symbolic items.

World Puppetry Day, on March 21, celebrates puppetry, one of the oldest forms of theatre, found in cultures all over the world. Shadow puppets, string marionettes, hand puppets and giant parade figures have long been used to tell stories, carry rituals and make audiences of every age laugh. The day is promoted by UNIMA, the international union of puppeteers, and was first marked in 2003. Puppet theatres, festivals and museums celebrate it with special shows, workshops and open rehearsals, often inviting children to make and perform with puppets of their own.

slogans.en: Pull the strings — tell the story.

descriptions.en: World Tattoo Day, on March 21, celebrates tattooing as an art form and the artists who practise it. Tattoos are among the oldest human arts: Ötzi the Iceman, who lived in the Alps more than 5,000 years ago, carries dozens of them, and cultures from Polynesia to Japan developed rich tattoo traditions of their own. Studios mark the day with open doors, special designs and charity events, and many people use it to share the stories behind the ink on their skin.

slogans.en: Every tattoo tells a story — wear yours with pride.

descriptions.en: Nauryz is Kazakhstan's spring new year, celebrated around the spring equinox on 21 March as a national holiday lasting several days. It belongs to the wider Nowruz tradition shared across Iran, Central Asia and beyond, with roots in ancient Iranian and Turkic spring customs. Long discouraged in the Soviet era, it is now one of the country's most loved festivals, a time of renewal, forgiveness and visiting. Families cook nauryz kozhe, a soup made from seven ingredients, set up yurts in town squares and gather for music, games and feasts.

World Water Day, on March 22, draws attention to the importance of fresh water and the billions of people who still lack safe water and sanitation. The United Nations General Assembly declared the day in 1992, and it has been observed every year since 1993. Each year has its own theme, from groundwater to climate change, coordinated by UN-Water. Governments, schools and charities hold events and campaigns, and many people use the day to think about how they use water and to support projects that bring clean water to communities in need.

Earth Hour is a worldwide event organised by WWF in which people, businesses and cities switch off non-essential lights for one hour as a sign of care for the planet. It began in Sydney in 2007 and quickly spread around the world. It usually takes place on a Saturday evening in late March, from 8:30 to 9:30 pm local time. Famous landmarks go dark, families spend the hour by candlelight, and many people use it to think about climate change and the small, everyday choices that save energy.

World Taxi Day, on March 22, honours the taxi drivers who keep cities moving day and night. Taxis take people to work, to airports and hospitals, and home safely late at night, often when no other transport is running. Drivers face long hours, heavy traffic and the pressures of a fast-changing industry, so the day is a chance to recognise their work. People mark it by thanking their driver, leaving a kind review or a tip, and remembering how much daily city life depends on them.

World Meteorological Day, on March 23, marks the date in 1950 when the convention creating the World Meteorological Organization came into force. It celebrates the work of meteorologists and weather services, whose forecasts and warnings protect lives and help farmers, pilots, sailors and whole cities prepare for storms, floods and heat. Each year the WMO chooses a theme, often linked to climate and early warnings. National weather services open their doors, share educational material and remind people how weather and climate shape everyday life.

World Puppy Day on 23 March celebrates the joy and unconditional affection puppies bring into our lives. It was started in 2006 by American animal advocate Colleen Paige, who also used it to speak up for adoption and against puppy mills. People share photos of their dogs, visit or donate to shelters, and many families choose the day to adopt. It is also a reminder that a puppy is a long commitment that needs time, training and care.

Pakistan Day, on March 23, is a national holiday that commemorates the Lahore Resolution of 1940. On that day the All-India Muslim League called for a separate homeland for the Muslims of the Indian subcontinent, a demand that led to the creation of Pakistan in 1947. The date gained further meaning in 1956, when Pakistan adopted its first constitution and became an Islamic republic. The day is marked with a military parade in Islamabad, flag-raising ceremonies, national awards and gatherings at the Minar-e-Pakistan in Lahore, where the resolution was passed.

World Tuberculosis Day on 24 March raises awareness of TB, a preventable and curable disease that is still one of the world's deadliest infections. The date recalls 24 March 1882, when Robert Koch announced in Berlin that he had discovered the bacterium that causes it, opening the way to diagnosis and treatment. Led by the World Health Organization, the day brings campaigns, free screenings and talks. Health workers and patients use it to call for faster diagnosis, full treatment and an end to stigma.

Greek Independence Day on 25 March marks the start of the 1821 uprising against Ottoman rule that led to the founding of the modern Greek state. The date also falls on the Feast of the Annunciation, so the day is both a national holiday and a major church feast. Schoolchildren parade in towns and villages carrying flags, and a military parade is held in Athens. Many families eat fried salted cod with garlic sauce, a dish traditional for the day.

Tolkien Reading Day (March 25) encourages fans around the world to celebrate the life and work of J.R.R. Tolkien, author of The Lord of the Rings. March 25 marks the date on which the One Ring was destroyed in the fires of Mount Doom.

slogans.en: Not all those who wander are lost.

descriptions.en: Bangladesh Independence Day on 26 March marks the 1971 declaration of independence from Pakistan, made after the Pakistani army began a violent crackdown in what was then East Pakistan. Nine months of war followed, ending with victory on 16 December, which Bangladesh celebrates as Victory Day. The day is a national holiday: the state honours the fallen at the National Martyrs' Memorial in Savar, and buildings fly the red and green flag. Parades, cultural programmes and patriotic songs fill the day.

Purple Day on 26 March is a worldwide awareness day for epilepsy, a common neurological condition that causes seizures. It was started in 2008 by Cassidy Megan, a nine-year-old girl from Nova Scotia, Canada, who lived with epilepsy and wanted others with the condition to know they were not alone. People wear purple, the colour linked to lavender, and share facts about epilepsy. The aim is to replace fear and myths with understanding, including knowing how to help someone having a seizure.

slogans.en: Wear purple. Stand up for epilepsy awareness.

descriptions.en: World Theatre Day on 27 March celebrates theatre as a living art that brings people together. It was created in 1961 by the International Theatre Institute and has been marked every year since 1962. Each year a leading theatre figure writes an international message, which is translated into many languages and read out before performances around the world. Theatres also offer special shows, open rehearsals and discounted tickets to welcome new audiences.

slogans.en: Theatre and a culture of peace.

descriptions.en: World Piano Day celebrates the piano and everyone who plays it, from beginners to concert performers. German pianist and composer Nils Frahm started it in 2015 and placed it around the 88th day of the year, a nod to the 88 keys of a standard piano. Pianists share performances online, venues hold concerts and open-piano sessions, and anyone with access to a keyboard is invited to sit down and play, even if only for a few minutes.

World Bipolar Day raises awareness of bipolar disorder, a mental health condition marked by shifts between periods of high energy and deep depression. It falls on 30 March, the birthday of Vincent van Gogh, whom many believe lived with the condition. The day aims to replace stigma with understanding: mental health groups share accurate information, people living with bipolar disorder tell their own stories, and everyone is encouraged to seek help and support early.

World Backup Day is a reminder to make copies of the files that matter most, from family photos to work documents, before a lost phone, broken drive or cyberattack wipes them out. It began in 2011 as a grassroots tech initiative and sits on 31 March for a playful reason: back up today so you are not made a fool of on April Fools' Day. People mark it by setting up automatic backups, copying data to an external drive or cloud service, and checking that their backups actually restore.

slogans.en: Don't be an April Fool. Backup Your Files!

descriptions.en: International Transgender Day of Visibility celebrates transgender and gender-diverse people and the contributions they make to their communities. It was started in 2009 by American activist Rachel Crandall, who noticed that the only widely known trans observance mourned those who had been killed and wanted a day to honour the living. Each 31 March, people share their stories, allies show support, and organisations draw attention to the discrimination trans people still face around the world.

Lebanon Cedars Day honours the cedar of Lebanon, the tree at the centre of the national flag and a symbol of the country's endurance. Prized since antiquity for its fragrant, durable wood and mentioned many times in the Bible, the cedar once covered the mountains but now survives in scattered groves such as the Cedars of God, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The day draws attention to threats from climate change, pests and past logging, and to the replanting efforts working to bring the forests back.

slogans.en: The tree on the flag needs the country's help.

descriptions.en: April Fools' Day, on 1 April, is a day for harmless pranks, hoaxes and jokes, with the trickster finally revealing the joke to the victim. Its origins are unclear, but the custom has been around for centuries in Europe. In France and Italy children try to stick a paper fish on someone's back, which is why Türkiye calls the day Nisan Balığı, the April fish. Today newspapers, broadcasters and brands join in with fake stories, the most famous perhaps the BBC's 1957 report on Swiss spaghetti trees.

slogans.en: Don't believe everything you read today.

descriptions.en: World Autism Awareness Day is marked on 2 April. The United Nations General Assembly declared it in 2007, and it was first observed in 2008. Autism is a lifelong difference in how people communicate, sense the world and relate to others, and it looks different in every person. The day calls for understanding, acceptance and equal rights for autistic people at school, at work and in public life. Buildings are lit in blue, and families, schools and autistic people themselves share their stories.

International Children's Book Day is held every year on 2 April, the birthday of the Danish storyteller Hans Christian Andersen. The International Board on Books for Young People (IBBY) started it in 1967 to spark a love of reading in children and to draw attention to good children's books. Each year a different national section of IBBY chooses a theme and shares a message and a poster with the world. Schools, libraries and bookshops mark the day with readings, storytelling sessions and book swaps.

slogans.en: Every child deserves a great book.

descriptions.en: International Fact-Checking Day falls on 2 April, the day after April Fools' Day, when spotting a false story is on everyone's mind. Fact-checkers around the world, together with the International Fact-Checking Network, use it to remind people how quickly misinformation spreads and why checking claims before sharing them matters. Newsrooms publish their best debunks, while schools and libraries run media literacy sessions. Pausing before you share, checking the source and looking for a second report is the simplest way to take part.

slogans.en: Don't get fooled — check the facts.

descriptions.en: World Party Day on 3 April is a light-hearted invitation to celebrate life together. It has no official sponsor; the idea is simply that friends, neighbours and strangers set aside their worries for one evening and share food, music and laughter. A party does not have to be big to count: a picnic in the park, a dance in the living room or a shared table on the street all do. Many people use the day to reconnect with someone they have not seen in a while.

International Boxing Day on 5 April celebrates boxing, one of the oldest combat sports in the world, practised in some form since ancient times. The day honours the discipline, courage and respect the sport demands, from children taking their first lessons in a local gym to professionals fighting for world titles. Clubs open their doors for trial sessions and sparring, and fans revisit great fights. It is also a reminder that boxing keeps many young people off the streets and teaches them self-control.

slogans.en: Float Like a Butterfly, Sting Like a Bee

descriptions.en: Chakri Day on 6 April commemorates the founding of the Chakri dynasty in 1782, when King Rama I came to the throne and made Bangkok the capital of Siam. The dynasty still reigns in Thailand today, and the day is a public holiday. The king leads ceremonies in honour of the earlier monarchs of the dynasty, and government officials and ordinary Thais lay flowers and wreaths before royal statues and portraits. Many families use the day off to visit temples or spend time together.

On 6 April, Sudanese people remember two popular uprisings. In 1985, mass protests and a general strike brought down President Jaafar Nimeiry. On the same date in 2019, protesters began a sit-in outside the army headquarters in Khartoum, and within days Omar al-Bashir's thirty-year rule came to an end. The date belongs to ordinary people rather than the state, and Sudanese at home and abroad mark it with marches, songs and remembrance of those who lost their lives.

World Health Day falls on 7 April, the date in 1948 when the constitution of the World Health Organization came into force. Each year the WHO picks one theme, such as mental health, safe motherhood or universal access to care, and uses the day to draw attention to it worldwide. Hospitals, schools and health ministries hold free check-ups, talks and campaigns. It is also a good moment for anyone to think about their own health and the right of every person to good care.

World Parkinson's Day raises awareness of Parkinson's disease, a progressive neurological condition that affects movement, sleep, mood and much more for millions of people worldwide. April 11 is the birthday of the English doctor James Parkinson, born in 1755, whose 1817 essay on the "shaking palsy" first described the disease in detail. Patient groups mark the day with information campaigns, walks and fundraisers, often under the red tulip that has become the symbol of the Parkinson's community.

Yuri's Night is a worldwide celebration of space held on and around 12 April, the day Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space in 1961. The date is doubly special, as the first Space Shuttle mission also launched on 12 April 1981. Since it began in 2001, Yuri's Night has grown into parties, talks and gatherings in many countries. Planetariums, science centres and space fans mark it with music, stargazing and lectures that share the excitement of space exploration.

slogans.en: The universe is yours to explore.

descriptions.en: World Space Day on 12 April marks the anniversary of Yuri Gagarin's flight in 1961, when he became the first person to travel into space. The United Nations also observes this date as the International Day of Human Space Flight. The day celebrates what people have achieved in space, from the first orbit to space stations and robotic explorers, and the science that has come from it. Planetariums, schools and space agencies hold talks and stargazing events to inspire future explorers.

Cosmonautics Day on 12 April marks the day in 1961 when Yuri Gagarin became the first person to travel into space, orbiting the Earth once aboard Vostok 1. The Soviet Union made the date a holiday the following year, and Russia still honours it today. It celebrates the country's cosmonauts, engineers and scientists and their place in the history of space exploration. People visit space museums and Gagarin monuments, lay flowers, and schools hold lessons and events about space.

Baisakhi, also spelled Vaisakhi, is the spring harvest festival of Punjab, falling on 13 or 14 April when the wheat is ready to be cut. For Sikhs it is also one of the most important days of the year: in 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, at Anandpur Sahib. People visit gurdwaras, join colourful street processions called nagar kirtan, share food and dance bhangra and gidda at village fairs.

slogans.en: Harvest, heritage, and the spirit of Khalsa.

descriptions.en: Songkran is the traditional Thai New Year, celebrated from 13 to 15 April as a national holiday. Its name comes from the Sanskrit word for the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign, and water is at its heart as a symbol of cleansing and a fresh start. Families visit temples to make merit, pour scented water over Buddha images and the hands of elders to ask for their blessing, and then fill the streets with cheerful water fights.

World Art Day on 15 April celebrates art and the role it plays in creativity, culture and dialogue between people. The date honours the birthday of Leonardo da Vinci, born on 15 April 1452, as a symbol of freedom of expression and curiosity. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2019, and it is marked with open museum days, exhibitions, workshops and street art events that invite everyone to make and enjoy art.

slogans.en: Art Speaks Where Words Are Unable to Explain.

descriptions.en: World Hemophilia Day on 17 April raises awareness of hemophilia and other inherited bleeding disorders, in which the blood does not clot properly. The date honours the birthday of Frank Schnabel, who founded the World Federation of Hemophilia. Many people with these disorders still have no diagnosis or treatment, so the day calls for better access to care, and landmarks around the world are lit up in red in solidarity.

slogans.en: Treatment for all — no one left behind.

descriptions.en: International Haiku Poetry Day on 17 April celebrates haiku, the short poem form born in Japan. A traditional haiku has seventeen sound units in three phrases of five, seven and five, and often includes a word hinting at the season; the 17th-century poet Matsuo Bashō is its best-known master. Today haiku is written in many languages, and people mark the day by writing their own, sharing them online and holding readings.

Syria's Independence Day marks 17 April 1946, when the last French troops left the country and full sovereignty took effect. It is also known as Evacuation Day, because the departure of foreign forces is what turned independence from a declaration into a fact. It is a national holiday, marked with flags, official ceremonies and gatherings that remember those who struggled for the country's freedom.

slogans.en: The day the last soldier left.

descriptions.en: World Heritage Day, officially the International Day for Monuments and Sites, is marked every year on April 18. It was proposed by ICOMOS, the International Council on Monuments and Sites, in 1982 and approved by UNESCO the following year. The day draws attention to the old buildings, historic towns, archaeological sites and cultural landscapes that tell the story of humanity, and to the work it takes to keep them standing. Museums and monuments often open their doors for free, and guided walks, talks and restoration visits invite people to look again at the heritage around them.

slogans.en: Heritage is our legacy from the past, what we live with today, and what we pass on to future generations.

descriptions.en: World Cycling Day on April 19 celebrates the bicycle as a simple, affordable way to get around and a sport for every age. Riding a bike strengthens the heart and lifts the mood, while cutting traffic, noise and carbon emissions in our cities. It is a separate occasion from the United Nations' World Bicycle Day on June 3. People mark the day by riding to work or school, joining group rides, tuning up an old bike in the garage or teaching a child to pedal for the first time.

World Creativity and Innovation Day is observed on April 21, and the United Nations General Assembly recognised it in 2017. It reminds us that creativity is not only for artists: new ideas and fresh ways of solving problems help tackle poverty, climate change and other challenges of sustainable development. The day falls within World Creativity and Innovation Week. Schools, companies and communities mark it with brainstorming sessions, workshops, hackathons and art projects, and many people simply set aside time to try something new.

Tiradentes Day on April 21 is a national holiday in Brazil honouring Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, known as Tiradentes, or "tooth-puller", because he also worked as a dentist. He was a leader of the Inconfidência Mineira, a 1789 plot in Minas Gerais to free the region from Portuguese rule. The plot was betrayed, and Tiradentes was hanged in Rio de Janeiro on April 21, 1792, later becoming a symbol of Brazilian independence. The day is marked with civic ceremonies, especially in the historic town of Ouro Preto, and a long weekend for many families.

slogans.en: A patriot's sacrifice, a nation's inspiration.

descriptions.en: Earth Day is held every year on April 22 to show support for protecting the environment. It began in the United States in 1970, when millions of people joined rallies, teach-ins and clean-ups to protest pollution, and it has since become one of the largest civic observances in the world. The day reminds us that clean air, water and soil depend on choices made by governments and individuals alike. People mark it by planting trees, picking up litter, saving energy and joining climate events in their towns.

World Book and Copyright Day, set up by UNESCO in 1995, celebrates books, reading and the authors and publishers who create them, and also highlights copyright. The date of 23 April is linked to the deaths of William Shakespeare, Miguel de Cervantes and Inca Garcilaso de la Vega in 1616, and to the Catalan tradition of giving books on Saint George's Day. Libraries, schools and bookshops mark it with readings, book swaps, author visits and gifts of books.

slogans.en: Read, so you never have to stop traveling.

descriptions.en: National Sovereignty and Children's Day marks 23 April 1920, when the Grand National Assembly of Turkey opened in Ankara and placed sovereignty in the hands of the nation. Atatürk later dedicated the day to children, the country's future, and it is a public holiday across Türkiye. Schools hold shows with songs, poems and folk dances, children symbolically take the seats of officials, including in parliament, and young guests from many countries join the celebrations.

St George's Day on 23 April is the feast of Saint George, the patron saint of England. George was a soldier said to have been martyred in the early fourth century, and the legend of him slaying a dragon made him a symbol of courage and good overcoming evil. Although it is not a public holiday in England, many people fly the red-cross flag of St George, wear a red rose, and enjoy parades, church services, folk dancing and pub gatherings.

names.en: World Day for Animals in Laboratories

descriptions.en: World Day for Animals in Laboratories, started in 1979 by the UK's National Anti-Vivisection Society, draws attention to the animals used in scientific research and product testing. It falls on 24 April, the birthday of Lord Dowding, a former president of the society. Animal welfare groups use the day and the week around it to call for an end to animal experiments and for more humane alternatives such as cell cultures and computer models, with protests, vigils and awareness campaigns.

World Malaria Day, on 25 April, highlights the fight against malaria, a disease caused by a parasite and spread by the bite of infected mosquitoes. The World Health Assembly created it in 2007, building on Africa Malaria Day, which had been held on this date since 2001. Malaria is preventable and treatable, yet it still kills hundreds of thousands of people each year, most of them young children in Africa. The day brings campaigns for bed nets, testing, treatment and research funding.

World Penguin Day, on 25 April, celebrates these flightless seabirds, which live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere, from Antarctica to the coasts of South America, Africa and Australia. The date is often linked to Adélie penguins, which head north toward the Antarctic pack ice around this time of year. Many penguin species are under pressure from warming oceans, overfishing and pollution. Zoos, aquariums and conservation groups mark the day with talks, feeding sessions and fundraising for penguin research.

ANZAC Day on 25 April is a national day of remembrance in Australia and New Zealand. It marks the landing of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps on the Gallipoli peninsula in Türkiye in 1915, during the First World War, and now honours everyone from both countries who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations. People gather for dawn services, veterans' marches and wreath-laying, and many also attend the dawn service held at Gallipoli itself.

Liberation Day, the Festa della Liberazione, is a national holiday in Italy. It marks 25 April 1945, when the resistance called a general uprising in the north and the country's liberation from Nazi German occupation and the Fascist regime drew to a close. The president lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Rome, and towns hold marches, concerts and ceremonies honouring the partisans. Many people sing the resistance song "Bella ciao".

World Intellectual Property Day, on 26 April, looks at how patents, copyright, trademarks and designs shape everyday life, from medicines to music. The World Intellectual Property Organization launched it in 2000 and chose the date on which its founding convention came into force in 1970. Each year has a theme, and IP offices, universities and creative groups hold talks, workshops and exhibitions. The day celebrates inventors and artists and asks how their work can be both protected and shared.

slogans.en: IP and You: Driving a Better Future.

descriptions.en: King's Day, Koningsdag, is the Netherlands' national holiday, held on 27 April for the birthday of King Willem-Alexander; if that date falls on a Sunday, it moves to the 26th. It replaced Queen's Day after he came to the throne in 2013. The whole country dresses in orange, the colour of the royal House of Orange. Streets turn into a huge flea market where anyone may sell, Amsterdam's canals fill with party boats, and the royal family visits a chosen town.

Freedom Day is a public holiday in South Africa on 27 April. It marks the country's first democratic elections in 1994, when South Africans of every race could vote for the first time, and the end of apartheid rule. Long queues of first-time voters became an enduring image, and Nelson Mandela soon became the country's first democratically elected president. The day is marked with official ceremonies, speeches, concerts and reflection on how far the country has come and how far it still has to go.

International Dance Day, on 29 April, celebrates dance as a language that crosses borders, cultures and generations. It was created in 1982 by the Dance Committee of the International Theatre Institute, and the date honours the birthday of Jean-Georges Noverre, the French ballet master who reshaped modern ballet. Each year a well-known dancer or choreographer writes a message that is shared around the world. Studios open their doors, companies stage free performances and people are invited simply to get up and dance.

slogans.en: Dance is an art that imprints on the soul.

descriptions.en: Golden Week is the run of national holidays that falls between late April and early May in Japan. It strings together Showa Day on 29 April, Constitution Memorial Day on 3 May, Greenery Day on 4 May and Children's Day on 5 May, and with a weekend or a few days off it can become a long break. It is one of the busiest travel periods of the year, as trains, airports and tourist spots fill up. Many people head home to family, go abroad or enjoy spring outings and festivals.

Showa Day, on 29 April, is a Japanese national holiday held on the birthday of Emperor Hirohito, known after his death as Emperor Showa, who reigned from 1926 to 1989. The date was first kept as Greenery Day after his death and took the name Showa Day in 2007. It asks people to look back on the turbulent Showa era, with its war, defeat and remarkable recovery, and to think about Japan's future. The day also opens the Golden Week holidays, so many families spend it travelling or outdoors.

slogans.en: Reflect on history, hope for peace.

descriptions.en: International Jazz Day, on 30 April, celebrates jazz as a music of freedom, dialogue and cooperation between people. UNESCO proclaimed it in 2011 at the initiative of pianist Herbie Hancock, and it was first marked in 2012. Jazz was born in African American communities in the United States and grew into a language spoken by musicians all over the world. Each year a host city stages an all-star concert, while clubs, schools and radio stations everywhere hold concerts, jam sessions and workshops.

Walpurgis Night, on the night of 30 April, is a spring festival celebrated in Germany, Sweden and Finland. It takes its name from Saint Walpurga, an eighth-century English abbess who worked in Germany, and folk belief held that witches gathered on this night, above all on the Brocken in the Harz Mountains. Today Germans hold costumed parties and witch festivals, and Swedes gather around large bonfires and sing to welcome spring. In Finland it opens Vappu, when students wear their white caps and celebrate into 1 May.

slogans.en: Dance around the bonfire — spring has arrived!

descriptions.en: Reunification Day, on 30 April, is a Vietnamese public holiday marking the fall of Saigon in 1975, which ended the Vietnam War and opened the way to reuniting North and South. Saigon was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City, and the country was formally united the following year. Streets are hung with flags, and major anniversaries bring parades and fireworks, especially in Ho Chi Minh City. Coming right before Labour Day on 1 May, it also gives many families a long holiday break.

slogans.en: One country, one heart, forever united.

descriptions.en: International Workers' Day, on 1 May, honours working people and their struggle for fair pay and decent conditions. It goes back to the 1886 Haymarket events in Chicago, part of the fight for an eight-hour working day, and in 1889 an international socialist congress chose 1 May as a day of workers' action. It is a public holiday in Germany and in Türkiye, where it has been officially called Labour and Solidarity Day since 2009. Trade unions hold marches, rallies and gatherings in many countries.

slogans.en: Workers united will never be defeated.

descriptions.en: Labour and Solidarity Day is a public holiday in Turkey celebrated on May 1. While workers' movements had observed this date since the early 20th century, it was officially recognised as a national holiday in Turkey in 2009. The day honours the contributions of workers and trade unions and is marked with rallies and events across the country.

slogans.en: Labour is the foundation of dignity.

descriptions.en: No Meat May is a month-long challenge that invites people to give up meat for all of May. It began in Australia and has since grown into an international campaign. The idea is simple: thirty-one days is long enough to discover new dishes, rethink everyday eating habits and see how food choices touch health, animals and the planet. Participants sign up, swap recipes, try plant-based meals with friends and family, and many keep some of the new habits once June arrives.

slogans.en: One month. No meat. Massive impact.

descriptions.en: National Photography Month every May celebrates photography as art, communication, and memory. Officially recognized by the US Congress in 1987, the medium itself dates back to 1826 when Joseph Nicéphore Niépce captured the world's first permanent photograph. Use this month to take more photos, visit galleries, or learn a new technique.

slogans.en: Every photo tells a story worth keeping.

descriptions.en: World Tuna Day, on May 2, draws attention to fish that feed millions of people and support some of the world's largest fisheries. The UN General Assembly adopted the day in December 2016 and it was first observed in 2017, to stress that tuna stocks must be managed sustainably. Some tuna species have been heavily overfished, yet tuna remains a vital source of food and income for many coastal nations, especially small island states in the Pacific. The day encourages choosing responsibly caught tuna and backs efforts to keep stocks healthy for the future.

World Press Freedom Day, held on 3 May, reminds governments of their duty to respect freedom of expression and honours journalists who have lost their lives or liberty for their work. It was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1993, following a UNESCO recommendation inspired by the 1991 Windhoek Declaration, a call by African journalists for a free and independent press. UNESCO marks the day with a global conference and the Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize, while newsrooms and press groups around the world publish reports on the state of media freedom.

slogans.en: A press for the planet: journalism in the face of the environmental crisis.

descriptions.en: Constitution Day on 3 May is one of Poland's most important national holidays. It marks the adoption of the Constitution of 3 May 1791, Europe's first modern written national constitution and the second in the world after that of the United States, passed as the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth tried to reform itself in the face of powerful neighbours. Poles mark the day with flags on homes and buildings, official ceremonies and a military parade in Warsaw, and many families enjoy a long spring weekend together.

Star Wars Day on 4 May is an unofficial holiday for fans of the Star Wars saga, the space adventure that began with George Lucas's 1977 film. The date comes from an English pun on the famous Jedi blessing "May the Force be with you", which turns into "May the Fourth be with you". Fans celebrate by rewatching the films, dressing up as their favourite characters, holding themed parties and sharing jokes online, and the franchise itself now joins in with special releases and events.

World Drone Day celebrates unmanned aerial vehicles, better known as drones, and the many ways they are changing everyday life. Once mainly a military technology, drones now film movies and sports, map land, inspect bridges and power lines, help farmers watch over their crops and support search and rescue after disasters. Hobby pilots and clubs mark the day with flying meetups, photo and video showcases and races, and it is also a good moment to learn the local rules for flying safely and respecting other people's privacy.

slogans.en: The Sky is Not the Limit

descriptions.en: Anti-Bullying Day draws attention to bullying in schools, workplaces and online, and asks everyone to stand up for those who are targeted. Bullying can leave lasting marks on a person's confidence and mental health, and it often continues because bystanders stay silent. Schools hold talks and workshops on kindness and respect, families talk openly with children about what happens at school and online, and many people share messages of support for those who have been bullied.

slogans.en: Stand up, speak out, stop bullying.

descriptions.en: Cinco de Mayo, Spanish for "the fifth of May", commemorates the Mexican army's victory over French forces at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862. Led by General Ignacio Zaragoza, the outnumbered Mexican troops held off a larger French army, and the win became a symbol of courage and national pride, though it is often confused with Mexico's Independence Day, which falls on 16 September. In Mexico it is celebrated mainly in Puebla with parades and battle re-enactments, while in the United States it has grown into a lively festival of Mexican culture, music, dance and food.

Children's Day, Kodomo no Hi, is a Japanese national holiday on 5 May that celebrates children's happiness and wishes them health and strength. It grew out of Tango no Sekku, an old seasonal festival traditionally held for boys, and became a holiday for all children in 1948; it is also one of the days of Golden Week. Families fly colourful carp-shaped streamers called koinobori, since the carp that swims upstream stands for perseverance, display samurai helmets and dolls, eat rice cakes wrapped in oak leaves, and take baths with iris leaves.

Liberation Day, Bevrijdingsdag, on 5 May marks the end of the German occupation of the Netherlands in 1945, after five years of war that ended with the bitter Hunger Winter in the west of the country. The surrender of the German forces in the Netherlands was settled in the town of Wageningen, and the day follows National Remembrance Day on 4 May, when the country falls silent for two minutes to honour the war dead. Liberation festivals with free concerts fill cities across the country, celebrating freedom and reflecting on what it takes to keep it.

International No Diet Day, on 6 May, invites people to take a day off from dieting and accept their bodies as they are. It began in Britain in 1992, started by Mary Evans Young, and has since spread to many countries. The day questions diet culture, warns against weight discrimination and the risks of extreme dieting, and puts health and wellbeing ahead of a number on the scale. People mark it by eating without guilt, sharing body-positive messages and wearing a light blue ribbon.

slogans.en: Your body is beautiful — no diet needed.

descriptions.en: World Athletics Day, held on 7 May, celebrates track and field, the oldest form of organised sport. It was launched by the sport's world governing body, then called the IAAF and now World Athletics, to bring young people into athletics and encourage them to stay active. Running, jumping and throwing need little equipment, which makes the sport open to almost anyone. Schools and clubs mark the day with races, open training sessions and fun events for children.

slogans.en: Run, Jump, Throw: Athletics for All.

names.en: World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day

descriptions.en: World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day is held on 8 May, the birthday of Henry Dunant, who was born in Geneva in 1828. After seeing the wounded left untended at the Battle of Solferino in 1859, he pushed for neutral aid to all victims of war, which led to the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross in 1863. Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. The day honours the volunteers and staff of the movement's national societies, who help people through wars, disasters and everyday emergencies.

slogans.en: Everything we do starts with humanity.

descriptions.en: World Ovarian Cancer Day, on 8 May, brings patients, families, doctors and charities together to raise awareness of ovarian cancer. It was started in 2013 by a group of ovarian cancer organisations from around the world. There is no reliable screening test, and early signs such as persistent bloating, feeling full quickly, pain in the abdomen or pelvis, and needing to urinate more often are easy to dismiss. Knowing these symptoms and seeing a doctor early can save lives, and many people wear teal on the day.

VE Day, Victory in Europe Day, marks 8 May 1945, when Nazi Germany's surrender took effect and the Second World War ended in Europe. The surrender was first signed in Reims, in northern France, on 7 May. In France, 8 May is a public holiday known as Victoire 1945. Towns hold ceremonies at their war memorials, laying wreaths and observing a minute of silence, while in Paris the President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe.

Europe Day, on 9 May, celebrates peace and unity in Europe. It marks the anniversary of the Schuman Declaration of 1950, in which French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed placing French and German coal and steel under a shared authority so that war between them would become impossible. That plan was the first step towards today's European Union. EU institutions open their doors to visitors, and cities across the continent hold concerts, talks and festivals under the blue flag with its circle of gold stars.

Victory Day on 9 May marks the defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945, the end of what Russia calls the Great Patriotic War. The surrender took effect late on 8 May in Europe, when it was already 9 May in Moscow, which is why the day falls a day later than in Western Europe. People lay flowers at war memorials and eternal flames, honour veterans and remember the millions who died.
