National S'mores Day on 10 August celebrates the campfire treat of a toasted marshmallow and a square of chocolate pressed between two graham crackers. The name is a contraction of "some more", which is exactly what most people ask for after the first one. An early printed recipe appeared in a Girl Scouts guidebook in the 1920s, and the snack has been a fixture of North American camping trips and backyard fires ever since. People mark the day by gathering round a fire pit, inventing new versions with peanut butter or cookies, or making s'mores in the oven.

World Lion Day on 10 August draws attention to the lion, one of the world's most recognisable animals and a species in serious decline. Wild lions now survive mainly in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, with a small population of Asiatic lions in India's Gir Forest, and they have vanished from most of their former range. Habitat loss, shrinking prey, conflict with livestock farmers and poaching are the main threats. Zoos, conservation groups and schools mark the day with talks, fundraising and awareness campaigns.

slogans.en: Roar for the king of the savanna.

descriptions.en: National Classic Movie Day on 10 August celebrates the films that have stood the test of time. It looks back especially to Hollywood's golden age, roughly the 1930s to the 1950s, when studios turned out the screwball comedies, musicals, westerns and film noir whose stars, lines and scenes still echo in cinema today. Classics matter because they shaped the language of film that later directors borrowed, and because many of them still entertain. Fans mark the day by watching an old favourite, introducing a younger viewer to a black-and-white gem or going to a revival screening.

Vlogging Day celebrates video bloggers, the creators who share their lives, hobbies, travels and opinions through regular videos online. What began as simple diaries filmed on webcams has grown into a craft and, for some, a career, with communities built around everything from cooking and study tips to gaming and daily life. The day honours that mix of storytelling and connection, and the way a phone camera has given almost anyone the chance to be heard. Creators mark it with special videos and collaborations, while newcomers are encouraged to film and share their very first vlog.

National Lazy Day on 10 August is an open invitation to slow down and do as little as possible. Its origins are unknown, but its point is easy to grasp: in a culture that prizes being busy, rest is often treated as something to earn rather than something we need. A day off from productivity gives body and mind a chance to recover, and many people find ideas come more easily once they stop forcing them. People mark it by sleeping in, reading in a hammock, watching films on the sofa or simply leaving the to-do list for tomorrow.

Mountain Day, Yama no Hi, is a Japanese national holiday on August 11 for getting close to the mountains and being grateful for what they give. It was written into law in 2014 and first observed in 2016, in a country where mountains cover most of the land. Many people use the day to hike, climb or escape the summer heat in the highlands, often as part of the Obon holiday season.

Play in the Sand Day, on August 11, is an invitation to slip off your shoes and dig into sand at the beach, a lakeshore or a backyard sandbox. It is an informal summer day with no official origin, and its point is simple: sand play is one of the oldest, freest kinds of fun, for children and adults alike. People mark it by building sandcastles, sculpting figures, burying their feet or going on a buried-treasure hunt.

Navasard is the ancient Armenian New Year, which by the old Armenian calendar began on August 11. Armenian tradition links the date to the legendary forefather Hayk and his victory over the tyrant Bel, and in pre-Christian times it was a great harvest festival with sacrifices, feasts, songs and athletic games. Today cultural groups and enthusiasts revive it with folk music, dance, sports contests and gatherings at historic sites.

slogans.en: An ancient new year, still alive.

descriptions.en: International Youth Day, on August 12, is a United Nations day that puts young people and the issues they face at the centre of attention. The UN General Assembly endorsed it in 1999, following a recommendation by the world's youth ministers, and it was first observed in 2000. Each year has its own theme, and governments, schools and youth organisations mark it with forums, campaigns, concerts and volunteer projects led by young people.

slogans.en: Green skills for youth: towards a sustainable world.

descriptions.en: World Elephant Day, on August 12, draws attention to the plight of Asian and African elephants. First held in 2012, it highlights the threats these intelligent, deeply social animals face, from poaching for ivory to habitat loss, conflict with people and mistreatment in captivity. Zoos, sanctuaries and conservation groups mark it with events and talks, and people are encouraged to learn about elephants, support protection work and avoid ivory and exploitative elephant rides.

Thailand celebrates its national Mother's Day on August 12, the birthday of Queen Sirikit, the mother of King Vajiralongkorn, whom many Thais regard as the mother of the nation. The date was chosen to honour her as a model for all mothers, and it is also a public holiday. Buildings are decorated with blue and her portraits, while children kneel before their mothers to offer jasmine garlands, the flower of the day, in thanks.

slogans.en: Honoring the Mother of the Nation.

descriptions.en: International Left-Handers Day, on August 13, celebrates left-handed people, roughly one in ten of us, and the way they navigate a world built mostly for right-handers. It was first observed in 1976 and has since grown into a worldwide day of awareness about everyday obstacles, from scissors and can openers to desks and notebooks. Left-handers share stories and tips, schools talk about handedness, and right-handers are invited to try a day using their other hand.

Obon is a Japanese Buddhist tradition held each August 13–15 to honor the spirits of ancestors. Families return home, clean grave sites, and light lanterns to guide spirits back. The festival features Bon Odori folk dances, floating paper lanterns on rivers, and a profound sense of togetherness across generations.

Tunisian Women's Day is a national holiday held every 13 August. It marks the day in 1956 when Tunisia, under Habib Bourguiba, promulgated the Code of Personal Status, which abolished polygamy, replaced repudiation with divorce through the courts, required both spouses' consent to marriage and set a minimum age for it. The code is still seen as one of the most far-reaching reforms for women's rights in the Arab world. Tunisians mark the day with official ceremonies, awards for women's achievements and public debate about how far equality has come and what remains to be done.

Pakistan Independence Day, on 14 August, marks the birth of Pakistan in 1947, when British India was partitioned and Pakistan became an independent state. The country was founded under the leadership of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, honoured as Quaid-e-Azam, the Great Leader. The day begins with gun salutes and the raising of the national flag in the capital, Islamabad. Across the country, streets, homes and cars are decorated in green and white, and people gather for parades, patriotic songs and fireworks.

World Lizard Day, on 14 August, celebrates one of the most varied groups of reptiles on Earth. There are more than 7,000 lizard species, from tiny geckos that can climb glass to the Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard. Lizards live on every continent except Antarctica and play an important part in ecosystems by eating insects and serving as food for birds and other animals. Zoos, schools and reptile lovers mark the day by sharing facts, watching lizards in the wild and raising awareness of species threatened by habitat loss.

Financial Awareness Day, held on 14 August, puts the spotlight on money management as an everyday life skill. Knowing how to budget, save, handle debt and plan ahead helps people weather surprises and make choices with less stress, whatever their income. The day is a prompt to take stock: review a budget, check subscriptions and bills, set a savings goal or talk openly about money with family. Banks, schools and financial educators often use it to share simple guides and tips.

slogans.en: Know your money, own your future.

descriptions.en: The Sarajevo Film Festival is the largest film festival in Southeast Europe, held in the Bosnian capital every August. It was first held in 1995, while the city was still under siege during the Bosnian War, as an act of cultural resistance and hope. Today it brings together filmmakers, critics and audiences from across the region and beyond, with a strong focus on films from Southeast Europe. Its top prize, the Heart of Sarajevo, is awarded at the closing ceremony, and open-air screenings fill the city's summer evenings.

Every two years, Brussels' Grand Place transforms into a breathtaking carpet of hundreds of thousands of begonias, arranged in an intricate new design each edition. Created in 1971 by landscape architect E. Stautemans, the biennial display celebrates Belgium's horticultural artistry at the UNESCO World Heritage square.

India's Independence Day, on 15 August, marks the end of British rule in 1947, after a long freedom struggle in which Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru played leading roles. On the eve of independence, Nehru, the country's first Prime Minister, gave his famous 'Tryst with Destiny' speech. Each year the Prime Minister raises the national flag at the Red Fort in Delhi and addresses the nation. Across the country people hoist the tricolour at schools, offices and homes, hold cultural programmes and, in many cities, fly kites.

Korea Liberation Day, on 15 August, marks the end of Japanese colonial rule over the Korean Peninsula in 1945, when Japan surrendered at the close of the Second World War. In South Korea it is called Gwangbokjeol, 'the day the light returned', and it also commemorates the founding of the South Korean government on the same date in 1948. North Korea also marks the liberation as a national holiday. In the South, people fly the national flag, and official ceremonies honour the independence activists who resisted colonial rule.

slogans.en: Gwangbokjeol: Light Returns to the Nation.

descriptions.en: Assumption Day, on 15 August, is the Christian feast celebrating the belief that the Virgin Mary was taken up body and soul into heaven at the end of her earthly life. The Catholic Church formally declared this a dogma in 1950, though the feast itself is far older. In Germany it is a public holiday in Saarland and in the predominantly Catholic communities of Bavaria. Catholics attend Mass and processions, and in many places bundles of herbs and flowers are blessed in church, a custom known as Kräuterweihe.

National Relaxation Day is an informal observance that gives everyone permission to slow down and do a little less for one day. It matters because constant work, screens and busy schedules leave many people tired and stressed, and real rest helps both body and mind recover. People mark it by taking a long walk, reading, napping, enjoying a bath or simply switching off the phone and spending unhurried time with the people they love.

The Nile Festival, known in Egypt as Wafaa El-Nil, honours the river that has sustained life in the country for thousands of years. Its roots lie in the ancient celebrations of the yearly summer flood, which spread fertile silt over the fields of the valley before the Aswan High Dam tamed it. Today the festival is marked in mid-August with concerts, folk dancing, boat parades and cultural events along the riverbanks, as a moment of gratitude to the Nile.

World Greatness Day celebrates the greatness found in ordinary people rather than in fame, wealth or headline achievements. It matters because most of the good in the world comes from quiet, everyday acts: a parent's patience, a teacher's encouragement, a neighbour who shows up when needed. People mark it by thanking someone whose small kindnesses made a difference, noticing their own modest victories and doing one generous thing that lifts someone else up.

National Science Week is Australia's yearly festival of science, held every August since 1997. Across the country, schools, universities, museums, libraries and research centres open their doors with experiments, talks, science shows and stargazing nights. The week celebrates the work of Australian scientists and invites people of every age to ask questions, try things out and discover how science shapes everyday life.

Ferragosto, on 15 August, is the high point of the Italian summer. Its name comes from the Latin Feriae Augusti, the 'holidays of Augustus', a festival introduced by the Roman emperor Augustus, and the Church later made the date the feast of the Assumption of Mary. It is a public holiday, and many Italians take their holidays around it, so cities empty while beaches and mountains fill up. People mark the day with long family lunches, picnics, trips to the sea, religious processions and fireworks.

names.en: Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

descriptions.en: On August 15 Catholics celebrate the Assumption, the belief that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was taken body and soul into heaven at the end of her earthly life. In Poland it is a public holiday, popularly called the feast of Our Lady of the Herbs, when people bring bouquets of herbs, flowers and grain to church to be blessed. Thousands of pilgrims arrive on foot at Jasna Góra in Częstochowa, and the same day is also marked as Polish Armed Forces Day.

slogans.en: She is taken up, hearts lift with her.

descriptions.en: National Rum Day, on August 16, raises a glass to one of the oldest spirits of the Americas. Rum is distilled from sugarcane juice or from molasses, a by-product of sugar making, and took shape on the sugar plantations of the Caribbean in the 17th century, a history bound up with colonial trade and slavery. Bars and distilleries mark the day with tastings and classic rum cocktails such as the daiquiri and the mojito, and fans use it to try a new bottle or learn the story behind an old favourite.

slogans.en: Raise a glass, it's Rum Day!

descriptions.en: Indonesia's Independence Day marks the proclamation of independence read by Sukarno, with Mohammad Hatta at his side, in Jakarta on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan's surrender ended its wartime occupation. Years of struggle against the returning Dutch followed before the Netherlands transferred sovereignty in 1949. Today the red-and-white flag is raised at a ceremony at the presidential palace, and neighbourhoods across the archipelago hold festive games such as sack races, krupuk-eating contests and climbing greased poles for prizes.

Black Cat Appreciation Day celebrates black cats and pushes back against the old superstitions that cast them as bad luck. In medieval Europe they were linked with witchcraft, yet in Japan and parts of Britain a black cat crossing your path has long been seen as a sign of good fortune. People mark the day by sharing photos of their black cats, learning the facts behind the myths and considering adopting a black cat from a local shelter.

slogans.en: Black cats bring good luck too.

descriptions.en: National Nonprofit Day, on August 17, celebrates the charities, foundations and community groups that work for the public good rather than for profit. Across the United States they run food banks and shelters, fund research, support schools and the arts, and respond when disasters strike, often powered largely by volunteers and small donations. The day is a chance to recognise that work and the people behind it. Mark it by volunteering a few hours, donating to a cause you trust or telling others about a local nonprofit.

Bullying. No Way! Week unites Australian schools, students, and families in tackling bullying together. Thousands of schools take part in activities that help young people recognize bullying, understand its impact, and take positive action to build safer, more inclusive communities.

National Couple's Day is a day for partners to celebrate each other and the life they have built together. Falling in mid-August, roughly half a year after Valentine's Day, it offers a second, quieter chance to say thank you without the pressure of roses and reservations. Couples mark it with a shared meal, a walk somewhere meaningful, an old photo album or simply an evening set aside for each other.

Serendipity Day celebrates happy accidents: the lucky finds and chance meetings that turn out better than anything we could have planned. The word was coined in 1754 by the English writer Horace Walpole, inspired by the Persian tale of The Three Princes of Serendip, Serendip being an old name for Sri Lanka. People mark the day by taking an unplanned route, saying yes to an unexpected invitation or recalling the coincidence that changed their own life.

Never Give Up Day celebrates the stubborn, everyday courage it takes to keep going after a setback. It matters because most goals worth reaching, from learning a skill to recovering from illness, are won through small steps repeated long after the first excitement fades. People mark it by returning to a project they had shelved, sharing a story of a comeback, or checking in on a friend who is going through a hard stretch.

Solidarity Day in Chile falls on August 18, the anniversary of the death in 1952 of Alberto Hurtado, the Jesuit priest who founded the charity Hogar de Cristo to shelter the poor. Hurtado was canonised in 2005 and remains one of the most loved figures in the country. Chileans mark the day by volunteering, collecting food and clothing for families in need, and supporting the many charities that carry on his work.

International Delivery Driver Appreciation Day thanks the couriers and drivers who bring meals, groceries and parcels to our doors in every kind of weather. Their work keeps cities running, yet it is often rushed, physically demanding and taken for granted, especially since online ordering became part of daily life. People mark the day with a warm thank-you, a fair tip, a kind review, a cold drink on a hot afternoon or simply a few minutes of patience when a delivery runs late.

World Humanitarian Day, held every August 19, honours aid workers who risk their lives to help people caught in wars and disasters. The date recalls the 2003 bombing of the United Nations headquarters at the Canal Hotel in Baghdad, which killed 22 people, among them the UN envoy Sérgio Vieira de Mello; the UN General Assembly designated the day in 2008. It is marked with memorials, campaigns that tell the stories of people in crisis, and calls to protect humanitarian staff.

World Photography Day celebrates the art, craft and science of capturing light. It falls on August 19 because on that day in 1839 the French government announced the daguerreotype, the first practical photographic process, and presented it as a free gift to the world. Photographers and amateurs alike mark the day by sharing their pictures, joining photo walks and exhibitions, or simply looking at the world a little more carefully through a lens.

slogans.en: A Photo Captures a Moment Forever

descriptions.en: National Aviation Day was established in 1939 by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to honor the birthday of Orville Wright and celebrate the impact of flight. The day recognizes the Wright brothers' pioneering achievements and decades of aviation progress that transformed how the world travels.

slogans.en: Look up — the sky's the limit.

descriptions.en: National Potato Day celebrates one of the world's most important food crops. The potato was domesticated thousands of years ago in the Andes of South America and reached Europe in the 16th century with Spanish ships, going on to feed growing populations across the globe. Fans mark the day by cooking it every way they know, from mash and roast potatoes to fries, gratins and a simple baked potato with butter.

Established by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1930s to coincide with Orville Wright's birthday, National Aviation Week honors the pioneers and breakthroughs of flight. It celebrates how aviation connected the world and inspires the next generation of pilots, engineers and dreamers.

World Mosquito Day falls on 20 August, the date in 1897 when the British doctor Ronald Ross found malaria parasites inside an Anopheles mosquito. His discovery proved that mosquitoes carry malaria, earned him a Nobel Prize and changed how the world fights the disease. Ross himself asked that the date be remembered as Mosquito Day. Today health groups use it to talk about malaria, dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses and the simple steps, such as nets and clearing standing water, that keep people safe.

National Radio Day celebrates the medium that brought news, music and voices into homes long before screens did. The date recalls August 20, 1920, when the Detroit station 8MK, later known as WWJ, began regular broadcasts, among the first commercial stations in the United States. Radio still keeps people company on commutes, at work and in emergencies, and listeners mark the day by tuning in to a favourite station, discovering a new podcast or calling in to a show.

slogans.en: Tune in and turn it up.

names.en: International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism

descriptions.en: On 21 August the United Nations remembers people killed, injured or traumatised by terrorist attacks around the world. The General Assembly created the day in 2017, and it was first marked the following year. Its aim is to make sure victims and survivors are heard, supported and not forgotten once the news moves on. Memorial ceremonies, moments of silence and survivors' testimonies are held in many cities, and governments are reminded of their duty to help those affected rebuild their lives.

National Senior Citizens Day is a US observance held every 21 August. President Ronald Reagan proclaimed it in 1988 to thank older people for what they have given their families, communities and country. It is a day to visit grandparents and older neighbours, listen to their stories and ask for their advice. Many people also use it to check on someone who lives alone, since loneliness is one of the hardest parts of growing old.

National Eat a Peach Day on 22 August is an American food holiday that falls at the height of peach season. The peach was first grown in China thousands of years ago and travelled west along trade routes before reaching orchards across the world. The idea is simple: pick or buy a ripe peach and enjoy it, whether eaten fresh over the sink, grilled, baked into a cobbler or turned into jam. Farm stands and bakeries often join in with peach pies and desserts.

Ride the Wind Day marks 23 August 1977, when the Gossamer Condor, a featherlight aircraft powered only by its pilot's pedalling, flew a figure-of-eight course in California and won the Kremer Prize. Designed by Paul MacCready and flown by Bryan Allen, it was the first human-powered aircraft to make a sustained, controlled flight. The day celebrates that dream of flying under your own power. People mark it by flying kites, sailing, windsurfing, paragliding or simply spending a breezy afternoon outdoors.

slogans.en: Catch the breeze, chase the sky.

descriptions.en: International Blind Dog Day on 23 August celebrates dogs who have lost their sight and the people who love them. Dogs rely far more on smell and hearing than on vision, so most adapt surprisingly well and go on to live full, happy lives. The day challenges the belief that a blind dog is a sad case or a burden, and encourages people to adopt one from a shelter. Owners share photos and tips online, such as keeping furniture in place and using sounds and scents to guide their dogs around the home.

Valentino Day commemorates the life and legacy of Rudolph Valentino, the Italian-born silent film star known as 'The Latin Lover,' who died on August 23, 1926. An estimated 100,000 people attended his funeral in New York City, and his death at just 31 shocked the world. The day pays homage to his short but iconic career in films like The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, The Sheik, and Son of the Sheik.

Find Your Inner Nerd Day is about dropping the mask and letting your quirks lead the way — whether you love space facts, board games, comic books, or coding projects. Founded in 2022 by speaker and author Beth Ziesenis, the day gives people a chance to share their true interests, especially the ones they might usually keep quiet. In 2026 it was officially added to the National Day Calendar.

slogans.en: Wear your weird like a badge.

descriptions.en: Legacy Week is Australia's annual tribute to the families of military personnel who lost their lives or health in service, anchored by Legacy — an organization founded by Captain Stanley Savige in Melbourne in 1923 to care for the widows and children of his fallen comrades. The week honours service and sacrifice through memorial services like the Memorial Day Wreath Ceremony on the USS Midway, fundraising appeals, movie nights celebrating heroes, memory walls, charity bake sales, community picnics and storytelling evenings with veterans. Legacy supports over 43,000 beneficiaries annually, with the Legacy badge symbolising mateship, compassion and fairness.

slogans.en: Keep the promise. Carry their light.

descriptions.en: Ukraine's Independence Day marks August 24, 1991, when the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence as the Soviet Union was breaking apart. More than 90 percent of voters confirmed the decision in a referendum on December 1 of that year. The day follows National Flag Day on August 23, and Ukrainians mark it with blue-and-yellow flags, embroidered shirts, concerts and ceremonies, and since 2022 also with tributes to those defending the country.

Vesuvius Day remembers the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, which buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and volcanic debris. August 24 is the traditional date, taken from manuscripts of Pliny the Younger's letters describing the disaster in which his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died; newer finds suggest it may have happened in the autumn instead. The buried towns lay forgotten until excavations began in the 18th century, and the day is a chance to read about them, explore their streets online or reflect on the power of volcanoes.

International Strange Music Day invites everyone to listen beyond their comfort zone. It was created by New York composer Patrick Grant, who wanted people to discover music that sounds unusual to them, whether experimental electronics, throat singing or a folk tradition from the other side of the world. People mark it by playing something they have never heard before, digging through unfamiliar genres and sharing their oddest finds with friends.

Pluto Demoted Day recalls August 24, 2006, when the International Astronomical Union, meeting in Prague, adopted a formal definition of a planet. Pluto, discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930 and counted as the ninth planet for 76 years, did not meet it and was reclassified as a dwarf planet, leaving the solar system with eight planets. Space fans mark the day by revisiting the debate, sharing images from NASA's New Horizons flyby of 2015 and raising a toast to the little world at the edge of the solar system.

slogans.en: Still a planet in our hearts.

descriptions.en: Belgian Beer Week raises a glass to one of the world's richest brewing traditions. Belgium brews a remarkable range of styles, from Trappist ales made in monasteries to sour, spontaneously fermented lambics, and in 2016 UNESCO added Belgian beer culture to its list of intangible cultural heritage. People mark the week by tasting styles they have never tried, visiting local breweries and cafés, and pouring each beer into its own glass, as Belgians traditionally do.

Kiss and Make Up Day is a gentle reminder to end quarrels and let go of old grudges. Nobody knows for certain who started it, but its message is simple: pride and silence cost more than a sincere apology. People mark the day by calling a friend they have drifted from, settling a family disagreement, or simply saying sorry to a partner with a kiss or a warm hug.

slogans.en: Let it go, make it right.

descriptions.en: National Secondhand Wardrobe Day celebrates clothes that get a second life. Its origins are unclear, but its point matters more than ever: the fashion industry uses huge amounts of water and energy, and much of what it makes is thrown away after only a few wears. People mark the day by browsing thrift and vintage shops, swapping clothes with friends, mending old favourites, or donating what they no longer wear.

International Dog Day on August 26 celebrates dogs of every breed and mix, from pedigree show dogs to shelter mutts. It was started in 2004 by American pet lifestyle expert Colleen Paige to honour the loyalty and companionship dogs give us, and to encourage people to adopt rather than buy. Dog lovers mark it by spoiling their pets with a long walk or a new toy, donating to or volunteering at a local shelter, and sharing photos of their four-legged friends.

slogans.en: Every Dog Deserves a Loving Home.

descriptions.en: Women's Equality Day marks August 26, 1920, the day the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution was certified, barring states from denying citizens the vote because of their sex. In 1971, at the urging of Congresswoman Bella Abzug, Congress designated the date to honour the generations of suffragists who fought for that right. Today it is marked with talks, voter registration drives and events that look at how far equality has come and what remains to be done.

International Lottery Day celebrates the small thrill of buying a ticket and wondering, just for a moment, what you would do if you won. Lotteries are centuries old: in the 15th century towns in the Low Countries were already raising money for walls and for the poor this way, and many lotteries still fund good causes today. People mark the day by trying their luck with friends or family, ideally with a small, sensible stake.

World Lake Day, on August 27, was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 2024 and first observed in 2025. Lakes hold much of the planet's accessible fresh water, supply drinking water, food and work for millions of people, and shelter a rich variety of wildlife, yet many are shrinking or polluted. The day is marked with shoreline clean-ups, water-quality checks, nature walks and talks on protecting and restoring lakes.

National Just Because Day, observed in the United States on August 27, gives everyone permission to do something for no particular reason. Its origins are unclear, but its point is simple: kindness and fun don't need an occasion. People mark it by sending a surprise note or small gift, calling an old friend, treating themselves to something spontaneous, or doing a good turn for a stranger, just because.

Festa do Vinho is the Madeira Wine Festival, held at grape-harvest time on the Portuguese island of Madeira. Vines have been grown on its steep terraces since the island was settled in the 15th century, and its fortified wine became famous around the world. The festival brings grape picking and traditional stomping in the countryside, folk music and dancing, tastings and colourful parades through the streets of Funchal.

National Red Wine Day, observed in the United States on August 28, raises a glass to red wine in all its styles, from light Pinot Noir to bold Cabernet Sauvignon. Winemaking is one of humanity's oldest crafts, with the earliest known traces found in the South Caucasus about 8,000 years ago; red wine gets its colour from fermenting the juice with the dark grape skins. People mark the day by opening a favourite bottle, trying a new grape or pairing a glass with a good meal.

Rainbow Bridge Remembrance Day, on August 28, is a gentle day to remember the pets who have died. It takes its name from the Rainbow Bridge, a short prose poem of uncertain authorship that imagines lost animals waiting, healthy and happy, in a green meadow until their people come to cross the bridge with them. Many owners mark the day by lighting a candle, looking through old photos, sharing stories of their companions or donating to an animal shelter in their memory.

names.en: International Read Comics in Public Day

descriptions.en: International Read Comics in Public Day invites fans to take their comics, graphic novels and manga out of the house and read them where everyone can see. It falls on August 28, the birthday of Jack Kirby, the artist who co-created Captain America, the Fantastic Four and the X-Men. Readers mark it by flipping pages on park benches, in cafés and on buses and trains, showing that comics are a medium for all ages.

The International Day Against Nuclear Tests falls on 29 August, the date in 1991 when the Semipalatinsk test site in Kazakhstan was closed after decades of Soviet nuclear testing. The UN General Assembly declared the day in 2009, at Kazakhstan's initiative, and it was first observed in 2010. It highlights the harm nuclear tests have done to people and the environment and calls for a complete ban on them. Conferences, exhibitions and educational events around the world promote a future free of nuclear weapons.

slogans.en: For a world free of nuclear tests.

descriptions.en: Individual Rights Day is marked on 29 August, the birthday of the English philosopher John Locke, born in 1632. Locke argued that every person holds natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that governments exist to protect them; his ideas shaped later declarations of rights. The day is a reminder of freedoms such as free speech and freedom of belief, which are easy to take for granted. People mark it by reading about these rights, discussing them and standing up for them in everyday life.

India's National Sports Day falls on 29 August, the birthday of the hockey legend Major Dhyan Chand, born in 1905. Famed for his ball control, he helped India win Olympic gold in hockey in 1928, 1932 and 1936. The day celebrates sport as a source of health, discipline and national pride. Schools, colleges and sports bodies hold matches, races and fitness events, and the country's national sports awards are traditionally presented around this date.

National Beach Day, founded in 2014 by animal activist and lifestyle expert Colleen Paige, is a call to clean the places we love most. Beaches nourish millions of outdoor memories — swimming, surfing, sandcastles, picnics, and quiet mornings — yet they degrade under pollution and climate pressure. The day invites everyone to do their part: grab a bag and a few friends, join or organize a beach cleanup, support groups like Surfrider Foundation, Oceana or The Nature Conservancy, and help keep our coastlines beautiful and sustainable for generations to come.

National Grief Awareness Day, founded by Angela Cartwright, honors the reality that grief is part of life — a response to losing someone or something we love. It exists to remind us how to be there for others: presence over advice, listening over fixing. The day talks about the well-known five stages — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — not as a linear path but as a loop we move through differently in every moment. The invitation is simple: be there. Bring a meal, lend an ear, share a laugh, or just sit.

Victory Day (Zafer Bayramı) on 30 August marks the Turkish victory at the Battle of Dumlupınar in 1922, known in Turkey as the Commander-in-Chief's Battle. Led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the Turkish army broke the Greek front, a turning point that decided the War of Independence and opened the way to the Republic in 1923. It is a national holiday across Turkey. People mark it with official ceremonies, military parades, visits to Anıtkabir and streets hung with Turkish flags.

International Whale Shark Day on 30 August celebrates the largest fish in the world. Despite its size, often more than 12 metres, the whale shark is a gentle filter feeder that lives on plankton and small fish in warm seas. The species is listed as endangered, threatened by fishing, collisions with boats and disturbance from poorly run tourism. Aquariums, divers and conservation groups mark the day with talks, beach clean-ups and campaigns for responsible whale shark watching.

slogans.en: The gentle giant needs a gentle hand.

descriptions.en: Frankenstein Day marks Mary Shelley's 1818 novel, the book that invented modern science fiction. Written when she was just 19, it tells the story of Victor Frankenstein and the Creature he stitches together from cadavers and jolts to life with lightning — a haunting meditation on ambition, creation, isolation, and what it means to be human. Readers, watchers, and writers celebrate the novel by revisiting the book, watching one of dozens of film adaptations, dressing up, exploring Frankenstein-themed video games, or simply talking about how a teenager gave us an idea that has haunted every scientific breakthrough since.

slogans.en: One spark, one monster, one legend.

descriptions.en: We Love Memoirs Day was founded in 2013 by memoir authors Victoria Twead and Alan Parks to bring readers and writers together around one of literature's most intimate forms. A memoir focuses on a single, significant period or moment rather than the whole sweep of a life — The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank is perhaps the most famous example. The day is celebrated with online writing circles, where new memoirists pick up tips, make friends and share drafts; by starting a personal memoir of one's own; and simply by recommending a favourite memoir to someone who hasn't read it.

slogans.en: Every life hides a story worth telling.

descriptions.en: National Eat Outside Day celebrates the oldest trick in the human playbook — taking the meal outdoors. The tradition stretches back centuries: medieval hunters packed provisions for the trail, Bavarian beer gardens opened in the 17th century, picnics caught on in 18th-century American 'pleasure gardens,' and Charles Feltman's Coney Island sausage sandwich birthed the hot dog in 1884. The day invites a picnic in the park, a few friends around a backyard grill, a patio table at a favourite restaurant — any excuse to skip the dining room while the weather still cooperates.

slogans.en: Eat outside. That's the whole rule.

descriptions.en: National Matchmaker Day was founded in 2016 by jewellery house ArtCarved Bridal to honour the people — professional or amateur — who spend their lives putting others in the same room and hoping something sparks. Matchmakers pre-screen for compatibility in ways no app can match, and they carry awkward conversations and fragile confidence for their clients. The day is a low-stakes chance to thank whoever set you up, play Cupid between two single friends, host a mixer, or share your own love story inspired by someone else's match.

slogans.en: Cupid called. He's on a coffee run.

descriptions.en: World Distance Learning Day celebrates the freedom to learn without borders. Its roots go back further than the internet: in 1728 Caleb Phillips taught shorthand by mail in Boston; in the 1840s Isaac Pitman taught the same subject by postcard; in 1858 the University of London became the first to grant degrees to remote students. Radio, television and the internet each widened access further — and distance learning now lets parents, night-shift workers and rural learners study on their own schedule, at any hour. The day invites trying a free online class, sharing what you learned, helping someone start a course, or joining a virtual study group.

names.en: International Day for People of African Descent

descriptions.en: The International Day for People of African Descent was established by the United Nations General Assembly in 2020 and first observed in 2021. It rests on three principles — recognition, justice, and development — and asks the world to confront the centuries of injustice that people of African descent have endured: the Transatlantic slave trade, colonial rule, and the ongoing discrimination and systemic racism that shape justice systems today. The day invites joining community events, reading books and watching documentaries about the African diaspora, standing up against inequity, and supporting organisations working on education and legal aid.

Malaysia's National Day, Hari Merdeka, on 31 August marks the independence of the Federation of Malaya from British rule in 1957. On that morning Tunku Abdul Rahman, the first prime minister, read the proclamation at Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur and led the crowd in shouts of "Merdeka!", meaning freedom. Malaysia itself was formed later, in 1963, but this date remains the country's main national celebration. It is marked with a grand parade, fireworks and homes, cars and streets decked in the Jalur Gemilang flag.

International Overdose Awareness Day on 31 August is the world's largest annual campaign to end overdose. It began in Melbourne, Australia, in 2001 and has since spread to communities around the world. The day remembers without stigma the people who have died of an overdose, acknowledges the grief of their families and friends, and spreads the message that overdose is preventable. People wear silver or purple, hold candlelit vigils and memorial walks, and share information on prevention and support.

World Alzheimer's Month is an international campaign held every September to raise awareness of dementia and challenge the stigma that still surrounds it. Alzheimer's Disease International launched the month in 2012, building on World Alzheimer's Day, which has been marked on 21 September since 1994. Organisations around the world run memory walks, information events and memory screenings, and many people use the month to learn the early signs, support carers and talk openly about living with dementia.

Suicide Prevention Month, observed throughout September, raises awareness of suicide as a major and preventable public health issue. It encourages open conversations about mental health, reduces stigma, and points people toward support and crisis resources. The month reminds everyone that reaching out, checking in, and listening can save lives.

slogans.en: Reach out, check in, save a life.

descriptions.en: Rtveli is the grape harvest in Georgia, a season of picking, pressing and celebration that runs from late summer into autumn, especially in the wine region of Kakheti. Georgia has one of the oldest winemaking traditions in the world, with archaeological traces going back about 8,000 years, and its method of fermenting wine in buried clay jars called qvevri is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. Families and neighbours harvest together, then gather at a supra feast with songs, toasts led by a tamada and sweets such as churchkhela made from grape juice and nuts.

Ginger Cat Appreciation Day is a day to celebrate orange cats, from sleepy sofa companions to the confident strays that rule many a city street. Every ginger cat carries tabby markings of some kind, and most are male, because the gene for orange fur sits on the X chromosome. Owners mark the day by sharing photos of their marmalade friends, while others feed neighbourhood strays or support local shelters where orange cats wait for a home.

slogans.en: Every ginger cat is a little tiger with a big heart.

descriptions.en: World Letter Writing Day celebrates the timeless art of hand-written correspondence. From scented paper to sealing wax, letters carry a personal touch that digital messages can never match. Founded by Richard Simpkin to revive the joy of finding a handwritten letter in the mailbox, the day encourages people to slow down and reconnect with friends, family, mentors, or even their future selves.

slogans.en: Put pen to paper. Send joy.

descriptions.en: National Hotel Employee Day honours the people who keep hotels running in the United States, from front desk staff and housekeepers to cooks, porters, maintenance crews and night auditors. They greet tired travellers at any hour, clean and prepare rooms with care, and quietly solve the small problems that can make or break a stay. Their work makes holidays, business trips and weekend getaways possible. On your next stay, thank the staff by name, leave a note or tip for housekeeping, or write a kind review that mentions them.

slogans.en: Behind every great stay is a great team.

descriptions.en: Yogurt Day celebrates one of the world's oldest fermented foods, made when friendly bacteria turn milk thick and tangy. People across the Middle East, Central Asia and the Balkans have made it for thousands of years, and the word itself comes from Turkish. Fans mark the day by enjoying yogurt in its many forms, from a bowl with fruit and honey to cooling drinks like ayran, garlicky dips like cacık or tzatziki, and sauces spooned over mantı.

slogans.en: Spoon into something good for you.

descriptions.en: Read A New Book Month runs through September and invites readers of every age to pick up a title they have never read before. It is a nudge to step beyond familiar favourites and try a new author, genre or language, just as schools and routines start again after summer. People mark the month by visiting libraries and bookshops, swapping books with friends, joining a reading club, or passing on books they have finished to someone else.

slogans.en: Open a book. Open a world.

descriptions.en: Knowledge Day on September 1 marks the start of the school and university year in Russia, a tradition dating back to Soviet times. It is a working day, but for pupils it is a festive one: schools hold a ceremony known as the First Bell, and first-graders arrive in their best clothes with bouquets of flowers for their teachers. Often an older pupil carries a first-grader on their shoulder, ringing a small bell to open the new year, and families take photos to remember the milestone.

slogans.en: Open the books, light the future.

descriptions.en: Vietnam's Independence Day, also called National Day, falls on September 2, the date in 1945 when Ho Chi Minh read the Declaration of Independence in Ba Dinh Square in Hanoi. That speech proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, the forerunner of today's Socialist Republic of Vietnam. It is a national public holiday: streets fill with red flags, families travel or gather, and major anniversaries bring parades in Hanoi and fireworks in cities across the country.

slogans.en: Độc lập – Tự do – Hạnh phúc (Independence – Freedom – Happiness)

descriptions.en: World Coconut Day on September 2 celebrates the coconut palm, a tree that gives food, drink, oil, fibre and timber to millions of people across the tropics. The date marks the founding of the Asian and Pacific Coconut Community, now the International Coconut Community, in 1969. Growers' groups and governments use the day to promote coconut farming, while cooks and shops showcase everything from coconut water to curries and sweets.

Vietnam National Day on September 2 is the country's most important civic holiday. On this day in 1945, Ho Chi Minh read the Declaration of Independence in Hanoi's Ba Dinh Square, proclaiming the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Today it is a public holiday: streets fill with red flags, families travel and gather, and major anniversaries bring parades and fireworks over Hanoi.

slogans.en: Độc lập — Tự do — Hạnh phúc!

descriptions.en: Pierce Your Ears Day celebrates one of the oldest forms of body adornment, the simple earring. Ear piercing has been practised across cultures for thousands of years: the funerary mask of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun shows pierced earlobes, and in many families, including in Türkiye, a first pair of earrings is a cherished gift for a baby or young girl. People mark the day by getting a first or extra piercing at a professional studio with sterile equipment, choosing new earrings, or sharing the story behind a favourite pair.

National Live Fearless Day is an American observance that encourages people to face their fears instead of letting them make the decisions. Courage here does not mean feeling no fear at all, but choosing to move forward while still feeling it, whether that means speaking up, starting something new or asking for help. People mark the day by taking one small brave step, such as signing up for a class, making a difficult phone call or finally having a postponed conversation, and by sharing stories of courage that might inspire others.

slogans.en: Courage isn't the absence of fear. It's moving anyway.

descriptions.en: Merchant Navy Day on September 3 honours the seafarers of Britain's merchant fleet, who carry most of the goods the country depends on. The date recalls the SS Athenia, a passenger liner torpedoed by a German U-boat on 3 September 1939, the day Britain entered the Second World War; thousands of merchant sailors were lost in the war that followed. Across the UK the Red Ensign, the merchant fleet's flag, is flown from public buildings, and services are held at memorials.

slogans.en: The silent force that keeps the world turning.

descriptions.en: National Skyscraper Day is celebrated on September 3rd each year to mark the birthday of Louis H. Sullivan, the American architect widely regarded as the father of skyscrapers. From the world's first skyscraper — the ten-story Home Insurance Building in Chicago, 1885 — to today's 163-floor Burj Khalifa, the day honours the architects, engineers, and construction crews who keep pushing buildings toward the sky.

slogans.en: From ten stories to the sky.

descriptions.en: National Wildlife Day on September 4 is an American day for learning about endangered animals and the habitats they need. It was started in 2005 by animal advocate Colleen Paige, and it has also come to honour the conservationist Steve Irwin, who died on 4 September 2006. People mark it by visiting zoos and sanctuaries, supporting rescue groups, planting for pollinators and learning which species near them are at risk.

slogans.en: Protect the wild that protects us.

descriptions.en: International Taekwondo Day on September 4 celebrates the Korean martial art known for its fast, high kicks. The date recalls 4 September 1994, when the International Olympic Committee voted to make taekwondo an official Olympic sport, first contested at the Sydney 2000 Games. World Taekwondo set up the day in 2006, and clubs around the world mark it with demonstrations, open classes and belt tests.

The International Day of Charity on September 5 encourages giving, volunteering and solidarity as ways to ease poverty and suffering. The United Nations General Assembly declared it in 2012, choosing the anniversary of the death of Mother Teresa, who died on this day in 1997 after a lifetime serving the poor in Kolkata. People mark it by donating, volunteering with local groups, and supporting food banks, shelters and other charities.

Unification Day, on 6 September, is a Bulgarian public holiday marking the 1885 union of the Principality of Bulgaria with Eastern Rumelia, an autonomous Ottoman province. The union was proclaimed in Plovdiv after an almost bloodless uprising organised by the Bulgarian Secret Central Revolutionary Committee under Zahari Stoyanov, and Prince Alexander I soon accepted it. Bulgaria defended the union later that year in the Serbo-Bulgarian War. Today the day is marked with flags, wreath-layings and ceremonies, with the biggest celebrations in Plovdiv.

Brazil's Independence Day, on 7 September, marks the day in 1822 when Prince Regent Pedro declared the country's break from Portugal on the banks of the Ipiranga stream in São Paulo. His cry of 'Independence or death!', remembered as the Grito do Ipiranga, became the founding moment of the Empire of Brazil, and Pedro was soon crowned its first emperor, Pedro I. Today it is a national holiday, celebrated with military and civic parades, the largest in Brasília, along with flags, music and school events.

names.en: International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies

descriptions.en: The International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, on 7 September, draws attention to air pollution, one of the greatest environmental threats to human health. The UN General Assembly established the day in 2019, and it has been observed every year since 2020, with the UN Environment Programme leading the campaign. Cities, schools and organisations mark it by sharing air-quality data, promoting cleaner transport and energy, and urging everyone to act together so that the air we breathe is safe.

International Literacy Day was proclaimed by UNESCO in 1966. It reminds the public of the importance of literacy as a matter of dignity and human rights, and to advance the literacy agenda towards a more literate and sustainable society. Around 773 million adults worldwide lack basic literacy skills.

slogans.en: Promoting literacy for a world in transition: building the foundation for sustainable and peaceful societies.

descriptions.en: World Physical Therapy Day, on 8 September, celebrates physiotherapists and the work they do to help people move, recover and stay independent after injury, surgery or illness. The date marks the founding of World Physiotherapy, then called the World Confederation for Physical Therapy, in 1951, and the day has been held since 1996. Each year has its own theme, and physiotherapists around the world run free check-ups, exercise sessions and campaigns showing how movement supports health at every age.

International Pardon Day, on 8 September, is a day about forgiveness: letting go of old grudges, offering an apology or accepting one. The date recalls 8 September 1974, when US President Gerald Ford granted Richard Nixon a full pardon for any crimes he may have committed during the Watergate scandal. People mark it by reaching out to someone they have fallen out with, forgiving a debt or a mistake, or simply going easier on themselves.

Technical Analysts Day on September 9 celebrates the traders and analysts who study price charts, trading volume and market patterns to judge where prices may head next. The craft traces back to Charles Dow, whose writing on market trends in the late 1800s became known as Dow Theory, and today it relies on tools such as moving averages, RSI and MACD. It is a fitting day to thank the chart readers in your life, or to learn what those lines and candles actually mean.

Teddy Bear Day on September 9 celebrates the cuddly toy that has comforted children for more than a century. Its name goes back to 1902, when US President Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear that had been tied up for him on a hunting trip in Mississippi. A newspaper cartoon made the story famous, and toymakers soon began selling stuffed 'Teddy's bears'. People mark the day by hugging an old favourite, giving a bear to a child or donating one to a hospital.

World Suicide Prevention Day is observed on September 10 each year. It was launched in 2003 by the International Association for Suicide Prevention together with the World Health Organization, to show that suicide can be prevented and that everyone has a part to play. Groups around the world hold talks, walks and candlelight vigils, share information about crisis lines, and encourage people to reach out to anyone who may be struggling. A simple conversation can help someone feel less alone.

Patriot Day honours the memory of the 2,977 people killed in the attacks of September 11, 2001, and the 411 emergency responders who died trying to save them. Across the United States flags fly at half-staff and a moment of silence is held at 8:46 a.m., the minute the first plane struck. Communities gather at memorials and firehouses to remember those lost and to thank those who still answer the call.

National SUP Day celebrates stand-up paddleboarding, the fastest-growing paddle sport in the world. Founded by AquaPaddle, it invites people of every age and fitness level onto lakes, rivers and coastlines for a day on the water. Alongside the paddling, the day raises money for charity and encourages everyone who enjoys the water to help look after it.

slogans.en: Find your balance on the water.

descriptions.en: Bravehearts Day, once known as White Balloon Day, brings people together to confront child sexual assault and to stand with survivors. White balloons are released and worn as a symbol of hope and solidarity, turning a subject people avoid into one they are willing to name out loud. Money raised funds education programmes, counselling and legal support for affected families.

For eleven days each September, Toronto turns into one of the most important stops on the film calendar. TIFF premieres everything from awards-season heavyweights to first features nobody has heard of yet, and audiences rather than juries decide its headline prize. The People's Choice Award has proved such a reliable predictor of Oscar success that the industry watches the vote closely.

slogans.en: Where the year's best films meet their audience.

descriptions.en: High blood pressure has earned the name the silent killer because it usually announces itself with no symptoms at all. Run by Blood Pressure UK, Know Your Numbers! Week sets up thousands of free Pressure Stations across the country so people can find out their reading in a couple of minutes. The campaign is aimed especially at the over-40s, where a single check can be the difference between a quiet warning and a stroke.

Most people assume the electric car is a recent idea, when in fact some of the earliest automobiles ever built ran on batteries. Started by Plug In America in 2011 as a single day, this campaign grew into a week and then a full month of test drives, owner meet-ups and community events. The pitch is simple: stop reading about electric cars and go and sit in one.

slogans.en: The future already has a plug.

descriptions.en: World Dolphin Day, on 12 September, celebrates dolphins and draws attention to the dangers they face. These social, playful animals live in close-knit groups, communicate with whistles and clicks, and are among the most intelligent creatures in the sea. Many populations are threatened by fishing nets, pollution, noise, habitat loss and hunting. People mark the day by learning about dolphins, joining beach and ocean clean-ups, choosing responsible wildlife tours and supporting marine conservation groups.

slogans.en: Protect the minds of the sea.

descriptions.en: Gym Day on September 12 celebrates the gym as a place for getting stronger, clearing your head and being part of a community. Coming as summer ends and routines return, it is a natural moment to start a new training habit or get back to one that slipped. Gyms often mark it with open days, free trial classes and group workouts, while regulars might bring a friend along, try a class they have never done, or simply thank the trainers and staff who keep them going.

German Language Day celebrates one of Europe's most widely spoken languages, the mother tongue of people in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and parts of Italy and Belgium. The idea of a Day of the German Language comes from the Verein Deutsche Sprache, a German language association that launched it in 2001 to encourage pride in German and careful use of it. People mark it by reading a German author, learning a few new words or enjoying the language's famously long compound nouns.

National Police Woman Day, on 12 September in the United States, honours the women who serve in law enforcement. The date recalls 12 September 1910, when Alice Stebbins Wells was sworn in by the Los Angeles Police Department, often cited as one of the first policewomen in the country with full police powers. Today women serve at every rank, and the day is marked with thanks from departments and communities, stories of trailblazers, and encouragement for young women considering the career.

slogans.en: Honour the women who answer the call.

descriptions.en: National Chocolate Milkshake Day on September 12 is an American food day devoted to the thick, cold blend of ice cream, milk and chocolate. Milkshakes became a fixture of soda fountains in the early 1900s, and a well-known story credits a Walgreens soda fountain in Chicago with popularising the malted milkshake by adding ice cream to malted milk in 1922. Fans mark the day by ordering one at a favourite diner or making their own at home, with whipped cream and a cherry on top.

slogans.en: If it won't suck through a straw, it's not a milkshake.

descriptions.en: International Programmers' Day falls on the 256th day of the year: 13 September, or 12 September in leap years. The number was chosen because 256 is the count of distinct values a single eight-bit byte can hold, and it is a power of two. Russia made it an official professional holiday in 2009, and developers worldwide have adopted it since. Programmers mark it with team celebrations, coding challenges, tech talks and a bit of self-mocking humour about bugs and deadlines.

slogans.en: There are 10 types of people in the world.

descriptions.en: Roald Dahl Day, on 13 September, celebrates the birthday of the storyteller Roald Dahl, born on that day in 1916 in Llandaff, Wales, to Norwegian parents. He wrote some of the best-loved children's books of all time, including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda, The BFG and The Witches, full of mischief, wordplay and children who outwit grown-ups. Schools and libraries mark the day with readings, and children often dress up as their favourite characters.

slogans.en: A little nonsense now and then is relished by the wisest men.

descriptions.en: Bald is Beautiful Day, on 13 September, celebrates people without hair and the confidence it takes to wear a bare head proudly. Hair loss is common, whether through genetics, age, illness or medical treatment, yet it is often treated as something to hide. The day challenges that idea and says baldness is simply another way to look good. People mark it by showing off their shaved or bald heads, sharing photos, and offering support to anyone struggling with hair loss.

slogans.en: No hair, no problem — shine on!

descriptions.en: The International Day of Democracy, observed every 15 September, was established by the UN General Assembly in 2007 and first marked in 2008. The date recalls the Universal Declaration on Democracy, adopted by the Inter-Parliamentary Union on 15 September 1997. The day is a chance to look honestly at the state of democracy around the world and to remember that it depends on free elections, accountable institutions and active citizens. Parliaments, schools and civil society groups mark it with debates, open days and campaigns encouraging people to take part.

Greenpeace Day on 15 September recalls the day in 1971 when a small group of activists set sail from Vancouver on a chartered fishing boat, the Phyllis Cormack, to protest a US nuclear test on Amchitka Island in Alaska. They called the voyage Greenpeace, and the name stayed with the movement that grew from it. The boat was turned back before reaching the island, but public pressure grew, and nuclear testing on Amchitka ended the following year. Supporters mark the day with environmental campaigns and actions.

Dates Day celebrates the fruit of the date palm, which has fed and shaded the Middle East and North Africa for thousands of years. Across the region dates are a sign of hospitality: they are offered to guests with Arabic coffee, served at weddings and feasts, and traditionally used to break the fast at iftar during Ramadan. People mark the day by sharing dates with family and neighbours, tasting varieties such as Khudri, Medjool and Deglet Nour, and visiting date markets and festivals.

World Ozone Day, held on 16 September, marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol in 1987, the treaty that set out to phase out the chemicals destroying the ozone layer. This thin band of gas high in the atmosphere shields life on Earth from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 1994, and the Protocol has since been ratified by every country in the world. Schools, scientists and environmental groups use the day to show how global cooperation can repair real damage to the planet.

slogans.en: Montreal Protocol: fixing the ozone layer and reducing climate change.

descriptions.en: Mexican Independence Day on 16 September marks the start of Mexico's war of independence from Spain. Before dawn on that day in 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo rang the church bell in the town of Dolores and called on people to rise up, a moment known as the Grito de Dolores; independence was won in 1821. Celebrations begin on the night of 15 September, when the president repeats the cry from the balcony of the National Palace in Mexico City and the crowd answers "¡Viva México!". The next day brings military parades, fireworks, music and festive food.

Malaysia Day on 16 September marks the formation of Malaysia in 1963, when the Federation of Malaya joined with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore; Singapore left two years later. The day is distinct from Independence Day on 31 August, which recalls Malaya's independence from Britain in 1957, and it carries special meaning in Sabah and Sarawak. It has been a national public holiday since 2010. Malaysians mark it with flags, concerts, cultural performances and gatherings that celebrate the country's many peoples, languages and faiths.

World Patient Safety Day on 17 September was established by the World Health Assembly in 2019 to raise awareness of patient safety and reduce avoidable harm in health care. Each year the World Health Organization chooses a theme, such as medication safety or safe childbirth, and calls on patients, health workers and governments to act together. Hospitals hold training and awareness events, and landmarks around the world are lit in orange, the day's colour. Its message is simple: no one should be harmed while receiving care.

World Manta Day on 17 September celebrates manta rays, the gentle giants of tropical seas, and raises awareness of the threats they face. Mantas glide through the water feeding on tiny plankton, and they have some of the largest brains of any fish. They breed very slowly, often having a single pup every few years, so fishing for their gill plates and accidental capture in nets hit them hard. Both species are listed as threatened on the IUCN Red List, and divers, aquariums and conservation groups use the day to share their story.

slogans.en: Protect the gentle giants of the sea.

descriptions.en: Chile's national day on 18 September commemorates the First National Government Junta of 1810, the first step on the road to independence, which was formally declared in 1818. Together with Army Day on 19 September, it is the heart of the Fiestas Patrias, the biggest celebration of the Chilean year. Families and friends gather at fondas and ramadas, festive stands serving empanadas, grilled meat and chicha. Flags fly from homes, and the cueca, the national dance, is danced across the country.

World Bamboo Day, on September 18, celebrates one of the most useful plants on Earth. It was declared by the World Bamboo Organization at the World Bamboo Congress held in Bangkok in 2009. Some bamboo species are among the fastest-growing plants known, and bamboo is used for building, furniture, paper, food and textiles while its roots help hold soil in place. People mark the day with planting events, craft and design exhibitions, and talks about bamboo as a renewable material.

International Equal Pay Day, on September 18, calls for equal pay for work of equal value, whoever does the work. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2019, and it was first observed in 2020. Women around the world are still paid less than men on average, and the gap is often wider for mothers, migrants and women of colour. Governments, unions and employers use the day to review pay data, publish salary gaps and commit to closing them.

slogans.en: Equal pay for equal work — always.

names.en: International Talk Like a Pirate Day

descriptions.en: International Talk Like a Pirate Day, on September 19, is a light-hearted holiday when people swap everyday speech for pirate talk. It was invented in 1995 by two friends from Oregon, John Baur and Mark Summers, and spread worldwide after the humour columnist Dave Barry wrote about it in 2002. People greet each other with 'Ahoy, matey!' and 'Arr!', dress up in eye patches and tricorn hats, and some cafés, schools and charities join in with themed games and fundraisers.

In Chile, September 19 is the Day of the Glories of the Army, widely known as Armed Forces Day, a national holiday that follows Independence Day on September 18. It honours the Army, Navy and Air Force and their part in the country's history, and it closes the main days of the Fiestas Patrias. The highlight is the Great Military Parade in Santiago's O'Higgins Park, attended by the president, while families spend the holiday at fondas with empanadas, cueca dancing and barbecues.

slogans.en: Service, honor, and unity for Chile.

descriptions.en: World Cleanup Day is a global volunteer action in September, when people in countries around the world head out on the same day to pick up litter from streets, parks, beaches, rivers and forests. It grew out of Let's Do It!, a movement born in Estonia in 2008, when tens of thousands of volunteers cleared illegally dumped rubbish from the whole country in a single day. Today local groups, schools, companies and families organise their own cleanups, sort what they collect and use the day to talk about cutting waste at its source.

The International Day of Peace, observed on 21 September, invites everyone to commit to peace beyond their differences and to help build a culture of peace. The United Nations General Assembly established it in 1981, and in 2001 fixed its date and declared it a day of global ceasefire and non-violence. Each year the Peace Bell is rung at UN headquarters in New York, and around the world people gather for vigils, a minute of silence, concerts, peace walks and school activities.

slogans.en: Actions for peace: our ambition for the #GlobalGoals.

descriptions.en: World Alzheimer's Day on 21 September raises awareness of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia and challenges the stigma that still surrounds them. It was launched in 1994 by Alzheimer's Disease International, the worldwide federation of Alzheimer associations, and since 2012 the whole of September has been marked as World Alzheimer's Month. Associations, hospitals and families hold information events, charity walks and free memory checks, and many people use the day to support carers and talk openly about the early signs of dementia.

Software Freedom Day is a worldwide celebration of free and open-source software, held each year in September. First held in 2004 and coordinated by the non-profit Software Freedom International, it aims to show the public why the freedom to use, study, change and share software matters. Local teams of volunteers, user groups and universities organise talks, workshops and install fests where people can try free programs and operating systems for themselves.

slogans.en: Free Software for a Free World

descriptions.en: Oktoberfest opens in Munich on a Saturday in late September and runs for about two weeks into early October on the Theresienwiese meadow. It began in 1810 with the horse races held to celebrate the wedding of Bavarian Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese, after whom the grounds are named. On opening day a parade of brewery horse carts and festival hosts makes its way to the grounds, and at noon the mayor taps the first keg with the cry “O'zapft is!” (It's tapped!) before crowds in dirndls and lederhosen raise their steins.

slogans.en: O'zapft is! — Let the Festivities Begin!

descriptions.en: Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Day, on 21 September, marks the birthday of Kwame Nkrumah, born in 1909, who led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957 and became the country's first prime minister and then its first president. A leading voice of pan-Africanism, he championed African unity and was among the founders of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963. It is a public holiday in Ghana, marked with wreath-laying at his mausoleum in Accra, lectures and school events, while the separate Founders' Day on 4 August honours the wider independence movement.

World Rhino Day on 22 September draws attention to the five surviving rhino species: the white and black rhinos of Africa and the greater one-horned, Javan and Sumatran rhinos of Asia. WWF South Africa announced the day in 2010, and it soon grew into a worldwide event against the poaching driven by the illegal trade in rhino horn and against the loss of their habitat. Zoos, conservation groups and schools mark it with talks, fundraisers and campaigns, and many people share pictures of rhinos to spread the message.

slogans.en: Five rhino species, five reasons to act.

descriptions.en: Hobbit Day on 22 September celebrates the birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins, the beloved heroes of J. R. R. Tolkien's The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. In the books the two hobbits share a birthday, and The Lord of the Rings opens with the grand party Bilbo throws on that date. Tolkien fans mark it in true Shire style, with hearty meals, hobbit costumes, going barefoot and reading the books aloud together.

slogans.en: In a hole in the ground, there lived a hobbit.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Sign Languages, on 23 September, celebrates sign languages as full, natural languages and as the key to the human rights of deaf people. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2017 at the request of the World Federation of the Deaf, choosing the date on which the federation was founded in 1951, and it falls during the International Week of the Deaf. Deaf communities, schools and institutions mark it with events in sign language, and many people use it to learn their first few signs.

slogans.en: Sign language — a language of inclusion.

descriptions.en: Celebrate Bisexuality Day, also called Bi Visibility Day, falls on 23 September and honours bisexual people, their history and their community. It was first marked in 1999, started by American bisexual rights activists Wendy Curry, Michael Page and Gigi Raven Wilbur, who wanted bi people to be seen both within and beyond the LGBTQ+ community. People mark it with gatherings, talks and the pink, purple and blue bisexual pride flag, and many use it to speak up against biphobia and bi erasure.

Saudi National Day, on 23 September, marks the day in 1932 when King Abdulaziz Al Saud proclaimed the unification of his lands as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. A royal decree joined the kingdoms of Hejaz and Najd under one name, laying the foundation of the modern state. It is a public holiday: streets and buildings turn green with flags and lights, and families enjoy fireworks, air shows, concerts and traditional performances such as the ardah sword dance.

Heritage Day, on 24 September, is a South African public holiday that celebrates the many cultures, languages and traditions of the 'rainbow nation'. In KwaZulu-Natal the date was long marked as Shaka Day in memory of the Zulu king Shaka, and after the end of apartheid it became a national day for the heritage of all South Africans. People wear traditional dress and attend cultural events, and many gather with friends and family around a braai, the South African barbecue, which is why it is also called National Braai Day.

World Gorilla Day, on 24 September, celebrates gorillas, among our closest living relatives, and supports the people working to protect them. It was first marked in 2017, on the 50th anniversary of Dian Fossey founding the Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park. Both gorilla species are critically endangered, threatened by poaching, habitat loss and disease. Zoos and conservation groups hold talks and fundraisers, and many people support park rangers or recycle old mobile phones, whose minerals are mined in gorilla habitat.

World Pharmacists' Day is celebrated every year on September 25 — the anniversary of the founding of the International Pharmaceutical Federation (FIP) in 1912. Established by FIP in 2009, the day highlights the vital role pharmacists play in improving health worldwide, promoting safe medication use, and advancing pharmaceutical science. Each year focuses on a specific theme set by FIP.

World Environmental Health Day, held every year on September 26, looks at how the places we live shape our health. It was launched by the International Federation of Environmental Health to draw attention to the work of environmental health professionals. Clean air, safe drinking water, sound food hygiene and healthy ecosystems all protect people quietly every day. Each year the day carries a theme, and health inspectors, municipalities and schools mark it with talks, campaigns and local clean-up projects.

National Pancake Day on September 26 celebrates America's love for the fluffy stacks that define weekend mornings. From classic buttermilk to blueberry and banana, pancakes are a canvas for creativity and a warm comfort food shared across generations. Stack 'em high and pour on the syrup!

Revolution Day on September 26 commemorates the 1962 uprising in which army officers overthrew the Mutawakkilite Kingdom, ending centuries of rule by the Zaydi imams in northern Yemen. The revolution proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic and was followed by years of civil war before the republic took hold. It remains one of the defining dates of modern Yemeni history. The anniversary is a national holiday, marked by lighting torches and bonfires on the eve, flags, patriotic songs and public gatherings.

World Tourism Day on September 27 highlights tourism's social, cultural and economic value around the world. It was established by the World Tourism Organization, now known as UN Tourism, and has been held since 1980; the date marks the anniversary of the adoption of the organization's statutes in 1970. Tourism supports millions of jobs and connects people across cultures, but it also has to protect the places it depends on. Each year a different host country leads celebrations around a theme, with conferences, open museum days and local events.

National Chocolate Milk Day on September 27 is an American food holiday devoted to the childhood classic that turns a plain glass of milk into a treat. Cocoa and a little sugar stirred into milk have been a favorite for generations, served cold in summer and warm on chilly mornings. Many athletes also reach for a glass after a workout, since it pairs carbohydrates with protein. People mark the day simply by pouring a glass, trying homemade chocolate syrup or sharing a nostalgic sip with their kids.

World Rabies Day on September 28 raises awareness of rabies, a viral disease that is almost always fatal once symptoms appear but entirely preventable.
