The date marks the death of Louis Pasteur, who developed the first rabies vaccine, and the day was started in 2007 by the Global Alliance for Rabies Control. Most human cases come from dog bites, so vaccinating dogs is the most effective way to stop the disease, and the global goal is zero human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030. Vets, health services and animal shelters mark it with free vaccination drives and bite-prevention lessons.

In Taiwan, September 28 honors the birthday of Confucius, the Chinese philosopher and teacher born in the state of Lu in 551 BCE. His teachings on family duty, respect, learning and good government have shaped East Asian life for more than two thousand years. Because he is revered as the model teacher, the day is also Taiwan's Teachers' Day. At dawn, Confucius temples hold a solemn ceremony with traditional music and the ancient ritual dance, and students thank their teachers with cards and small gifts.

slogans.en: Honor the master, walk the path.

descriptions.en: World Heart Day on September 29 reminds people that cardiovascular disease, including heart attack and stroke, is the world's leading cause of death. The day was created by the World Heart Federation, which runs it each year with heart foundations and health organizations around the world. Much of this disease can be prevented by not smoking, eating well, staying active and keeping blood pressure and cholesterol in check. People mark it with free heart check-ups, charity walks and runs, landmarks lit in red and campaigns that encourage small daily changes.

International Translation Day is celebrated on September 30, the feast of St. Jerome, who translated most of the Bible into Latin and is the patron saint of translators. The International Federation of Translators promoted the day for decades, and in 2017 the United Nations General Assembly officially recognised it. It honours translators and interpreters, whose work lets literature, science, diplomacy and everyday conversation cross language borders. Universities, publishers and translator associations mark it with talks, workshops and awards.

International Podcast Day, on September 30, celebrates the podcast: spoken audio that anyone can record and anyone can listen to, whenever they like. Podcasts carry news, interviews, comedy, true stories and lessons into commutes, kitchens and late-night walks. Listeners mark the day by trying a new show, recommending a favourite to a friend or leaving a kind review, while creators often release special episodes or record live.

The International Day of Older Persons is observed on October 1. It was established by the United Nations in 1990. The day celebrates the contributions of older people and raises awareness of the opportunities and challenges of ageing in today's world.

International Coffee Day on 1 October celebrates one of the world's most popular drinks and the people who grow it. The International Coffee Organization launched the official day in 2015, bringing together many national coffee days that had been held on different dates. Coffee is grown by millions of small farmers in tropical countries, and the day draws attention to their work and to fair prices for their beans. Cafés mark it with tastings and special offers, while coffee lovers try new beans and share a cup with friends.

China's National Day on October 1 marks the founding of the People's Republic of China, proclaimed by Mao Zedong in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1949. It is one of the country's biggest public holidays and opens Golden Week, a stretch of days off when hundreds of millions of people travel home or go sightseeing. Flag-raising ceremonies, fireworks, flower displays and, in some anniversary years, a grand military parade in Beijing mark the occasion.

slogans.en: Long live the People's Republic of China!

descriptions.en: Nigeria's Independence Day on October 1 marks the end of British colonial rule in 1960, when the green-white-green flag was raised for the first time. Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, home to hundreds of ethnic groups and languages, and the day is a public holiday celebrating that shared nationhood. The president addresses the nation, and people mark the day with parades, flag-waving, music, dance and family gatherings at home and across the diaspora.

slogans.en: Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress.

descriptions.en: World Vegetarian Day on October 1 celebrates meat-free eating and the people who choose it. The North American Vegetarian Society established the day in 1977, and the International Vegetarian Union soon endorsed it; it also opens Vegetarian Awareness Month. Vegetarians and the simply curious mark it by cooking a meatless meal, sharing recipes, trying dishes from cuisines with long vegetarian traditions, or talking about how food choices touch health, animals and the planet.

LGBTQ+ History Month celebrates the achievements, struggles, and trailblazers of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer community. Founded in 1994 by U.S. teacher Rodney Wilson, it is observed in October in the United States, timed around National Coming Out Day, while the UK marks it in February. It provides role models and educates about LGBTQ+ contributions to society.

slogans.en: Remembering the past, inspiring the future.

descriptions.en: National Pitbull Awareness Month celebrates these often-misunderstood dogs and works to counter negative stereotypes. It highlights that pit bulls are loyal, affectionate companions that score remarkably well in temperament testing. First held in 2007 by the organization Bless the Bullys, it promotes responsible ownership, adoption, and a fairer reputation for the breed.

The International Day of Non-Violence falls on October 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India's independence movement through peaceful resistance. The UN General Assembly established the day in 2007 to spread the message of non-violence through education and public awareness. In India the date is also Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday. Around the world, schools, peace groups and communities mark it with talks, silent marches, readings of Gandhi's words and efforts to resolve conflicts without force.

slogans.en: Be the change you wish to see in the world.

descriptions.en: German Unity Day is Germany's national holiday, marking the reunification of East and West Germany on 3 October 1990. Less than a year after the fall of the Berlin Wall, the two states, divided since the aftermath of the Second World War, became one country again. It is a public holiday across Germany, and the main celebration, a large citizens' festival with music, food and stands from every federal state, moves to a different host city each year.

Gaecheonjeol, which means "the day the heavens opened", is South Korea's National Foundation Day, held on 3 October. It celebrates the legendary founding of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, by Dangun, traditionally dated to 2333 BCE. The day is a public holiday, and a traditional rite is held at the Chamseongdan altar on Mount Mani on Ganghwa Island, which legend links to Dangun himself, while families enjoy a day off together.

Iraq Independence Day recalls 3 October 1932, when Iraq was admitted to the League of Nations as a sovereign state and the British mandate came to an end. It was the first Arab country under a mandate to gain membership, a milestone in the region's modern history. Today Iraq observes the date as its National Day, a public holiday marked with flags in the streets, official ceremonies and gatherings that celebrate the country's long history and shared identity.

World Animal Day, on 4 October, is an international day of action to improve the lives and welfare of animals everywhere. It was first held in Berlin in 1925 and later moved to 4 October, the feast day of Saint Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals. Shelters hold open days and adoption drives, schools run activities about caring for animals, and many people donate to animal charities or simply give extra attention to the animals around them.

slogans.en: Creating a world where animals are always recognized as sentient beings.

names.en: Feast of St. Francis of Assisi

descriptions.en: The Feast of St. Francis of Assisi (October 4) honors the patron saint of animals, the environment, and Italy. Many churches hold Blessing of the Animals ceremonies. Francis is celebrated for his love of nature and creatures.

slogans.en: All creatures great and small — blessed.

descriptions.en: World Teachers' Day, on 5 October, celebrates teachers around the world and the difference they make in people's lives. It marks the anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, which set out teachers' rights and responsibilities, and it has been held since 1994. Students thank their teachers with cards and small gifts, schools hold ceremonies, and education unions use the day to speak up for better conditions; Türkiye celebrates its own Teachers' Day on 24 November.

slogans.en: Teachers at the Heart of Education Recovery.

descriptions.en: World Cerebral Palsy Day, on 6 October, is a global movement led by people with cerebral palsy and their families. Cerebral palsy is a lifelong condition caused by damage to the developing brain, and it affects movement, posture and muscle control in very different ways from person to person. The day calls for a world where people with CP have the same rights, access and opportunities as anyone else. Organisations hold events, share personal stories and light up buildings in green, the day's colour.

Egypt's Armed Forces Day, on 6 October, honours the country's military and commemorates the crossing of the Suez Canal at the start of the 1973 October War. On that day Egyptian forces crossed the canal and broke through the Bar Lev Line on the eastern bank, an event remembered in Egypt as a moment of national pride. It is a public holiday, marked with official ceremonies, tributes to the fallen, television documentaries and patriotic songs heard across the country.

Evacuation Day, on 7 October, recalls the expulsion of Libya's Italian community in 1970, the year after Muammar Gaddafi took power. Italy had ruled Libya as a colony until the Second World War, and some twenty thousand Italian settlers still lived there; their property was confiscated and they were made to leave. Under Gaddafi the date was a public holiday, one of several that marked the end of foreign presence in the country. It was dropped from the official calendar after 2011, but it remains part of how Libyans remember the colonial era.

slogans.en: The last of the bases closed.

descriptions.en: World Post Day, on 9 October, marks the founding of the Universal Postal Union in Bern, Switzerland, in 1874. The union made it possible to send a letter across borders under shared rules, and it is now a United Nations agency; the UPU Congress declared the day in 1969. Today the post still carries letters, parcels and online orders, and in many places offers banking and other services too. Postal services mark it with special stamps, open days and letter-writing activities for children.

slogans.en: Post for planet: Together for a sustainable future.

descriptions.en: Hangul Day, on 9 October, is a national holiday in South Korea celebrating Hangul, the Korean alphabet. It was created under King Sejong the Great in 1443 and proclaimed in 1446 so that ordinary people, not only scholars of Chinese characters, could read and write. Its letters are built on a clear logic, with consonant shapes modelled on the mouth and tongue as they make each sound. Koreans mark the day with calligraphy contests, exhibitions and ceremonies, many of them around King Sejong's statue in central Seoul.

slogans.en: Celebrating the Beauty of the Korean Script

descriptions.en: World Mental Health Day, held every year on 10 October, puts mental health on the global agenda. It was first observed in 1992 at the initiative of the World Federation for Mental Health, and the World Health Organization now supports it with a yearly theme. The day aims to break the silence and stigma around mental illness and to push for care that everyone can reach. People mark it with talks, campaigns and open conversations, and by checking in on themselves and the people around them.

slogans.en: Mental Health is a Universal Human Right

descriptions.en: Double Ten Day, Taiwan's National Day, falls on 10 October, the tenth day of the tenth month. It marks the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911, the revolt that brought down China's last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China on 1 January 1912. In Taipei the day centres on a ceremony in front of the Presidential Office Building, with the president's address, honour guards and marching bands. Fireworks, flags and concerts fill the evening across the island.

slogans.en: Ten ten, a century of pride.

names.en: International Day of the Girl Child

descriptions.en: The International Day of the Girl Child, on 11 October, draws attention to the challenges girls face simply because they are girls and to their right to shape their own futures. The UN General Assembly declared the day in 2011, and it was first observed in 2012. It highlights issues such as access to education and health care, child marriage and violence, while celebrating what girls achieve when given a fair chance. Schools, charities and UN agencies mark it with campaigns, events and stories told by girls themselves.

slogans.en: Our time is now — our rights, our future.

descriptions.en: National Coming Out Day, on 11 October, supports LGBTQ+ people in sharing who they are with family, friends and colleagues. It began in the United States in 1988, on the first anniversary of the 1987 National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights. The idea behind it is simple: when people know someone who is openly LGBTQ+, prejudice is harder to hold on to. Today it is marked well beyond the US with events, personal stories and messages reminding everyone that coming out happens in one's own time and safety comes first.

slogans.en: Be yourself. Everyone else is taken.

descriptions.en: Spain's National Day, the Fiesta Nacional de España, falls on 12 October, the date in 1492 when Christopher Columbus's expedition first reached the Americas. Also known as the Día de la Hispanidad, it celebrates the language and cultural ties that link Spain with Latin America, though the anniversary is viewed very differently across the Americas. The main event is a military parade in Madrid led by the King, with an air force display trailing the colours of the flag. The date is also the feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, which Zaragoza celebrates with its biggest fiesta of the year.

Bald and Free Day, on 14 October, is a lighthearted day for celebrating baldness instead of hiding it. Whether hair has thinned with age, fallen out through illness or been shaved off by choice, the day invites people to wear their heads with pride. It is an unofficial observance with no single founder, but its message is a kind one: confidence is not measured in hair. People mark it by leaving the hats at home, sharing photos and jokes, and showing some love to the bald people in their lives.

slogans.en: Free your head, free your mind.

descriptions.en: Global Handwashing Day, on 15 October, promotes one of the simplest ways to stay healthy: washing your hands with soap. It was first held in 2008 and is led by the Global Handwashing Partnership, a group of public and private organisations working on hygiene. Washing hands with soap at key moments, such as after using the toilet and before eating or handling food, helps stop the spread of diarrhoea, respiratory infections and other illnesses. Schools and communities mark the day with demonstrations, songs and games that turn handwashing into a lasting habit.

slogans.en: Clean Hands Are a Human Right.

descriptions.en: World Food Day is held every year on 16 October, the date the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) was founded in 1945. It was first observed in 1981 and now carries a yearly theme on hunger, nutrition or how food is grown and shared. Governments, schools and charities mark it with food drives, talks and campaigns against waste, and many people use it to think about where their own food comes from.

slogans.en: Water is life, water is food. Leave no one behind.

descriptions.en: World Bread Day on 16 October celebrates one of humanity's oldest foods, eaten in some form in almost every culture. Promoted by international bakers' associations, it shares its date with World Food Day, a reminder that bread has long stood for daily nourishment and food security. Bakeries open their doors, schools hold baking lessons, and people bake at home, share loaves with neighbours and try breads from other kitchens, from flatbreads to sourdough.

World Spine Day highlights the importance of spinal health. Back and neck pain affect 1 in 10 people and are the leading cause of disability worldwide. The day promotes active and healthy lifestyles for spine care.

names.en: International Day for the Eradication of Poverty

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, on 17 October, stands for a world where no one is left to live in extreme poverty. It traces back to 17 October 1987, when around a hundred thousand people gathered at the Trocadéro in Paris to honour victims of poverty, hunger and violence; the UN made the date official in 1992. The day is marked with gatherings, testimonies from people living in poverty and calls for fairer policies on work, housing and education.

slogans.en: Decent work and social protection: putting dignity into practice for all.

descriptions.en: World Menopause Day, on 18 October, draws attention to menopause, the natural stage when periods stop, usually in a woman's late forties or early fifties. Led by the International Menopause Society, it picks a theme each year, from sleep and bone health to mood and heart health. Clinics, doctors and women's groups share information, encourage women to talk openly about symptoms such as hot flushes and poor sleep, and point to the treatments and support available.

St. Luke's Day on 18 October is the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist, traditionally held to be the author of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. Called "the beloved physician" by Paul, and by legend a painter, he became the patron saint of doctors and artists. In Denmark the date is a quiet one in the church calendar rather than a public holiday, a day to remember Luke through readings and his link to healing and art.

Independence Restoration Day marks 18 October 1991, when Azerbaijan's Supreme Council adopted the Constitutional Act on State Independence as the Soviet Union was breaking up. The act restored the independence of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, first declared in 1918, which had lasted only until 1920. Across Azerbaijan the day is marked with official ceremonies, flags on public buildings, concerts and speeches recalling the long road to sovereignty.

World Statistics Day celebrates the official statistics that help governments, businesses and citizens make informed decisions. The United Nations General Assembly established it, and it was first held on 20 October 2010; it is formally observed every five years. Reliable figures on population, health, jobs and prices underpin public policy and hold leaders to account. National statistics offices mark the day with open data releases, talks and school activities that show how numbers shape everyday life.

slogans.en: Connecting the World with Data We Can Trust.

descriptions.en: World Osteoporosis Day raises awareness of osteoporosis, a disease that makes bones thin and fragile, often without any symptoms until a bone breaks. The day is led by the International Osteoporosis Foundation, which works with patient groups and health bodies around the world. Hip, spine and wrist fractures caused by the disease can take away independence, especially in older women. On the day, campaigns encourage bone density checks, enough calcium, vitamin D and protein, regular exercise and fall prevention.

World Candy Day is a light-hearted celebration of sweets of every kind, from chocolate and caramel to gummies, lollipops and hard candy. Its origins are informal, but nearly every culture has its own beloved sweets, often tied to holidays, childhood and family traditions. People mark the day by sharing treats with friends and colleagues, trying a sweet from another country or revisiting a favourite from childhood, ideally in moderation.

slogans.en: Life is sweeter when you share it.

descriptions.en: World Iodine Deficiency Day, also known as Global Iodine Deficiency Disorders Day, highlights a small nutrient with a big role. The body needs iodine to make thyroid hormones, and a lack of it can cause goitre and, during pregnancy and early childhood, harm brain development. Iodine deficiency is one of the most preventable causes of learning problems in children worldwide. The simplest remedy is iodised salt, so health campaigns on the day encourage families to choose it and to keep it covered and away from heat.

Back to the Future Day celebrates 21 October 2015, the date Marty McFly and Doc Brown travel to in Back to the Future Part II, released in 1989. The film imagined that future with hoverboards, self-lacing sneakers, flying cars and video calls, some of which have come surprisingly close to reality. When the real date arrived in 2015, fans around the world celebrated it, and the day has stuck. Fans mark it by rewatching the trilogy, gathering around DeLoreans and comparing the film's predictions with today.

slogans.en: Where we're going, we don't need roads.

descriptions.en: International Snow Leopard Day honours the elusive big cat of the high mountains of Central and South Asia. It marks 23 October 2013, when the countries where snow leopards live signed the Bishkek Declaration in Kyrgyzstan, pledging to protect the cat and its mountain home together. Snow leopards are listed as vulnerable, threatened by poaching, retaliatory killing by herders, loss of prey and climate change. Conservation groups mark the day with talks, camera-trap images and support for communities that share the mountains with the cats.

slogans.en: Ghost of the mountains needs our protection.

descriptions.en: United Nations Day falls on 24 October, the anniversary of the UN Charter coming into force in 1945. On that day the new organisation formally came into being, created after the Second World War to keep the peace, protect human rights and help nations work together. The UN General Assembly declared the anniversary United Nations Day in 1947. It is marked with concerts, debates and school events, and landmarks around the world are often lit up in UN blue.

slogans.en: The future we want, the United Nations we need.

descriptions.en: World Origami Day on 24 October celebrates origami, the art of folding a sheet of paper into a figure, usually without cutting or glue. Paper folding has a long history in Japan, where it once had ceremonial uses, and today it is enjoyed everywhere, from simple cranes to complex designs built on geometry. The date honours Lillian Oppenheimer, a pioneer of origami in the United States, and opens a stretch of origami events running to 11 November. Folders share models, teach workshops and fold paper cranes for peace.

slogans.en: One sheet of paper, endless possibilities.

descriptions.en: In Norway, 24 October is United Nations Day, one of the country's official flag days. It marks the date in 1945 when the UN Charter came into force and the organisation was founded after the Second World War. Norway was a founding member, and the first UN Secretary-General, Trygve Lie, was Norwegian. On the day the Norwegian flag flies from public buildings, and schools and organisations hold events on peace, human rights and international cooperation.

World Pasta Day on 25 October celebrates one of the world's most popular foods. The date goes back to the first World Pasta Congress, held in Rome on 25 October 1995, and pasta makers' organisations promote the day. Classic Italian dried pasta is made simply from durum wheat semolina and water, and almost every cuisine has its own noodles or filled dough, from Turkish mantı to Chinese noodles. People mark the day by cooking a favourite dish, sharing recipes or trying a new shape.

Austria's National Day on 26 October recalls 26 October 1955, when the Austrian parliament passed the law declaring the country permanently neutral. It came months after the State Treaty restored Austria's full independence, and just after the last occupying troops had left. The day is a public holiday. Many Austrians spend it visiting government buildings and parliament, which open their doors to the public, while the armed forces present themselves to visitors on Vienna's Heldenplatz.

Pet Day of the Dead, on 27 October, is a newer custom within Mexico's Día de los Muertos season, when the spirits of the dead are believed to return home for a visit. On this day families remember the pets they have lost. They set up a small ofrenda, or home altar, with a photo of the animal, its favourite toy, some food or water and marigold flowers. The custom has spread beyond Mexico as a gentle way to honour the bond between people and their animals.

slogans.en: Their spirit returns — light a candle, share a memory.

descriptions.en: Oxi Day, on October 28, is one of Greece's two national holidays. It marks the morning in 1940 when Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas rejected Mussolini's ultimatum to let Italian troops occupy Greek territory, an answer remembered by the single word "Oxi" (No). Greece entered the Second World War that day, and the refusal became a lasting symbol of national courage. Towns and cities hold school and military parades, buildings fly the blue-and-white flag, and churches hold services of thanksgiving.

slogans.en: Oxi! Greece Said No to Fascism.

descriptions.en: Republic Day is the most important national holiday in Turkey. It celebrates the proclamation of the Republic of Turkey on October 29, 1923, by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. The day is marked with ceremonies, parades, and fireworks throughout Turkey.

World Stroke Day, on October 29, raises awareness of stroke, one of the leading causes of death and long-term disability worldwide. The World Stroke Organization launched the day in 2006 to spread the message that many strokes can be prevented and that fast treatment saves lives and brain function. Campaigns teach the warning signs, such as a drooping face, a weak arm and slurred speech, urge people to call emergency services at once, and promote healthy habits like controlling blood pressure, staying active and not smoking.

National Cat Day, on October 29, is an American celebration of cats and the people who love them. Beyond the photos and treats, it was created to draw attention to the many cats waiting in shelters for a home each year. People mark it by sharing pictures of their own cats, donating food or money to rescue groups, volunteering at shelters, or adopting a cat themselves.

slogans.en: Every Cat Deserves a Loving Home

descriptions.en: Internet Day, on October 29, remembers the first message ever sent over ARPANET, the network that grew into today's internet. On the evening of October 29, 1969, a student programmer at the University of California, Los Angeles tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute; the system crashed after two letters, so the first word to cross the network was "lo". The day is a chance to look back at how far connectivity has come, and many people use it to think about online safety, digital skills and the billions still offline.

slogans.en: The World is Connected — Happy Internet Day!

descriptions.en: Halloween falls on October 31, the eve of All Saints' Day, and is one of the most widely celebrated nights of the year. Its roots reach back to the Celtic festival of Samhain, when people lit bonfires and wore disguises on the night the boundary between the living and the dead was believed to grow thin. Today it means costumes, trick-or-treating, carved jack-o'-lanterns and a good scary film.

World Cities Day on October 31 was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2013 and first observed in 2014. The date recalls the closing day of the 2010 Shanghai World Expo, whose theme was Better City, Better Life. With more than half of humanity now living in cities, the day is used to discuss housing, transport, climate and how to make urban life fairer.

World Handstand Day celebrates one of the simplest and hardest moves in movement training: balancing your whole body on your hands. Handstands sit at the heart of gymnastics, yoga, breakdance and circus arts, and they build strength in the shoulders, wrists and core. People mark the day by trying a first wall-supported handstand or by sharing photos of their best upside-down balance.

Reformation Day marks October 31, 1517, when Martin Luther made public his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences in Wittenberg. The protest set off the Protestant Reformation, which split Western Christianity and reshaped Europe's churches, languages and politics. It is a public holiday in several German states and is marked with church services, concerts and Luther-themed events.

slogans.en: Here I stand, I can do no other.

descriptions.en: World Savings Day was established in 1924 by delegates at the first International Savings Bank Congress in Milan. The aim was to rebuild trust in saving after the First World War and to teach families, especially children, the habit of putting money aside. It is still marked on October 31, often with school visits, piggy banks and campaigns about building a financial cushion.

World Vegan Day on November 1 celebrates a way of living without animal products in food, clothing and everyday goods. It was created in 1994 by Louise Wallis, then president of the UK Vegan Society, to mark 50 years since the society was founded in November 1944 and the word vegan was coined. People mark it by cooking plant-based meals, trying vegan recipes and sharing what led them to the choice.

All Saints' Day on November 1 honours all Christian saints, known and unknown. The feast was fixed on this date in Rome in the 8th century and spread across the Western Church in the following decades. In many Catholic countries it is a public holiday when families visit cemeteries, clean graves and leave flowers and candles, often chrysanthemums.

slogans.en: In memory of all who have gone before us.

descriptions.en: On November 1, 1954, the National Liberation Front (FLN) launched coordinated attacks across Algeria, beginning the war of independence against French rule. The war lasted nearly eight years, cost hundreds of thousands of lives and ended with independence in 1962. Revolution Day is a national holiday, marked with flag ceremonies, tributes to the martyrs and fireworks at midnight.

Day of the Dead, celebrated in Mexico on November 1 and 2, welcomes the souls of loved ones back for a brief visit. Families build ofrendas, home altars with photos, candles, marigolds, sugar skulls, pan de muerto and the favourite food and drink of the departed, and spend time at decorated graves. Blending Indigenous and Catholic traditions, the celebration was added to UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

Culture Day (Bunka no Hi) on November 3 is a national holiday in Japan dedicated to culture, freedom and peace. The date was the birthday of Emperor Meiji, and Japan's postwar constitution was proclaimed on November 3, 1946; the holiday took its present name in 1948. The Emperor presents the Order of Culture to leading artists and scholars, and museums, schools and towns hold exhibitions, festivals and parades.

Unity Day on November 4 is a Russian public holiday introduced in 2005. It commemorates the liberation of Moscow from Polish-Lithuanian forces in 1612 by a people's militia led by the merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, which ended the period known as the Time of Troubles. The day is marked with concerts, rallies and flowers laid at the Minin and Pozharsky monument on Red Square.

World Tsunami Awareness Day on November 5 was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2015 at Japan's proposal. The date recalls the Japanese story of Inamura-no-hi, in which a villager set fire to his rice sheaves in 1854 to lead his neighbours to high ground before a tsunami struck. The day promotes early warning systems, evacuation drills and the simple rule that a strong earthquake near the coast means moving inland at once.

Bonfire Night, or Guy Fawkes Night, on November 5 recalls the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605, when a group of Catholic conspirators tried to blow up the House of Lords and kill King James I. Guy Fawkes was caught guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament, and Londoners lit bonfires to celebrate the king's survival. Across Britain, people still gather for bonfires, fireworks displays, toffee apples and, in some towns, the burning of a straw guy.

slogans.en: Remember, Remember the Fifth of November.

descriptions.en: National STEM Day on November 8 celebrates science, technology, engineering and mathematics and encourages young people to explore them. These fields drive medicine, clean energy, computing and space exploration, and many of tomorrow's jobs will depend on them. Schools and families mark the day with experiments, coding challenges, building projects and visits to science centres, with a special push to welcome girls and students who rarely see themselves in these careers.

slogans.en: Science + Technology + Engineering + Math = Our Future.

descriptions.en: On the evening of November 9, 1989, an East German official announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border, apparently effective immediately. Crowds gathered at the checkpoints in Berlin until guards opened the gates, and people began climbing on the Wall and chipping pieces from it. The fall of the Wall opened the way to German reunification on October 3, 1990, and became a symbol of the end of the Cold War.

World Freedom Day is a US observance on November 9, the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. It was proclaimed by President George W. Bush in 2001 to commemorate the end of communist rule in Central and Eastern Europe. The day is used to honour those who resisted oppression and to reflect on the value of democracy and free speech.

slogans.en: Freedom is not free — cherish it.

descriptions.en: Carl Sagan Day on November 9 celebrates the birthday of the American astronomer and science communicator, born in New York in 1934. Sagan helped plan NASA's planetary missions, including the Golden Records carried by the Voyager probes, and brought the universe into living rooms with his 1980 television series Cosmos. Fans mark the day with stargazing nights, public lectures and readings from Pale Blue Dot, his reflection on Earth seen from deep space.

slogans.en: Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.

names.en: World Science Day for Peace and Development

descriptions.en: World Science Day for Peace and Development on November 10 was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2001 and first celebrated in 2002. It highlights the role science plays in everyday life, from vaccines to clean water and climate research, and the need to keep the public involved in debates about new discoveries. Universities, museums and research institutes mark it with open labs, public lectures and events for schools.

slogans.en: Open science for a global transformation.

descriptions.en: November 11 marks the armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918. In the UK and Commonwealth it is Remembrance Day, with two minutes' silence at 11 a.m. and red poppies inspired by the poem In Flanders Fields. In the United States it has been called Veterans Day since 1954 and honours everyone who has served in the armed forces.

Singles Day on November 11 began as a joke among students at Chinese universities in the 1990s, chosen because 11/11 looks like four people standing alone. In 2009 the e-commerce company Alibaba began offering big discounts on the date, and it has since grown into the largest online shopping event in the world. Many people still mark it the original way, with gatherings of single friends, blind dates and a little self-celebration.

Poland's National Independence Day on November 11 marks the rebirth of the Polish state in 1918, after 123 years in which its lands were partitioned between Russia, Prussia and Austria. On that day Józef Piłsudski took command of Polish forces in Warsaw, and the new republic soon took shape. Banned under communist rule, the holiday was restored in 1989 and is marked with flags, parades, concerts and the changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

slogans.en: Jeszcze Polska nie zginęła! (Poland has not yet perished!)

descriptions.en: Armistice Day in France marks November 11, 1918, when the armistice signed in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne came into force at 11 a.m., ending the fighting of the First World War. It has been a public holiday in France since 1922 and is also a national holiday in Belgium. Ceremonies take place at war memorials in every town, and the President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe.

Rakı Day is celebrated in Türkiye on November 11, a date chosen because 11.11 looks like two tall rakı glasses standing beside each other. Rakı is an anise-flavoured spirit distilled from grapes that turns milky white when water is added, which is why it is nicknamed lion's milk. It is drunk slowly over a long table of meze and fish, with friends, conversation and often music, and the day is a reason to raise a glass to that ritual.

slogans.en: Two glasses, two fish — cheers to tradition.

descriptions.en: World Kindness Day on November 13 was introduced in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organisations from several countries. It encourages people to look past differences of nationality, religion and politics and to treat one another with care. People mark the day with small acts: paying for a stranger's coffee, writing a thank-you note, helping a neighbour or simply being patient.

World Diabetes Day on November 14 was created in 1991 by the International Diabetes Federation and the World Health Organization, and became an official UN day in 2006. The date is the birthday of Frederick Banting, who discovered insulin with Charles Best in 1921, turning a fatal disease into a manageable one. Its symbol is a blue circle, and the day is marked with free blood-sugar tests, blue-lit landmarks and campaigns on prevention and access to care.

Shichi-Go-San, meaning seven-five-three, is a Japanese festival held around November 15 for girls aged three and seven and boys aged three and five. The custom dates back centuries to a time when many children did not survive early childhood, and families gave thanks at these ages. Children dress in kimono or formal clothes and visit Shinto shrines with their parents, and they receive chitose-ame, long red and white sweets symbolising a long life.

slogans.en: Bless the little ones as they grow.

descriptions.en: Proclamation of the Republic Day on November 15 marks the day in 1889 when a military movement led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca overthrew Brazil's monarchy. Emperor Pedro II was sent into exile in Europe, and Brazil became a federal republic, with Deodoro as its first president. It is a national public holiday, marked with official ceremonies, flag-raisings and parades.

slogans.en: From empire to republic, Brazil united.

descriptions.en: On November 15, 1988, the Palestinian National Council meeting in Algiers adopted the Palestinian Declaration of Independence, read aloud by Yasser Arafat. The text was written largely by the poet Mahmoud Darwish and proclaimed the State of Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital. The anniversary is a national holiday for Palestinians, marked with flags, speeches, school events and gatherings at home and in the diaspora.

The International Day for Tolerance on November 16 marks UNESCO's adoption of the Declaration of Principles on Tolerance in 1995, the UN Year for Tolerance. A year later the UN General Assembly invited countries to observe the day every year. It promotes respect for the world's diversity of cultures, beliefs and ways of life, and UNESCO uses it to award a prize for work that builds tolerance and non-violence.

slogans.en: Tolerance is not passive. It is an active recognition of universal human rights.

descriptions.en: World Prematurity Day on November 17 raises awareness of babies born too early, before 37 weeks of pregnancy. About one in ten babies worldwide is born preterm, and complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of death in children under five. The day was started in 2008 by parent organisations in Europe, and hospitals and families mark it with purple lights, stories from neonatal units and calls for better care.

International Students' Day on November 17 recalls 1939, when Nazi forces stormed universities in Prague after student protests against the occupation of Czechoslovakia. Nine student leaders were executed, more than a thousand students were sent to concentration camps, and all Czech universities were closed until the end of the war. Fifty years later, on November 17, 1989, a student march in Prague began the Velvet Revolution, and the day now celebrates student activism and the right to education.

slogans.en: Students are the future — protect their rights.

descriptions.en: World AMR Awareness Week, held from November 18 to 24, was launched by the World Health Organization in 2015 as World Antibiotic Awareness Week. Antimicrobial resistance happens when bacteria and other microbes evolve to survive the medicines meant to kill them, making common infections harder to treat. The week urges people not to demand antibiotics for colds and flu, to finish courses as prescribed, and calls on farmers and doctors to use these medicines carefully.

Morocco's Independence Day on November 18 recalls 1955, when Sultan Mohammed V, back from two years of exile imposed by France, announced the end of the French protectorate in his Throne Day speech. Full independence followed in March 1956, and the sultan later took the title of king. The day is a national holiday marked with flags, official ceremonies, concerts and tributes to the independence movement.

Oman's National Day is celebrated on November 20 and 21 under a royal decree issued by Sultan Haitham bin Tarik in 2025. It was previously held on November 18, the birthday of Sultan Qaboos bin Said, who ruled from 1970 to 2020 and led the country's modern development. In the weeks before, streets and buildings are decorated with flags and lights, and the celebrations include military parades, fireworks and a public holiday that is often moved to create a long weekend.

slogans.en: Green, red and white from coast to coast.

descriptions.en: International Men's Day on November 19 was revived in 1999 in Trinidad and Tobago by Dr Jerome Teelucksingh, who chose the date of his father's birthday. It focuses on men's and boys' health, positive male role models and better relations between the sexes. The day is marked in many countries with talks on men's mental health and suicide prevention, health checks, and events celebrating fathers, mentors and community volunteers.

slogans.en: Helping men live longer, happier and more fulfilling lives.

descriptions.en: World Toilet Day on November 19 was started in 2001 by the World Toilet Organization, founded in Singapore by Jack Sim, and became an official UN day in 2013. Around 3.5 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions have no toilet at all, which spreads disease and puts women and girls at risk. The day mixes humour with serious campaigning to raise money and political will for toilets, sewers and clean water.

Universal Children's Day was recommended by the UN General Assembly in 1954 as a day for all countries to promote the welfare of children and understanding between them. November 20 later became its date because the UN adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child on that day in 1959 and the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989. Some countries celebrate children on their own dates, such as Türkiye on April 23, but November 20 is the shared global moment for children's rights.

World Children's Day on November 20 is UNICEF's global day of action for children, built on the anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989. Each year children are invited to take over roles usually held by adults, from presenting the news to sitting in parliaments, to show that their voices matter. Buildings and landmarks around the world light up in blue, and schools hold debates on the issues children say matter most to them.

slogans.en: A World Fit for Every Child.

descriptions.en: Revolution Day in Mexico commemorates November 20, 1910, the date Francisco I. Madero set in his Plan of San Luis Potosí for an uprising against the long rule of Porfirio Díaz. The revolution that followed lasted about a decade, brought figures such as Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa to fame and produced the 1917 Constitution. It is a national holiday, now observed on the third Monday of November, with sports parades and civic ceremonies.

slogans.en: Viva la Revolución! — Celebrating Mexican Heritage

descriptions.en: Transgender Day of Remembrance on November 20 honours transgender people who have been killed because of anti-trans hatred. It was started in 1999 by writer and activist Gwendolyn Ann Smith as a vigil for Rita Hester, a Black trans woman murdered in Massachusetts in 1998 whose killing was never solved. Communities around the world gather for candlelight vigils where the names of those killed in the past year are read aloud.

slogans.en: Remembering our trans family who are no longer with us.

descriptions.en: Africa Industrialization Day on November 20 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1989. It focuses on helping African countries move from exporting raw materials to processing them and manufacturing goods at home, creating jobs and adding value to their economies. Governments, the African Union and the UN industrial development agency mark it with forums on manufacturing, trade, energy and skills for young workers.

National Sovereignty Day on November 20 commemorates the Battle of Vuelta de Obligado in 1845, when Argentine forces stretched chains across the Paraná River to stop an Anglo-French fleet. The fleet broke through, but the resistance and the costly campaign that followed led Britain and France to recognise Argentina's control of its rivers a few years later. The day was established by law in 1974 and is now a public holiday, usually moved to a Monday.

World Television Day on November 21 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1996, the year the first World Television Forum met at the UN on that date. The day is not meant to celebrate the screen itself but television's power to inform, to bring distant conflicts and crises into people's homes, and to shape public debate. Broadcasters and media schools use it to reflect on public-service journalism, children's programming and trust in the news.

slogans.en: TV: A Window to the World.

descriptions.en: World Hello Day on November 21 was started in 1973 by two brothers, Brian and Michael McCormack, in response to the Yom Kippur War between Israel and its Arab neighbours. Their idea was that conflicts begin when people stop talking, so the day asks everyone to greet at least ten people. Since then it has been observed in many countries, and people mark it by saying hello to strangers, neighbours and anyone they have not spoken to in a while.

Lebanon's Independence Day on November 22 marks the end of the French Mandate in 1943. Earlier that month the French authorities arrested President Bechara El Khoury, Prime Minister Riad Al Solh and other leaders after parliament removed French privileges from the constitution, and held them in the citadel of Rashaya. Under popular protest and international pressure they were released on November 22, and the day is now marked with a military parade in Beirut and flags across the country.

slogans.en: One flag, one cedar, one day.

descriptions.en: Fibonacci Day is celebrated on November 23 because the date written as 11/23 matches the start of the Fibonacci sequence: 1, 1, 2, 3. In the sequence each number is the sum of the two before it, and it was introduced to Europe by the Italian mathematician Leonardo of Pisa in his book Liber Abaci in 1202. The same numbers appear in sunflower heads, pine cones and spiral shells, and teachers use the day for nature walks and maths puzzles.

names.en: International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25 was designated by the UN General Assembly in 1999. The date honours the Mirabal sisters, three political activists murdered in 1960 on the orders of the Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo. It opens the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, and governments, organisations and individuals mark it with orange lights, marches and calls to protect women and girls and end impunity.

slogans.en: UNiTE! Invest to prevent violence against women and girls.

descriptions.en: Mauritania's Independence Day on November 28 marks 1960, when the country became independent from France. Moktar Ould Daddah, who had led the territory toward self-government, became the first president of the new Islamic Republic of Mauritania. The day is a national holiday, marked with a military parade and official ceremonies in Nouakchott, flags across the country and cultural events.

Computer Security Day on November 30 was started in 1988 by a Washington, D.C. chapter of the Association for Computing Machinery, the same month the Morris worm spread across the early internet. It began as a way to make people think about protecting their computers and data, at a time when few home users did. Today it is a reminder to update devices, use a password manager and two-factor authentication, back up important files and watch out for phishing messages.

slogans.en: Protect your data. Protect your life.

descriptions.en: St Andrew's Day on November 30 is the feast of Saint Andrew, one of Jesus's twelve apostles and the patron saint of Scotland. Tradition holds that he was crucified on an X-shaped cross, which became the white saltire on a blue background of the Scottish flag. Since 2006 it has been an official bank holiday in Scotland, celebrated with ceilidh dances, traditional music, Scottish food such as haggis and cranachan, and events across the country.

slogans.en: Scotland the Brave — Happy St. Andrew's Day!

descriptions.en: World AIDS Day on December 1 was first observed in 1988, making it the first global health day. It remembers the more than 40 million people who have died of AIDS-related illnesses and supports the tens of millions living with HIV today. People wear the red ribbon, introduced in 1991, and the day promotes HIV testing, treatment that lets people live long and healthy lives, and the fight against stigma.

Romania's National Day on December 1 marks the Great Union of 1918, when an assembly in Alba Iulia proclaimed the union of Transylvania with the Kingdom of Romania. Together with the earlier unions of Bessarabia and Bukovina that year, it created the state Romanians call Greater Romania. Since 1990 it has been the national holiday, celebrated with a military parade in Bucharest, ceremonies in Alba Iulia and flags across the country.

names.en: International Day for the Abolition of Slavery

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Abolition of Slavery on December 2 marks the adoption by the UN General Assembly in 1949 of the Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in Persons and of the Exploitation of the Prostitution of Others. Slavery is banned everywhere, yet the International Labour Organization estimates that around 50 million people live in modern slavery, through forced labour, forced marriage, debt bondage and human trafficking. The day calls for ending these practices and supporting the people who escape them.

UAE National Day on December 2 marks 1971, when six emirates united to form the United Arab Emirates under its first president, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan; Ras Al Khaimah joined early the following year. In a few decades the country grew from a small pearling and trading region into a global centre of trade, aviation and tourism. Celebrations include fireworks, parades, light shows and buildings decorated in the national colours.

slogans.en: One nation, seven Emirates, endless pride.

names.en: International Day of Persons with Disabilities

descriptions.en: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities on December 3 has been observed since 1992 by decision of the UN General Assembly. About 1.3 billion people, or one in six worldwide, live with a significant disability and face barriers in buildings, transport, education, work and technology. The day promotes the rights set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and calls for a world designed with everyone in mind.

slogans.en: United in action to rescue and achieve the SDGs for, with and by persons with disabilities.

descriptions.en: December 3 is the second day of the UAE National Day holiday, continuing the celebrations of the country's founding in 1971. With schools and many offices closed, families use it for outings, heritage events, desert trips and gatherings with relatives. Public spaces keep their decorations, and many cities host concerts, fireworks and traditional performances.

World Cookie Day on December 4 celebrates the small baked treat loved in almost every country. The word cookie comes from the Dutch koekje, meaning little cake, and Dutch settlers brought the word to North America. Whether chocolate chip, oatmeal, shortbread or gingerbread, it is a day to bake a batch and share it with friends, family or colleagues.

slogans.en: Life is Short, Eat More Cookies.

descriptions.en: National Cookie Day on December 4 is an American food holiday with perfect timing, just as holiday baking season begins. The chocolate chip cookie, the most famous American cookie, was created in the 1930s by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts. Bakeries hand out deals and free cookies, and many families use the day to start their holiday baking or swap cookies with neighbours.

slogans.en: Life is Short, Eat More Cookies!

descriptions.en: Wildlife Conservation Day on December 4 was launched in 2012 by then US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who called on the world to fight the illegal wildlife trade. Poaching and trafficking threaten elephants, rhinos, pangolins, tigers and many less famous species, and the trade is often run by organised crime networks. The day encourages people never to buy products made from endangered animals and to support rangers and conservation groups.

slogans.en: Wildlife crime is a global crisis.

descriptions.en: Eid il-Burbara, Saint Barbara's Day on December 4, is celebrated by Christians in Lebanon and parts of the Levant. Tradition says the young Barbara disguised herself to escape her father, who persecuted her for her faith, so children dress up in costumes and masks and go door to door singing for sweets. Families cook burbara, a dish of boiled wheat sweetened with sugar and spiced with anise, topped with pomegranate seeds and nuts, and bake qatayef and other sweets.

slogans.en: Costumes at the door, burbara on the stove.

descriptions.en: International Volunteer Day on December 5 was established by the UN General Assembly in 1985. It celebrates the millions of people who give their time to help others, from community kitchens and disaster relief to coaching, mentoring and caring for the sick. Organisations use the day to thank their volunteers, and many people mark it by signing up for a cause in their own neighbourhood.

slogans.en: If everyone did a little, we could achieve a lot.

descriptions.en: World Soil Day on December 5 was proposed by the International Union of Soil Sciences in 2002 and adopted by the UN General Assembly, with the first official observance in 2014. The date honours King Bhumibol of Thailand, a champion of the day. Healthy soil grows most of our food, filters water and stores carbon, yet erosion, pollution and overuse are degrading it, and the day promotes ways of farming and building that protect it.

Thailand's National Day on December 5 is the birthday of King Bhumibol Adulyadej, Rama IX, born in 1927, who reigned from 1946 until his death in 2016, the longest reign in Thai history. The day is also Thailand's Father's Day, as the late king was regarded as a father figure to the nation. People wear yellow, the colour of his birthday, offer alms to monks and attend candle-lighting ceremonies in his memory.

slogans.en: Long Live Thailand — Land of Smiles.

descriptions.en: Krampusnacht, on the night of December 5, is an Alpine tradition from Austria, Bavaria and nearby regions. Krampus is a horned, furry figure from folklore who accompanies Saint Nicholas: while Nicholas rewards good children with sweets, Krampus rattles chains and bells to scare the naughty ones. In many towns young men dress in elaborate hand-carved masks and costumes for Krampus runs, noisy parades through the streets.

Nikolaustag on December 6 is the feast of Saint Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop of Myra, in today's Türkiye, known for his secret gifts to the poor. On the evening of December 5, children in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and other countries clean their boots and leave them outside the door. By morning Nikolaus has filled them with nuts, oranges, chocolate and small gifts, and in some regions he visits in person to ask whether the children have been good.

slogans.en: Good things come to those who are kind.

descriptions.en: Finnish Independence Day on December 6 marks 1917, when the Finnish parliament declared independence from Russia in the turmoil after the Russian Revolution. It is a quiet, dignified holiday: many families light two blue-and-white candles in their windows in the evening. Millions watch the President's Independence Day reception at the Presidential Palace on television, and there are ceremonies at war graves and a torch parade by students.

International Anti-Corruption Day on December 9 was established after the UN General Assembly adopted the United Nations Convention against Corruption in 2003, which opened for signature on this date in Mérida, Mexico. Corruption diverts money from schools, hospitals and infrastructure, weakens trust in institutions and hits the poorest hardest. The day highlights the role of whistleblowers, journalists, courts and ordinary citizens in exposing and preventing it.

Human Rights Day on December 10 marks the day in 1948 when the UN General Assembly, meeting in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, it set out for the first time the rights every person is entitled to, from freedom of speech and religion to education and fair trial. It has been translated into hundreds of languages, and the day is marked with campaigns, debates and the UN Human Rights Prize.

slogans.en: Our rights, our future, right now.

descriptions.en: Nobel Prize Day on December 10 marks the anniversary of the death of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and inventor of dynamite, who died in 1896. In his will he left most of his fortune to fund prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace, first awarded in 1901. On this day the laureates receive their medals and diplomas in Stockholm, and the Peace Prize is presented in Oslo.

International Mountain Day on December 11 has been observed since 2003, following the UN International Year of Mountains in 2002. Mountains cover about a quarter of the Earth's land surface, are home to around 15 percent of the world's people and provide fresh water for roughly half of humanity. The day highlights threats such as climate change and melting glaciers, and promotes sustainable tourism and support for mountain communities.

National Tango Day in Argentina falls on December 11, the shared birthday of two tango legends: the singer Carlos Gardel, born in 1890, and the bandleader Julio De Caro, born in 1899. Tango was born in the late 19th century in the working-class neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, mixing African, European and local rhythms. UNESCO added it to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009, and on this day milongas, concerts and open-air dances fill the streets of Buenos Aires.

slogans.en: Let the rhythm of tango move your soul.

descriptions.en: Jamhuri Day on December 12 is Kenya's most important national holiday, and its name means republic in Swahili. It marks two anniversaries on the same date: independence from Britain in 1963, and the country becoming a republic a year later, in 1964, with Jomo Kenyatta as its first president. Kenyans celebrate with the president's speech at a national stadium, military parades, traditional dance, family feasts of nyama choma and flags flying everywhere.

Kenya became independent from Britain on December 12, 1963, after years of struggle that included the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s. Jomo Kenyatta, who had been imprisoned by the colonial authorities, became the country's first prime minister and later its first president. The anniversary is celebrated as Jamhuri Day with flag ceremonies, a presidential address, parades and music across the country.

The Day of Reconciliation on December 16 has been a public holiday in South Africa since 1995, the first year of democracy after apartheid. The date carried opposite meanings before: Afrikaners marked it as the Day of the Vow, after the Battle of Blood River in 1838, while the liberation movement remembered it as the day its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, was founded in 1961. By joining these histories into one day, the new South Africa chose to promote healing, national unity and an honest look at the past.

slogans.en: One nation, many stories, one future.

descriptions.en: Kazakhstan's Independence Day on December 16 marks 1991, when Kazakhstan became the last Soviet republic to declare independence, days before the Soviet Union dissolved. The date also recalls the Jeltoqsan protests of December 1986 in Almaty, when young Kazakhs demonstrated against Moscow's appointment of a non-Kazakh party leader. The holiday is marked with official ceremonies, concerts, fireworks and flags in Astana, Almaty and across the country.

Bahrain's National Day on December 16 commemorates the founding of the modern state of Bahrain by Ahmed Al Fateh in 1783, and the accession of Sheikh Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa as ruler on December 16, 1961. Bahrain became fully independent from Britain in August 1971, and the December celebrations grew into the country's main national festival. Streets and buildings are decked in red and white, and the holiday brings fireworks, concerts and heritage events across the islands.

slogans.en: Two days, one island, one celebration.

descriptions.en: December 17 is the second day of Bahrain's national holidays, known as Accession Day. It honours the accession of Sheikh Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, who became ruler in 1961 and led Bahrain to full independence in 1971. Together with National Day on December 16, it forms the country's main civic celebration of the year, with parades, fireworks, cultural shows and family gatherings.

slogans.en: The second day of the celebration.

descriptions.en: International Migrants Day on December 18 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2000. It marks the adoption on December 18, 1990, of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. Around 280 million people live outside the country where they were born, and the day highlights their contributions to the societies they join, the dangers many face on the way, and their right to be treated with dignity.

slogans.en: Harnessing the potential of human mobility.

descriptions.en: World Arabic Language Day on December 18 celebrates a language that shaped science, poetry and faith across three continents. Written from right to left in an alphabet of 28 letters, Arabic gave many languages words such as algebra, coffee, sugar and zero, and its script became one of the great art forms through calligraphy. Schools, museums and cultural centres mark the day with calligraphy workshops, poetry readings and talks on the language's many dialects.

slogans.en: Arabic: a language of history, beauty, and wisdom.

descriptions.en: Qatar National Day on December 18 commemorates 1878, when Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani succeeded his father and began uniting the peninsula's tribes into a single state. Celebrated as National Day since 2007, it honours Qatar's founder and the country's journey from a pearl-diving coast to a modern state. The Doha Corniche hosts a military parade, air shows and fireworks, and families visit the Darb Al Saai heritage festival with its traditional crafts, food and camel rides.

Yule is an ancient midwinter festival of the Germanic and Norse peoples, held around the winter solstice to mark the turning point when the days begin to grow longer. Its traditions included feasting, burning a great log through the long night, and bringing evergreens indoors as a sign of life that survives the winter. Many of these customs passed into Christmas, which is still called jul in the Scandinavian languages, and today Yule is also celebrated by modern pagans.

slogans.en: The sun returns — light conquers darkness.

descriptions.en: The Night of the Radishes, La Noche de Rábanos, is held on December 23 in the main square of Oaxaca, Mexico. Since 1897, farmers and artisans have carved oversized radishes into elaborate scenes of nativity figures, saints, dancers, animals and local legends, competing for prizes. Because the carvings wilt within hours, crowds line up the same evening to see them, and the festival has become one of Oaxaca's best-loved Christmas traditions.

Jólabókaflóð, the Christmas Book Flood, is the Icelandic tradition of giving books on Christmas Eve and spending the night reading them. It took shape during the Second World War, when imports were restricted but paper was not, so books became the gift of choice. Every autumn a free catalogue of new titles goes to every household, publishers release most of their year's books before Christmas, and Iceland remains one of the countries that publishes and reads the most books per person.

slogans.en: A book as a gift — the best Christmas tradition.

descriptions.en: Libya became independent on December 24, 1951, as the United Kingdom of Libya under King Idris I, uniting the regions of Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and Fezzan. It was the first country to gain independence through a decision of the United Nations, after Italian colonial rule and a period of British and French administration following the Second World War. The anniversary is a national day in Libya, marked with flags, official ceremonies and gatherings in Tripoli and Benghazi.

slogans.en: The first independence the UN ever granted.

descriptions.en: Christmas Day on December 25 celebrates the birth of Jesus, and it is both the central Christian feast of the winter and a cultural holiday marked by billions of people around the world. The date was set in Rome by the 4th century, and Orthodox churches that follow the Julian calendar celebrate on January 7. Families gather for church services, festive meals and gift-giving, homes are decorated with trees and lights, and traditions such as carol singing and Santa Claus vary from country to country.

slogans.en: Peace on earth and goodwill to all.

descriptions.en: Ukraine celebrates Christmas on December 25 after a 2023 law moved the national holiday from January 7, following the Orthodox Church of Ukraine's switch to the Revised Julian calendar. The change was seen as a step away from Russian church tradition and towards Europe, while some families still also keep the old date. Ukrainians mark Holy Supper on Christmas Eve with twelve meatless dishes, beginning with kutia, display a didukh sheaf of wheat, and go carolling with koliadky.

The International Festival of the Sahara is held each winter in Douz, a desert town in southern Tunisia known as the gateway to the Sahara. Begun as a camel festival in 1910, it is one of the oldest desert festivals in North Africa and celebrates the culture of the region's nomadic peoples. Over several days there are camel races, horsemanship displays, saluki hunting demonstrations, traditional weddings, poetry, music and crafts in the dunes.

slogans.en: Where the desert throws a party.

descriptions.en: December 26 is the Second Day of Christmas, a public holiday in all German states and in many other European countries. In the church calendar it is the feast of Saint Stephen, honoured as the first Christian martyr, who was stoned to death in Jerusalem, according to the Acts of the Apostles. In Germany families use the day to continue the celebrations, visit relatives they did not see on Christmas Eve, go for a winter walk and attend church.

Kwanzaa is a week-long celebration of African heritage held from December 26 to January 1, mainly by African Americans. It was created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, and its name comes from a Swahili phrase meaning first fruits of the harvest. Each day honours one of seven principles, the Nguzo Saba, such as unity, self-determination and creativity, marked by lighting a candle on a seven-branched kinara, with a feast called karamu near the end.

slogans.en: Seven days, seven principles — the spirit of African heritage.

descriptions.en: Rizal Day on December 30 is a national holiday in the Philippines honouring José Rizal, the writer, doctor and reformer executed by the Spanish colonial authorities in Manila on that date in 1896. His novels Noli Me Tángere and El Filibusterismo exposed abuses under Spanish rule and inspired the independence movement, and his execution fuelled the revolution that had begun that year. Filipinos mark the day with wreath-laying at the Rizal Monument in Luneta Park, where he was shot, and with flags at half-mast.

slogans.en: Remember the hero, honor the legacy.

descriptions.en: New Year's Eve on December 31 is the last night of the Gregorian year and one of the most widely celebrated evenings on Earth. As midnight moves around the planet, from the Pacific islands to Sydney, Tokyo, Istanbul, London and New York, crowds count down together and fireworks light up the sky. Customs vary everywhere, from eating twelve grapes in Spain to wearing red underwear for luck, but most people end the year with friends, family and a toast to what comes next.

slogans.en: Out with the old, in with the new.

descriptions.en: Chinese New Year, or the Spring Festival, is the most important traditional holiday in China and is celebrated by Chinese communities around the world. It begins on the new moon of the first month of the lunar calendar, between January 21 and February 20, and each year is linked to one of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac; in 2024 UNESCO added its customs to the list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Hundreds of millions travel home for the reunion dinner on New Year's Eve, and the celebrations bring red envelopes of money, firecrackers, lion and dragon dances, and end on the fifteenth day with the Lantern Festival.

slogans.en: Gong Xi Fa Cai — Wishing You Prosperity!

descriptions.en: World Pangolin Day, on the third Saturday of February, speaks up for pangolins, the shy, scaly mammals of Asia and Africa. Pangolins are widely described as the most trafficked wild mammals in the world, hunted for their meat and for their keratin scales, which are used in traditional medicine. All eight species are threatened. On this day zoos, conservation groups and schools share facts about the animal, campaign against the illegal trade, and invite people never to buy pangolin products.

slogans.en: Protecting the World's Most Trafficked Mammal

descriptions.en: World Pancake Day falls on Shrove Tuesday, the day before Ash Wednesday, and is also known as Pancake Day. Christians traditionally used up rich foods such as eggs, milk, butter and sugar before the Lent fast began, and pancakes were the easiest way to do it. Families flip pancakes at home and top them with lemon and sugar, syrup or fruit, and some towns in England hold pancake races in which runners toss a pancake in a pan as they go.

slogans.en: Flip for Joy — It's Pancake Day!

descriptions.en: World Sleep Day falls each year on the Friday before the March equinox. It is organised by the World Sleep Society, a body of sleep doctors and researchers, to remind people that good sleep matters as much to health as diet and exercise. Sleep clinics, hospitals and health groups use the day to talk about insomnia, sleep apnoea and other disorders, and to share simple habits for better rest. It is also a good excuse to switch off screens early and go to bed on time.

World Laughter Day, on the first Sunday of May, celebrates the power of laughter to bring people together. It was started in 1998 in Mumbai by Dr Madan Kataria, the Indian doctor who founded the Laughter Yoga movement. The idea is that shared laughter lifts the mood, eases stress and builds friendship across borders, and in that way serves peace. Laughter clubs meet in parks and public squares for group laughing sessions, and people are encouraged simply to laugh together.

Mother's Day honours mothers and the people who raise and care for us. The modern day grew out of Anna Jarvis's campaign in the United States in the early twentieth century, and it spread from there around the world. The date varies by country: Türkiye, the United States and Germany mark it on the second Sunday in May, many Arab countries on 21 March, and Mexico on 10 May. Families give flowers, cards and small gifts, share a meal, or simply call to say thank you.

slogans.en: Celebrating the Heart of Every Home

descriptions.en: Vesak Day, also known as Buddha Day, honors the birth, enlightenment, and passing into Nirvana of Siddhartha Gautama. Observed on the full moon of the Vaisakha lunar month — usually in May — it is the most sacred day in the Buddhist calendar. Millions mark it with meditation, temple visits, lantern releases, and acts of compassion. The UN officially recognized it as an international day in 1999.

slogans.en: May all beings be happy and free.

descriptions.en: Global Running Day, on the first Wednesday of June, is a worldwide celebration of running in all its forms. It grew out of National Running Day in the United States and became a global event in 2016, inviting everyone to make a pledge to run, however fast, far or slow. Runners join group runs, races and school events, share their routes online, and many people use the day to lace up for the very first time.

slogans.en: One Day. One Run. One World.

descriptions.en: Donut Day falls on the first Friday of June and celebrates the ring-shaped fried treat loved around the world. It began in Chicago in 1938, when the Salvation Army created it to raise funds and to honour its volunteers who fried and served doughnuts to American soldiers in France during the First World War. Those volunteers became known as the Doughnut Lassies. Today bakeries and coffee shops mark the day with free or discounted donuts, and many people simply share a box with friends or colleagues.

World Pet Memorial Day, held on the second Tuesday of June, is a day to remember the animals who shared our lives and are no longer with us. Losing a dog, a cat or any companion animal can hurt as much as losing a family member, and the day gives that grief a gentle place. People mark it by lighting a candle, visiting a pet's grave, looking through photos or sharing memories with others who loved them. Some choose to honour a lost pet by helping an animal shelter.

slogans.en: Their love leaves paw prints on our hearts forever.

descriptions.en: Father's Day honours fathers and father figures and the love, care and guidance they give. In Türkiye, the United States and many other countries it falls on the third Sunday of June, while others mark it on different dates, such as March 19, the feast of Saint Joseph. The modern custom grew from Spokane, Washington, where Sonora Smart Dodd organised a celebration in 1910 to honour her father, who had raised six children alone. Families mark the day with cards, small gifts, shared meals and time spent together.

names.en: Take Your Dog to Work Day

descriptions.en: Take Your Dog to Work Day invites employers to open their doors to employees' dogs for one day, on the Friday after Father's Day in the United States. Pet Sitters International started it in 1999 to celebrate dogs as companions and to encourage people to adopt from shelters and rescue groups. Offices set out water bowls and treats, colleagues meet each other's dogs, and many workplaces use the day to collect donations or share adoption listings from local shelters.

slogans.en: Because who ever heard of working like a cat?

descriptions.en: Social Justice Sunday is observed across Australia, anchored in a tradition begun by Australian Catholic bishops in 1940 to address pressing social, economic, and ecological concerns. Each year the bishops release a statement focusing on a different theme — poverty, inequality, environmental care — calling on the Catholic community and beyond to reflect, act, and engage. The day invites personal action plans, community panels, food drives, letter-writing to representatives, social-justice movie nights, and volunteering to make solidarity and compassionate action feel tangible.

slogans.en: Reflect, act, and stand for fairness.

descriptions.en: The Philippines' National Heroes Day falls on the last Monday in August, marking the 1896 Cry of Pugad Lawin that launched the Philippine Revolution against the Spanish Empire. The day honours figures like Andres Bonifacio, who founded the Katipunan, and Apolinario Mabini, the brilliant paralysed strategist known as the Sublime Paralytic, alongside every Filipino who served and sacrificed for the nation. Observed since 1931 with parades, wreath-layings, fireworks, and quiet reflection, the modern celebration was moved to its long-weekend date in 2007. Other countries honour their own heroes on different dates — Zimbabwe remembers its Liberation War heroes on the second Monday of August, Indonesia on 10 November, the Cayman Islands on the fourth Monday in January.

The Late Summer Bank Holiday (also called the August Bank Holiday) falls on the last Monday in August in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, marking the third three-day weekend British workers earn each summer.
