Introduced by the Bank Holidays Act of 1871 to improve conditions for industrial workers, it was moved to the last Monday of August in 1971's Banking and Financial Dealings Act so families could enjoy a long weekend. The day sees millions take short holidays, fire up barbecues for one of the last outdoor meals of the season, head to Brighton or Blackpool, and crowd the Notting Hill Carnival.

slogans.en: One last long weekend. Make it count.

descriptions.en: National Day of Joy, held on the last Wednesday of June, encourages people to find and share happiness in everyday moments. Created in 2019 by Comfort Keepers — an in-home senior care organization — the day grew from the observation that small moments of happiness often bring the biggest smiles. Joy isn't reserved for weekends or special occasions: it's a skill that can be practiced, noticed, and shared every single day.

slogans.en: Joy is a skill — practice it today.

descriptions.en: Dream Big Day, held on the last Friday of June, inspires children to explore their interests, break down barriers, and imagine ambitious futures. Organized by Careermap and sponsored by Pearson, Barclays, and Lifeskills, the day connects UK employers with primary schools to bring real-world career education to young learners. Research shows children's career aspirations narrow dramatically by age seven — so introducing diverse possibilities early makes a lasting difference.

slogans.en: Every big life starts with a big dream.

descriptions.en: National SAFER Workplace Day, held on the last Friday of June, encourages workers across all industries to Stop, Assess, Formulate, Execute, and Review safety in their daily tasks. Founded in 2023 by tec.nicum (part of the Schmersal Group), the day began with a focus on machine safety before expanding to cover all workplaces — offices, factories, warehouses. It emphasizes real actions over just talk: hazard discussions, safety reviews, and proactive risk identification.

slogans.en: Safety starts with a single smart step.

descriptions.en: Global Smurf Day fills the streets with blue faces, white hats, and wide smiles. Established in 2011 by Sony Pictures Animation to celebrate the birthday of Peyo — the Belgian artist who created the little blue characters in 1958 — the inaugural event earned a Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of people dressed as Smurfs. Held on the Saturday closest to June 25, the day celebrates imagination, kindness, and teamwork through costumes, parties, and comic marathons.

UK Armed Forces Day, held on the last Saturday of June, celebrates the entire British military community — serving personnel, reservists, veterans, cadets, and military families. It began in 2006 as Veterans' Day and was renamed and expanded in 2009 to honour the armed forces as an active part of national life. Through parades, family events, and community open houses, the day helps bridge the gap that can form between military and civilian life.

slogans.en: Show your support for our Armed Forces.

descriptions.en: National Pet Memorial Day, held in the United States on the second Sunday of September, is a day to remember the animals we have loved and lost. A dog, cat or bird is often part of the family for many years, and the grief when it dies is real but rarely given space. Owners mark the day by lighting a candle, visiting a grave or a favourite walking spot, looking through old photos, or sharing a memory with friends.

slogans.en: Gone but never forgotten — always in our hearts.

descriptions.en: World First Aid Day falls on the second Saturday of September. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies started it in 2000 to remind people that first aid saves lives and that anyone can learn it. Red Cross and Red Crescent societies around the world run free demonstrations and short courses on the day, teaching skills such as CPR, stopping bleeding and helping someone who is choking. Learning the basics means you can help in the minutes before professional help arrives.

slogans.en: Know First Aid, Save a Life

descriptions.en: The Federal Fast, in German the Eidgenössischer Dank-, Buss- und Bettag, falls on the third Sunday of September. It is a day of thanksgiving, repentance and prayer shared by Swiss of different faiths, set on a common date for the whole country in the nineteenth century to bring the cantons and churches together. Many people attend ecumenical services or spend a quiet day outdoors, and a traditional meal is a simple plum tart; in the canton of Vaud the following Monday is a public holiday.

slogans.en: One for All, All for One.

descriptions.en: World Smile Day falls on the first Friday of October. It was started in 1999 by Harvey Ball, the American commercial artist from Worcester, Massachusetts, who drew the yellow smiley face in 1963 and later felt it had lost its meaning to commercialism. His motto for the day was simple: "Do an act of kindness. Help one person smile." People mark it with small kindnesses, from a compliment or a handwritten note to helping a stranger or a neighbour.

slogans.en: Do an Act of Kindness. Help One Person Smile.

descriptions.en: World Habitat Day, on the first Monday of October, is a United Nations day to reflect on the state of our towns and cities and on everyone's right to adequate shelter. The UN General Assembly created it in the 1980s, and UN-Habitat leads it with a new theme each year, from affordable housing to climate-resilient cities. Governments, city planners and community groups hold conferences, publish reports and organise local events that put housing and liveable neighbourhoods on the agenda.

World Architecture Day falls on the first Monday of October and celebrates the role of architecture in shaping the places where we live, work and gather. It was established by the International Union of Architects, which chooses a theme each year, and it shares its date with the United Nations' World Habitat Day. Architects' associations, schools and cities mark it with talks, exhibitions, open buildings and guided walks that invite people to look again at the streets and buildings around them.

World Egg Day falls on the second Friday of October and celebrates one of the most affordable and nourishing foods on the planet. It was started by the International Egg Commission in 1996 to remind people how much good nutrition a single egg packs: high-quality protein and a range of vitamins and minerals. Eggs turn up in nearly every cuisine, from a simple breakfast to cakes and sauces. The day is marked with cooking events, school activities, egg donations to food banks and, quite simply, a good egg dish at home.

World Sight Day, held on the second Thursday of October, draws global attention to blindness and vision impairment. It is coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness, which brings together eye-care groups, health workers and governments. Its central point is that much of the world's sight loss could be prevented or treated with something as simple as an eye test, a pair of glasses or cataract surgery. On the day, clinics offer free screenings, campaigns urge people to get their eyes checked, and organisations push for eye care that reaches everyone.

World Philosophy Day is celebrated by UNESCO on the third Thursday of November. First held in 2002 and made an annual UNESCO day in 2005, it highlights the value of philosophical thinking for questioning assumptions, debating ideas and living together in diverse societies. Universities, schools and cafés around the world host lectures, debates and philosophy workshops for children and adults on the day.

Thanksgiving in the United States falls on the fourth Thursday of November and traces its story to a harvest feast shared by English colonists and the Wampanoag people at Plymouth in 1621. President Abraham Lincoln made it a national holiday in 1863, in the middle of the Civil War, and in 1941 Congress fixed it on the fourth Thursday. Families gather for roast turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie, watch parades and football, and take a moment to say what they are grateful for.

slogans.en: Grateful for Everything. Thankful for Everyone.

descriptions.en: Regaib Kandili is observed on the night before the first Friday of Rajab, the seventh month of the Islamic calendar, and opens the three holy months that lead to Ramadan. In Türkiye it is one of the five kandil nights, named after the lamps that were lit on minarets in Ottoman times. Families visit mosques, pray and read the Quran, exchange good wishes and share kandil simidi, a small sesame bread made for these nights.

slogans.en: Bu mübarek gecede kalpler huzur bulur.

descriptions.en: Thaipusam is a Hindu festival of the Tamil community held at the full moon in the Tamil month of Thai, in January or February, in honour of the god Murugan. It recalls the day his mother Parvati gave him a vel, a divine spear, to defeat the demon Soorapadman. Devotees fast and pray, then carry kavadi, decorated frames, or pots of milk on pilgrimages, some with their skin pierced by hooks and skewers; the largest gathering is at the Batu Caves near Kuala Lumpur, where hundreds of thousands climb 272 steps to the shrine.

Up Helly Aa is a fire festival held in Lerwick, in Scotland's Shetland Islands, on the last Tuesday of January. It grew out of rowdy 19th-century midwinter celebrations and took its Viking theme in the late 1800s, honouring the islands' Norse heritage. A squad dressed as Vikings, led by the Guizer Jarl, marches through the dark streets with around a thousand torchbearers, who then throw their torches into a full-size replica longship and burn it, before a night of parties in halls across the town.

slogans.en: Fire and Viking spirit ignite the night.

descriptions.en: Miraç Kandili is the Turkish name for the night of Isra and Mi'raj, observed on the eve of the 27th of Rajab in the Islamic calendar. It commemorates the Prophet Muhammad's night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and his ascension to the heavens, during which, according to tradition, the five daily prayers were made obligatory. In Türkiye it is one of the five kandil nights: mosques are lit up, families pray, read the Quran and exchange good wishes, and kandil simidi is shared.

slogans.en: Göklere yükselen o gece nur oldu.

descriptions.en: The Lantern Festival falls on the 15th day of the first lunar month, the first full moon of the year, and closes the Chinese New Year season. It matters as a night of reunion and light that sends the new year off with hope. Streets, temples and parks glow with paper lanterns, people guess the riddles hung on them, families share tangyuan, sweet glutinous rice balls, and lion and dragon dances wind through crowds in China, Taiwan, Singapore and Chinese communities everywhere.

slogans.en: Light up the night — the new year's final glow.

descriptions.en: Berat Kandili is observed on the night before the 15th of Sha'ban, the eighth month of the Islamic calendar, about two weeks before Ramadan begins. Known elsewhere as Shab-e-Barat or Laylat al-Bara'ah, it is regarded as a night of forgiveness, when, according to tradition, God's mercy is especially near and the coming year's destinies are recorded. In Türkiye it is one of the five kandil nights, when mosques are lit, families pray and read the Quran, visit the graves of loved ones and exchange kandil greetings.

slogans.en: Affın kapıları bu gece sonuna kadar açık.

descriptions.en: Pink Shirt Day is an anti-bullying day celebrated on the last Wednesday in February. It started in Canada in 2007 when two students stood against bullying by wearing pink shirts. Today millions around the world wear pink to take a stand.

Rare Disease Day falls on the last day of February, and on 29 February in leap years, itself a rare date. It was started by the European patient alliance EURORDIS in 2008 to raise awareness of rare diseases and their impact on patients and their families. Each disease affects few people, but together they touch more than 300 million people worldwide, many of whom wait years for a diagnosis and have no approved treatment. Patient groups, hospitals and supporters mark the day with events, campaigns and landmarks lit up in the day's colours.

slogans.en: Share your colours — rare is many, rare is strong.

descriptions.en: Open Data Day is held each year around the first Saturday of March to celebrate data that anyone can freely use, share and build on. Coordinated by the Open Knowledge Foundation, it brings together local groups around the world who believe open data makes governments more transparent and research and services better. Communities mark it with workshops, hackathons, mapping parties and talks that turn public data into tools and stories people can use.

slogans.en: Open data for open government and open society.

descriptions.en: Mothering Sunday is the British day for honouring mothers, held on the fourth Sunday of Lent, three weeks before Easter. It began as a church custom: on this Sunday people went back to their 'mother church', the main church of their home parish, and young people working away in service were often given the day off to visit their families. Over time it became a day for mothers themselves, marked with flowers, cards, family meals and sometimes a simnel cake. It is older than the American Mother's Day and falls on a different date.

slogans.en: For all the love our mothers give.

descriptions.en: Commonwealth Day is the yearly celebration of the Commonwealth of Nations, the voluntary association of 56 countries, most of them once part of the British Empire. It grew out of Empire Day, first held on Queen Victoria's birthday, and since 1977 it has been kept on the second Monday of March. The monarch, as Head of the Commonwealth, sends a message to its peoples, a multi-faith service is held at Westminster Abbey in London, and schools and communities in member countries mark the day with flags and events.

World Kidney Day, on the second Thursday of March, raises awareness of how much our kidneys do and how often kidney disease goes unnoticed. It was started in 2006 by the International Society of Nephrology and the International Federation of Kidney Foundations. Chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms until it is advanced, and diabetes and high blood pressure are its main causes. On the day, hospitals and health groups offer free screenings and share simple advice: check your blood pressure and blood sugar, eat well and keep active.

Red Nose Day is Comic Relief's big fundraising day in the UK, held in March. The charity began it in 1988 with a simple idea: use comedy and a cheap plastic red nose to get the whole country giving. People wear red noses, dress up, hold bake sales and silly sponsored challenges at school and work, and the day ends with a long evening of comedy on BBC television. The money goes to projects tackling poverty and injustice in the UK and around the world.

slogans.en: We're all in this together — do something funny for money.

descriptions.en: World Social Work Day, held on the third Tuesday of March, honours the social workers who support families, children, older people and anyone facing hardship. The International Federation of Social Workers leads the day each year, and it is also marked at the United Nations. Each year has a theme tied to social justice, human rights and community well-being. Social work schools, agencies and associations hold conferences, share stories from the field and thank colleagues whose work is often unseen.

Good Friday is the Christian day that remembers the crucifixion and death of Jesus, observed on the Friday before Easter Sunday. For believers it is one of the most solemn days of the year, a time of mourning before the joy of Easter. In Germany it is a public holiday everywhere, and also a protected silent day, when dance events and other loud entertainment are restricted in many states. Churches hold quiet services, often at three in the afternoon, and many families eat fish instead of meat.

Easter Monday is the day after Easter Sunday, extending the celebration of Jesus's resurrection into a second day of rest. In Germany it is a public holiday in every federal state, as it is in many other countries with a Christian tradition. With shops and offices closed, families use it for visits, spring walks and leftover Easter treats, and in some regions people keep up the custom of an Easter Monday walk recalling the disciples' journey to Emmaus.

Laylat al-Qadr — Kadir Gecesi in Turkish — is the holiest night of the Islamic year, falling in the last ten nights of Ramadan, traditionally on the 27th. The Quran describes it as 'better than a thousand months'. Muslims spend the night in prayer believing their supplications are especially answered. In Turkey, mosques are packed with worshippers and minarets glow throughout the night.

The International Day of Pink is an anti-bullying day held on the second Wednesday of April. It began in Canada, inspired by two Nova Scotia high school students who in 2007 handed out pink shirts after a classmate was bullied for wearing pink. Today schools, workplaces and communities around the world wear pink to stand against bullying, discrimination, homophobia and transphobia, and to show that everyone deserves to feel safe.

International Guide Dog Day, on the last Wednesday of April, celebrates the dogs that help blind and partially sighted people move about safely and independently. Each guide dog, often a Labrador, golden retriever or German shepherd, spends its puppyhood with volunteer families and then months in training before it is matched with a partner. The day thanks the dogs, their trainers and the volunteers who raise them. Guide dog schools hold open days and fundraisers and remind businesses that guide dogs are welcome.

slogans.en: Guide dogs — independence and loyalty in one.

descriptions.en: World Password Day falls on the first Thursday in May and reminds everyone to look after their passwords. It was launched in 2013 by the technology company Intel and is now promoted by security firms worldwide. A strong password is long, unique to each account and never shared, and turning on two-step verification adds a second lock. People mark the day by changing old or reused passwords, trying a password manager and checking which of their accounts have appeared in data leaks.

slogans.en: A strong password is your best defence.

descriptions.en: Ascension Day is the Christian feast of Jesus Christ's ascension into heaven, as told in the New Testament. It falls on the fortieth day of Easter, counting Easter Sunday as the first, so it is always a Thursday, 39 days later. Churches hold special services, and in Germany it is a public holiday. Germans also know it as Vatertag, Father's Day, when groups of men traditionally go out walking together, often pulling a handcart of food and drink.

Pentecost, or Whitsun, is the Christian feast that recalls the Holy Spirit coming down on the apostles in Jerusalem, as told in the Acts of the Apostles. It falls on the seventh Sunday after Easter, the fiftieth day of the Easter season, and is often called the birthday of the Church. Churches hold festive services, often with red vestments and decorations for the flames of the Spirit. In Germany, Pentecost Sunday and Whit Monday make a long holiday weekend.

slogans.en: The spirit is poured out on all people.

descriptions.en: Whit Monday is the day after Pentecost Sunday, fifty days after Easter by the traditional count. It extends the feast that recalls the Holy Spirit coming down on the apostles, and in many countries it has long been kept as a day of rest. In Germany it is a public holiday in every state, and churches hold services, sometimes ecumenical ones in the open air. Many families use the long weekend for outings, hikes, cycling trips and local spring festivals.

slogans.en: The spirit moves through all things.

descriptions.en: Victoria Day is a Canadian public holiday held on the last Monday before 25 May, honouring the birthday of Queen Victoria, born on 24 May 1819, and today also the reigning monarch's official birthday in Canada. It is often called the unofficial start of summer, when cottages open, gardens get planted and the long weekend is nicknamed May Two-Four. Communities mark it with fireworks, parades and picnics; in Quebec the same day is National Patriots' Day.

slogans.en: May long weekend — summer begins in Canada!

descriptions.en: Corpus Christi is a Catholic feast honouring the presence of Christ in the Eucharist, held on the Thursday 60 days after Easter. It began in Liège in the 13th century and Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264. In Germany it is a public holiday in Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland. Towns hold solemn processions behind the consecrated host, often over carpets of flowers laid in the streets.

Vardavar is Armenia's joyful water festival, when people of all ages soak each other with buckets, bottles and water pistols in the streets. Its roots are usually traced to a pre-Christian summer feast linked to Astghik, the Armenian goddess of love and beauty; today it coincides with the Armenian Church's Feast of the Transfiguration, held 98 days after Easter, so the date moves each year. Alongside the water fights, families go to church, share meals and enjoy a long summer day outdoors.

slogans.en: Cool down with joy — happy Vardavar!

descriptions.en: World Calligraphy Day, held on the second Wednesday of August, celebrates the art of beautiful writing in every script. Calligraphy has shaped cultures for centuries, from Chinese and Japanese brushwork to Arabic and Ottoman scripts and the lettering of medieval Western manuscripts. Calligraphers mark the day with workshops, exhibitions and demonstrations, and many people simply pick up a pen or brush and write a few letters slowly and with care.

slogans.en: Every letter, a stroke of art.

descriptions.en: World Honey Bee Day falls on the third Saturday of August and celebrates the honey bee and the beekeepers who care for it. Bees pollinate many of the fruits, vegetables and nuts we eat, yet they face pressure from habitat loss, pesticides, disease and a changing climate. Beekeepers open their hives to visitors, markets offer honey tastings, and schools teach children how a colony works. Anyone can join in by planting bee-friendly flowers or buying honey from a local beekeeper. It is not the same as the UN's World Bee Day, held on 20 May.

slogans.en: Save the bees, save the world.

descriptions.en: The Hungry Ghost Festival falls on the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, at the heart of what many Chinese communities call Ghost Month. Rooted in Taoist and Buddhist tradition, it rests on the belief that the gates of the underworld open and spirits wander among the living. Families set out food and burn incense and joss paper for their ancestors and for spirits with no one left to remember them. In Singapore and Malaysia, open-air getai concerts are staged, with the front row left empty for the ghostly guests.

La Tomatina is a tomato fight held on the last Wednesday of August in Buñol, a town near Valencia in Spain. It is said to have begun in 1945, when a scuffle among young people at a parade ended with them pelting each other with tomatoes from a market stall, and it grew into a yearly tradition. Trucks bring in tons of overripe tomatoes, the battle lasts about an hour, and then fire hoses wash the streets and the crowd clean; numbers are now limited by ticket.

R U OK? Day is an Australian day for suicide prevention, held on the second Thursday of September. It began in 2009, started by Gavin Larkin after losing his father to suicide, and grew into a national movement. Its message is simple: ask the people around you 'Are you OK?', listen without judgement and help them find support if they need it. Workplaces, schools and sports clubs mark it with morning teas, conversations and check-ins with friends and colleagues.

slogans.en: Are you ok? Ask someone today.

descriptions.en: Mevlid Kandili celebrates the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad on the 12th of Rabi' al-Awwal. In Turkey it is a deeply observed holy night. The tradition of the Mevlid — a poem praising the Prophet written by Süleyman Çelebi in 1409 — is recited in mosques across the country. Families gather, special prayers are held, and minarets are illuminated.

International Coastal Cleanup Day falls on the third Saturday of September and is one of the largest volunteer efforts for the health of the ocean. It is coordinated by the US-based Ocean Conservancy, which has run its International Coastal Cleanup since the 1980s with partners in more than a hundred countries. Volunteers gather on beaches, riverbanks and lakeshores to pick up litter and record what they find, so the data can show where plastic pollution comes from.

Batman Day, held on the third Saturday of September, celebrates one of the world's best-known superheroes. Created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger, Batman first appeared in Detective Comics #27 in 1939 and has lived on ever since in comics, cartoons, films and games. DC Comics first held Batman Day in 2014 to mark the character's 75th anniversary. Comic shops, bookstores and libraries celebrate with free comics, costume contests and special events, as fans gather in capes and cowls to honour the Dark Knight of Gotham City.

slogans.en: I am the night. I am Batman.

descriptions.en: World Rivers Day celebrates the world's rivers on the fourth Sunday of September. It grew out of BC Rivers Day in British Columbia, Canada, and became a worldwide event in 2005. Rivers carry drinking water, feed farmland and shelter countless species, yet many suffer from pollution, damming and over-extraction. People mark the day with riverbank clean-ups, guided walks, paddling trips, tree planting and school activities that bring communities back to their local waterways.

slogans.en: Celebrate our rivers — protect their future.

descriptions.en: Native American Day honours the history, cultures and contributions of the Indigenous peoples of the United States. California observes it on the fourth Friday of September, recognising the tribes who lived on the land long before the state existed and who remain part of its life today. Schools, museums and tribal communities mark it with powwows, traditional dance and food, storytelling and lessons on Native history, and the day is also a time to speak up for tribal sovereignty and Indigenous rights.

slogans.en: Honor the past, celebrate the present, build the future.

descriptions.en: Ada Lovelace Day, held on the second Tuesday of October, celebrates women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. It is named after Ada Lovelace (1815–1852), the English mathematician whose 1843 notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine included what is often called the first computer program. Lovelace also saw that such a machine could work with more than numbers, a striking idea for her time. On the day, schools, universities and companies hold talks and events and share the stories of women in STEM to give girls role models they can see themselves in.

slogans.en: Inspiring women in STEM, one pioneer at a time.

descriptions.en: World Quality Day, held on the second Thursday of November, celebrates the role of quality in products, services and public life. Promoted by quality professionals worldwide, including the Chartered Quality Institute in the UK, it highlights how getting things right the first time saves money, reduces waste and protects people. Organisations mark it with workshops, staff recognition and reviews of how their work could be done better.

slogans.en: Quality — doing it right the first time.

descriptions.en: Loy Krathong is a Thai festival held on the full moon of the twelfth month of the traditional Thai lunar calendar, usually in November. People make krathongs, small floating baskets of banana leaves decorated with flowers, candles and incense, and set them on rivers, canals and lakes. The offering thanks the water goddess, Phra Mae Khongkha, and is a way to let go of bad luck and grudges, and the night is filled with lights, fireworks and beauty contests.

slogans.en: Float away the worries, welcome the light.

descriptions.en: World COPD Day, held on a Wednesday in November, is organised by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) and was first marked in 2002. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a long-term lung condition that makes breathing harder over time and is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. The day promotes early diagnosis with simple breathing tests, quitting smoking, cleaner air and better access to treatment and rehabilitation.

Stir-Up Sunday is the last Sunday before Advent, the traditional day in Britain for making the Christmas pudding. Its name comes from the Book of Common Prayer, whose prayer for that Sunday begins Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord. By Victorian custom each member of the family stirs the mixture from east to west, in honour of the Wise Men, and makes a secret wish, sometimes adding a silver coin for luck, so the pudding can mature for weeks before Christmas Day.

slogans.en: Stir, wish, and let Christmas magic begin.

descriptions.en: Buy Nothing Day is an international day of protest against overconsumption, held on Black Friday in North America and on the following Saturday elsewhere. It was started in Vancouver in 1992 by artist Ted Dave and promoted by the Canadian magazine Adbusters. Participants spend 24 hours buying nothing at all, and use the day to swap, repair, give away or simply think about the environmental and social cost of what they buy.

slogans.en: 24 hours of not spending — can you do it?

descriptions.en: International Blues Music Day celebrates the blues, the music that grew out of African American communities in the American South in the late 19th century. Rooted in work songs, field hollers and spirituals, it turned hardship into song and later shaped jazz, rock and roll, soul and much of the popular music that followed. People mark the day by listening to classic recordings, going to live gigs and jam sessions, and discovering the musicians who carry the tradition today.

National Sunflower Day celebrates the tall, golden flower that brightens late summer fields across the United States. Sunflowers are native to North America, where Indigenous peoples grew them for seeds and oil long before European settlers arrived, and Kansas is nicknamed the Sunflower State. People mark the day by visiting sunflower farms, planting seeds in their gardens, snacking on roasted seeds and sharing photos of the cheerful blooms.

slogans.en: Turn your face to the sun.

descriptions.en: Sandcastle Day invites people of all ages to head to a beach, lakeshore or sandbox and build the best sandcastle they can. It celebrates creativity, teamwork and the simple joy of making something beautiful that the next tide will wash away. Families grab buckets and spades, mix sand with just enough water to make it hold, and shape towers, moats and walls, while some seaside towns hold sand sculpture contests.

National Sisters Day falls on the first Sunday of August in the United States and celebrates the bond between sisters, whether by birth, adoption or chosen friendship. Sisters are often our first playmates, fiercest defenders and keepers of family memories, and the day is a reminder to appreciate a relationship that can last a lifetime. People mark it by calling or visiting their sisters, sharing old photos and stories, sending small gifts or planning a day out together. Many also use it to honour close friends who feel like sisters.

slogans.en: The bond that knows you best.

descriptions.en: National Friendship Day is celebrated in the United States on the first Sunday of August. It is separate from the United Nations' International Day of Friendship on July 30, though both share the same idea: friends deserve to be told they matter. In a busy week it is easy to let friendships drift, and the day offers a gentle nudge to reconnect. People mark it by spending time together, sending cards or messages, swapping friendship bracelets or getting in touch with an old friend.

Psychic Day, observed in the United States on the first Sunday of August, is a lighthearted day for curiosity about intuition, hunches and the unexplained. Fortune telling in its many forms, from tarot cards and palm reading to tea leaves, has fascinated people across cultures for centuries, and the day celebrates that playful wonder rather than any scientific claim. People mark it with guessing games, such as predicting who is calling or the colour of the next card, a tarot evening with friends, or simply by listening to their gut feelings for a day.

Festival Monday falls on the first Monday of August, at the height of the British summer; in Scotland this is the date of the summer bank holiday. Long summer weekends like this one are when many towns hold their carnivals, agricultural shows and outdoor concerts. People mark the day with parades, live music, picnics and family days out. It is a chance to make the most of the long evenings before autumn arrives.

Commerce Day, known in Iceland as Frídagur verslunarmanna, is a public holiday on the first Monday of August. It began as a day off for shop and office workers, the country's commercial staff, and has grown into a holiday for everyone. It closes Verslunarmannahelgi, the busiest long weekend of the Icelandic summer, when many people go camping and head to outdoor festivals around the country. The best known is Þjóðhátíð in the Westman Islands, where crowds gather for music, a bonfire and a big hillside singalong.

Natal Day is a civic holiday in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, held on the first Monday of August. It began as a celebration of the founding of Halifax in 1749 and has grown into a province-wide summer festival. Towns across Nova Scotia mark it with parades, concerts, community breakfasts, sports events and fireworks, and in Halifax and Dartmouth the festivities often fill the whole long weekend.

National Night Out is a community-building campaign in the United States, held since 1984 and usually on the first Tuesday of August. It encourages neighbors to step outside, meet one another and get to know the police officers and firefighters who serve their area. Streets fill with block parties, cookouts, parades and safety demonstrations, and many residents leave their porch lights on that evening as a sign that the neighborhood looks out for itself.

Professional Engineers Day, held on the first Wednesday of August, honors licensed professional engineers in the United States. The National Society of Professional Engineers launched it in 2016, and it looks back to 1907, when Wyoming became the first state to license engineers. Firms, universities and engineering societies use the day to thank the engineers who design and safeguard bridges, roads, water systems and power grids, and to encourage young people to join the profession.

slogans.en: Building the world, one design at a time.

descriptions.en: International Beer Day falls on the first Friday of August and celebrates one of the oldest drinks people have ever made. It began in Santa Cruz, California, in 2007 and soon spread to bars and breweries around the world. People mark it by raising a glass with friends, trying a local or unfamiliar style, thanking the brewers and bartenders who serve them, and, as the day's own spirit insists, drinking responsibly.

International Hangover Day is a tongue-in-cheek day that falls right after International Beer Day, when many people are paying for the night before. It treats the headache, thirst and tiredness of the morning after with humour rather than lecturing. People mark it by taking things slowly, drinking plenty of water, eating a hearty breakfast, swapping favourite recovery tips, and perhaps promising themselves to drink more moderately next time.

Melon Day is a national holiday in Turkmenistan, held on the second Sunday of August when the melon harvest is at its peak. Turkmen farmers grow hundreds of melon varieties, and the sweet, fragrant fruit has long been a point of national pride and a staple of summer tables. Markets and squares fill with melon displays, tastings and contests for the best fruit, along with music, dancing and family gatherings.

slogans.en: A taste of paradise, one slice at a time.

descriptions.en: Ekka People's Day is a public holiday in Brisbane that falls during the Royal Queensland Show, known to everyone simply as the Ekka. The show has long brought the country to the city, giving Queensland's farmers a stage for their best livestock, produce and skills. On the day, families head to the Brisbane Showgrounds for animal judging, woodchopping, sideshow rides, showbags and the famous strawberry sundaes.

Nag Panchami is a Hindu festival honouring the Nagas, the serpent deities of Hindu tradition, held on the fifth day of the bright half of the monsoon month of Shravana. Snakes emerge in the rains, and the festival grew from an old wish to live at peace with them and seek their protection for home and family. Devotees pray at serpent shrines, offer milk, flowers and sweets to images of cobras, and draw snakes on walls, though wildlife groups urge people not to feed milk to live snakes.

National Finance Brokers Day thanks the mortgage and finance brokers who help people find their way through loans, rates and paperwork. For many households a home loan is the biggest financial decision they will ever make, and a good broker compares lenders, explains the fine print and stays with the client until settlement. The day is marked by industry events and messages of thanks, and it is a good moment for anyone to review their own loans.

The Gold Cup Parade is a summer highlight in Charlottetown, the capital of Prince Edward Island, Canada. It belongs to the island's late-summer festivities, held as part of Old Home Week, and is tied to the Gold Cup and Saucer, the province's best-known harness race. Thousands of spectators line the streets to watch decorated floats, marching bands, vintage cars and giant balloons wind through downtown.

Mawlid al-Nabi celebrates the birth of the Prophet Muhammad. Many Muslims mark it on the 12th of Rabi al-Awwal, the third month of the Islamic lunar calendar, so its Gregorian date moves earlier each year. Customs vary from country to country: people gather for prayer, recite poems and hymns in praise of the Prophet, share food and give to charity. In Türkiye it is observed as Mevlid Kandili, a night when mosques are lit up and Süleyman Çelebi's Mevlid poem is recited.

National Burger Day is a tribute to one of the world's most popular foods: a grilled patty in a soft bun. The hamburger takes its name from the German city of Hamburg, and several American towns and cooks claim to have first served one around the turn of the 20th century, a debate that has never been settled. People mark the day by firing up the grill, trying a new burger joint, or building their own with everything from classic beef to plant-based patties.

slogans.en: Stack it high, bite it deep.

descriptions.en: Raksha Bandhan is a Hindu festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters, held on the full-moon day of the month of Shravan, usually in August. A sister ties a rakhi, a decorated thread, around her brother's wrist, prays for his wellbeing and feeds him sweets, and he promises to protect her and gives her a gift in return. Across India and Nepal and wherever their diasporas live, families gather for the ritual, and many people also tie rakhis for cousins and close friends.

slogans.en: A thread of love and protection.

descriptions.en: International Cosplay Day celebrates the fans who bring characters from comics, anime, films and games to life through costume and performance. The word cosplay, a blend of 'costume' and 'play', was coined in Japan in the 1980s, and the hobby has since grown into a worldwide community. Cosplayers mark the day by sewing, sculpting and finishing their outfits, gathering for photo shoots and meet-ups, and sharing their work online.

Franchise Appreciation Day recognises the franchise businesses found on high streets and in shopping centres everywhere. In a franchise, a local owner runs an outlet under a familiar brand name, using its recipes, systems and training while investing their own money and hiring people from the neighbourhood. The day is a chance to thank those owners and their staff, often by stopping in at a favourite franchise, leaving a kind review or simply saying thanks at the counter.

World Beard Day, held on the first Saturday of September, is a light-hearted celebration of beards and the people who grow them. Facial hair has carried meaning in many cultures, standing at different times for wisdom, faith, strength or simply style. On the day, bearded men share photos, barbers offer grooming tips, and clubs hold friendly contests, sometimes raising money for charity along the way.

International Vulture Awareness Day, held on the first Saturday of September, speaks up for some of the world's most misunderstood birds. Vultures clean up carcasses before disease can spread, yet many species are now threatened by poisoning, loss of habitat and veterinary drugs in livestock. The day grew out of awareness days run by South Africa's Birds of Prey Programme and England's Hawk Conservancy Trust, and today zoos, reserves and schools hold talks, bird counts and flying displays.

Labor Day, on the first Monday of September, is the United States' public holiday honouring workers and the labour movement that fought for safer workplaces and shorter hours. It grew out of a workers' parade in New York City on 5 September 1882 and became a federal holiday in 1894. Today it is a long weekend of parades, barbecues and last trips to the beach, and it marks the unofficial end of summer before the school year begins.

slogans.en: Honour the hands that built the country.

descriptions.en: The West Indian Day Parade turns Brooklyn's Eastern Parkway into a sea of colour every Labor Day, with steel bands, soca and calypso music, and dazzling feathered costumes. The tradition began among Caribbean immigrants in Harlem and moved to Brooklyn in the late 1960s, growing into one of the largest street festivals in North America. Celebrations start before dawn with J'ouvert, then masquerade bands parade for hours while crowds wave island flags and share food such as jerk chicken, roti and doubles.

slogans.en: One Caribbean, one Brooklyn, one parade.

descriptions.en: Carnival is Brazil's biggest celebration, filling the days before Lent with music, dancing and street parties. It grew from the pre-Lenten feasts the Portuguese brought over, reshaped by African rhythms into samba and many regional styles. Rio de Janeiro's samba schools parade through the Sambadrome in huge costumes and floats, Salvador dances behind trucks carrying live bands, and in Recife and Olinda crowds follow street groups playing frevo, while neighbourhood bands bring the party to towns across the country.

Nyepi, the Day of Silence, is the Balinese Hindu New Year, which opens the Saka calendar year. For 24 hours, from dawn to dawn, the island goes still: no fires or lights, no work, no travel and no entertainment, and even the airport closes while people fast, pray and reflect. The days before are loud and busy, with purification rites at the sea and, on the eve, parades of huge ogoh-ogoh effigies representing evil spirits, which are carried through the streets and often burned.

Waisak, known elsewhere as Vesak, is the holiest day of the Buddhist year and a national holiday in Indonesia. Falling on the full moon of the month of Waisak, usually in May or sometimes June, it commemorates the birth, enlightenment and passing of the Buddha. The best-known celebration takes place in Central Java, where monks and pilgrims walk in procession from Mendut Temple to Borobudur. There they meditate and pray at the moment of the full moon, and the night often ends with lanterns released into the sky.

slogans.en: Buddha's light shines across the world.

descriptions.en: Midsommar is one of Sweden's best-loved holidays, celebrated around the summer solstice, with Midsummer Eve on a Friday between 19 and 25 June and Midsummer Day on the Saturday after. Its roots mix old summer festivities with the Christian feast of John the Baptist, and Midsummer Eve is the day most Swedes actually celebrate. Families and friends raise a leafy maypole, wear crowns of wild flowers, dance and sing around it, and share a meal of pickled herring, new potatoes and strawberries late into the light evening.

slogans.en: Welcome the light, dance till dawn.

descriptions.en: Tết, short for Tết Nguyên Đán, is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year and the most important holiday of the year in Vietnam. It falls on the first day of the lunar calendar, usually in late January or February, and welcomes the spring while honouring family and ancestors. In the days around it, people clean and decorate their homes with peach or yellow apricot blossoms and kumquat trees, travel home to their families, offer food at ancestral altars, cook sticky rice cakes called bánh chưng and give children lucky money in red envelopes.

slogans.en: New year, new blessings, together again.

descriptions.en: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day of the Jewish year and falls on the 10th of Tishrei, ten days after Rosh Hashanah. It closes the Days of Awe, a period of reflection on the past year and of seeking forgiveness from God and from other people. Many Jews fast for about 25 hours, from sunset to nightfall the next day, and spend much of it in synagogue, from the evening Kol Nidre prayer to the closing Neilah service ended by a blast of the shofar. In Israel, traffic and broadcasting almost stop and the streets fall quiet.

slogans.en: A sacred day of reflection and renewal.

descriptions.en: Lag BaOmer is a joyful Jewish holiday on the 33rd day of the Omer, the seven-week count between Passover and Shavuot. Tradition links it to the anniversary of the death of the sage Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and to the end of a plague among the students of Rabbi Akiva. It breaks the Omer's mourning period, so weddings and music return. In Israel families light bonfires, children go on outings, and many thousands make a pilgrimage to Meron.

slogans.en: Light the bonfire, honor the sage.

descriptions.en: Matariki is the Māori New Year, marked when the Matariki star cluster, known in English as the Pleiades, reappears in the pre-dawn sky in midwinter, in June or July. Since 2022 it has been a public holiday in New Zealand, the first to honour a Māori tradition. People gather to remember those who died in the past year, celebrate the present with shared food and music, and look ahead to the year to come, often rising early to see the stars or flying kites.

slogans.en: Stars rise, a new year awakens.

descriptions.en: National Farmers' Day in Ghana falls on the first Friday of December and has been celebrated since 1985. It honours the farmers and fisherfolk who feed the nation, at a time when agriculture employs a large share of Ghana's workers. The highlight is the award of National Best Farmer, along with regional and district prizes such as tractors, tools and houses, and the day is a public holiday.

slogans.en: Thank a farmer, feed the future.

descriptions.en: Juhannus, Finnish Midsummer, celebrates the lightest time of the year, with Midsummer Eve on a Friday and Midsummer Day on the Saturday between 20 and 26 June. Its name comes from John the Baptist, whose feast falls at this time, but many customs are older and tied to the summer solstice. Cities empty as people head to lakeside cottages for sauna, swimming and grilling, bonfires called kokko burn late into the bright night, and Midsummer Day is also Finland's Flag Day.

slogans.en: Light the bonfire, greet the sun.

descriptions.en: Chung Yeung Festival falls on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month and is a public holiday in Hong Kong. Nine was considered a yang number, so the doubled nine gave the day its name, and an old legend tells of a family who escaped a deadly disaster by climbing a hill on this date. Families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep them and leave offerings. Many also hike to high ground, a custom said to keep misfortune away, while chrysanthemums and autumn outings round off the day.

Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, marks the end of Ramadan, the month in which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. It falls on the first day of Shawwal, so its date moves through the seasons with the lunar calendar, and in many countries the holiday lasts several days. The morning begins with a special Eid prayer, and before it every family that can gives zakat al-fitr, a charity so the poor can celebrate too. Then come new clothes, visits to elders and relatives, sweets for guests and gifts for children.

Eid al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice, is the greater of Islam's two festivals and begins on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, as pilgrims in Mecca complete the main rites of the Hajj. It recalls the Prophet Ibrahim's readiness to sacrifice his son at God's command, and the ram that God sent in the son's place. Families start the day with the Eid prayer, sacrifice a sheep, goat or cow, and share the meat with relatives, neighbours and people in need, then spend the holiday visiting one another.

Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains in India and around the world, and falls in October or November with the new moon of the month of Kartika. For many Hindus it marks Rama's return to Ayodhya and honours Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity; Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas and Jains the nirvana of Mahavira. Families clean and light their homes with oil lamps, draw rangoli patterns, share sweets, wear new clothes and set off fireworks.

Easter Sunday is the most important feast of the Christian year, celebrating the resurrection of Jesus three days after his crucifixion on Good Friday. Western churches set the date by an old formula: the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after 21 March, so it moves between late March and late April. Families go to church, often at sunrise, then share a festive meal, decorate eggs and send children hunting for eggs and chocolate left by the Easter Bunny.

slogans.en: Celebrate hope, renewal, and new life.

descriptions.en: Ramazan Bayramı, also called Şeker Bayramı (the Sugar Feast), is how Turkey celebrates Eid al-Fitr, the festival that ends the fasting month of Ramadan. Its date follows the Islamic lunar calendar, so it comes about eleven days earlier each year. The first morning begins with the Eid prayer at the mosque, followed by three days of visits to elders, relatives, neighbours and the graves of loved ones, with baklava and Turkish delight on every table. Children kiss the hands of their elders and receive sweets or pocket money in return.

Eid al-Adha — Kurban Bayramı in Turkey — commemorates the willingness of Ibrahim to sacrifice his son as an act of obedience to God. It is celebrated for four days. Families who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, cow, or goat, and distribute the meat to neighbours, relatives, and those in need. It is one of the two major Islamic festivals and a public holiday in Turkey.

Islamic New Year falls on the first day of Muharram, the opening month of the Hijri calendar. The calendar counts its years from the Hijra, the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622, and because it follows the moon the new year comes about eleven days earlier each year. For most Muslims it is a quiet, reflective day rather than a festive one, marked with prayer, good wishes and time with family. For Shia Muslims, the start of Muharram also opens a period of mourning for Imam Husayn.

slogans.en: A new year on the lunar calendar.

descriptions.en: Ashura falls on the tenth day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar, and is observed across the Muslim world in different ways. In Sunni tradition it is a day of voluntary fasting linked to the deliverance of Moses and his people from Pharaoh; for Shia Muslims it is a solemn day of mourning for Imam Husayn, the Prophet Muhammad's grandson, who was killed at Karbala in 680. In Türkiye the day is known for aşure, a sweet pudding of grains, pulses and dried fruit cooked in large pots and shared with neighbours.

The first day of Ramadan opens the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, the holiest month of the year for Muslims. Ramadan is the month in which, according to Islamic belief, the Quran was first revealed, and its start depends on the sighting of the new crescent moon, so it moves about eleven days earlier each year. Throughout the month, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, share a meal called suhoor before dawn and break the fast at iftar, pray, read the Quran and give to people in need until the month ends with Eid al-Fitr.

The Day of Arafat falls on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the day before Eid al-Adha, and is the high point of the Hajj pilgrimage. Pilgrims gather on the plain of Arafat near Mecca, where the Prophet Muhammad gave his farewell sermon, and spend the day standing in prayer and asking for forgiveness. Standing at Arafat is the essential rite of Hajj. Muslims who are not on pilgrimage often fast, pray and give to charity, and in Türkiye the day is known as arefe, a time for visiting graves and preparing for the holiday.

Isra and Mi'raj, observed on the 27th of Rajab in the Islamic calendar, commemorates two parts of one miraculous night in the life of the Prophet Muhammad. In the Isra he travelled from Mecca to the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, and in the Mi'raj he ascended through the heavens, where, according to tradition, the five daily prayers were given. Muslims mark the night with extra prayers, Quran recitation and talks about its meaning, and in some countries it is a public holiday.

Rosh Hashanah marks the beginning of the Jewish new year, observed on the first and second days of Tishrei. It is a day of prayer, reflection and the sounding of the shofar, marking the start of the High Holy Days that culminate ten days later in Yom Kippur. Apples dipped in honey and round challah with raisins symbolise sweetness and the cycle of the year.

slogans.en: A new year, written in the book of life.

descriptions.en: Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles, begins five days after Yom Kippur on the 15th of Tishrei and lasts seven days. Families build and eat meals in a sukkah — a temporary hut with a roof of natural materials — to remember the Israelites' forty years in the desert. The festival also marks the autumn harvest.

slogans.en: Dwell in the sukkah, give thanks for the harvest.

descriptions.en: Simchat Torah celebrates the completion of the annual cycle of Torah readings and the immediate beginning of the new cycle. Observed on the 22nd of Tishrei (the day after Sukkot's final day), synagogues unroll the entire Torah scroll and congregants dance and sing with the scrolls through the night. In Israel it coincides with Shemini Atzeret.

slogans.en: Dance with the Torah, end and begin again.

descriptions.en: Hanukkah, the Festival of Lights, is an eight-day celebration beginning on the 25th of Kislev. It commemorates the rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem after the Maccabean victory over the Seleucids in 164 BCE, and the miracle of a single cruse of oil lasting eight days. Each night a candle is added to the menorah, and families exchange gifts, eat fried foods and play dreidel.

slogans.en: Light the candles, remember the miracle.

descriptions.en: Tu BiShvat, the 15th of Shevat, marks the new year for trees in the Jewish calendar. Originating in the Mishnah for agricultural tithe purposes, it is now celebrated by planting trees, eating fruit — especially the seven species of the Land of Israel — and in modern Israel by schoolchildren planting saplings across the country. It also falls at the start of spring in the Mediterranean climate.

slogans.en: A new year for the trees.

descriptions.en: Purim is a joyful Jewish holiday held on the 14th of Adar (Adar II in a leap year). It recalls how the Jews of ancient Persia were saved from Haman's plot to destroy them, as told in the Book of Esther. In synagogue the Megillah, the scroll of Esther, is read aloud, and listeners drown out Haman's name with noisemakers. People dress in costumes, send gifts of food to friends, give charity to the poor, share a festive meal and eat hamantaschen, three-cornered pastries filled with poppy seed or jam.

slogans.en: A feast of joy, masks and giving.

descriptions.en: Passover, or Pesach, begins on the 15th of Nisan and lasts seven days (eight in the diaspora). It commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt as told in the Book of Exodus. Families gather for the Seder on the first two nights, reading the Haggadah, eating matzah and avoiding leavened products (chametz). The holiday ends with the counting of the Omer toward Shavuot.

slogans.en: Tell the story of the Exodus.

descriptions.en: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, falls seven weeks after Passover on the 6th of Sivan. It commemorates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai and marks the end of the barley harvest and the start of the wheat harvest. Tradition includes an all-night study session (Tikkun Leil Shavuot), dairy meals, the reading of the Book of Ruth, and the decorating of synagogues with greenery.

slogans.en: The day the Torah was given.

descriptions.en: Yom HaShoah, Israel's Holocaust Remembrance Day, is observed on the 27th of Nisan. Established by the Israeli Knesset in 1953, it commemorates the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. At 10:00 a siren sounds across Israel, traffic stops and people stand in silence. Public ceremonies, memorial services and the reading of victims' names take place throughout the day.

Yom HaZikaron, Israel's Memorial Day, is observed on the 4th of Iyyar, the day before Yom Ha'atzmaut. It honours the more than 24,000 soldiers and security personnel killed in the line of duty since 1860, as well as civilian victims of terrorism. A one-minute siren sounds at 20:00; memorial ceremonies are held at military cemeteries, and flags are lowered to half-mast.

Supernatural Day, on 13 September, celebrates the American TV series Supernatural, which premiered on that date in 2005. The show followed brothers Sam and Dean Winchester, played by Jared Padalecki and Jensen Ackles, as they hunted ghosts, demons and monsters across the United States. It ran for fifteen seasons until 2020, one of the longest runs for a fantasy drama, and built a famously devoted fan community. Fans mark the day with rewatches, fan art, cosplay and online tributes.

slogans.en: Where the story never truly ends.

descriptions.en: National Sober Day, on 14 September in the United States, celebrates people who live free of alcohol and other substances, whether in recovery from addiction or simply by choice. Getting and staying sober takes daily effort, and many people still face shame or silence around it. The day aims to break that stigma and show that a full, joyful life without drinking is possible. People mark it by sharing their sobriety milestones, joining recovery meetings and events, and checking in on friends who are struggling.

Frevo Day on 9 February honours the fast, acrobatic dance and brass-band music born in the streets of Recife, Pernambuco, in the late nineteenth century. The date recalls the first known appearance of the word "frevo" in a Recife newspaper in 1907, and UNESCO added frevo to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity in 2012. Dancers spin small, colourful umbrellas as they leap and squat, and the day brings concerts, dance classes and a foretaste of carnival.

Remember Me Thursday, held on the fourth Thursday of September, is a worldwide moment of remembrance and hope for pets in shelters that are still waiting for a home. The campaign was started by the Helen Woodward Animal Center, an animal welfare organisation in California, to encourage people to adopt rather than buy. Supporters light a real or virtual candle and share photos of their adopted pets online, while shelters hold vigils and adoption events to help more animals find families.

slogans.en: Light a candle. Save a life.

descriptions.en: Collect Rocks Day on 16 September invites people of all ages to look down and pick something up: a smooth pebble, a sparkling crystal or a stone studded with fossils. Rock collecting is one of the oldest and most accessible hobbies, and every stone carries a story of volcanoes, oceans or ancient rivers. People mark the day by walking a beach or riverbank in search of interesting rocks, sorting and labelling a collection with children, or visiting a geology museum. Just remember to collect only where it is allowed.

Fiesta de San Pacho is the great feast of Quibdó, capital of Colombia's Chocó department on the country's Pacific side, held every year from 20 September to 4 October. It honours Saint Francis of Assisi, known locally as San Pacho, and blends Catholic devotion with the Afro-Colombian traditions of the region; UNESCO added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2012. Each neighbourhood takes its turn with masses, processions, costumed parades and the brass-and-drum music called chirimía, until the festival closes on the saint's feast day.

slogans.en: Faith and rhythm in the streets.

descriptions.en: Hispanic Heritage Month runs from 15 September to 15 October in the United States, honouring the histories, cultures and contributions of Americans with roots in Spain, Mexico, Central and South America and the Caribbean. It began as a week-long observance in 1968 and was extended to a full month in 1988. The start date matches the independence days of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua, with Mexico and Chile following on 16 and 18 September. Schools, museums and communities mark it with festivals, music, food and talks.

Mayflower Day on 16 September marks the departure of the Mayflower from Plymouth, England, in 1620, carrying the passengers later remembered as the Pilgrims to the New World. After 66 days at sea the ship reached Cape Cod, and before going ashore the men signed the Mayflower Compact, an early agreement on self-government. The settlement they founded at Plymouth became one of the first lasting English colonies in North America. The anniversary is marked with talks, museum visits and readings about the voyage and its legacy, including its impact on Native peoples.

slogans.en: A voyage that changed the world.

names.en: National Sit With a Stranger Day

descriptions.en: National Sit With a Stranger Day on November 9 encourages people to put their phones down and talk to someone they do not know. Studies on everyday conversation suggest that a brief chat with a stranger on a train or in a café tends to leave both people happier than they expected. Mark the day by sharing a bench or a table, saying hello and seeing where the conversation goes.

Responsible Dog Ownership Day falls on the third Saturday of September and is promoted by the American Kennel Club. It reminds people that a dog is a commitment for its whole life, with daily needs for exercise, training, healthy food, vet care and companionship. Kennel clubs and shelters across the United States mark it with training demonstrations, microchip and health clinics, adoption events and family-friendly activities that help new and future owners prepare.

slogans.en: Love them well. Train them right.

descriptions.en: Australian Citizenship Day on 17 September is a chance for all Australians to reflect on what citizenship means. Introduced in 2001, it celebrates the shared values, rights and responsibilities that unite people of many different backgrounds. Councils and communities across the country hold citizenship ceremonies where new citizens make their pledge, often with family and friends looking on. Existing citizens can take part too by making an affirmation, and schools run activities about democracy and living together.

Time's Up Day on 17 September is a reminder that some things have waited long enough. It invites people to set aside old grudges and reach out to someone they have fallen out with, before more time slips away. Life is too short to carry feuds for years, and a simple call, message or apology can close a distance that once seemed permanent. People mark the day by making that first move, mending a friendship or finally saying sorry.

Constitution Day on 17 September marks the day in 1787 when delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia signed the United States Constitution. Officially called Constitution Day and Citizenship Day, it also honours everyone who has become an American citizen, whether by birth or by naturalisation. Schools hold lessons on the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, and many naturalisation ceremonies take place on or around the date. It is a day to think about the rights and duties shared by every citizen.

slogans.en: A document that still shapes us.

descriptions.en: Global Company Culture Day, on September 18, celebrates the shared values, habits and relationships that shape how a workplace feels. Culture is what decides whether people feel trusted, heard and able to do their best work, so it matters as much as any strategy or product. Teams mark the day by thanking colleagues, sharing stories about what makes their workplace special and talking honestly about what could make it fairer and more welcoming.

slogans.en: Culture is how we work together.

names.en: National HIV/AIDS and Aging Awareness Day

descriptions.en: National HIV/AIDS and Aging Awareness Day, on September 18, focuses on older adults living with HIV in the United States. It was started in 2008 by The AIDS Institute, at a time when effective treatment meant more people with HIV were living into their fifties and beyond; today about half of Americans with diagnosed HIV are over fifty. The day encourages testing at every age, care that fits ageing bodies, and respect for long-term survivors who lived through the early years of the epidemic.

National First Love Day, on September 18, invites you to remember the first person who ever made your heart race. Whether that memory is sweet, bittersweet or long faded, a first love often shapes how we understand affection, longing and ourselves. People mark the day by looking through old letters and photos, replaying the songs from that time, or simply smiling at a memory, and some even reach out to say hello.

Comic Book Day, on 25 September, celebrates the art of telling stories in sequential pictures, from the newspaper strips of the late 19th century to today's graphic novels, manga and webcomics. Comics have given the world superheroes and much-loved characters as well as serious works of memoir and history, and for many readers they were the first books they loved. Fans mark the day by rereading old favourites, starting a new series, drawing their own panels or visiting a local comic shop or library.

Good Neighbor Day on September 28 invites everyone to reach across the fence — literally and figuratively. The day traces back to Becky Mattson of Arizona in the 1970s and was formalised by President Jimmy Carter's 1978 proclamation; in 2003 the date was fixed at September 28. It is a small annual nudge to introduce yourself, lend a hand, and remember that strong communities start with the people next door.

slogans.en: Start with the neighbour next door.

descriptions.en: Chic Spy Day on October 5 was created in 2015 by fashion website The Chic Spy to celebrate the anniversary of James Bond's first film, Dr. No, released on October 5, 1962. The day salutes the timeless blend of espionage, elegance, and style that has defined 007 across six decades of cinema.

Sweetest Day falls on the third Saturday of October and is celebrated mainly in the American Midwest, around the Great Lakes. It began in Cleveland, Ohio, in the early 1920s, when local candy makers promoted a day of handing out sweets, including to people who were often forgotten. Today it works as a second, smaller Valentine's Day: people give candy, cards and flowers to partners, friends and family, simply to show they care.

slogans.en: A little sweetness goes a long way.

names.en: Pretend to Be a Time Traveler Day

descriptions.en: Pretend to Be a Time Traveler Day on December 8 invites people to spend the day acting as if they have just arrived from another era. You might dress in old-fashioned clothes and marvel at smartphones, or act puzzled by today's prices as if you came from the past, or hint at future inventions as if you came from tomorrow. It is a playful way to notice how much everyday life has changed, and how strange the present might look to someone else.

slogans.en: Live the day like it is any other year.

descriptions.en: Wright Brothers Day on December 17 marks the anniversary of the Wright brothers' first successful powered flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. The 12-second, 120-foot hop aboard the Wright Flyer launched the age of aviation. The day has been an official US observance since 1959.

slogans.en: Twelve seconds that changed the world.

descriptions.en: Underdog Day, observed on the third Friday of December, honours the people and teams nobody expects to win. It celebrates the second-in-command, the backup player, the small business up against giants and the quiet worker whose effort makes others shine. The day invites people to cheer for an underdog, thank someone who works behind the scenes, and remember that many great stories began with the side nobody backed.

slogans.en: Cheer for the one no one is watching.

descriptions.en: Forget-Me-Not Day on November 10 takes its name from the small blue flower long linked with remembrance and faithful love. It is a day to remember people we have lost and to reconnect with friends and family we have drifted away from. It also draws attention to causes tied to memory, such as dementia care and missing people, and many mark it by calling an old friend or writing to someone they miss.

International Animation Day, on October 28, celebrates the art of bringing drawings, puppets and pixels to life. It was proclaimed in 2002 by ASIFA, the International Animated Film Association, and recalls October 28, 1892, when Émile Reynaud gave the first public show of his Théâtre Optique in Paris, projecting hand-painted moving pictures for a paying audience. Festivals, cinemas and schools around the world mark it with screenings, workshops and talks that honour animators of every style, from hand-drawn to stop-motion to computer animation.

slogans.en: Frame by frame, worlds come alive.

descriptions.en: Curious Events Day, on 9 October, is an informal day for the strange, the unexplained and the simply odd. Its origins are unclear, but the idea is easy to follow: take a break from routine and look at the puzzles that still surround us, from unsolved mysteries to UFO sightings and legendary creatures. It is a reminder that curiosity is where discovery begins. People mark it by swapping strange stories, reading up on an unsolved case or watching a good mystery documentary.

Swap Ideas Day on September 10 is a friendly nudge to share a good idea with someone and take one home in return. Its origins are unclear, but the point is easy to see: the best thinking often comes from talking with people who see the world differently. You might trade tips with a colleague over coffee, swap book or recipe suggestions with a friend, or ask someone outside your usual circle how they would solve a problem you are stuck on.

slogans.en: One idea in. One idea out.

descriptions.en: Be a Millionaire Day on 20 May is a light-hearted invitation to spend a day imagining life as the wealthiest version of yourself. Its origin is unclear, but its appeal is easy to understand: daydreaming about money is a quick way to discover what you really value. People mark it by planning a dream trip, picking pretend stocks or writing a wish list. Some use it more seriously, to set a savings goal or take a first small step toward financial security.

Fun at Work Day, on 1 April, is a light-hearted reminder that people do their best work when they enjoy where they work and who they work with. Sharing a date with April Fools' Day, it encourages teams to break the routine and lift the mood without losing sight of the job. Colleagues mark it with small surprises, team games, shared snacks or a lunch together, and the best celebrations leave everyone with a laugh and a little more goodwill for the weeks ahead.

Science Fiction Day on January 2 is held on the official birthday of Isaac Asimov, born around 1920 in Russia and raised in New York. A biochemistry professor, he wrote or edited around 500 books, including the Foundation series and the robot stories that introduced the Three Laws of Robotics. Fans mark the day by reading a classic or a new science-fiction novel, watching a favourite film and imagining the futures the genre has explored.

slogans.en: Read a future before it happens.

descriptions.en: International Music Day celebrates the power of music to unite people across cultures. Established in 1975 by the International Music Council, a UNESCO affiliate, the day promotes musical art in all sectors of society. It encourages people worldwide to share in five goals: to express themselves through music, to learn musical skills, to access musical involvement, to develop as artists, and to obtain fair recognition for their work.

World Sake Day is a global celebration dedicated to traditional Japanese rice wine. Launched in 1978 by the Japan Sake and Shochu Makers Association, it marks the start of the sake brewing season and the cultural craftsmanship behind every bottle. The day unites sake fans worldwide, from casual sippers to connoisseurs, in appreciation of the rice farmers and brewers who bring this ancient drink to life.

slogans.en: Crafted by hand, shared by heart.

descriptions.en: Ukraine Defenders Day honors those who serve and have served in defense of Ukraine. Established in 2014 by President Petro Poroshenko and first observed on October 14, 2015, the day was moved to October 1 in 2023. It separates Ukrainian military commemorations from those of Russia and the former Soviet Union, paying respect to fallen defenders and to the veterans who have fought for the country's independence.

World Farm Animals Day draws attention to the lives of the billions of animals raised for food each year. It is held on 2 October, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, in honour of his belief that all living beings deserve compassion. People mark it with vigils, information stands and shared plant-based meals, and many use the day to look more closely at where their food comes from and to support groups working for better farm animal welfare.

Guardian Angel Day honors the belief that each person is accompanied by a quiet, unseen protector through life's joys and difficulties. Rooted in Catholic tradition and added to the Church's calendar by Pope Paul V in 1608, the day has spread beyond any single faith. People mark it with reflection, kind acts for others, angel-inspired art, or simply pausing to feel less alone.

National Techies Day is an American day for the people who keep our computers, networks and connected devices running, from office IT staff to the friend who fixes the family Wi-Fi. Much of their work goes unnoticed until something breaks, so the day is a chance to say thank you. It also aims to spark young people's interest in technology careers. People mark it by thanking their help desk, treating the tech team to coffee, or sharing what first got them curious about how things work.

Mean Girls Day celebrates the cult 2004 film written by Tina Fey, named after the scene where Cady Heron answers that it's October 3rd. The day invites fans to quote along, wear pink, host themed parties, and revisit the movie that became a Broadway musical. It's a playful annual moment for one of pop culture's most quoted comedies.

International Ethical Hackers Day celebrates the cybersecurity professionals who find and fix vulnerabilities before malicious hackers can exploit them. Launched in 2020 by the EC-Council — a credentialing body recognized by the US Department of Defense — the day launches National Cyber Security Awareness Month each October. It promotes awareness of ethical hacking as a career and celebrates the digital shield these professionals provide.

Frugal Fun Day, on the first Saturday of October, celebrates good times that cost little or nothing. It was created by Shel Horowitz, an American author who writes about frugal living, to show that saving money and having fun go hand in hand. People mark it with a picnic in the park, a library visit, a board-game night, a hike, a swap party with friends or an evening of stargazing, and by sharing their best free ideas with others.

slogans.en: Joy that doesn't cost a fortune.

descriptions.en: Manufacturing Day, observed on the first Friday of October, opens the doors of American factories to students, families, and the curious. Founded in 2012 by The Manufacturing Institute and FABTECH International, the day reframes modern manufacturing as a high-tech, opportunity-rich field. Hundreds of facilities across all 50 states host tours, job fairs, and demonstrations, reaching tens of thousands of community members each year.

National Hair Day, observed in the United States on 5 March, celebrates hair in all its textures, colours and styles, and the stylists and creativity behind it. Hair has always been a way to express identity, culture and mood, from braids passed down through generations to the latest salon trends. People mark the day by trying a new cut or style, treating their hair to some extra care, or thanking the stylist who knows them best.

slogans.en: Every day can be a good hair day.

descriptions.en: ROK Alliance Day celebrates the enduring partnership between the United States and the Republic of Korea. Anchored by the 1953 U.S.-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty, the alliance has grown beyond military cooperation to include economic, technological, and cultural exchanges. The day honors the veterans and shared values that hold the partnership together and the cooperation that addresses regional and global challenges.

Walk Your Dog Week, held in the first week of October, is a seven-day reminder that dogs need regular exercise, fresh air and time with their people. A daily walk helps keep a dog at a healthy weight, burns off energy that might otherwise turn into chewing or barking, and gives the nose a world of new smells to explore. Owners mark the week by adding an extra walk, trying a new route or park, or joining friends and their dogs for a group stroll.

slogans.en: A walk a day keeps the vet away.

descriptions.en: Sekaten is a vibrant Javanese celebration honoring the birth of the Prophet Muhammad, blending Islamic teaching with local customs.
