Founded in the 15th century during the reign of Sultan Hamengkubuwono I of Yogyakarta, the festival uses gamelan music, parades, traditional dance, and market stalls to draw crowds and share Islamic teachings. Today it remains a cherished cultural and spiritual moment across Java.

slogans.en: Faith and culture, side by side.

descriptions.en: National Vodka Day raises a glass to one of the world's most versatile spirits. Although often associated with Russia, vodka is produced and enjoyed across many countries, from Poland and Sweden to the United States. The Slavic word means "little water," and the spirit dates to the Middle Ages, when monks likely first distilled it from grains or potatoes. After World War II, vodka spread globally and became the foundation of countless cocktails, from the martini to the Moscow Mule.

Global James Bond Day celebrates 007, the superspy created by Ian Fleming in his 1953 novels and brought to the silver screen in 1962 with Dr. No. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, the world's most famous secret agent has defined cinematic cool across generations — fast cars, exotic locations, sharp suits, and a license to kill. The day invites fans to revisit the books, marathon the films, or just feel a little more dashing for a day.

National Get Funky Day is a chance to break out of a rut and shake off the dust. Founded in 2016 by Funkytown Fitness in St. Augustine, Florida, the day invites everyone to step outside their comfort zone — through dance, music, a flash of color, or just bringing a little more joy to those around them. Born from a wish to lift spirits after Hurricane Matthew, it's a reminder that getting funky is really about reconnecting with what makes you feel alive.

names.en: National Get Out N Drive Day

descriptions.en: National Get Out N Drive Day celebrates the simple joy of being behind the wheel. Started in 2020 by Joann Meyer, co-creator of the Get Out N Drive Podcast, the day invites people to rediscover driving as a passion rather than a chore. Whether you take the vintage out for a spin, hit the open road without a map, or just cruise with friends and good music, the day is about motion, freedom, and the stories that happen between point A and point B.

National Noodle Day celebrates the simple, soothing comfort of noodles in every shape and form. From Italian pasta to Japanese ramen, Chinese lo mein to Thai khao soi, noodles have been a foundation of working-class cuisine across cultures for two thousand years. The day invites you to try a new variety, host a noodle potluck with friends, or simply enjoy a steaming bowl of something familiar.

slogans.en: A bowl of comfort, anywhere in the world.

descriptions.en: National German-American Day, on 6 October, honours the millions of Americans with German roots and what their families brought to the United States. The date recalls 6 October 1683, when thirteen families from Krefeld landed in Philadelphia and went on to found Germantown, among the first German settlements in America. President Ronald Reagan proclaimed the day in 1983 for the 300th anniversary, and Congress made it an annual observance in 1987. Heritage clubs mark it with German food, music, folk dancing and talks on family history.

National Plus Size Appreciation Day celebrates bodies of every shape and pushes back against narrow beauty standards. Established in 2016 by Women Rock, Inc., the day promotes self-love, body positivity, and the inclusive spirit of communities that have long been left out of mainstream fashion and media. Attend a plus-size fashion show, host a clothing swap, or simply treat the people around you — and yourself — to kinder words in the mirror.

National Depression Screening Day encourages people to check in on their mental health through free, confidential screenings. Founded in 1990 by Harvard psychiatrist Dr. Douglas Jacobs and first observed in 1991, the day opens the door to conversations that often stay hidden. Schools, clinics, and workplaces now participate, offering simple tools that can guide someone toward care — and reminding anyone struggling that asking for help is the first step toward brighter days.

slogans.en: Asking for help is the first step.

descriptions.en: National Inner Beauty Day shines a light on the qualities that can't be measured by a mirror — kindness, creativity, courage, and resilience. Founded in 2017 by Roma Newton of 6° Degrees Management in partnership with the National Day Calendar, the day also raises awareness of human trafficking and the people affected by it. The invitation is simple: appreciate what's within yourself, extend that grace to others, and let inner beauty be the standard.

slogans.en: The truest beauty comes from within.

descriptions.en: You Matter To Me Day is a reminder to tell the people in your life how much they mean to you. Started in 2010 by Linda Jew of California after losing a friend and his son without ever saying those four words, the day falls on the New Moon in Libra each year — a phase associated with fresh starts and balance in relationships. Send a note, make a call, share a meal. The gesture is small, but the ripple can be enormous.

The Baku Jazz Festival fills the streets of Azerbaijan's capital with music every autumn. Founded in 2005 by saxophonist Rain Sultanov to celebrate a genre that had been banned during the Soviet era, the festival has grown into a multi-venue citywide showcase. World-class artists like Herbie Hancock and Al Jarreau have shared the stage with local Azerbaijani talents, and the festival is now a UNESCO International Jazz Day partner — a powerful symbol of jazz's universal reach.

slogans.en: Jazz from the shores of the Caspian.

descriptions.en: World Space Week is the largest annual space event on Earth, celebrated in over 95 countries during the week of October 4–10. Designated by the United Nations General Assembly in 1999, the dates honor two milestones: the launch of Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, and the signing of the Outer Space Treaty on October 10, 1967. Each year carries a new theme, with schools, agencies, and enthusiasts hosting rocket launches, stargazing nights, and conversations about how space technology shapes our daily lives.

Oktoberfest in Blumenau is the largest German heritage festival outside Germany, held annually in the Brazilian city founded by German immigrants. Started in 1984 as a morale-booster after a devastating flood, the festival has grown into a multi-week celebration of Bavarian traditions — dirndls and lederhosen, bratwurst and pretzels, oompah bands and folk dances. Hundreds of thousands gather each year to celebrate German-Brazilian heritage with parades, food, and plenty of Gemütlichkeit.

slogans.en: Brazil's German heart beats loudest in October.

descriptions.en: Fire Prevention Week is observed annually in the United States during the week containing October 9, commemorating the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. Sponsored since 1922 by the National Fire Protection Association and proclaimed a national observance by President Calvin Coolidge in 1925, the week teaches families and communities how to prevent fires and respond safely if one starts. Schools lead the charge with classroom drills and educational programs every fall.

Active Aging Week celebrates the positive contributions older adults make to their communities and promotes healthy, engaged living at every age. Launched in 2003 by the International Council on Active Aging under its CEO Colin Milner, the week brings senior centers, retirement communities, and local organizations together for fitness events, brain games, social gatherings, and travel. The message is simple: aging well is a team sport, and it starts with staying active — physically, mentally, and socially.

slogans.en: Age is an attitude, not a number.

descriptions.en: National Dance Week celebrates the art and joy of dance in all its forms. Started in 1981 by the Coalition for National Dance Week (now the National Dance Foundation), the week brings more than a thousand events to communities across the United States — dance mobs, classes, performances, and social dances. After 40+ years in April, the celebration moved to the fall in 2024, anchoring the week around two full weekends of movement and community.

slogans.en: Move your body, lift your spirit.

descriptions.en: World Octopus Day celebrates one of the ocean's most extraordinary creatures. Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood, and around 500 million neurons distributed between brain and arms — letting them solve problems, use tools, and change color with a creativity that rivals any land animal. Fossils date back more than 300 million years, predating dinosaurs. The day invites us to learn about them, share their strangeness, and recognize the intelligence hiding beneath the waves.

slogans.en: Eight arms, three hearts, infinite wonder.

descriptions.en: International Off-Road Day brings together drivers and riders who chase the trail less traveled. Launched in 2021 by Can-Am Off-Road (a BRP brand), the day celebrates the thrill of venturing beyond paved roads — on ATVs, dirt bikes, and 4x4s — across deserts, forests, and mountain passes. It's also a moment to honor the responsibility that comes with it: respect for the land, safe riding practices, and a global community bonded by shared dust and shared trails.

slogans.en: Beyond the pavement, into the wild.

descriptions.en: World Dyslexia Day shines a light on a learning difference that affects how the brain processes words — but doesn't touch intelligence or creativity. Launched in 2013 by the European Dyslexia Association, the day replaces old myths with real conversations: people with dyslexia often excel in design, storytelling, music, and seeing patterns others miss. Across schools, workplaces, and communities, the day invites honest discussion, supportive tools, and a reminder that the difference isn't a weakness — a lack of support is.

National Mall Walking Day invites everyone to step outside and reconnect with movement, nature, and history. Started in 2019 by the Shopkick app, the day encourages casual strolls in scenic places — the National Mall in Washington, D.C. is the flagship — with its monuments, open lawns, and shaded paths. It's not about steps or pace; it's about the simple, restorative act of walking somewhere meaningful, whether alone, with coworkers, or with family.

National Sneakers Day celebrates the everyday shoes that carry us through every part of life. From soft rubber-soled plimsolls in the late 1800s to today's collaborations between sportswear brands and musicians, sneakers have grown from gym gear into cultural artifacts. Started as a celebration of sneaker culture and now observed by collectors, runners, and streetwear fans alike, the day is a chance to pull on your favorite pair, share what you love, and maybe donate the ones gathering dust.

World Homeless Day raises awareness of the more than 100 million people worldwide without adequate housing. First observed in 2005 and born from conversations among aid workers across continents, the day carries a simple slogan: 'locals act locally on a global day.' It invites grassroots campaigns, fundraisers, and education in your own community, while standing in solidarity with everyone working on homelessness around the world. The day's message is that the path out of homelessness runs through local action — and that every person deserves safety, autonomy, and a place to call home.

National Motorcycle Ride Day fires up engines every second Saturday in October. Established in 2015 by Chad Geer of Dunlop Motorcycle Tires to mark the end of the traditional riding season, the day invites bikers to take one last ride through crisp autumn air before colder weather sets in. It's both a celebration of the freedom and community of motorcycling — and a reminder of the safety advances like the pneumatic tire that made riding accessible. Group rides, charity events, and rallies fill the day worldwide.

Pastor Appreciation Day honors the clergy whose work rarely fits into a 9-to-5 schedule — preparing sermons, sitting with families in crisis, leading weddings and funerals, and carrying the spiritual weight of their congregations. Established in 1992 as Clergy Appreciation Day and championed by Focus on the Family, the day is celebrated on the second Sunday of October as part of Pastor Appreciation Month. Congregations mark the occasion with notes, gifts, surprise sermons, or simply covering a Sunday service so their pastor can rest.

slogans.en: For the shepherds who never clock out.

names.en: Procession of Our Lady of Nazareth

descriptions.en: The Procession of Our Lady of Nazareth — Círio de Nazaré — is one of the largest Catholic processions in the world, drawing more than two million faithful to the streets of Belém, Brazil each year on the second Sunday of October. The tradition dates to 1793, when a humble caboclo named Plácido José de Souza reportedly found a small statue of the Virgin Mary near the Murutucu stream. Believers carry the image through the city in a tide of prayer, music, and flowers — a moving expression of Brazilian Catholic faith that UNESCO added to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2013.

slogans.en: Two million faithful, one tide of prayer.

descriptions.en: It's My Party Day, observed on October 11, invites anyone to throw a celebration — birthday or not, big or small. The day takes its name from Lesley Gore's 1963 hit, which turned a teenager's lament about a ruined party into an anthem for claiming joy on your own terms. Whether it's a costume bash, a karaoke night, or a quiet dinner with friends, the day's invitation is the same: don't wait for an occasion — make one. Life is short, the cake can be store-bought.

slogans.en: Don't wait for an occasion. Make one.

descriptions.en: Dysautonomia Awareness Month, observed every October since 2012, shines a light on a family of conditions that affect the autonomic nervous system — the part that regulates heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, temperature, and digestion. Launched by Dysautonomia International, the month raises awareness, lowers diagnostic delays, and supports the more than 70 million people worldwide who live with these conditions. Turquoise is the awareness color; wearing a turquoise ribbon or sharing resources is a simple, visible way to start a conversation.

slogans.en: Awareness shortens the path to diagnosis.

descriptions.en: Seed Gathering Season, observed in the UK from late September through October, invites communities to collect seeds from local trees, flowers, and fruits as autumn sets in. Launched in the early 2000s by The Tree Council under Director of Trees Jon Stokes, the season started as a single day and expanded to a month so different species' ripening times could all be included. Seed swaps, guided walks, and workshops teach plant identification and seed collection while supporting biodiversity and native species preservation.

slogans.en: Gather, share, plant — the future starts in your hands.

descriptions.en: The Phuket Vegetarian Festival — known locally as the Nine Emperor Gods Festival — transforms Phuket, Thailand into a vibrant hub of devotion each year in early October. Believed to have begun in the early 19th century when a Chinese opera troupe recovered from illness after adopting a strict vegetarian diet and honoring the Nine Emperor Gods, the festival is now famous for daily processions, fire-walking, body-piercing rituals, and streets filled with yellow-flagged vegetarian stalls. Tens of thousands of participants and tourists gather to share in the spiritual purification and the food.

slogans.en: Nine gods, nine days, one shared feast.

descriptions.en: The Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta is the world's largest balloon festival, drawing hundreds of hot air balloons of every shape and color to the New Mexico desert each October. Held annually since 1972 and running about nine days in early October, the fiesta features mass ascensions where hundreds of balloons lift off at once, glowing night glows where envelopes are illuminated like lanterns, and special-shape balloons that defy belief. The event transforms the Albuquerque skyline into a moving painting each fall.

slogans.en: Where the desert sky becomes a sea of color.

descriptions.en: AgitÁgueda is an annual urban art festival held in Águeda, Portugal each July. Streets are transformed with colorful floating umbrella canopies, art installations, performances, and street art spread across the town. The festival turns an ordinary Portuguese municipality into a walkable open-air gallery, drawing visitors from across Europe for its bold combination of color, sound, and creative expression.

The Fuji Shibazakura Festival is a springtime floral celebration at the base of Mount Fuji in Japan. Each year, around 500,000 shibazakura (pink moss) flowers bloom across the Fuji Five Lakes region, creating a sweeping carpet of pink beneath Japan's most iconic mountain. Held from mid-April through late May, the festival combines nature walks, local food stalls, and some of the most photographed floral scenery in the country.

slogans.en: Half a million flowers beneath Mount Fuji.

descriptions.en: Holi Festival of Color is the joyful Hindu celebration of the triumph of good over evil and the arrival of spring. Celebrated primarily in India and Nepal around the March full moon, the festival has spread worldwide as a celebration of color, where friends throw vibrant powders at each other in the streets, share sweets, and let go of the year's grievances. From Delhi street parties to community festivals in major cities across the world, Holi has become a global invitation to play, laugh, and start fresh.

slogans.en: Throw color. Shake off the past.

descriptions.en: SF Pride is San Francisco's annual celebration of LGBTQIA+ community, identity, and visibility, held each year on the last Sunday of June. What began in 1970 to commemorate the Stonewall Riots now draws more than a hundred thousand people to one of the oldest and largest Pride parades in the world. The weekend brings street parties, performances, and an unmistakable message of belonging across the city's Castro district and Civic Center.

slogans.en: One of the oldest, still the loudest.

descriptions.en: The Jaisalmer Desert Festival is a three-day celebration of Rajasthani culture held every February in the golden city of Jaisalmer, India. Folk music and dance, camel polo and races, turban-tying contests, and processions against the backdrop of the Sam Sand Dunes bring the Thar Desert to vivid life. The festival culminates under the full moon with a sound-and-light show that lights up the sandstone walls of the fort.

slogans.en: Three days where the desert sings.

descriptions.en: Burning Man is an annual experiment in temporary community, art, and self-expression held in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada each year on the Sunday before and through Labor Day. Founded in 1986 on San Francisco's Baker Beach, the event has grown into a pop-up city of more than 70,000 participants who build massive art installations, perform, barter, and ultimately burn a giant wooden effigy on the final night. The principles — radical self-expression, radical self-reliance, gifting, decommodification, and leaving no trace — define what makes Black Rock City unlike anywhere else on Earth.

slogans.en: Where the desert becomes a city.

descriptions.en: Austin City Limits Music Festival, better known as ACL, turns two October weekends in Austin's Zilker Park into one of the largest music festivals in the United States. Inspired by the long-running PBS concert series of the same name, ACL features dozens of headliners across eight stages, with a focus on indie rock, country, hip-hop, and electronic music. Beyond the music, the festival showcases Austin's legendary food scene, art installations, and the city's famously warm hospitality.

slogans.en: Two weekends, one city, every stage.

descriptions.en: Honolulu's Floating Lanterns Festival takes place annually on Memorial Day at Moana Beach Park, drawing thousands of people to release floating lanterns onto the water. Each lantern carries a handwritten message honoring a loved one who has passed, creating a luminous, deeply moving ceremony against the Hawaiian sunset. The festival blends Japanese hanauma tradition with Pacific Island ceremony, offering a quiet space for remembrance amid one of America's most beautiful settings.

slogans.en: Light a lantern. Send a message. Remember.

descriptions.en: Art Basel Miami Beach is the American edition of the prestigious Art Basel fair, held annually the first week of December. The Miami Beach Convention Center becomes a temporary mecca for over 4,000 artists and 200 modern and contemporary galleries from across the world. Beyond the fair itself, the week brings satellite shows across Wynwood, the Design District, and Miami's beaches, plus parties and installations that turn the city into a week-long celebration of contemporary art.

slogans.en: A week where Miami becomes the art world.

descriptions.en: The Harbin Ice Festival is China's premier winter spectacle, held annually from late December through February in the sub-zero city of Harbin. Massive ice and snow sculptures — some the size of multi-story buildings — are carved and illuminated with colored lights, drawing millions of visitors to see the world's largest ice festival. The festival includes the Harbin Ice and Snow World, ice swimming competitions, and Siberian Tiger Park visits, transforming one of China's coldest cities into a luminous winter kingdom.

slogans.en: A city of ice, lit from within.

descriptions.en: San Diego Comic-Con is the largest comic book and pop culture convention in the world, drawing around 130,000 attendees each summer to the San Diego Convention Center. What began in 1970 as a small gathering of comic book fans has grown into a four-day cultural phenomenon where Hollywood studios unveil blockbuster trailers, artists sketch legendary characters, and fans celebrate every corner of genre storytelling. The convention has shaped mainstream entertainment for over 50 years.

slogans.en: Where the world's biggest stories meet their fans.

descriptions.en: Mardi Gras is the centuries-old carnival celebration culminating on the day before Ash Wednesday, with the largest celebration held each year in New Orleans, Louisiana. The season officially begins on Twelfth Night (January 6) and runs until Fat Tuesday, featuring parades led by social clubs known as krewes, masquerade balls, brass band concerts, and the iconic purple, green, and gold colors. What began as a European pre-Lenten tradition has become one of America's most distinctive cultural celebrations, rooted deeply in New Orleans' French and Creole heritage.

Glastonbury Festival is England's largest greenfield music festival, held annually on the last weekend of June at Worthy Farm in Somerset. Drawing nearly 200,000 people to a town that normally holds fewer than 9,000, Glastonbury transforms a dairy farm into a pop-up city for five days of music, theater, circus, and political expression. Headliners from rock, pop, and electronic music share stages with emerging artists across dozens of venues, while the surrounding Somerset countryside becomes a temporary home to hundreds of thousands of tents.

The August Moon Festival is Greece's annual celebration of the full moon in August, when the country's archaeological sites, museums, and monuments open their doors after hours for concerts, theatrical performances, poetry readings, and guided tours beneath moonlight. From the Acropolis and the Roman Agora in Athens to ancient theatres across the islands, more than a hundred sites participate in a single night of culture and starlight. Locals and visitors gather where the past meets the moonlit present.

Calan Gaeaf, the first day of winter in the old Welsh calendar, falls on November 1 and closes the harvest season. The night before, Nos Calan Gaeaf, was an ysbrydnos, a spirit night, when people lit bonfires, marked stones with their names and avoided churchyards and crossroads. Tales warned of the ladi wen, a white lady, and the hwch ddu gwta, a tailless black sow said to chase stragglers home.

slogans.en: When the veil between worlds grows thin.

descriptions.en: Zero Tasking Day lands on the first Sunday of November, just as clocks fall back. It invites everyone to use the extra hour not for more to-dos, but for a long walk, an unhurried book, or simply a nap — anything that lets the mind drift. Coinciding with the end of daylight saving time, it is a quiet nudge toward rest, reflection, and the underrated art of doing nothing.

Prime Meridian Day marks the International Meridian Conference in Washington, which ended on November 1, 1884. Delegates from 25 nations chose the meridian passing through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, as zero degrees longitude. That line still anchors world maps, navigation and the time zones measured from Greenwich, and visitors to the observatory stand with one foot in each hemisphere.

slogans.en: The line that holds the world together.

descriptions.en: On the first Sunday of November, daylight saving time ends across most of the United States and clocks fall back one hour at 2 a.m. The rules come from the Uniform Time Act of 1966, and the November date has applied since 2007. Many households use the extra hour to reset clocks, test smoke alarms and enjoy a brighter morning.

slogans.en: One hour back. One more morning light.

descriptions.en: Kannada Rajyotsava marks November 1, 1956, when the Kannada-speaking regions of southern India were united into one state under the States Reorganisation Act. The state was first called Mysore and was renamed Karnataka in 1973. Every year the red-and-yellow Kannada flag flies across the state, schools and towns hold cultural programmes, and the government presents the Rajyotsava Awards to people who have served Karnataka.

slogans.en: One state. One language. One pride.

descriptions.en: National Animal Shelter Appreciation Week, held in the first full week of November, was established by the Humane Society of the United States in 1996. It honours the staff and volunteers who care for lost, abandoned and surrendered animals and work to find them new homes. People mark the week by adopting or fostering a pet, donating food and blankets, or volunteering a few hours at a local shelter.

slogans.en: Every shelter pet is a second chance.

descriptions.en: World Communication Week, held in the first full week of November, celebrates the skills that let people understand one another. It focuses on clear speaking, careful listening and honest writing, whether between colleagues, within families or across cultures. Workplaces and schools use the week for workshops, public-speaking events and simple exercises in listening better.

Samhain is the ancient Celtic festival at the heart of the harvest-to-winter turn, observed from October 31 into November 1. It marks the night when the veil between the living and the dead is believed to grow thin — a time for bonfires, dumb suppers, and reading the year ahead. Many of its customs travelled with Irish and Scottish emigrants and grew into the Halloween now celebrated worldwide.

slogans.en: Where the year turns, and the veil thins.

descriptions.en: Polar Bear Week, organised by Polar Bears International, takes place in early November, when polar bears gather near Churchill, Manitoba, waiting for the sea ice on Hudson Bay to freeze. Polar bears hunt seals from the ice, so a shorter ice season means a longer fast on land. The week draws attention to the effects of a warming Arctic, with live bear cams, school lessons and calls to cut carbon emissions.

slogans.en: Their ice is melting. Act now.

descriptions.en: Truffle Days in Croatia celebrate the autumn truffle season in Istria, centred on the village of Livade at the edge of the Motovun Forest. The damp woods along the Mirna River are famous for white truffles, among the most prized ingredients in the world, and black truffles grow there too. Over several autumn weekends visitors can join truffle hunters and their trained dogs, watch cooking demonstrations, and taste truffle dishes alongside Istrian wine, olive oil and cheese. For many local families, truffle hunting is a skill handed down through generations.

slogans.en: Where the forest hides its treasure.

descriptions.en: Lung Cancer Awareness Month in November draws attention to the cancer that kills more people worldwide than any other. In the United States the month is recognised by presidential proclamation, and patient groups use it to push for screening, which can find the disease early when it is most treatable. Campaigns also fight the stigma that lung cancer only affects smokers, since many patients have never smoked.

National Children's Month is observed in the Philippines every November under a 2015 law, Republic Act 10661. November was chosen because the UN adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child on November 20, 1989, and the Philippines ratified it the following year. Government agencies, schools and charities use the month for programmes on child protection, health, nutrition and education.

slogans.en: Every child deserves a chance to thrive.

descriptions.en: Recreation Day is a public holiday in northern Tasmania, Australia, held on the first Monday of November. It gives the north a long weekend to balance Royal Hobart Regatta Day, which is a holiday in the south of the state. With spring well underway, people use it for barbecues, bushwalks, fishing, gardening and the first outdoor outings of the warm season.

slogans.en: A day off, before the long summer.

descriptions.en: International Doge Day on November 2 celebrates Kabosu, the Shiba Inu from Japan whose sideways glance became the Doge meme. Her owner, kindergarten teacher Atsuko Sato, posted the photo on her blog in 2010, and it spread around the world with captions in broken, cheerful English. Kabosu died in 2024, and fans now mark her birthday by sharing Doge memes, donating to animal charities and repeating her motto, Do Only Good Everyday.

All Souls' Day on November 2 is the Christian day of prayer for all the faithful departed. The custom of a yearly commemoration on this date was set by Abbot Odilo of Cluny around the year 1000 and spread across the Western Church. Families visit cemeteries, light candles on graves and attend memorial services for relatives and friends who have died.

National Housewife Day, also called National Homemaker Day, is observed in the United States on November 3. It honours the unpaid work of running a home: cooking, cleaning, managing budgets and raising children, work that keeps families going but rarely gets recognised. People mark it by thanking a homemaker in their life, sharing the chores, or giving them a day off.

slogans.en: Running a home is real work.

descriptions.en: Melbourne Cup Day, the first Tuesday of November, is built around the race that stops a nation. First run in 1861 at Flemington Racecourse, the Melbourne Cup is a 3,200-metre handicap and a public holiday in metropolitan Melbourne. Across Australia, offices hold sweepstakes, racegoers dress up in hats and suits, and the country pauses for about three minutes to watch the race.

slogans.en: The race that stops a nation.

descriptions.en: US Election Day falls on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, a date set for federal elections by Congress in 1845. In a farming country, November came after the harvest and before harsh winter travel, and Tuesday let voters travel to the county seat without missing Sunday worship or Wednesday market day. Americans vote for offices from local school boards to Congress, and every four years for president.

Eating Healthy Day, on the first Wednesday of November, was promoted by the American Heart Association to encourage better everyday food choices. Diet plays a major role in heart disease, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, and small changes add up over a lifetime. The day suggests simple steps: more vegetables, fruit and whole grains, less salt and added sugar, more water, and cooking at home with family.

Flag Day in Panama on November 4 honours the national flag, first raised in 1903 when Panama separated from Colombia. It was designed by Manuel Encarnación Amador and sewn by María de la Ossa de Amador; its blue and red stand for the country's two traditional political parties and its white for the peace between them. The day falls between Separation Day and Colón Day, and schools and towns fill the streets with marching bands and parades.

slogans.en: The flag that won a country.

descriptions.en: National Cancer Awareness Day is observed in India on November 7, the birthday of Marie Curie, whose work on radioactivity laid foundations for cancer treatment. It was announced in 2014 by Union Health Minister Harsh Vardhan to promote early detection, since many cancers in India are diagnosed late. Hospitals and health groups mark the day with free screening camps, talks on tobacco and diet, and campaigns against the stigma around cancer.

Eat a Red Apple Day on December 1 celebrates one of the world's most familiar fruits. Apples were first domesticated in Central Asia, in the mountains of today's Kazakhstan, and thousands of varieties are now grown around the world. They are rich in fibre and vitamin C, travel well in a lunchbox, and the day is a simple nudge to pick one up instead of a sweet snack.

slogans.en: An apple a day, shared with joy.

descriptions.en: Advent in Zagreb turns the Croatian capital into a Christmas market that spreads across its squares, parks and streets from late November to early January. Visitors find wooden stalls selling mulled wine, sausages and fritule doughnuts, an ice rink at King Tomislav Square, concerts and a lights display in Zrinjevac park. Readers of the travel website European Best Destinations voted it the best Christmas market in Europe three years running, from 2016 to 2018.

The Hornbill Festival is held every year from December 1 to 10 at the Naga Heritage Village of Kisama, near Kohima in the Indian state of Nagaland. Started by the state government in 2000, it brings together all of Nagaland's tribes, and its opening day coincides with Nagaland Statehood Day. It takes its name from the hornbill, a bird that appears throughout Naga folklore, and fills the days with traditional dances, songs, crafts, food, archery and a rock music contest.

Play Basketball Day on December 2 celebrates the simple pleasure of picking up a ball and shooting a few hoops. The game was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, a physical education teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts, using two peach baskets as goals. People mark the day with pickup games at the local court, shooting contests and a game with friends or family.

World Computer Literacy Day on December 2 was launched in 2001 by the Indian IT training company NIIT. It draws attention to the digital divide, the gap between people who can use computers and the internet and those who cannot, which often falls along lines of income, age and gender. Schools, libraries and volunteers mark it with free classes that teach basic digital skills, from typing and email to staying safe online.

Make a Gift Day on December 3 encourages people to skip the shop and make a present by hand. It could be a batch of cookies, a knitted scarf, a drawing, a photo album, a playlist or a heartfelt letter. Homemade gifts often mean more because of the time and thought behind them, and the day is a good moment to start on them before the holiday rush.

Celebrate Shelter Pets Day honours the dogs, cats and other animals waiting in shelters, and the many adopted pets who once waited there too. Millions of animals enter shelters every year, and adoption gives them a second chance while freeing space for others in need. People mark the day by sharing photos of their adopted pets, donating to a local shelter or meeting the animals available for adoption.

slogans.en: Every shelter pet deserves a story.

descriptions.en: National Blue Jeans Day on December 5 celebrates denim jeans, first patented in 1873 by tailor Jacob Davis and merchant Levi Strauss, who reinforced work trousers with copper rivets. Made for miners and labourers, jeans later became a symbol of youth culture and are now worn almost everywhere. The day is an easy excuse to wear a favourite pair, and some charities use it for denim-themed fundraising.

slogans.en: Live in denim. Love in denim.

descriptions.en: Crate Day falls on the first Saturday of December in New Zealand and marks the unofficial start of the Kiwi summer. It began in 2010 as a promotion by The Rock radio station and has grown into a popular tradition of gathering friends for a barbecue and sharing a crate of beer. Organisers and health groups also use it to promote drinking responsibly, staying hydrated in the sun and arranging a safe way home.

slogans.en: Crack a crate. Crack a smile.

descriptions.en: National Miners Day on December 6 honours mine workers in the United States and the risks they take to supply coal, metals and minerals. The date recalls the Monongah mining disaster in West Virginia on December 6, 1907, the deadliest mining accident in American history, which killed hundreds of men and boys. The day remembers those lost in mining accidents and recognises the safety laws that came after them.

names.en: Canada National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women

descriptions.en: Canada's National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence against Women on December 6 was established by Parliament in 1991. It marks the anniversary of the 1989 shooting at the École Polytechnique in Montreal, where fourteen women were murdered because they were women. Canadians mark the day with vigils, moments of silence and flags at half-mast, and use it to act against gender-based violence today.

The Rakia and Spirits Festival is held in Sofia, Bulgaria, in early December and celebrates rakia, the fruit brandy that is a national drink across much of the Balkans. Rakia is distilled from grapes, plums, apricots and other fruit, and many families still make their own in the autumn. The festival brings together distillers and visitors for tastings, competitions and talks on traditional production.

slogans.en: Sip the spirit of the Balkans.

descriptions.en: Operation Santa Paws runs from December 1 to December 24 and asks animal lovers to support shelters and rescued pets during the season of giving. Shelters often fill up in winter, when strays need protection from the cold and some pets are given up. People take part by donating food, blankets and toys, volunteering their time, or fostering an animal through the holidays.

slogans.en: Give a little love to those who give it all year.

descriptions.en: National Cat Lovers Month in December celebrates the bond between cats and the people who share their homes with them. Cats were first domesticated around 10,000 years ago in the Near East, probably drawn to farming villages by the mice in stored grain, and today they are among the world's most popular pets. The month is a chance to spoil a cat, read up on its health and behaviour, and help shelter cats waiting for a home.

Decembeard is a December fundraising campaign in which people grow a beard, or wear a fake one, to raise money and awareness for bowel cancer. It is run in the UK by the charity Bowel Cancer UK, and similar campaigns run elsewhere. Bowel cancer is one of the most common cancers, but it is far more treatable when caught early, so the month also encourages people to know the symptoms and take part in screening.

slogans.en: Grow it. Talk it. Beat it.

descriptions.en: Walt Disney Day on December 5 marks the birthday of Walt Disney, born in Chicago in 1901. With his studio he created Mickey Mouse, who appeared with synchronised sound in Steamboat Willie in 1928, and made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length cel-animated feature film, in 1937. He later opened Disneyland in 1955, and fans celebrate the day by watching classic films and revisiting the characters he brought to life.

slogans.en: Dreams are made where imagination lives.

descriptions.en: World Techno Day on December 9 celebrates techno, the electronic dance music that emerged in Detroit in the 1980s. It was shaped by three friends from the Detroit suburb of Belleville, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, who blended funk, electro and European synth music into a sound built on drum machines and synthesisers. Techno later found a second home in Berlin's clubs after the fall of the Wall, and the day is marked with DJ sets and parties around the world.

slogans.en: Feel the pulse of the machine.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Commemoration and Dignity of the Victims of the Crime of Genocide and of the Prevention of this Crime is observed on December 9. It was established by the UN General Assembly in 2015 and marks the adoption on that date in 1948 of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. The day honours the victims of past genocides and calls for education, early warning and action to prevent new ones.

International Animal Rights Day on December 10 was started in 1998 by the British animal rights group Uncaged, choosing the same day as Human Rights Day. Its organisers argue that animals, too, can suffer and deserve protection from cruelty and exploitation. People mark it with vigils, information stands and choices such as cruelty-free products and plant-based meals.

names.en: Festival for the Souls of Dead Whales

descriptions.en: The Festival for the Souls of Dead Whales on December 10 is a day of remembrance for whales killed by hunting, pollution, fishing nets and ship strikes. It echoes old traditions in coastal communities in Japan and elsewhere, where people built memorials and held services for the whales they relied on. People mark the day with art, beach clean-ups, documentaries and support for groups working to protect whales and the oceans.

Constitution Day in Thailand on December 10 marks 1932, when King Prajadhipok, Rama VII, granted the country's first permanent constitution. It followed the revolution of June that year, which ended absolute monarchy and made Thailand a constitutional monarchy. The day is a public holiday, and government offices, schools and ceremonies honour the constitution and the democratic principles it introduced.

slogans.en: A constitution is a promise to the people.

descriptions.en: Global Family Day on January 1 grew out of the UN's call for One Day in Peace at the start of the new millennium, and invites people to begin the year with a day of peace and togetherness. Its idea is that peace starts at home: families, neighbours and communities sharing a meal, forgiving old quarrels and reaching out across divides. People mark it by gathering with relatives, ringing bells, sharing food with neighbours and making a resolution to treat others with kindness.

The Philadelphia Mummers Parade takes place every New Year's Day and is one of the oldest folk parades in the United States, held as a city-sanctioned event since 1901. Its roots lie in European mumming traditions brought by immigrants, in which masked revellers went door to door at the turn of the year. Thousands of members of comic brigades, fancy brigades and string bands march in sequins, feathers and huge costumes, playing banjos and saxophones and performing choreographed routines.

slogans.en: Strut the New Year in feathers.

descriptions.en: Euro Day on January 1 marks the launch of the euro in 1999, when eleven European Union countries fixed their exchange rates and began using it for banking and accounting. Euro notes and coins followed on January 1, 2002, replacing currencies such as the Deutsche Mark, the French franc and the Italian lira. Today the euro is used by more than 20 countries and hundreds of millions of people, making it the world's second most important currency after the US dollar.

The World Day of Peace on January 1 was established by Pope Paul VI, who announced it in December 1967 and first celebrated it on January 1, 1968, during the Vietnam War and the Cold War. Each year the pope publishes a message for the day on a theme such as justice, dialogue, migration or the environment. It is observed by Catholics around the world with prayers for peace, and the message is sent to world leaders.

slogans.en: Be peacemakers in a small corner of the world.

descriptions.en: Haitian Independence Day on January 1 marks 1804, when Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independence of Haiti after the only successful slave revolution in history. Former slaves led by Toussaint Louverture and then Dessalines defeated the armies of Napoleon's France, and Haiti became the first Black republic and the second independent nation in the Americas. Haitians celebrate by eating soup joumou, a pumpkin soup once forbidden to the enslaved, a tradition added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2021.

slogans.en: Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité — and liberté for all.

descriptions.en: The Solemnity of Mary, the Holy Mother of God, is celebrated by the Catholic Church on January 1, the octave, or eighth day, of Christmas. It honours Mary's role as the mother of Jesus, a title, Theotokos, affirmed by the Council of Ephesus in 431, and in its current form dates from the calendar reforms of 1969. In many countries it is a holy day of obligation, and since 1968 the Catholic Church has also observed it as the World Day of Peace.

Saint Basil's Day on January 1 honours Basil the Great, the 4th-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, in today's Türkiye, remembered for his writings and for founding one of the first hospitals for the poor. In Greece and Cyprus he is the gift-bringer, Agios Vasilis, who arrives on New Year's Day. Families cut a vasilopita, a sweet bread or cake with a coin baked inside, and whoever finds the coin is said to have good luck for the year.

slogans.en: Generous as Basil, bright as New Year.

descriptions.en: Dry January is a month-long break from alcohol that began in the UK in 2013, launched by the charity now called Alcohol Change UK. It has since spread to many countries as a way to reset after the indulgence of the holidays. Many participants report better sleep, more energy and money saved, and the month often prompts people to rethink their drinking habits for the rest of the year.

Veganuary is a January pledge to try plant-based eating for a month, launched in the UK in 2014 by Jane Land and Matthew Glover. What began as a small campaign has grown into a worldwide movement, with millions of people signing up and supermarkets and restaurants launching new vegan products each January. Participants try new recipes and cuisines, and many keep eating more plant-based meals after the month ends.

National Pet Travel Safety Day on January 2 comes as many families travel home after the holidays with their pets. Loose animals in a car can distract the driver and be badly hurt in a sudden stop, so experts recommend secured crates or harnesses, regular breaks, water and never leaving a pet alone in a parked car. The day is also a reminder to keep identification tags and microchip details up to date in case a pet gets lost on the road.

Festival of Sleep Day on January 2 is an unofficial holiday for catching up on rest after the late nights of the festive season. Sleep matters more than it is often given credit for: adults need around seven to nine hours a night, and too little is linked to poorer concentration, mood and long-term health. The day invites people to have a lie-in or a nap, switch off screens early and start the year with better sleep habits.

Women Rock! Day on January 3 celebrates women in rock, pop and every corner of music, and the barriers many still face in the industry. It recalls 1987, when Aretha Franklin became the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. People mark the day by listening to and sharing music by women artists, from pioneers like Sister Rosetta Tharpe to today's bands, and by supporting women musicians, producers and engineers.

slogans.en: Play her music. Tell her story. Change the ratio.

descriptions.en: Perihelion Day falls around January 3, when Earth reaches the point in its slightly oval orbit closest to the Sun, about 147 million kilometres away. That is roughly 5 million kilometres closer than in early July, at aphelion. It surprises many people that the Northern Hemisphere's winter happens when Earth is nearest the Sun: the seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not from our distance to the Sun.

Pop Music Chart Day on January 4 marks the date in 1936 when Billboard magazine published its first music popularity chart, a list of the most-played songs on network radio. The first song at the top was Stop! Look! Listen! by Joe Venuti and his orchestra. Charts went on to shape the music industry for decades, from the Hot 100 to today's streaming rankings, and the day is a fun excuse to look up what was number one in the year you were born.

slogans.en: The charts turn scattered hits into history.

descriptions.en: National Bird Day on January 5 is a US observance that celebrates birds and draws attention to the threats they face. Habitat loss, pesticides, collisions with windows and climate change have contributed to a decline of about three billion birds in North America since 1970, according to a 2019 study. The day also raises concerns about the trade in wild-caught parrots and other pet birds, and coincides with the Christmas Bird Count, a citizen-science survey begun in 1900.

slogans.en: Look up. Learn a bird's name.

descriptions.en: Twelfth Night, the evening of January 5, marks the end of the twelve days of Christmas and the eve of Epiphany. In England it was once a night of feasting and role reversal, with a Twelfth Cake hiding a bean, and whoever found it became king of the revels, a custom that inspired the title of Shakespeare's comedy Twelfth Night. Many people still take down their Christmas decorations by this date for luck, and in cider country orchards are wassailed with songs to bless the coming harvest.

slogans.en: Twelve days complete. Bring on the cake.

descriptions.en: The National Day of Dialogue on January 5 encourages people to sit down and talk with someone whose views differ from their own. At a time of deep political and social division, it promotes listening to understand rather than to win an argument. Schools, faith groups, neighbourhoods and workplaces use the day to host structured conversations, practise curiosity and find the common ground that often hides beneath disagreements.

Three Kings Day on January 6, the Christian feast of Epiphany, celebrates the arrival of the Magi with their gifts for the infant Jesus. In Spain and much of Latin America it is the main day for children's presents: on the evening of January 5 the Three Kings parade through towns in the cabalgata, and children leave out shoes, and sometimes grass or water for the camels. Families share a ring-shaped sweet bread, the roscón or rosca de reyes, with a small figure hidden inside.

slogans.en: The journey ends. The gifts begin.

descriptions.en: The Armenian Apostolic Church celebrates Christmas on January 6, together with Theophany, the baptism of Jesus, keeping the early Christian custom of marking both feasts on one day. Armenia was the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion, traditionally dated to 301, and the church holds to this ancient practice; in Jerusalem it is observed on January 19 under the Julian calendar. Families attend a candlelit service on Christmas Eve, share a meal of fish, rice and dried fruits, and attend the blessing of water on Christmas Day.

slogans.en: The first to believe. The first to celebrate.

descriptions.en: The Alilo Parade is a joyful Georgian Christmas tradition held every January 7th. Participants of all ages dress in traditional attire, march through cities and villages, sing carols, and carry icons and flags. The streets fill with music and warmth as people share small gifts and donations, gathering at a church for a final blessing.

Orthodox Christmas Day is celebrated by Orthodox Christians worldwide on January 7th, following the Julian calendar. It marks the birth of Jesus Christ and begins a season that culminates in Epiphany on January 19th. Traditions vary across Greece, Russia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Serbia, and beyond, with liturgies, feasts, and folk customs unique to each culture.

Coptic Christmas, celebrated on January 7th, is a deeply cherished day in the Coptic Orthodox Church, marked by joy, reverence, and spiritual reflection. Homes and churches glow with candles, families gather for traditional meals like fava bean stew, and a midnight mass unites communities in prayer and song. The day honors the birth of Jesus Christ and reminds believers of the light and hope He brought into the world.

Earth's Rotation Day marks the anniversary of Léon Foucault's 1851 demonstration of the planet's spin at the Paris Panthéon. By suspending a heavy pendulum from the dome, Foucault showed that the swing's plane appears to rotate as the Earth turns beneath it. Today, Foucault Pendulums in science museums worldwide continue to make this invisible motion visible.

National Australian Shepherd Day honors the bright mind, tireless energy, and loyal heart of the Aussie. Bred to herd and built to work, Australian Shepherds thrive when given a job, a trail, or a backyard challenge. The day invites owners to celebrate with an outdoor adventure, a training session, or simply extra time together.

International Choreographers Day honors the creators behind every dance, from Broadway and film to television and concert stages. From Jean-Georges Noverre, the father of modern ballet, to today's Tony and Emmy winners, choreographers shape how the world moves. The day celebrates their craft, vision, and the joy their work brings to millions.

The Golden Globe Awards honor the year's best in film and American television, broadcast live from Beverly Hills on the first Sunday of January. Founded in 1944 by the Hollywood Foreign Correspondents Association, the ceremony is famed for its glamorous red carpet, surprise wins, and free-flowing champagne. The iconic golden statuette encircled by a film strip remains one of the most-watched entertainment events of the year.

Heritage Treasures Day raises awareness of the artifacts, monuments, and traditions that connect us to the past. Established by the Heritage Lottery Fund in the UK, the day promotes preservation of archaeological sites, museum collections, and historic architecture. It's a reminder that our shared history shapes who we are and deserves to be protected for future generations.

slogans.en: Protect the past, inspire the future.

descriptions.en: Gold Heart Day, founded in 1991 by Marsha Rae Ratcliff of Variety International, celebrates acts of kindness while raising awareness for children in need, including those facing childhood cancer. The gold heart symbolizes the inherent value of every person and the ripple effect of compassion. Across communities, people wear gold heart pins, host charity events, and share uplifting gestures.

names.en: Cigarettes Are Hazardous to Your Health Day

descriptions.en: Cigarettes Are Hazardous to Your Health Day cuts through the noise to deliver a blunt reminder: tobacco packs over 7,000 chemicals, including dozens known to cause cancer, and damages nearly every organ in the body. Secondhand smoke harms children, older adults, and the immunocompromised. The day encourages quit attempts, smoke-free spaces, and honest conversations about the real cost of smoking.

Coming of Age Day, observed on the second Monday of January in Japan and recognized in many cultures worldwide, celebrates the transition into adulthood. From Japan's Seijin no Hi to Latin America's Quinceañera and the Jewish bar and bat mitzvah, the day honors the rituals, rights, and responsibilities that mark this milestone. Newly recognized adults often gain the right to vote, drive, and make decisions that shape their future.

National Dark Chocolate Day on February 1 is an American food day for chocolate with a high share of cocoa and little or no milk. Its roots go back to the cacao drinks of Mesoamerica, where the Olmec, Maya and Aztecs prepared ground cacao beans as a bitter, often spiced drink long before sugar reached it. People mark the day by tasting bars of different cocoa percentages and origins, baking with dark chocolate or pairing it with coffee, fruit or nuts.

National Freedom Day on February 1 marks the day in 1865 when President Abraham Lincoln signed the joint resolution of Congress proposing the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery in the United States once it was ratified later that year. The observance was championed by Major Richard R. Wright Sr., who had been born into slavery, and President Harry Truman signed it into law in 1948. It opens Black History Month and is marked with readings, wreath-layings and talks on the long struggle for civil rights.

Women's Heart Week, held in the United States in the first week of February, raises awareness of heart disease, the leading cause of death among American women. It is promoted by the Women's Heart Foundation and falls at the start of American Heart Month, alongside National Wear Red Day. The week stresses that women's heart attack symptoms can differ from men's, such as shortness of breath, nausea, fatigue or pain in the back or jaw, and encourages checks of blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar.

World Interfaith Harmony Week is held in the first week of February each year. It was proposed by King Abdullah II of Jordan and adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2010, building on the idea that the world's religions share the commandments to love God and to love one's neighbour. Mosques, churches, synagogues, temples and schools mark it with open days, joint prayers, shared meals and community service projects that bring people of different faiths together.

The Carnival of Venice takes place in the weeks before Lent and is famous for its elaborate masks and 18th-century costumes. Its origins are often traced to celebrations of a Venetian victory over the Patriarch of Aquileia in 1162, and in the following centuries masks allowed people of every class to mix freely. Banned under Austrian rule and fading for much of the 19th and 20th centuries, it was revived in 1979, and today it opens with the Flight of the Angel from St Mark's Campanile and fills the city with masked balls and costume contests.

The Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show is the best-known dog show in the United States, held in New York since 1877. It is America's second-longest continuously held sporting event, after only the Kentucky Derby, and thousands of dogs from more than two hundred breeds compete to be judged closest to their breed standard. Winners of the seven groups meet in the final for Best in Show, while agility and obedience contests and a huge television audience make the event a celebration of dogs well beyond the show ring.

African Heritage and Health Week is held in the first week of February, at the start of Black History Month, by Oldways, a US nonprofit that promotes traditional diets. It celebrates the cooking traditions of Africa and the African diaspora in the Caribbean, South America and the American South, which rest on greens, beans, yams, okra, rice, peanuts and spices. Since diet-related illnesses such as high blood pressure and diabetes weigh heavily on many African American communities, the week shares recipes, cooking demonstrations and classes that bring these healthy heritage foods back to the table.

slogans.en: Taste the heritage, embrace the health.

descriptions.en: Black History Month in February honours the achievements, culture and struggles of African Americans throughout the history of the United States. It grew out of Negro History Week, launched in 1926 by the historian Carter G. Woodson and set in the second week of February to include the birthdays of Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass; it was expanded to a full month and recognised by President Gerald Ford in 1976. Schools, libraries, museums and media mark the month with lessons, exhibitions, films and events that tell the stories of Black Americans from the era of slavery to the civil rights movement and today.

The Festival of Iemanjá on February 2 honours the orixá of the sea in the Afro-Brazilian religions Candomblé and Umbanda, whose worship came to Brazil with enslaved Yoruba people from West Africa. Its best-known celebration is in the Rio Vermelho district of Salvador, Bahia, where fishermen and devotees have kept the tradition for generations. Dressed in white, crowds bring flowers, perfume, mirrors and combs to the shore, and boats carry baskets of offerings out to sea to ask Iemanjá for protection and a good catch.

The Feast of Candelaria on February 2 is the Catholic feast of Candlemas, the Presentation of Jesus in the Temple, when candles are blessed in churches as a sign of Christ as the light of the world. In the Canary Islands it honours the Virgin of Candelaria, the islands' patron saint, whose image according to tradition was found by Guanche shepherds on a beach in Tenerife before the Spanish conquest, and pilgrims gather at her basilica in the town of Candelaria. In Puno, Peru, the feast becomes a huge festival of music and costumed dance listed by UNESCO, and in Mexico families share tamales, paid for by whoever found the figure of the Christ Child in the Three Kings cake on January 6.

National Golden Retriever Day on February 3 celebrates one of the world's best-loved dog breeds. Golden Retrievers were bred in the Scottish Highlands in the 19th century to fetch game birds from water and land, which gave them a soft mouth, a love of swimming and an eagerness to work with people. Today they are family dogs, guide dogs and therapy dogs, and owners mark the day with long walks, a game of fetch and donations to Golden Retriever rescues.

St Blaise's Day on February 3 honours Saint Blaise, a bishop of Sebaste in Armenia who, according to tradition, was martyred in the early 4th century. He is the patron saint of Dubrovnik, and the city's Festivity of Saint Blaise, inscribed on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009, fills the old town with flags, processions carrying his relics, the release of white doves and folk music. In Catholic churches elsewhere, priests bless throats with two crossed candles, recalling the story that Blaise saved a boy choking on a fish bone.

Time to Talk Day is a UK day in early February that encourages everyone to have a conversation about mental health. It was launched in 2014 by Time to Change, the anti-stigma campaign run by the charities Mind and Rethink Mental Illness, to show that talking openly can break down shame and help people feel less alone. Friends, families, schools and workplaces take part by setting aside time to check in with one another, hosting tea-and-talk events and simply listening without judgement.

Optimist Day on February 1 is a reminder to look at the year ahead with hope rather than worry. Optimism is not ignoring problems but expecting that effort can make things better, an attitude that research links with greater resilience in hard times. People mark the day by writing down a few things they look forward to, sharing good news, doing a small kindness or spending time with friends who lift their spirits.

World Muay Thai Day, on February 6, celebrates Thailand's national martial art, known as the Art of Eight Limbs because fighters strike with fists, elbows, knees and shins. The date honours King Sanphet VIII of Ayutthaya, remembered as Phra Chao Suea, the Tiger King, who loved the sport and is said to have fought in village contests in disguise. Gyms and fighters around the world mark the day with the wai khru ram muay, a ritual dance of respect for teachers, along with group training, demonstrations and exhibition bouts.

Bloco da Lama is a carnival tradition in Paraty, on the coast of Rio de Janeiro state in Brazil, where revellers cover themselves from head to toe in dark mud. It began in the 1980s, when a group of local young people smeared themselves with mud from the mangroves at Jabaquara beach and paraded through town, and it has grown into one of the town's best-known carnival events. On the day, thousands of mud-caked participants march through the streets to drums and samba, many carrying bones, branches or homemade props, before washing it all off in the sea.

Sami National Day, on February 6, celebrates the Sami, the Indigenous people whose homeland stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. The date marks the first Sami congress, held in Trondheim in 1917, when Sami from different countries met to work together on their shared rights and future. Communities raise the Sami flag, sing the Sami national anthem, wear the traditional gákti and gather for joik singing, reindeer races, food and cultural events.

National Eighties Day is a light-hearted American celebration of the 1980s, a decade remembered for synth-pop, neon colours, big hair and blockbuster films. It invites people who grew up in the eighties to relive their favourite moments, and lets younger fans discover the music, fashion and games that still shape pop culture today. People mark it by dressing in leg warmers and shoulder pads, playing classic arcade games, watching eighties movies and sharing retro playlists with friends.

National Wear Red Day, held on the first Friday of February in the United States, asks people to wear red to raise awareness of heart disease, a leading cause of death among women. It began with The Heart Truth campaign of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, which made the red dress a national symbol of women's heart health, and the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women movement has joined it. On the day, offices, schools and landmarks turn red, and people are encouraged to learn their risk, get a checkup and choose healthier habits.

The Yukon Quest is a famous long-distance sled dog race held each February in the far north of North America. First run in 1984, it was known for its roughly 1,000-mile course between Fairbanks, Alaska, and Whitehorse, Yukon, following trails once used by Klondike Gold Rush prospectors and mail carriers, and it is now organised as separate races on each side of the border. Mushers and their dog teams cross frozen rivers and mountain passes in deep cold, while fans follow the race and greet the teams at checkpoints and finish lines.

The Goa Carnival is a lively street festival held in the days before Lent in the Indian state of Goa. It took root during the long period of Portuguese rule, when the pre-Lenten carnival tradition arrived with Catholic settlers, and it has since absorbed Goan music, food and humour. Each year the playful King Momo is crowned and takes charge of the celebrations, as parades of colourful floats, dancers and brass bands wind through Panaji, Margao, Vasco and Mapusa, and the festivities close with the Red and Black dance in Panaji.

The Carnival of Barranquilla, held in the four days before Ash Wednesday, is Colombia's biggest folk festival and was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2003. It blends African, Indigenous and European traditions in dances such as the cumbia, the congo and the mapalé, and in characters like the long-nosed Marimonda and the Torito. Its opening highlight, the Battle of Flowers, has paraded through the city since 1903, followed by days of floats, music, masks and street dancing.

The Chiang Mai Flower Festival takes place on the first weekend of February, when the cool season brings the city's gardens into full bloom. It celebrates the flowers of northern Thailand, especially the damask rose that is a symbol of Chiang Mai, along with chrysanthemums, orchids and other blossoms. Highlights are a parade of floats covered in flowers that winds through the old city to Suan Buak Haad park, flower and garden displays in the park, traditional Lanna music and dance, and a festival beauty pageant.

Ghost Hunting Day falls on the last Saturday of September and opens the spooky season for anyone drawn to ghost stories and the unexplained. Tales of haunted houses, castles and graveyards exist in almost every culture, and many old buildings carry legends that have been passed down for generations. People mark the day with night-time ghost tours, visits to famously haunted places, amateur investigations with cameras and recorders, or simply by sharing a good ghost story with the lights turned off.

Neurodiversity Pride Day, observed on June 16, celebrates the strengths of neurodivergent minds and pushes back against the idea that there is one 'right' kind of brain. Anchored by the slogan 'Every Brain Is Beautiful,' the day centres autistic, ADHD, dyslexic, dyspraxic, Tourette's and other neurodivergent voices. It falls inside ND Pride Week, with meetups, panels and art that reframe how the world sees minds that don't fit the neurotypical template.

Neurodiversity Celebration Week is a global, week-long initiative held annually in March that challenges stereotypes and celebrates the strengths of neurodivergent minds in schools, workplaces and communities. Schools run talks and inclusion workshops; employers spotlight accommodations and neurodivergent colleagues; advocacy groups share resources. The week reframes neurological differences — autism, ADHD, dyslexia, dyspraxia, Tourette's and more — as part of how humans vary, not something to fix.

ADHD Awareness Month, observed every October, raises understanding of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and the millions of adults and children who live with it. Across the month, ADHD advocacy groups, healthcare providers, educators and employers run screening campaigns, talks and resource drives that reframe ADHD away from stereotypes and toward support, treatment and acceptance. The month's message: ADHD is a real, often life-long difference in how the brain regulates attention, emotion and impulse — and people who have it build, create and lead every day.

My Way Day is a quiet rebellion against doing things the way everyone else does them. Founded by Thomas and Ruth Roy — the couple behind Wellcat Herbs and dozens of offbeat observances — the day reframes 'It's my way or the highway' as something kinder: a reminder that personal agency, deliberate choices, and doing things your own way can be an act of meaning. Inspired by moments in history when someone had a bold idea and followed it through, it asks everyone to claim a small corner of their day back.

Daytona Pole Day is the qualifying session, held in the days before the Daytona 500, that decides who starts NASCAR's biggest race from the front row. Drivers go out one at a time for timed laps around the 2.5-mile Daytona International Speedway, which opened in 1959, and the two fastest lock in the first two starting spots. Its great moments include Bill Elliott's qualifying record of 210.364 mph in 1987, and Danica Patrick becoming the first woman to win the Daytona 500 pole in 2013. Fans fill the grandstands to see who will lead the field to the green flag.

Kosovo Independence Day on 17 February marks the day in 2008 when Kosovo's Assembly declared independence from Serbia. The declaration followed the war of 1998 to 1999 and nearly a decade of United Nations administration. Many countries recognise Kosovo, while Serbia and some others do not. The day is a public holiday with flags, concerts and fireworks. In Pristina crowds gather around the NEWBORN monument, unveiled on independence day and repainted with a new design each year.

International Flirting Week, observed during the second full week of February, is a lighthearted invitation to remember that flirting is a skill — and an art. The week is a chance to practice eye contact, playful conversation and small compliments, online or in person, after a decade in which dating has moved almost entirely into apps. It is not a dating week; it is a week to rediscover the easy, mutual fun of signalling interest without pressure.

Ramadan is the ninth and most sacred month of the Islamic lunar calendar, observed by nearly two billion Muslims worldwide as a month of fasting from dawn to sunset. Rooted in 610 CE, when the Prophet Muhammad is believed to have received the Quran from the angel Gabriel on Laylat al-Qadr, the month gathers families for suhoor before sunrise and iftar after Maghrib, and is read cover-to-cover in many mosques. Dates shift each year because the Islamic calendar follows the moon; crescent-and-star lanterns light streets from Jakarta to Casablanca.

slogans.en: A month of fasting, family, and reflection.

descriptions.en: World Human Spirit Day is a quiet invitation to slow down in a noisy, anxious world. It asks people to look past the daily rush and reconnect with the inner life that keeps them steady, through reading, walking, breathing, journaling or simply spending time with people they trust. Its message is practical: peace, healing and connection are not reserved for retreats or rare moments of insight, and they can be found in ordinary hours if you make room for them.

World Anthropology Day celebrates the discipline that studies what it means to be human, from our deep past to the way we live today. It began in 2015 as National Anthropology Day, launched by the American Anthropological Association, and was later renamed to reflect its worldwide reach. From excavations at Çatalhöyük to medical anthropology in hospitals and research inside tech companies, the field spans deep time and daily life. Schools, universities and museums mark the day with talks, exhibitions and open events.

slogans.en: What does it mean to be human?

descriptions.en: Pluto Day, observed on February 18, marks the day in 1930 when Clyde Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff identified a moving point of light on photographic plates — the first detection of what was then called the ninth planet. The name was suggested by 11-year-old Venetia Burney in Oxford, and for 76 years Pluto held its place in school textbooks. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union moved it to the new 'dwarf planet' category — a decision still argued over by anyone who learned their solar system before then.

World Care Day, founded in Australia by the Create Foundation and now observed in dozens of countries, raises a voice for children and young people who cannot live with their families — in foster care, kinship care, residential care, or aging out of it. The day centres care-experienced young people, who design the campaigns and tell the world what helped and what didn't, and pushes governments and communities to listen to them when child welfare policy is being shaped. It is a day about being seen, not saved.

National Arabian Horse Day, observed on February 21 in the United States, honours one of humanity's oldest and most influential horse breeds. Founded in 2021 by the Scottsdale Show and the Arabian Horse Association of Arizona, the day celebrates the Arabian's distinctive dished face, arched neck and endurance — qualities shaped over centuries in the deserts of the Arabian Peninsula and now carried by show horses, racing lines and family companions across North America. The day's events include parades, horse shows and educational seminars.

slogans.en: Bred for beauty. Built for endurance.

descriptions.en: Iwo Jima Day, observed on February 19, marks the day in 1945 when the U.S. 3rd, 4th and 5th Marine Divisions came ashore on the volcanic island of Iwo Jima in one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific War. Five days later, Joe Rosenthal photographed five Marines and a Navy corpsman raising a second American flag on Mount Suribachi — the image that won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize and became the model for the Marine Corps War Memorial near Arlington, dedicated by President Eisenhower in 1954. The day honours the more than 6,800 Americans who died taking the island.

slogans.en: Uncommon valor was a common virtue.

descriptions.en: Shivaji Jayanti, on February 19, marks the birth in 1630 of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, who founded the Maratha kingdom in western India and is remembered as one of the country's great rulers. He built his realm through campaigns against the Adil Shahi sultanate of Bijapur and the Mughal Empire, guarded it with a chain of hill forts and a navy, and was crowned in 1674. The social reformer Jyotirao Phule held the first public celebration in Pune in 1870; today it is a public holiday in Maharashtra, marked with processions, music and saffron flags.

slogans.en: Born to lead. Honoured to remember.

descriptions.en: National Love Your Pet Day, observed on February 20 in the United States, is a reminder to slow down and tell the dog, cat, rabbit or parrot exactly what they mean to you — with treats, a longer walk, a fresh grooming, or just a long cuddle. The day is part of a long tradition of pet appreciation days, rooted in the 12,000-year history of humans and animals living together. Pet stores, shelters and veterinary clinics often run special events, and many use the day to spotlight adoption and rescue work.

slogans.en: Spoil the one who spoils every day.

descriptions.en: No Politics Day asks for one simple thing: a single day's break from politics. It is a small American observance born of a familiar feeling, that political arguments have crept into dinners, friendships and family chats until little else gets talked about. The day is not against caring about public life; it is a reminder that people are more than their opinions. To mark it, switch off the news, skip the debates online and talk with someone about anything else at all.

World Whale Day, on the third Sunday of February, celebrates whales and the work of protecting them. It began on Maui, Hawaii, in 1980, started by Greg Kaufman, founder of the Pacific Whale Foundation, to draw attention to the humpback whales that spend the winter in Hawaiian waters and were then endangered. Maui marks it with a festival and parade, while people elsewhere join whale-watching trips, beach clean-ups and talks about the threats whales still face, from ship strikes and ocean noise to entanglement in fishing gear.

slogans.en: For the whales, and the oceans they call home.

descriptions.en: Makha Bucha Day is one of the most sacred days in the Buddhist calendar, observed on the full moon of the third lunar month to mark the day when 1,250 of the Buddha's enlightened disciples spontaneously gathered at the Veluvana Bamboo Grove in India — nine months after his enlightenment — without any prior arrangement. In Thailand it is a national holiday marked by candlelit processions around the temple, in Cambodia by offerings at the pagoda, and across Theravada Buddhist Southeast Asia by alcohol-free observance, mindful speech and quiet reflection. Dates shift each year with the lunar calendar.

slogans.en: A gathering that needed no words.
