descriptions.en: National Walking the Dog Day, observed in the United States on February 22, is a reminder that a daily walk is one of the best things you can do for your dog and for yourself. Regular walks keep dogs fit, calm and curious, give them a chance to sniff and explore, and build the bond between dog and owner. People who walk a dog also tend to move more and meet more neighbours. Mark the day with a longer walk, a new route or a trip to a park your dog has never smelled before.

slogans.en: Leash up. Lungs open. Day started.

descriptions.en: World Thinking Day, on February 22, is the shared day of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts around the world. The date was chosen at their world conference in 1926 because it is the birthday of both Robert Baden-Powell, founder of Scouting, and his wife Olave, who led the Guide movement. Each year the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts sets a theme, and members think of their sisters in other countries, raise money for the movement and take action on that theme in their own communities.

slogans.en: Think of each other. Act together.

descriptions.en: National California Day, observed on February 22, celebrates the U.S. state that became the 31st in 1850 — a place whose landscapes, from Yosemite granite to the San Andreas, helped shape its culture as much as its economy. Born as a passion-project of Californians who wanted to share the state's heritage, the day gained momentum through social media and now invites everyone to plan a Hollywood pilgrimage, a Napa wine tasting, a surf in Malibu, or a hike in the Sierra. It's a holiday about the world's fifth-largest economy and a coastline that runs 840 miles.

The Abu Simbel Festival celebrates the moment, twice a year, when the rising sun reaches deep inside the great rock-cut temple that Pharaoh Ramses II built in southern Egypt more than 3,000 years ago. Around February 22 and October 22, the light travels the length of the temple and falls on the seated statues in the inner sanctuary, while the statue of Ptah stays in shadow. Tradition links the dates to the pharaoh's birthday and coronation, though no record confirms it. The temples were moved to higher ground in the 1960s to escape the rising Lake Nasser, and crowds still gather before dawn to watch, followed by music and dancing in the town.

slogans.en: Sun, stone, and a king's birthday.

descriptions.en: Real Bread Week is the yearly celebration of the Real Bread Campaign, a project of the UK charity Sustain that has championed bread made without unnecessary additives since 2008. Held in February, it encourages people to bake their own loaves and to buy from small independent bakeries rather than factory production lines. Bakeries open their doors, run sourdough and baking classes and share recipes, while home bakers show off their loaves online and pass bread on to neighbours.

slogans.en: Bake it. Buy local. Skip the factory.

names.en: Take Down Tobacco National Day of Action

descriptions.en: Take Down Tobacco National Day of Action, held each April 1, is the youth-driven campaign of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids that asks young people to push back against the tobacco and nicotine industry. The day grew out of Kick Butts Day, founded in 1996, and was rebranded in 2019 to cover e-cigarettes, nicotine pouches, flavored products and the marketing tactics aimed at hooking a new generation. Events are typically youth-led: school assemblies, marketing-tactics pop-ups, awareness walks, classroom workshops and resource fairs. The day carries a clear message: health is not a trend, addiction is not a game, and young people are not a target market.

slogans.en: Stand up. Speak out. Take down tobacco.

descriptions.en: Harmonize Your Health Day, observed on April 1, was founded by the frequency-therapy company Somavedic to mark its brand anniversary and to invite people to take a quieter, more balanced approach to well-being. The day encourages decluttering, healthier eating, restful sleep, and small breaks from the digital world, drawing on the idea that true health weaves mind, body and environment together. Marked on the same day as April Fools' Day, it offers a serious counterpoint: instead of noise, a moment of stillness; instead of distraction, a chance to reset routines. People celebrate by simplifying their homes, planning nourishing meals, exploring meditation or breath work, and treating sleep as a foundation rather than an afterthought.

St. Stupid Day is the playful San Francisco holiday celebrated every April 1 with a costume parade through the Financial District, founded in 1979 by Ed Holmes — a.k.a. Bishop Joey of the First Church of the Last Laugh — and rooted in the city's deep tradition of political clowning from the San Francisco Mime Troupe. On weekday Aprils the parade starts at Embarcadero Plaza and winds through downtown; on weekend Aprils it begins at the Transamerica Building and climbs up Columbus. Participants dress in outlandish outfits, wave silly signs, toss pennies and confetti, and embrace the festival's central idea: that one of the unifying bonds in society is stupidity, and that mocking seriousness is its own form of honesty.

slogans.en: Mock the serious. March the absurd.

descriptions.en: National Cleaning Week, observed the last week of March into early April, is the annual public-awareness campaign of the ISSA — the worldwide cleaning industry association — built around the slogan 'the value of clean'. Founded to spotlight the impact that clean spaces have on public health, the environment and the economy, the week invites households, schools and professional cleaners to refresh their routines, run cleaning competitions, and recognise the people who keep our buildings, hospitals and homes running. Spring has long been a natural moment to clear out cobwebs and dust; the week makes that instinct a coordinated push, with seminars and industry events for cleaning professionals and practical challenges for everyone else.

The National Cherry Blossom Festival is the four-week spring celebration in Washington, D.C. that commemorates the 1912 gift of 3,020 cherry trees from Tokyo Mayor Yukio Ozaki to the U.S. capital, a gesture that became a lasting symbol of friendship between the United States and Japan. The festival has run officially since 1935 and now draws more than a million visitors each year for the Blossom Kite Festival on the National Mall, the Sakura Taiko Fest, paddle-boat rides on the Tidal Basin, cultural performances and a parade. Peak bloom typically falls in late March or early April, turning the Tidal Basin into a halo of pink and white and giving the city one of its most photographed weeks of the year.

slogans.en: A century of blossoms, a season of friendship.

descriptions.en: Jazz Appreciation Month — known as JAM — is the April-long celebration founded in 2001 by Smithsonian curator John Edward Hasse at the National Museum of American History, with an early boost from the Ella Fitzgerald Charitable Foundation. The month honours the heritage of jazz, born in late-19th-century New Orleans from the interweaving of African folk, blues and ragtime, and the musicians who shaped it: Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Miles Davis and John Coltrane. April was chosen because so many jazz greats were born in it, including Ellington, Fitzgerald, Holiday and Herbie Hancock. Schools, libraries and concert halls across the country host listening parties, lectures and jam sessions, while the Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra anchors the calendar with a weekend of concerts.

slogans.en: Honor the sound that shaped America.

descriptions.en: Move More Month is the April-long initiative of the American Heart Association that asks everyone — regardless of fitness level — to add a little more movement to each day. Launched in 2018, the month is anchored by National Walking Day on the first Wednesday of April and ties into the AHA's long-term mission of preventing heart disease and stroke. The message is plain: small things count. A walk around the block, a dance break in the living room, a stretch every hour, a game of fetch with the dog, a new sport tried for the first time — each builds toward the kind of steady, moderate activity that protects the heart and the brain. The campaign's tone is friendly, not punishing: progress, not perfection.

Walk to Work Day, observed each April 1, is the gentle challenge to swap the commute behind the wheel for a commute on foot. Created in 2004 by Prevention Magazine and quickly picked up by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the day builds on a simple public-health insight: brisk walking counts toward the WHO's 150-minutes-a-week target, and replacing even one car trip a day with footsteps cuts carbon emissions, eases traffic and clears the morning fog from the head. The day isn't for the rare few who live next door to the office — remote workers can take a brisk pre-shift loop, and long-distance commuters can walk to the bus or train.

Autism Acceptance Day, observed on April 2 alongside the United Nations' World Autism Awareness Day, is the community-led counterpart that reframes the conversation from awareness to acceptance. While World Autism Awareness Day, established by the UN in 2007, highlights diagnosis rates, research and the diversity of the spectrum, Acceptance Day focuses on moving autistic people from being the object of awareness campaigns to being heard, supported and included in everyday life. Schools, workplaces and families are invited to read autistic authors, listen to autistic voices, and reconsider the small habits — language, lighting, expectations — that can make a real difference. The day pairs naturally with Autism Acceptance Month throughout April.

Tangible Karma Day, observed each April 1, is a modern take on the ancient idea of karma — translated from 'what goes around comes around' into 'what can you do, physically, today?' The day is built around a simple question: instead of waiting for the universe to balance the scales, what small, real act of kindness can you perform? Declutter a closet and donate the bag, leave a kind note on a stranger's car, pay for the coffee of the person behind you, help an elderly neighbour carry groceries. Rooted in the same Eastern philosophical soil that gave the world karma in the first place — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, Taoism — the day is a reminder that good energy, like bad, starts with what we do in our own hands.

slogans.en: Do something kind. With your hands.

descriptions.en: Independent Artist Day, celebrated each April 3, was founded by Minted, the online design marketplace, to honour the thousands of artists who work outside the walls of large galleries and institutions. The day exists to celebrate independent creators and the path they've chosen — building studios, mailing lists, websites and livelihoods one piece at a time, often while balancing day jobs, families and the slow grind of being heard. It also pushes back against a moment when AI is flooding the creative marketplace, reminding the world that human imagination, craft and the courage to make something personal are still the most valuable things an artwork can carry.

slogans.en: Made by hand. Made by humans.

descriptions.en: The Pharaohs' Golden Parade, held on 3 April 2021 in Cairo, was the once-in-a-lifetime procession that carried 22 royal mummies of New Kingdom pharaohs and queens from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square to their new home at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Fustat. Stretched across about 7 kilometres and broadcast live on state television, the parade was a meticulously choreographed tribute to the pharaohs themselves, with each mummy placed in a climate-controlled, gold-trimmed capsule aboard a royal float designed to evoke the boats of the ancient Nile. The Royal Hall of Mummies, where the 22 royals — including Ramesses II, Seqenenre Tao and Hatshepsut — were installed, opened to the public on 18 April 2021.

Geologists Day, observed on the first Sunday in April, is the official professional holiday of geologists, geophysicists and geochemists in Russia and across the post-Soviet space, established in 1966. The day honours the scientists who read the Earth — from the chemistry of its crust to the physics of its core — and whose work underpins everything from mineral exploration and earthquake preparedness to climate modelling and the search for groundwater. The date is the first Sunday in April, which means it shifts each year but always falls in the same spring window when the snow thaws and the rocks start showing again in the Northern Hemisphere.

slogans.en: Read the rocks. Read the Earth.

descriptions.en: World Corporate Health Day, observed each April 4, is the annual prompt to put corporate health — the physical, mental and emotional wellbeing of working people — on the leadership agenda. The day exists because burnout, sedentary work, chronic stress and the quiet erosion of sleep are not just personal problems; they show up in the productivity, retention and culture of every company that ignores them. The day calls on employers, HR teams and managers to look honestly at what their workplaces do to the people inside them, and to invest in solutions: better ergonomics, mental-health support, time off that is actually used, and cultures where rest is not a weakness.

Victims of Violence Wholly Day, observed each April 4, is a day of remembrance and reflection on the human cost of violence in all its forms — from civil-rights assassinations to domestic abuse, from hate crimes to war. The date is no accident: April 4 is the anniversary of the 1968 assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in Memphis, a wound that still shapes the American conversation about race, justice and the violence done to those who demand change. The day invites communities to honour the lives lost, support the survivors among them, and recommit to the unfinished work of building a world where people can speak, march, love and live without fear.

The Edinburgh Science Festival, founded in 1989 by the Edinburgh Science Foundation, is the United Kingdom's largest science festival and one of the biggest in Europe, transforming Scotland's capital into a two-week laboratory of exhibits, workshops, lectures and family activities every spring. The inaugural festival was presided over by Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, and over the years has welcomed figures like Richard Dawkins, Brian Cox and Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell. The programme covers everything from personal health to planetary challenges, with a family hub at the City Art Centre, school shows, late-night debates and online workshops. The exact dates shift each year but the festival reliably fills the second half of March and the first half of April.

National Body Care Day, observed each April 5, was founded in 2018 by Kayo Body Care to highlight the importance of caring for the skin beyond the face — the body's largest organ. The day traces its roots much further back, to the Egyptians and Romans who built elaborate public baths around the idea that cleanliness was both a health practice and a spiritual one. Today, the day is a friendly nudge to indulge in self-care: roll out the yoga mat, run a bath, slather on a new lotion, host a pampering party with friends, or just cook a meal that loves your body back. Skincare of the whole body, the founders argue, is not vanity — it is a basic human right worth protecting from pollution, sun and modern neglect.

slogans.en: Your skin is your largest organ. Care for it.

descriptions.en: National Dandelion Day, observed each April 5, is the unofficial celebration of the small, stubborn, sun-yellow flower that most people pull out of their lawns and a few people put in their salads. The day nods to a plant whose taproot can punch 18 inches into compacted soil, whose seeds travel on the wind with parachutes of fluff, and whose greens out-spinach in vitamins A, C and K. The Dandelion Festival in Dover, Ohio — a community event that started in 1996 — is the best-known local anchor, and the holiday has spread online through nature lovers, gardeners and herbalists who want the rest of us to slow down and notice what's growing between the cracks. Folk medicines on four continents have used the plant for digestion, liver support and skin care for centuries.

slogans.en: Look closer. It's not a weed.

descriptions.en: Bohring-Opitz Syndrome Day, observed each April 6, raises awareness of the ultra-rare genetic condition caused by truncating variants in the ASXL1 gene — a chromatin regulator whose disruption reshapes development in ways that affect nearly every system in the body. Children with BOS often have distinctive facial features, joint stiffness in the arms, a small head, feeding difficulties, sleep apnea, frequent lung infections, and an increased risk of Wilms tumor. The day is rooted in a 2011 Facebook support group started by Sünne van Gemert-Godbersen and marked since 2015 under the leadership of Taylor Gurganus and other parents. Gold and denim — the BOS ribbon colors — are worn to spark conversation; small fundraisers and registry drives push research forward; and families find each other in a community that, before 2011, did not really exist.

slogans.en: Gold and denim for the rarest among us.

descriptions.en: International Asexuality Day, observed each April 6, is the annual effort to put asexual people — those who experience little or no sexual attraction — and the broader ace umbrella on the global awareness map. The day was launched in 2021 by a committee of organizers from several countries after almost a year of planning, and it orbits four themes: advocacy, celebration, education and solidarity. It exists to make 'ace' a familiar word, to give voice to asexual communities outside the West and the English-speaking world, and to support the spectrum that includes demisexual, graysexual, aromantic and many other lived experiences that fall under the ace umbrella. Related moments throughout the year include Ace Week in October, Pride Month in June, and LGBTQ+ History Month.

slogans.en: A is for ace. Always has been.

descriptions.en: New Beer's Eve, observed each April 6, is the celebration of the night before Prohibition ended in the United States — the moment when, after 13 years of dry law, Americans queued around the block at their local bars and pubs waiting for 12:01 a.m. on April 7, 1933, when legal beer could flow again. President Franklin D. Roosevelt famously remarked, 'I think this would be a good time for a beer,' and Anheuser-Busch delivered a Clydesdale-drawn carriage of brew straight to the White House. The first 24 hours of legal beer saw an estimated 1.5 million gallons consumed, and the day still invites pub crawls, brewery tours, beer-and-cheese pairings and home-brew experiments in honour of a long-overdue reunion between Americans and their pints.

slogans.en: A good time for a beer.

descriptions.en: Jump Over Things Day, observed each April 6, is the playful invitation to find something — anything — and leap over it. The holiday has no founder, no official club, no ribbon; just a small, sturdy idea that the body likes to move in more ways than walking, and that the brain enjoys the small math of distance, height and safe landing. The day's deeper roots run through Georges Hébert's natural-method training in early-20th-century France, the high jump's evolution at the modern Olympics, Evel Knievel's televised motorcycle leaps, and the rise of parkour and freerunning in the late 20th century. People celebrate by hopping over couch cushions, doing leapfrog in a park, organising a backyard obstacle course for kids, or just taking a moment to jump rope between tasks.

The International Day of Sarajevo Roses, observed each April 6, honours the lives lost during the Siege of Sarajevo and the resilience of the people who turned the scars of the Bosnian War into permanent memorials. The 'roses' are mortar-shell craters scattered across the city, filled after the war with red resin so each one blooms from the asphalt like a flower of remembrance, marking a place where someone died. April 6 marks the beginning of the siege in 1992, the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare. The day exists to remember the dead, support survivors, and turn local memory into global reflection — through walking tours, art exhibitions, rose-planting events, documentary screenings and quiet conversations that keep Sarajevo's story alive in cities far from Bosnia.

Parkinson's Awareness Week, observed annually with World Parkinson's Day on April 11, is the coordinated push to deepen public understanding of Parkinson's disease, the neurodegenerative condition that affects movement, balance and often mood, sleep and cognition. The week takes its cue from Dr. James Parkinson, the English surgeon who first described the condition in his 1817 monograph 'An Essay on the Shaking Palsy', and from figures like Muhammad Ali, Michael J. Fox, Alan Alda and Linda Ronstadt, whose public diagnoses pulled Parkinson's out of the shadows. Charities run fun walks, 5Ks and cycling challenges; clinics host seminars; advocates meet with lawmakers to push for research funding; and the red tulip — bred by J.W.S. Van der Wereld, a Dutch grower who himself had Parkinson's — is the universal symbol of solidarity.

slogans.en: Wear a red tulip. Speak a name.

descriptions.en: The Masters Tournament, played the first full week of April at Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia, is one of golf's four major championships and the only major played at the same course every year. Founded in 1934 by Bobby Jones and Clifford Roberts — after a first invitational in 1933 — the tournament has been the sport's most tradition-soaked event for more than 90 years. Patrons (not 'fans') watch in silence, cell phones are forbidden, broadcasting is limited to four hours a day, and the previous champion slips the famous green jacket onto the new winner's shoulders. Amen Corner — holes 11, 12 and 13 — has produced more dramatic swings than almost any stretch in golf. The Par-3 Contest on the Wednesday before the main event brings families onto the course.

Honor Our LGBT Elders Day, observed on May 16, celebrates the lives, wisdom and contributions of older LGBTQ+ individuals who built the foundation for the rights and acceptance many enjoy today. The day was created in 2015 by Nate Sweeney, director of SAGE at Chase Brexton Health Care in Baltimore, to recognize that the pioneers who fought for queer rights — often without family, social or legal support — still face unique challenges as they age, including isolation, financial hardship and limited access to affirming healthcare. Observing the day can be as simple as a phone call, a handwritten note, a shared meal, or a donation to an organization that serves LGBT elders; documenting their stories so the next generation hears them is one of its most lasting acts.

The International AIDS Candlelight Memorial, held the third Sunday of May, is the world's longest-running grassroots HIV awareness event, bringing people together in homes, parks and city squares to honor the lives lost to AIDS and to stand with those living with HIV today. The memorial began in 1983 in San Francisco and New York, when a small group of friends living with HIV created a quiet space to mourn during a time when grief was hidden, fear was widespread and public understanding lagged behind reality. Today the Global Network of People Living with HIV leads the observance worldwide, balancing remembrance with practical action: education, anti-stigma advocacy, testing access and support for the caregivers, researchers and friends who have carried communities through four decades of the epidemic.

International Invention Day, observed on May 16, celebrates the creative spark behind every invention — from the wheel and the printing press to the smartphone and the mRNA vaccine — and the people whose curiosity and persistence turn an idea into a tool the world uses. Founded by the engineering software company Vention, the day exists to honor past inventors whose breakthroughs reshaped daily life, to spotlight the working inventors of today, and to plant the seed in the next generation by encouraging kids and students to tinker, prototype, fail, and try again. The day pairs naturally with related observances: National Inventors' Day in February, National Kid Inventors' Day in January, and National Inventors Month in August.

American Craft Beer Week, observed the week of May 11–17, is the annual toast to the more than 9,000 small, independent U.S. breweries that turn local water, grain and hops into beer with a sense of place. Launched in 2006 by the Boulder-based Brewers Association and Craftbeer.com, the week encourages beer lovers to try a new-to-them independent brewery (the association notes that most Americans live within 10 miles of one), brew their own batch at home, cook with beer, or simply raise a glass to the small producers that keep American beer culture varied and alive. The week falls as the weather turns warm enough for backyards, barbecues and outdoor tables — exactly when a cold, locally made IPA, pilsner or saison tastes best.

Skin Cancer Awareness Month, observed every May in the United States, is the annual push to lower the country's skin cancer burden — the most common cancer in America, with more than 5 million new cases diagnosed each year — through prevention, early detection and public education. Coordinated by the Skin Cancer Foundation, the American Academy of Dermatology, the CDC and the American Association for Cancer Research, the month gives doctors, schools and community groups a shared moment to teach the basics: seek shade, cover up, skip indoor tanning, wear UV-blocking sunglasses, and use broad-spectrum SPF 15+ sunscreen on any skin that sees the sun. It also surfaces the stark numbers — 1 in 5 Americans will develop skin cancer by age 70; five or more sunburns doubles melanoma risk — so the habit changes feel personal, not theoretical.

slogans.en: Cover up. Check your skin. Catch it early.

names.en: World Telecommunication and Information Society Day

descriptions.en: World Telecommunication and Information Society Day, observed on May 17 each year, marks the 1865 founding of the International Telegraph Union — the ancestor of today's International Telecommunication Union and the world's oldest intergovernmental organization still in operation. The day celebrates the technologies that let people talk across distances, from the electric telegraph to the World Wide Web, and the people — researchers, engineers, standards-setters, advocates — who keep those networks open, safe and useful. Each year carries a fresh theme, from broadband for sustainable development to digital inclusion, and the ITU uses the day to publish reports, host online events and push for policies that bring the next billion people online.

slogans.en: Connect the world. Bridge the divide.

descriptions.en: Hari Raya Haji, also known as Eid al-Adha, is one of the two principal festivals of the Muslim world, observed on the 10th day of Dhu al-Hijjah — the final month of the Islamic lunar calendar. The day commemorates the story of Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God, with the animal he had prepared for slaughter replaced at the last moment by a ram; in the world's Muslim communities the story is honored through the ritual of Qurban, the sacrifice of a sheep, goat, cow or camel whose meat is divided into thirds for family, friends and those in need. Eid al-Adha also coincides with the end of the Hajj, the annual pilgrimage to Mecca that every able Muslim is encouraged to perform once in a lifetime, so the day arrives each year wrapped in prayer, family gatherings, new clothes and plates of rendang, biryani and other regional feast food shared across neighborhoods.

slogans.en: Faith, family, and the spirit of giving.

descriptions.en: National Vegetarian Week, observed the week of May 18–24, is the UK's annual nudge from the Vegetarian Society — the world's oldest vegetarian organization, founded in 1847 — to try a few more meat-free meals and to notice what happens when you do. Started in 1992, the week is built around community events, cooking classes, recipe swaps and restaurant partnerships that show plant-based eating can be as hearty, varied and satisfying as anything centred on meat, while pointing to the health, environmental and animal-welfare arguments for shifting a few dinners a week. The week also gives restaurants, schools and workplaces a shared moment to put plant-based dishes at the front of the menu and to show that eating more vegetables is as much about pleasure and culture as it is about health.

slogans.en: Try a few meatless meals. Notice what changes.

descriptions.en: Dementia Action Week, observed the week of May 18–24, is the Alzheimer's Society's annual UK-wide push to move dementia out of the 'awareness only' lane and into the action lane — funding, research, better care and stronger support for the families carrying the disease alongside the person who has it. First held in 1989 to mark the charity's 10th anniversary and renamed from Dementia Awareness Week in the 2000s, the week is built around practical asks: learn about the different forms of the disease, take part in local events, advocate for policy change, share stories on social media, and reach out to a caregiver. With millions of people living with dementia worldwide and no cure yet, the week's plain message — 'United against dementia' — is that the disease is too big for any of us to fight alone.

International Customer Support Day, observed on May 20, is the annual moment to step back from the day-to-day churn of tickets, calls and chats and recognize the people who turn 'this is broken' into 'this is fixed'. Customer support is often invisible when it works — that's the whole point — but it is the single biggest driver of whether a customer stays, churns or tells their friends, with industry studies showing that a majority of consumers will leave a brand after one bad interaction. The day is built for three audiences at once: customers are encouraged to leave specific, kind feedback (mention what actually helped, not just 'great service'); organizations are pushed to invest in training, mental-health support, and clear growth paths for their support staff; and the support professionals themselves get a public nod for the steady, often invisible work that keeps the rest of the economy running.

slogans.en: Thank the people who fix it.

descriptions.en: National Rescue Dog Day, observed on May 20, celebrates the more than 2 million dogs adopted from U.S. shelters every year and the shelters, foster families, trainers, veterinarians and volunteers who made those second chances possible. Founded in 2018 by children's-book author and Tails that Teach director Lisa Wiehebrink, the day pushes back on the idea that 'rescue' describes a particular kind of dog: shelters are full of every shape, size, age and breed, and what unites them is the simple fact that someone stepped in to keep them safe. The day encourages adoption and fostering, of course, but also donations, social-media shares of adoptable dogs, and the quieter work of helping a newly adopted dog decompress — because the celebration is not just the happy adoption photo, it is the months of patience and training that follow.

National High Heel Day, observed on May 20, is the annual celebration of one of fashion's most polarizing silhouettes — a shoe that is, depending on who's wearing it, design, engineering, attitude or a tiny bit of theater wrapped into something that fits in a box. Founded in 2021 by Supreme Court mediator Kimberly Lorenz with Judge Gisela Laurent, the day treats high heels as more than a fashion accessory: a cultural artifact with centuries of history (Persian horsemen, Louis XIV's red-heeled court, Dior's steel-shanked stilettos) and a deeply personal relationship to confidence, identity and self-expression. The day's tone is celebratory rather than prescriptive — wear them, photograph them, design around them, support the small designers making them, but also know that appreciating heels doesn't require owning a pair.

slogans.en: Step into the story you want to tell.

descriptions.en: International Academic Freedom Day, observed on May 20, is the annual reminder that the work of universities — teaching, research, public debate — only stays credible if scholars can do it without fear of censorship, dismissal or prosecution. The day ties together a long history: Wilhelm von Humboldt's 19th-century model of Lehrfreiheit and Lernfreiheit in Berlin, the AAUP's 1915 Declaration of Principles, UNESCO's 1997 Recommendation on Higher-Education Teaching Personnel, and the UN's recognition of academic freedom as an essential part of the right to education. Marking the day is mostly practical: read Mill's On Liberty, attend a panel, host a case-study discussion about real pressures facing researchers, and look hard at the policies and procedures that protect (or fail to protect) the people who do this work — because the Academic Freedom Index shows the state of academic freedom has been declining globally for over a decade, with roughly one-third of the world's population now living in countries where scholars face significant political pressure.

National Child Day on November 20 honours the anniversaries of two UN agreements: the Declaration of the Rights of the Child in 1959 and the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989. The Convention sets out children's rights to safety, health, education, play and a say in decisions that affect them, and it is the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history. Schools and communities mark the day by asking children what matters to them and by reviewing how well those rights are protected.

The Pushkar Camel Fair is held each autumn in the desert town of Pushkar in Rajasthan, India, during the Hindu month of Kartik. Herders bring thousands of camels, horses and cattle to trade on the sand dunes, and the fair has grown to include camel races, moustache and turban-tying contests, folk music and dance. It ends at the full moon of Kartik Purnima, when pilgrims bathe in the sacred Pushkar Lake beside the town's rare temple to Brahma.

slogans.en: Camels, colour, and the Rajasthani sun.

descriptions.en: Global Entrepreneurship Week, held each November, is billed as the world's largest celebration of people who start and grow businesses. It grew out of the UK's Enterprise Week and was launched globally in 2008, and it now runs in more than 180 countries. During the week, founders, students, investors and policymakers meet at workshops, pitch competitions, mentoring sessions and startup events.

slogans.en: Build the business. Build the community.

descriptions.en: The Surin Elephant Round-Up is held each November in Surin province in northeastern Thailand, a region long known for its elephant-keeping Kuy people. Since 1960 the festival has brought hundreds of elephants and their mahouts into town for parades, a huge fruit buffet for the elephants and re-enactments of historic battles. It celebrates the centuries-old bond between the Kuy and their elephants, alongside growing debate about how captive elephants should be cared for.

slogans.en: Where elephants and people walk together.

descriptions.en: Book Week Scotland is a nationwide celebration of reading run every year by the Scottish Book Trust, the charity that promotes books and literacy in Scotland. Since it began in 2012, it has brought free events to libraries, schools, bookshops and community spaces, from author talks to storytelling sessions. People of all ages are invited to share their favourite books, meet writers and discover the simple pleasure of reading together.

slogans.en: A book for everyone, a week for Scotland.

descriptions.en: The Cairo International Film Festival, founded in 1976, is one of the oldest film festivals in the Arab world and Africa. It is the only festival in the region accredited by the international federation of film producers in its top category, alongside events such as Cannes and Berlin. Each November it screens features and shorts from around the world at the Cairo Opera House and awards the Golden Pyramid to the best film in competition.

American Education Week is held each year in the week before Thanksgiving to celebrate public education in the United States. It was started in 1921 by the National Education Association and the American Legion, after many young men drafted for the First World War were found unable to read. Each weekday highlights a different group, from teachers and support staff to parents and substitute educators, and schools invite families in to see classes at work.

National Healthy Skin Month is a November campaign by the American Academy of Dermatology. It reminds people that skin is the body's largest organ, protecting against heat, germs and injury, and that it needs care in every season. Dermatologists use the month to promote daily sunscreen, gentle cleansing, moisturising in cold weather and regular checks for changing moles.

slogans.en: Healthy skin, every day of the year.

descriptions.en: Breast Cancer Awareness Month, observed every October, honors those who have faced breast cancer, those who survived it and those who were lost. It promotes early detection and teaches people what signs to look for. The pink ribbon is its symbol. Use this month to book a screening, learn how to check yourself, or support someone you love.

Liver Cancer Awareness Month, observed every October, raises awareness of liver cancer risks, prevention and treatment options. Often called the 'Silent Disease' because it rarely shows symptoms in its early stages, it is best caught by knowing your risk factors and getting checked. Its ribbon is emerald green.

slogans.en: The silent disease needs a loud voice.

descriptions.en: No Bra Day, held every October 13th during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, invites women to go bra-free for a day to start conversations about breast cancer and early detection. Many also enjoy the comfort of a day without one. Use it to talk about breast health, share the reminder to get screened, or support a related cause.

World Breast Cancer Research Day, observed every August 18th, focuses on global research efforts and long-term support in the search for a cure. It honors researchers and the people who take part in studies. Use it to learn about current research, donate to a research fund, or thank someone working toward better treatments.

Go For A Ride Day invites people to leave the usual routine behind and take a ride just for the pleasure of it. That might mean a bike ride, a scenic train journey, a ferry crossing, a horse ride or a slow drive down a road you have never taken. The point is the journey rather than the destination, and many people use the day to explore their own area from a new angle.

slogans.en: Pick a way. Enjoy the way.

descriptions.en: Humane Society Anniversary Day on November 22 celebrates the humane societies that have worked for more than two centuries to protect animals from cruelty. These organisations run shelters, rescue animals from neglect and disasters, campaign for animal welfare laws and help pets find new homes. People mark the day by donating to a local shelter, volunteering, or adopting rather than buying their next pet.

slogans.en: Compassion that lasts beyond a day.

descriptions.en: World Silambam Day on November 22 celebrates silambam, a martial art from Tamil Nadu in southern India that is fought with a long bamboo staff. It is mentioned in classical Tamil literature, and practitioners combine fast spinning strikes, footwork patterns and defence in a style that looks almost like a dance. On the day, schools and clubs in India, Malaysia, Sri Lanka and the Tamil diaspora hold demonstrations, workshops and competitions.

slogans.en: Staff in hand, tradition in heart.

descriptions.en: National Bible Week is observed in the United States during Thanksgiving week, from the Sunday before the holiday to the Sunday after. It was started in 1941 by the Laymen's National Bible Committee, at a time when the country was heading into the Second World War. Churches, families and study groups use the week for daily readings, discussion and reflection on what the biblical texts mean for everyday life.

slogans.en: Read it. Share it. Live it.

descriptions.en: National Game and Puzzle Week is held in the United States during Thanksgiving week, when families are together and looking for something to do. It celebrates board games, card games and jigsaw and word puzzles as a way to think, laugh and spend time together without screens. Schools, libraries and families mark it with game nights, puzzle swaps and the return of half-forgotten games from the back of the cupboard.

National Tree Week is the UK's largest annual celebration of trees, launched by The Tree Council in 1975 after Dutch elm disease had killed millions of elms across the country. It runs for about ten days from late November, the start of the winter planting season, when young trees can settle their roots before spring. Schools, community groups and councils plant saplings, look after hedgerows and learn about the trees in their own streets and parks.

Better Conversations Week is a US observance held each year in late November, created by conversation coach Loren Ekroth. It encourages people to slow down, listen more than they speak and ask questions out of genuine curiosity. Falling just before the holiday gatherings, it is a good moment to practise putting the phone away and letting a conversation go somewhere new.

Thankful For My Dog Day on November 23 is a chance to notice what dogs give us beyond the walks and the mess: company, comfort and a reason to get outside every day. Studies link living with a dog to more physical activity and less loneliness, and many dogs work as guides, therapy animals and rescue partners. Owners mark the day with a longer walk, a new toy or treat, and a donation to a dog rescue for the dogs still waiting for a home.

slogans.en: They give us everything. We give them thanks.

descriptions.en: Wolfenoot is a small holiday celebrated on November 23, invented by a young boy in New Zealand whose mother shared the idea online, where it quickly spread. It honours the spirit of the wolf and anyone who is kind to dogs: people who have been kind to dogs are said to find small gifts on the day. Celebrations include eating roast meat or a vegetarian feast, wolf-shaped cakes, and donations to dog rescues and wildlife groups.

slogans.en: Feed the wolf. Gift the dog.

descriptions.en: Celebrate Your Unique Talent Day on November 24 is a reminder that everyone can do something well, even if it never appears on a CV. It might be singing, sketching, juggling, baking, whistling, solving puzzles or making people laugh. The day invites people to share their talent with friends, family or colleagues, and to notice and praise the hidden talents of the people around them.

Kartika Purnima is the full-moon day of the Hindu month of Kartika, which falls in November. Hindus mark it with fasting, ritual bathing in sacred rivers and the lighting of lamps; in Varanasi, thousands of lamps line the ghats of the Ganges for Dev Deepawali, the Diwali of the gods. For Sikhs the same full moon is Guru Nanak Gurpurab, the birth anniversary of the founder of Sikhism, and Jains mark it as a sacred day of pilgrimage.

slogans.en: Light a lamp. Lift a prayer.

descriptions.en: Yi Peng is the lantern festival of northern Thailand, held on the full moon of the second month of the old Lanna calendar, the same night as Loy Krathong. In Chiang Mai and across the north, people release khom loi, paper lanterns lifted by a small flame, so that thousands of lights drift up into the night sky. Each lantern is said to carry away misfortune and bring good luck for the year ahead, and temples hold ceremonies with candles and prayer.

slogans.en: A thousand lanterns, a thousand hopes.

descriptions.en: Drinksgiving, also called Thanksgiving Eve or Blackout Wednesday, is the night before Thanksgiving in the United States and one of the busiest nights of the year for bars. Many young adults are back in their home towns for the holiday, so it becomes an informal reunion with old school friends. Because it is also one of the most dangerous nights on the roads, it is a good moment to plan a safe way home and leave the car keys behind.

names.en: Statehood Day in Bosnia and Herzegovina

descriptions.en: Statehood Day in Bosnia and Herzegovina on November 25 marks the first session of the State Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (ZAVNOBiH), held in Mrkonjić Grad in 1943. During the Second World War the council declared Bosnia and Herzegovina an equal federal unit of the future Yugoslavia, belonging to all its peoples. It is a public holiday in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, marked with concerts, school events and flag ceremonies, though it is not observed in Republika Srpska.

slogans.en: A republic of many, a state of one.

descriptions.en: The National Day of Mourning has been held on US Thanksgiving Day since 1970, organised by the United American Indians of New England on Cole's Hill in Plymouth, Massachusetts. It began after the Wampanoag leader Wamsutta Frank James was barred from giving a speech about the impact of colonisation at the 350th anniversary of the Pilgrims' landing. Participants gather to remember the violence, land loss and broken treaties Native peoples have endured, and to speak about Indigenous rights today.

Anti-Obesity Day on November 26 was started in India by the wellness company VLCC to raise awareness of the health risks of obesity. Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and some cancers, and rates have risen quickly in many countries as diets and daily routines have changed. The day encourages small, lasting habits rather than crash diets: more vegetables and whole foods, daily movement, enough sleep and regular health checks.

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has marched through Manhattan every Thanksgiving morning since 1924, ending outside Macy's flagship store at Herald Square. Giant character balloons, first added in 1927, float above the route alongside marching bands, floats and Broadway performances. Millions watch along the streets and on television, and the parade traditionally ends with the arrival of Santa Claus, signalling the start of the holiday season.

Native American Heritage Day is observed in the United States on the day after Thanksgiving, under a law passed by Congress in 2008. It falls within Native American Heritage Month and recognises the cultures, languages and contributions of the hundreds of Native nations, as well as their long history of resistance and survival. Schools, museums and tribal communities mark it with storytelling, dance, art and food, and many people use it to learn whose land they live on.

The National Day of Listening was launched by the nonprofit StoryCorps in 2008 and is held on the day after Thanksgiving in the United States. StoryCorps has recorded hundreds of thousands of conversations between ordinary people, many of them preserved at the Library of Congress. The day asks people to set aside shopping for an hour, sit down with a relative, friend or neighbour, and record a conversation about their life.

Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving in the United States, is the traditional start of the Christmas shopping season. The name was popularised by Philadelphia police in the 1960s to describe the crowds and traffic, and retailers later explained it as the day their accounts moved from red into black. Stores and websites around the world now offer deep discounts, so it is worth making a list, comparing prices and checking return policies before buying.

National Deal Week is the stretch of US shopping days around Thanksgiving, running from the Wednesday before the holiday through the following weekend. It gathers Black Friday, Small Business Saturday and the lead-up to Cyber Monday into one long season of discounts, online and in stores. It is a good week to compare prices, make a list before shopping and remember that the best deal is often not buying what you do not need.

The Pattaya International Fireworks Festival lights up the sky over Pattaya Bay on Thailand's Gulf coast with displays synchronised to music. Teams from several countries take turns over consecutive nights, each trying to outdo the others with colour, rhythm and scale. The beach fills with food stalls, concerts and crowds, and the festival has become one of the highlights of the city's year-end tourist season.

A Blue Christmas is an American observance that runs from Thanksgiving to New Year's Eve and honours the people who keep working while others celebrate. Police officers, firefighters, nurses, soldiers, shop staff and delivery drivers often spend the holidays on shift and away from their families. The idea is simple: notice them, thank them, and share a little of the season with them, whether through a card, a meal or a kind word.

slogans.en: For those who keep the lights on.

descriptions.en: Albanian Independence Day on November 28 marks 1912, when the Assembly of Vlorë, led by Ismail Qemali, declared Albania independent from the Ottoman Empire and raised the red flag with the black double-headed eagle. The date was chosen to echo November 28, 1443, when the national hero Skanderbeg is said to have raised the same flag at Krujë. Albanians in Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia and the diaspora celebrate with flags, parades, music and family gatherings.

slogans.en: One flag. One people. One day.

descriptions.en: National Chocolates Day on November 29 celebrates chocolate in every form, from bars and truffles to bonbons and hot cocoa. Chocolate comes from cacao beans, first prepared as a bitter drink by peoples of Mesoamerica such as the Olmec, Maya and Aztecs, and only sweetened after it reached Europe in the 16th century. People mark the day by sharing a box with colleagues, baking with chocolate or trying a bar from a small fair-trade maker.

International Jaguar Day on November 29 was launched in 2018 by the countries where the jaguar lives, from Mexico to Argentina, as part of a plan to protect the species and its habitat by 2030. The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and has already lost around half of its historic range to deforestation, hunting and conflict with ranchers. Conservation groups use the day to promote wildlife corridors linking forests across borders and ways for farmers and jaguars to coexist.

Albanian Liberation Day on November 29 marks 1944, when the last German forces withdrew from Albania at the end of the Second World War. The country had been occupied first by Italy from 1939 and then by Germany from 1943, and was freed by partisan resistance without the arrival of Allied armies. It is a public holiday, observed with wreath-laying at war memorials, official ceremonies and school programmes about the partisans and civilians who died.

slogans.en: Remember the cost. Honour the freed.

descriptions.en: Games Day on December 20 is an invitation to set aside work and play a game, whether on a board, with a deck of cards, on a console or in the backyard. Games are among the oldest pastimes humans have: boards for the Royal Game of Ur and the Egyptian game senet are thousands of years old. Falling just before the winter holidays, the day is a good excuse to bring family and friends around a table and play together.

slogans.en: Roll the dice. Play the game.

descriptions.en: International Human Solidarity Day on December 20 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2005 and first observed in 2006. It celebrates solidarity as one of the basic values of relations between people and nations: the idea that those who have more share with those who have less, and that no one is left behind. The day is used to promote action on poverty and inequality, and to encourage people to support community projects, charities and humanitarian appeals.

Saturnalia was the ancient Roman festival in honour of Saturn, god of sowing and agriculture, which began on December 17 and over time stretched to a week. Rome turned upside down for the holiday: work and business stopped, masters sometimes served their slaves at table, people wore the felt cap of freed slaves, and everyone greeted each other with Io Saturnalia. Romans exchanged small gifts such as candles and clay figurines, and several of these customs later found their way into Christmas and New Year celebrations.

World Basketball Day on December 21 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2023. The date marks December 21, 1891, when James Naismith's students played the first game of basketball at the YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, shooting at peach baskets nailed to a balcony. Today basketball is played by hundreds of millions of people in almost every country, and the day celebrates the sport's power to bring people together, from street courts to the Olympics.

National Crossword Puzzle Day on December 21 marks the publication of the first modern crossword in the New York World newspaper on December 21, 1913. Its creator, the Liverpool-born journalist Arthur Wynne, called it a word-cross and laid it out in a diamond shape. Crosswords became a craze in the 1920s and are now printed in newspapers in many languages, so the day is a good moment to sit down with a pencil and a fresh grid.

slogans.en: One across. Clue: a good day.

descriptions.en: National Short Story Day falls on December 21, the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, a fitting date for the shortest form of fiction. Short stories have a long history, from the tales of the Thousand and One Nights to the masters of the form such as Anton Chekhov, Edgar Allan Poe, Alice Munro and Sait Faik Abasıyanık. The day invites readers to pick up a story that can be finished in one sitting, and writers to try writing one.

slogans.en: Tell the story that lives in you.

names.en: Look On The Bright Side Day

descriptions.en: Look on the Bright Side Day falls on December 21, the winter solstice and the darkest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. The timing is the point: from this day on, the days start getting longer again. It is a gentle nudge to look for the good in a hard situation, write down a few things to be grateful for and share some optimism with someone who needs it.

World Meditation Day on December 21 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in December 2024 and first observed that month. Meditation practices have deep roots in Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, Islamic and other traditions, and research links regular practice with lower stress and better attention. The day invites people everywhere to take a few quiet minutes to breathe, sit still and pay attention to the present moment.

World Snowboard Day, held around the start of the northern winter season, invites people to try snowboarding for the first time. Snowboarding grew out of surfing and skateboarding culture in the United States in the 1960s and 1970s and became an Olympic sport at the 1998 Winter Games in Nagano. On the day, resorts and schools in many countries offer free or discounted lessons and gear, and experienced riders share the slopes with beginners.

National Homeless Persons' Memorial Day on December 21, the longest night of the year, was started in 1990 by the National Coalition for the Homeless in the United States. It remembers the people who died while homeless during the past year, many of them from illness, violence or exposure to the cold. Communities hold candlelight vigils and read the names aloud, and many use the day to push for affordable housing and to support local shelters.

The winter solstice, around December 21 in the Northern Hemisphere, is the moment the North Pole is tilted farthest from the Sun, giving the shortest day and the longest night of the year. From then on the days slowly lengthen, which is why so many cultures have marked it as the return of the light. People celebrate with festivals such as Yule and the Iranian Shab-e Yalda, sunrise gatherings at ancient sites like Stonehenge and Newgrange, and long evenings with family.

Gift of Sight Month in December encourages people to look after their eyes and to help others get the eye care they need. The World Health Organization estimates that at least a billion people have a vision problem that could have been prevented or has not yet been treated, often for lack of a simple eye test or a pair of glasses. The month is a reminder to book a routine eye exam and to support charities that provide glasses and cataract surgery.

slogans.en: Protect the windows to your world.

descriptions.en: Carols by Candlelight is an Australian Christmas Eve tradition that began in Melbourne in 1938, started by radio announcer Norman Banks after he saw a woman listening alone to carols by candlelight in her window. Each year tens of thousands of people gather at the Sidney Myer Music Bowl, and many more in parks and town squares across Australia, holding candles and singing carols under the summer night sky. The Melbourne concert is broadcast nationally and raises money for children's charities.

Christmas Eve, celebrated every December 24, is the quiet hush that falls on the world just before Christmas morning. Families gather for candlelit services, midnight Mass, and shared meals; in Christian tradition, it is the eve of the birth of Christ. The evening invites stillness and reflection, and remains for many the most meaningful night of the year.

Boxing Day on December 26 is a public holiday in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and other Commonwealth countries. Its name is usually traced to the Victorian custom of giving servants, tradespeople and the poor a Christmas box of money or gifts the day after Christmas. Today it is a day for family visits and leftovers, a full programme of football and horse racing, cricket's Boxing Day Test in Melbourne, and big post-Christmas sales.

The International Day of Epidemic Preparedness on December 27 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in December 2020, in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic. The date is the birthday of Louis Pasteur, born in 1822, whose work on germs and vaccines laid foundations of modern public health. The day calls on governments and communities to invest in strong health systems, early warning, research and cooperation, so the next outbreak can be stopped before it becomes a pandemic.

Holy Innocents' Day on December 28 remembers the young boys of Bethlehem whom, according to the Gospel of Matthew, King Herod ordered killed in his attempt to destroy the infant Jesus. The Western churches honour them as the first martyrs, while Orthodox churches mark the feast on December 29. In Spain and much of Latin America the day has a lighter side as the Día de los Santos Inocentes, when people play pranks much like April Fools' Day.

National Call a Friend Day on December 28 falls in the quiet days between Christmas and New Year, a natural moment to reconnect. Messages and likes are easy, but a real phone call carries tone, laughter and the chance to talk properly. The day is a nudge to ring an old friend, someone who might be lonely over the holidays, or anyone you have been meaning to call for months.

Hogmanay is the Scottish celebration of the last day of the year, with roots in older midwinter festivities. After the Reformation the Church of Scotland discouraged Christmas as too Catholic, so for centuries New Year became Scotland's biggest winter holiday. Traditions include first-footing, when the first visitor after midnight brings coal, shortbread or whisky for luck, singing Robert Burns's Auld Lang Syne, and huge street parties, torchlight processions and fire festivals in Edinburgh and beyond.

National Compliment Day on January 24 was started in 1998 by Kathy Chamberlin and Debby Hoffman in New Hampshire. It encourages people to give at least a few sincere, specific compliments during the day, to family, friends, colleagues and strangers alike. Research suggests that people underestimate how much a compliment brightens someone's day, and the best ones praise effort or character rather than appearance.

Change a Pet's Life Day on January 24 draws attention to the millions of dogs, cats and other animals waiting in shelters for a home. Adopting one animal frees a place for another in need, and adopted pets often arrive already vaccinated and neutered. For those who cannot adopt, the day suggests other ways to help: fostering, volunteering, donating food and supplies, or sharing photos of animals available for adoption.

National Bible Sunday is observed by some churches in the United States and elsewhere on a Sunday in late January, as a day to celebrate the Bible and encourage people to read it. Churches mark it with sermons on scripture, readings, and the giving of Bibles to children, new members and people who do not have one. The day also highlights the work of Bible societies, which translate the scriptures into new languages and distribute them around the world.

World Kiwanis Week, from January 21 to 26, marks the founding of Kiwanis on January 21, 1915, in Detroit, Michigan, as a club of local businessmen. It has since become Kiwanis International, a global network of volunteer clubs whose mission is to improve the lives of children, through projects such as reading programmes, playgrounds and campaigns against iodine deficiency and maternal and neonatal tetanus. During the week, clubs hold service projects, open meetings and thank-you events for their members.

Manuary is a January campaign in which men grow out their beards and moustaches through the coldest month, a follow-up to Movember. Participants use the challenge to start conversations about men's health and to raise money for related charities. It is also a light-hearted way to ease into the new year, and a reminder to book the health check-ups many men put off.

slogans.en: Grow the beard. Beat the cancer.

descriptions.en: St Dwynwen's Day on January 25 is the Welsh day of love, often called the Welsh Valentine's Day. Dwynwen was a 5th-century Welsh princess who, according to legend, turned away from an unhappy love, became a nun on Llanddwyn Island off Anglesey and prayed that all true lovers would find happiness. Couples in Wales exchange cards and carved wooden lovespoons, a traditional Welsh love token, and some visit the ruins of her church on Llanddwyn.

Better Business Communication Day, on the fourth Monday of January, encourages workplaces to look at how they talk to customers and to each other. Unclear emails, jargon and endless meetings waste time and cause mistakes, while plain language, active listening and honest feedback build trust. The day suggests small changes: shorter messages with one clear request, meetings with a purpose, and asking whether people actually understood.

Cancer Talk Week, held in the last week of January, encourages people to talk openly about cancer, a subject many still avoid. Talking can help people notice and act on possible symptoms sooner, ask about screening, and feel less alone during treatment or after losing someone. The week invites people to start a conversation with a friend, family member or doctor, and reminds everyone that support services are available for patients and their loved ones.

slogans.en: Talk about it. Beat it sooner.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Clean Energy on January 26 was declared by the UN General Assembly and first observed in 2024. The date marks the founding of the International Renewable Energy Agency, IRENA, on January 26, 2009, and the day supports the UN goal of affordable, reliable and modern energy for all. Around the world it is used to promote solar, wind and other renewables, to push for energy efficiency and to draw attention to the hundreds of millions of people who still live without electricity.

World Environmental Education Day on January 26 highlights the role of learning in protecting the planet. It draws on the Belgrade Charter of 1975, one of the first international frameworks to set out what environmental education should achieve: awareness, knowledge, skills and action. Schools, nature centres and environmental groups mark the day with outdoor lessons, clean-ups, tree planting and projects that teach children how to save water and energy and reduce waste.

slogans.en: Learn the Earth. Love the Earth.

descriptions.en: Vietnam Peace Day on January 27 marks the signing of the Paris Peace Accords in 1973, which ended direct US military involvement in the Vietnam War. The agreement brought a ceasefire and the release of prisoners of war, though fighting between North and South Vietnam went on until the fall of Saigon in 1975. The day is a moment to remember the millions of soldiers and civilians who died, to honour veterans and to reflect on the long work of making peace.

slogans.en: Remember. Reflect. Renew the hope for peace.

descriptions.en: On January 27, 1945, soldiers of the Soviet Red Army entered Auschwitz, the largest of the Nazi concentration and extermination camps, in occupied Poland. Around 1.1 million people were murdered there, the great majority of them Jews, along with Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others, and the soldiers found about 7,000 starving prisoners left behind. Each year survivors, leaders and visitors gather at the Auschwitz-Birkenau memorial in Oświęcim to lay wreaths, light candles and remember the victims.

National Daisy Day on January 28 celebrates the daisy, one of the most familiar flowers in gardens, meadows and lawns. Its English name comes from the Old English for day's eye, because the common daisy opens its petals in the morning and closes them at dusk. In the middle of winter the day is a small promise of spring, marked by giving a bunch of daisies, planning a flower bed or playing the old game of plucking petals to the words he loves me, he loves me not.

slogans.en: Plant a daisy, share a smile.

descriptions.en: Pop Art Day on January 28 celebrates the art movement that turned soup cans, comic strips, adverts and film stars into paintings and prints. Pop art emerged in Britain in the mid-1950s and took off in the United States in the 1960s, where Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein and Claes Oldenburg became its best-known names. It blurred the line between high art and popular culture, and people mark the day by visiting a gallery, making bright collages from magazines or turning an everyday object into art.

NASA's Day of Remembrance, held on the last Thursday of January, honours the astronauts who died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967, the Challenger explosion in 1986 and the loss of Columbia in 2003. The three tragedies all happened in the last week of January or the first days of February, which is why the agency chose this time of year. NASA flags fly at half-staff, wreaths are laid at Arlington National Cemetery and at NASA centres, and employees pause to reflect on the lessons for safety in spaceflight.

Seeing Eye Guide Dog Anniversary on January 29 marks the founding of The Seeing Eye in Nashville, Tennessee, in 1929, the oldest guide dog school still working in the United States. It was started by Dorothy Harrison Eustis, who had written about guide dogs being trained in Switzerland, and Morris Frank, a young blind man who travelled there to train with his German shepherd, Buddy. The day honours guide dogs, their handlers and the trainers, puppy raisers and donors behind every team, and is a reminder that guide dogs at work should not be petted or distracted.

Freethinkers Day on January 29 marks the birthday of Thomas Paine, born in Thetford, England, in 1737. His pamphlet Common Sense of 1776 rallied American colonists to independence, Rights of Man defended the French Revolution, and The Age of Reason challenged organised religion and made him one of the best-known freethinkers of his time. The day celebrates reason, evidence and the courage to question authority, and is marked with readings from Paine, talks and debates.

The Surva festival is held at the end of January in Pernik, Bulgaria, and has been an international festival of masquerade games since 1966. Thousands of mummers, known as survakari or kukeri, come from across Bulgaria and abroad wearing huge masks of fur, feathers and horns and heavy bells tied around their waists. Their noisy dances are meant to drive away evil spirits and bring health and a good harvest, and the Surova custom of the Pernik region is on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

slogans.en: Mask the past. Dance the future.

descriptions.en: National Escape Day on January 30 encourages people to step away from their routine and recharge. It falls in the long stretch of late winter, when the holidays are over, the days are still short and many people feel worn out. Ways to mark it range from a weekend trip or a long walk to a day without screens, a good book or simply planning the next holiday.

slogans.en: Step away. Breathe. Come back refreshed.

descriptions.en: World Leprosy Day is held on the last Sunday of January, a date chosen in 1954 by the French journalist and humanitarian Raoul Follereau to fall close to the anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi's death, since Gandhi had cared for people with leprosy. Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is caused by a slow-growing bacterium and is fully curable with multidrug therapy, recommended by the World Health Organization since 1981 and provided free of charge. Yet fear and discrimination still keep many people from seeking treatment, so the day is marked with awareness campaigns, screening drives and calls to end laws and attitudes that exclude those affected.

names.en: Inspire Your Heart With Art Day

descriptions.en: Inspire Your Heart With Art Day on January 31 invites people to make room for art in their lives, whether in a gallery, a concert hall, a book or their own sketchbook. Its origins are informal, but its message is backed by research linking looking at and making art with lower stress, better mood and a stronger sense of connection to others. People mark the day by visiting a museum, listening closely to a favourite piece of music, picking up a brush or instrument again, or taking a child to a creative workshop.

Nauru Independence Day on January 31 marks 1968, when the island became an independent republic after decades as a UN trust territory administered by Australia. The date was chosen to recall January 31, 1946, when Nauruans who had been deported by Japanese forces during the Second World War returned home from the island of Truk. The world's third-smallest country by area, after Vatican City and Monaco, celebrates with sports competitions, cultural performances, music and community feasts across the island.

Celebrate Older Adults, also called Wellderly Day, falls on the third Monday of March and celebrates growing older in good health and good spirits. The word "wellderly" joins "well" and "elderly", and the day's message is that what matters is not only adding years to life but adding life to years. It honours the experience older people bring to their families and communities, and reminds everyone that staying connected, active and curious helps at every age. People mark it by visiting older relatives and neighbours, sharing stories, and joining walks, classes or get-togethers.

slogans.en: Add life to years, not just years to life.

descriptions.en: National Brutus Day falls on March 15, the Ides of March, the day Julius Caesar was assassinated in Rome in 44 BC. Marcus Brutus, a trusted friend of Caesar, was among the senators who killed him. His name has stood for betrayal ever since, helped along by the famous line Shakespeare gave the dying Caesar: "Et tu, Brute". The day is a light-hearted reminder to watch out for backstabbers and to appreciate the loyal friends who have always had your back.

slogans.en: Watch for the Ides, but honor true friends.

descriptions.en: The International Day to Combat Islamophobia, observed every March 15, calls on people everywhere to reject fear, hatred and discrimination directed at Muslims. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2022, choosing the anniversary of the 2019 attacks on two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in which 51 worshippers were killed. It is marked with UN events, interfaith gatherings, talks and educational campaigns that promote tolerance, dialogue and respect for freedom of religion.

slogans.en: Stand against fear. Stand with Muslims.

descriptions.en: Belarus Constitution Day, observed every March 15, marks the adoption of the Constitution of the Republic of Belarus by the Supreme Council in 1994. The constitution set out the country's system of government and the rights and duties of its citizens a few years after Belarus became independent. The day is marked with official ceremonies, flag-raisings and events in schools and public institutions that focus on the country's laws and statehood.

Benito Juárez Day is a Mexican public holiday honouring Benito Juárez, born on March 21, 1806, and remembered as the country's first Indigenous president. A Zapotec who rose from poverty to lead the nation, he championed the Reform Laws that separated church and state and led the resistance against the French intervention. The holiday falls on the third Monday of March, when schools, banks and government offices close, and towns hold civic ceremonies and parades in his memory.

Global Money Week is an annual awareness campaign held each March to help children and young people learn how to manage money wisely and safely. Today it is coordinated by the OECD's International Network on Financial Education, which brings together governments, central banks and education groups from many countries. During the week, schools, banks and community organisations run lessons, games, competitions and workshops on saving, budgeting, spending and avoiding financial scams.

slogans.en: Protect your money. Secure your future.

descriptions.en: The Adelaide Fringe is a huge open-access arts festival held each year in Adelaide, South Australia, running for about a month from mid-February into March. It began in 1960 alongside the first Adelaide Festival of Arts, when artists left out of the official programme staged their own shows. Open access means any artist can take part, so comedy, theatre, music, cabaret, circus and visual art fill grand theatres, parks, pubs and pop-up tents. Locals and visitors spend warm evenings hopping from show to show.

names.en: National Drug and Alcohol Facts Week

descriptions.en: National Drug and Alcohol Facts Week is an annual US health observance held in March that gives teenagers science-based facts about drugs, alcohol and addiction. It was launched in 2010 by the National Institute on Drug Abuse to counter the myths young people hear from friends, films and the internet. During the week, schools, libraries and community groups hold quizzes, classroom activities and question sessions with experts so teens can make informed, healthy choices.

Universal Women's Week stretches the spirit of International Women's Day across a whole week in March. It is a time to celebrate what women have achieved in every culture and to look at the inequalities many still face, from pay and education to safety and political voice. Schools, workplaces and communities mark it with talks, exhibitions and events that tell the stories of women past and present, and with conversations about what still needs to change.

slogans.en: Rise together. Lift each other up.

descriptions.en: National Colon Cancer Awareness Month is observed in the United States every March, a tradition that began when President Bill Clinton proclaimed it in 2000. Colorectal cancer is one of the most common cancers, yet it is often preventable or treatable when caught early through regular screening. Throughout the month, doctors and health groups urge people to talk about symptoms and get checked, many wear blue ribbons, and survivors and families share their stories to ease the embarrassment that keeps many from seeking help.

Nutrition Month, held every March in the United States, encourages people to make informed food choices and build healthy eating and physical activity habits. It is organised by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, which began it in 1973 as a week-long campaign before expanding it to a full month. Each year brings a new theme, and dietitians, schools and community groups mark it with cooking demonstrations, healthy recipes, nutrition talks and tips on eating well on any budget.

names.en: Expanding Girls' Horizons in Science and Engineering Month

descriptions.en: Expanding Girls' Horizons in Science and Engineering Month is a March observance in the United States that invites girls to picture themselves as scientists, engineers and inventors. Women are still underrepresented in many science and technology careers, and early encouragement can shape which paths a girl believes are open to her. Schools, universities, museums and community groups mark the month with hands-on workshops, lab visits and talks by women working in these fields, giving girls the chance to meet role models and try the work for themselves.

National Panda Day on March 16 is a day to appreciate the giant panda, the black-and-white bear that has become a worldwide symbol of wildlife conservation. Wild pandas live only in the misty mountain bamboo forests of central China, where they spend much of each day eating bamboo. Years of habitat protection helped the species move from endangered to vulnerable, so the day mixes celebration with a reminder that the work goes on. People watch zoo panda cams, read up on the species and support conservation groups.

slogans.en: Protect the panda. Protect the bamboo forest.

descriptions.en: National Freedom of Information Day, observed every March 16, honors President James Madison on his birthday by celebrating the public's right to access government records. First celebrated in 1989 by the Freedom of Information Center, the day promotes access laws like the U.S. FOIA, encourages civic literacy, and reminds journalists and citizens of their right to petition agencies for documents.

St. Urho's Day on March 16 is a playful Finnish-American holiday honouring a saint who never existed. It was dreamed up in Minnesota's Finnish communities in the mid-20th century, partly as a cheeky answer to St. Patrick's Day the following day. According to the made-up legend, St. Urho drove the grasshoppers out of Finland and saved the grape harvest. Fans mark it by wearing purple and green, drinking grape juice or wine, holding small parades and shouting the saint's mock-Finnish chant at the grasshoppers.

March Madness is the nickname for the NCAA Division I basketball tournaments, the knockout championships of American college basketball for men and women. The men's tournament began in 1939 and the women's in 1982; today 68 teams start out in mid-March and the last four meet at the Final Four in early April.
