Its fame comes from surprise upsets, underdog runs and last-second shots. Across the United States, friends and offices fill in brackets predicting every game and gather to watch.

Goddess of Fertility Day on March 18 recalls the fertility goddesses honoured by ancient peoples, such as Inanna and Ishtar in Mesopotamia, Demeter in Greece and Venus in Rome. These goddesses stood for birth, love, harvests and the return of life after winter. Falling just before the spring equinox, the day ties those old beliefs to the season of new growth. People mark it by planting seeds, bringing fresh flowers indoors, reading ancient myths or simply taking time to notice spring arriving.

slogans.en: Plant seeds. Plant hopes. Plant joy.

descriptions.en: Global Recycling Day on March 18 celebrates recycling and the people who make it work, from waste collectors to sorting plant workers. It was launched in 2018 by the Bureau of International Recycling, a global industry body, which calls recyclable materials the world's "seventh resource" alongside water, air, oil, natural gas, coal and minerals. The day urges people, companies and governments to treat waste as something valuable. Many people mark it by sorting their rubbish more carefully, repairing instead of throwing away and joining local clean-ups.

slogans.en: Recycle today for a better tomorrow.

descriptions.en: National Public Defense Day, observed every March 18, celebrates the vital role of public defenders in ensuring fair access to legal representation, particularly for those who cannot afford a lawyer. The day recognizes the work of Gideon v. Wainwright, the Supreme Court ruling that established the right to counsel, and honors the attorneys who carry forward that legacy in courtrooms nationwide.

Operation Iraqi Freedom Day on March 19 marks the start of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, led by the United States with the United Kingdom and other allies. The campaign toppled Saddam Hussein's government within weeks, but it was followed by years of insurgency and sectarian violence, and US combat operations formally ended in 2010. The war cost many lives among soldiers and, above all, Iraqi civilians. The day is kept as a time of remembrance for the fallen and reflection on the war's lasting effects.

National Let's Laugh Day on March 19 is a cheerful reminder to make room for laughter in everyday life. Laughter eases stress, lifts the mood and brings people closer, and it is contagious: one person's laugh quickly sets off another's. The day has no grand history; its point is simply to share a good laugh. People mark it by swapping jokes, watching a favourite comedy, going to a stand-up show, trying laughter yoga or recalling funny memories with friends and family.

The Feast of Saint Joseph, on March 19, honours Joseph, the husband of Mary and the foster father of Jesus. The Catholic Church sees him as a model of quiet work, faithfulness and care for the family, and he is the patron saint of the universal Church. Italians, especially in Sicily, set up Saint Joseph's Tables laden with bread and sweets to share with the poor, and bakers fill their windows with zeppole. In Italy, Spain and Portugal the day is also Father's Day, and in Valencia it closes the Fallas festival.

slogans.en: Saint Joseph, patron of families and workers.

descriptions.en: National Native HIV/AIDS Awareness Day, on March 20 in the United States, focuses on HIV among American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian people. First held in 2007, it falls on the spring equinox, a time of renewal and balance in many Native traditions. The day encourages people to get tested, know their status and seek treatment, and works to break the stigma that keeps many from asking for help. Tribes, clinics and community groups hold free testing events, talks and gatherings rooted in their own cultures.

The March Equinox, usually on March 20, is the moment the Sun crosses the celestial equator heading north, so day and night are roughly the same length everywhere on Earth. It marks the start of astronomical spring in the Northern Hemisphere and of autumn in the Southern Hemisphere. People have watched for it since ancient times: Nowruz, the Persian new year celebrated across Iran, Central Asia and as Nevruz in Türkiye, begins at the equinox, and crowds gather at Chichén Itzá in Mexico to see a shadow serpent slide down the pyramid's steps.

slogans.en: Light and dark find their balance.

descriptions.en: Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere with the March equinox, around March 20, when days start to outgrow nights. After the cold months it is a time of renewal: trees bud, birds return and gardens come back to life. Many cultures greet the season with festivals and customs, from Nowruz, the new year celebrated as Nevruz in Türkiye with jumping over bonfires, to Holi, the Indian festival of colours. People also mark it with spring cleaning, planting seeds and the first walks and picnics outdoors.

Astrology Day falls on March 20, around the spring equinox, when the Sun enters Aries and the astrological year begins with the first sign of the zodiac. It is an informal day for people who enjoy astrology to celebrate a tradition that reaches back thousands of years, to the sky-watchers of ancient Mesopotamia. Enthusiasts mark it by drawing up birth charts, reading their horoscopes for the year ahead, and meeting at talks and gatherings where newcomers can learn from experienced astrologers.

International Color Day, held on 21 March around the spring equinox, celebrates the role of color in our lives. It was proposed by the Portuguese Color Association and taken up by the International Colour Association, which has promoted it since 2009. The day brings together everyone who works with color, from physicists and biologists to artists, designers and architects, and reminds us how much color shapes what we see and feel. It is marked with exhibitions, workshops, lectures and colorful events in schools and studios.

World Day for Glaciers, held on 21 March, draws attention to the world's glaciers and the fresh water they store. The United Nations declared the day alongside the International Year of Glaciers' Preservation, and it was first observed in 2025. Glaciers act as natural water towers, feeding the rivers that billions of people rely on for drinking water, farming and energy, yet they are shrinking fast as the climate warms. Scientists, schools and environmental groups mark the day with talks, exhibitions and calls for climate action.

slogans.en: Protect the ice that feeds the world.

descriptions.en: Big Bang Day celebrates the scientific story of how our universe began, about 13.8 billion years ago, from an extremely hot and dense state. It falls on 21 March, the date in 2013 when the European Space Agency released the Planck satellite's detailed map of the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of that early universe. The day honours the long chain of discovery, from Georges Lemaître's idea of an expanding cosmos to Edwin Hubble's observations of receding galaxies. Science centres and planetariums mark it with talks, stargazing and shows about the cosmos.

Semana Santa, or Holy Week, is the Christian week from Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday that recalls the last days, death and resurrection of Jesus. Its dates move each year with Easter. It is observed with special intensity in Spain, Portugal, Mexico and Guatemala, where Catholic faith and centuries of local tradition meet. Brotherhoods carry ornate floats called pasos through the streets in solemn processions, accompanied by drums and brass bands, and in Guatemala people lay colorful carpets of dyed sawdust and flowers along the routes.

Texas Independence Day, on 2 March, marks the day in 1836 when delegates meeting at Washington-on-the-Brazos adopted the Texas Declaration of Independence from Mexico. The declaration came while the Alamo was under siege, and Texan forces under Sam Houston secured independence with their victory at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836. The Republic of Texas remained independent until it joined the United States in 1845. Texans mark the day with reenactments, parades and celebrations, especially at the historic site where the declaration was signed.

names.en: National Aplastic Anemia & MDS Awareness Week

descriptions.en: National Aplastic Anemia & MDS Awareness Week, held in the United States in early March, shines a light on rare bone marrow failure diseases such as aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndromes. In these conditions the bone marrow stops making enough healthy blood cells, leaving people tired, prone to infection and at risk of bleeding. Patient groups, led by the Aplastic Anemia and MDS International Foundation, use the week to share patient stories, support families, encourage blood and marrow donor registration and raise funds for research into better treatments.

National Shareholders Day on January 10 recognises the ordinary people who own a piece of companies through shares, whether directly or through pension and investment funds. Shareholders provide the capital businesses use to grow, and in return they share in the profits and have a say through their votes at annual meetings. The day is a reminder to learn the basics of investing, think long-term and use the voting rights that come with owning shares.

Ratification Day on January 14 marks the day in 1784 when the Confederation Congress, meeting in Annapolis, Maryland, ratified the Treaty of Paris. Signed in September 1783, the treaty ended the American Revolutionary War, and Britain recognised the independence of the United States and its borders reaching west to the Mississippi. Congress had struggled for weeks to gather enough delegates to vote, and the ratified copy then had to cross the Atlantic before the deadline.

Makar Sankranti, usually on January 14 or 15, marks the sun's entry into the sign of Makara (Capricorn) in the Hindu calendar and the start of its northward journey, Uttarayana, bringing longer days. Unlike most Hindu festivals, it follows the solar calendar, so its date barely changes from year to year. It is celebrated across India and Nepal under many names, with holy dips in rivers such as the Ganges, sweets made of sesame and jaggery, bonfires, and kite flying that fills the skies of Gujarat and Rajasthan.

National Tulip Day in the Netherlands, on the third Saturday of January, opens the Dutch tulip season with a free picking garden of around 200,000 tulips on Dam Square in Amsterdam. Organised by Dutch tulip growers since 2012, it lets visitors walk in and pick their own bouquet for free. Tulips arrived in the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century, sparked the famous tulip mania of the 1630s, and the country now grows billions of bulbs every year.

slogans.en: Pick a tulip. Take spring home.

descriptions.en: Pongal is a four-day harvest festival celebrated by Tamils in mid-January, in Tamil Nadu, Sri Lanka and the diaspora, thanking the Sun, nature and cattle for the harvest. Its name comes from the sweet rice dish boiled in new clay pots with milk and jaggery until it overflows, a sign of abundance, as people cry Pongalo Pongal. The days include Bhogi, when old things are discarded, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal honouring cattle with painted horns, and Kaanum Pongal for family outings, and homes are decorated with kolam patterns.

The Feast of the Santo Niño, the Holy Child Jesus, is celebrated on the third Sunday of January in the Philippines, most famously in Cebu City with the Sinulog festival. It honours a small statue of the Christ Child that Ferdinand Magellan's expedition gave to the wife of a local ruler, Rajah Humabon, at her baptism in 1521, and which Spanish soldiers found again in 1565. Millions join the processions, masses and the Sinulog street dance, a rhythmic two-steps-forward, one-step-back movement performed in colourful costumes to drumbeats.

World Snow Day, on or around the third Sunday of January, was launched in 2012 by the International Ski Federation, FIS, to bring children and families to the snow. Ski resorts and clubs in dozens of countries offer free or discounted lessons, equipment and activities, from skiing and snowboarding to sledging and snowshoeing. The idea is to give children a first taste of winter sports and outdoor fun, and to encourage an active lifestyle in the colder months.

World Religion Day, on the third Sunday of January, was first observed in 1950 by the National Spiritual Assembly of the Bahá'ís of the United States. Inspired by the Bahá'í teaching of the oneness of religion, it highlights the values that the world's faiths share, such as compassion, honesty and care for others. Today it is marked in many countries with interfaith services, panel discussions and visits between places of worship.

Hunt for Happiness Week, held in the third week of January, invites people to look for what makes them happy at a time of year when many feel low. Its organisers suggest small, practical steps: noticing what went well each day, spending time with people you like, doing something kind and making room for things you enjoy. Research on wellbeing suggests that relationships, gratitude and a sense of purpose matter more for lasting happiness than possessions.

Take a Walk Outdoors Day on January 20 encourages people to step outside, even in the middle of winter, and go for a walk. Walking is one of the simplest forms of exercise: it strengthens the heart, helps control weight and blood sugar, and time outdoors in daylight can lift mood and improve sleep. A brisk twenty or thirty minutes in a park, along a river or around the neighbourhood is enough to feel the difference.

The International Day of Acceptance on January 20 was started in 2010 by Stevie Hopkins and the organisation 3E Love, in memory of his sister Annie Hopkins, a disability rights advocate who died on that date in 2009. Annie created the wheelchair heart symbol, a heart with a wheelchair figure inside, to show that disability is part of life and nothing to hide. The day invites people with disabilities to embrace who they are and asks everyone else to see the person, not the disability, and to remove barriers.

Mariachi Day celebrates the Mexican ensemble of violins, trumpets, guitars, the deep guitarrón and the high-pitched vihuela, whose musicians wear the traditional charro suit. Mariachi grew from rural string music in western Mexico, especially Jalisco, and became a symbol of Mexican identity in the 20th century through radio and film. UNESCO added it to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011, and the day is marked with performances in plazas, restaurants and concert halls.

slogans.en: Sounds of Mexico, soul of a nation.

descriptions.en: Thank Your Mentor Day falls in January during National Mentoring Month in the United States, a campaign launched in 2002 by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and MENTOR, the National Mentoring Partnership. It invites people to thank the teachers, coaches, managers and neighbours who guided them, often without being asked. Research shows that young people with mentors are more likely to stay in school and aim higher, and the day also encourages people to become mentors themselves.

names.en: Get to Know Your Customers Day

descriptions.en: Get to Know Your Customers Day falls on the third Thursday of each quarter, including January, and encourages businesses to step back from selling and listen. Owners and staff are invited to call regular customers, ask for honest feedback, learn why people choose them and what frustrates them. Small businesses in particular gain from knowing customers by name, and the day is a reminder that loyal customers are built through attention, not just advertising.

National Hug Your Puppy Day on January 21 celebrates the bond between people and their dogs, whatever their age. Studies have found that gentle contact between people and their dogs can raise levels of oxytocin, the hormone linked to bonding, in both species. The day is also a reminder that not every dog likes being squeezed: experts suggest reading your dog's body language, offering a calm cuddle or a scratch it enjoys, and letting it walk away if it wants.

Ash Wednesday opens Lent in Western Christianity, falling 46 days before Easter. The ashes recall the biblical words "you are dust, and to dust you shall return" and the ancient custom of wearing ashes as a sign of repentance. Worshippers go to church, where a priest or minister marks a cross of ash on their foreheads, and many begin the 40 days of prayer, fasting and giving that lead to Easter.

slogans.en: From dust we came. To dust we return.

descriptions.en: National Robotics Week, established by the U.S. House of Representatives in 2010 after a coalition of more than 140 robotics experts petitioned for recognition, invites students, educators, and the public to explore robotics through build sessions, demos, and competitions in all 50 states. Organized with iRobot and partner organizations, the week spotlights the people, technologies, and careers shaping the field of human-machine collaboration.

Innovation Day on 16 February honours new ideas and the people who turn them into something real. Every tool, medicine and gadget we rely on started as someone's question about how things could work better. The day invites everyone, not just scientists and engineers, to think creatively. People mark it by learning about inventors, trying a fresh approach to an everyday problem, sharing ideas with colleagues or encouraging children to tinker, build and experiment.

slogans.en: Think it. Build it. Try it.

descriptions.en: National Hospitality Workers Appreciation Day, on February 23, thanks the people who keep hotels, restaurants, bars, cafés and event venues running. Their work means long shifts, weekends and holidays on their feet, and a smile kept up for every guest. The day asks diners, travellers and employers to notice that effort. People mark it by thanking staff by name, tipping generously, leaving a kind review, or treating their own teams to a meal and a well-earned break.

Brunei National Day, Hari Kebangsaan, is celebrated on February 23. Brunei became fully independent from the United Kingdom on January 1, 1984, after nearly a century as a British protectorate, and the formal national celebration was set for February 23. The day is a show of loyalty to the sultan and pride in the nation. In Bandar Seri Begawan, crowds gather for a grand parade, students form colourful card mosaics, and prayers, music and fireworks are held across the country.

Fatherland Defenders Day is observed in Belarus on February 23 as the day of the country's defenders and its armed forces. The date goes back to the Soviet era, when February 23 was kept as the birthday of the Red Army, formed in 1918. Today it honours soldiers, veterans and everyone who has served. Wreaths are laid at war memorials, concerts and ceremonies are held, and in many families and workplaces it has also become an informal men's day, with cards and small gifts for fathers, sons and colleagues.

World Obesity Day, on 4 March, calls for better understanding of obesity as a chronic disease shaped by genes, environment, food systems and health care, not simply personal choice. It is led by the World Obesity Federation, which first held the day in October and moved it to 4 March in 2020. Health groups use the day to push for prevention, fair access to treatment and an end to weight stigma, with campaigns, events and personal stories shared around the world.

International HPV Awareness Day, on 4 March, encourages open talk about the human papillomavirus, a very common infection that most people catch at some point and that can lead to cervical and several other cancers. It was launched in 2018 by the International Papillomavirus Society. The day promotes HPV vaccination and regular screening, and works to remove the stigma that keeps people from asking questions and getting care.

International ASMR Day on 9 April celebrates ASMR, the calm, tingling feeling some people get from soft sounds and slow, careful movements. Whispering, tapping, page turning and hair brushing are common triggers, and millions of people watch ASMR videos online to relax or fall asleep. The day invites fans and the curious alike to try a video or two and find what works for them. Creators often share special videos and recommendations to mark the occasion.

Global Holistic Wealth Day, observed on 9 April, asks people to see wealth as more than money in the bank. The idea of holistic wealth brings together financial security, meaningful work, a sense of purpose, close relationships and inner wellbeing. The day encourages individuals, families and workplaces to take stock of all of these and plan for each of them. People mark it by setting goals, reviewing their finances or simply making time for what gives their life meaning.

National Hug Your Dog Day, observed in the United States on 10 April, celebrates the bond between people and their dogs. It encourages owners to slow down and give their dogs some extra attention, whether a cuddle, a favourite scratch or a long walk. The day also reminds owners to learn each dog's body language, because not every dog enjoys a tight hug. Many people share photos of their dogs online, and some visit animal shelters to give dogs waiting for a home a little affection.

slogans.en: Show the love. Watch the leash.

descriptions.en: The Grand National is the world's most famous steeplechase, run each spring at Aintree Racecourse near Liverpool. Horses race over more than four miles and around 30 fences, and the race has been held there since 1839. It has produced legends such as Red Rum, who won three times in the 1970s, and Rachael Blackmore, who in 2021 became the first woman to ride the winner. Across Britain, millions who never bet otherwise join office sweepstakes and gather to watch the race on a Saturday in April.

Golfer's Day on 10 April celebrates everyone who loves golf, from weekend players to professionals. The date is the anniversary of the founding of the Professional Golfers' Association of America in 1916. Golf is played on courses in almost every country, and its mix of skill, patience and fresh air keeps people playing at every age. Golfers mark the day by playing a round or practising at the range, while newcomers might try a lesson or a game of mini golf.

Chinese Language Day is celebrated on April 20 as one of the language days the United Nations set up in 2010 to honour its six official languages. The date pays tribute to Cangjie, the legendary figure said to have invented Chinese characters, and falls around Guyu, the spring solar term that tradition links to his story. The day celebrates one of the world's oldest written languages and the many spoken forms, from Mandarin to Cantonese, that share it. UN offices and schools mark it with calligraphy, poetry readings, film screenings and language lessons.

National Princess Week is a celebration in the United States held over a full week in late April. Rather than focusing on crowns and glitter, it celebrates qualities often linked to storybook princesses, such as kindness, courage and imagination. Children mark it with dress-up play, tea parties and favourite fairy tales, and families and schools use the week to encourage acts of kindness.

slogans.en: Be kind. Be brave. Be you.

names.en: Animal Cruelty / Human Violence Awareness Week

descriptions.en: Animal Cruelty / Human Violence Awareness Week is held each year in the third full week of April, mainly in the United States and the United Kingdom. It highlights a link that researchers and social workers have long observed: people who harm animals are more likely to harm people too, and abuse of a pet is often a warning sign of violence at home. Shelters, schools, vets and domestic-violence groups use the week to share warning signs, teach kindness to animals and encourage people to report abuse, protecting both pets and families.

Leprechaun Day on May 13 celebrates the mischievous little guardians of Irish folklore. Folk tales tell of leprechauns hiding pots of gold at the end of a rainbow and outsmarting anyone who tries to force the secret from them. It is a playful day of treasure hunts, green treats, shamrock crafts and telling the old stories by the fire.

slogans.en: Hunt for the pot of gold.

descriptions.en: The International Day of UN Peacekeepers on May 29 marks the first peacekeeping mission, launched in 1948. It honours the men and women who serve in conflict zones to protect civilians, watch ceasefires, escort aid and help communities rebuild. On this day the UN usually honours the fallen and celebrates the service of those still in the field.

International Everest Day on May 29 marks the first confirmed summit of Mount Everest, reached by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on 29 May 1953. Nepal founded the observance in 2008 to honour Sir Edmund after his death. It celebrates the mountain, the Sherpa communities who live on its slopes, and everyone who climbs it.

World MS Day on May 30 brings people together around multiple sclerosis, a condition in which the immune system damages the protective coating of nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord. The MS International Federation launched the day in 2009, and it is now marked by patient groups in many countries. People share their stories, raise money for research and call for better care, helping others see symptoms such as fatigue and numbness that are often invisible.

Statehood Day on 30 May is one of Croatia's main national holidays. It recalls 30 May 1990, when the first freely elected multi-party parliament, the Sabor, held its opening session, setting the country on its path to independence from Yugoslavia. The holiday returned to this date in 2020 after years on 25 June. It is a public day off, marked with official ceremonies, wreath-laying, concerts and the red-white-blue chequered flag flying everywhere.

Epilepsy Awareness Week, held in the third week of May, explains what epilepsy is: a common brain condition that causes repeated seizures and can affect anyone at any age. Its aim is to replace myths with accurate information, support research and end the stigma that still leads many people with epilepsy to hide it. Charities and clinics share simple first-aid steps, such as staying calm, timing the seizure and never putting anything in the person's mouth, and people tell their own stories online and at local events.

slogans.en: End the stigma, start the talk.

descriptions.en: The Feast of St. Anthony on June 13 honours the thirteenth-century Franciscan preacher from Padua. In Portugal and Italy people bring bread to church to be blessed, and it becomes the custom to give a piece away to the poor. Anthony is also the patron of lost things, so it is the day to ask him to find what has gone missing.

slogans.en: Bread, blessings and lost things found.

descriptions.en: International Albinism Awareness Day, on 13 June, builds understanding of albinism, an inherited condition in which the body makes little or no melanin, leaving skin, hair and eyes very pale and the eyes sensitive to light. The United Nations proclaimed the day in 2014, and first observed it in 2015, in response to the attacks and discrimination that people with albinism face, particularly in parts of Africa. It is marked with campaigns for sun protection, eye care, inclusion and equal rights.

America the Beautiful Week, in the first full week of June, celebrates one of the best-loved patriotic songs in the United States and the landscapes it describes. The words began as a poem by Katharine Lee Bates, inspired by the view from the summit of Pikes Peak in Colorado in 1893, and are usually sung to Samuel A. Ward's hymn tune Materna. People mark the week by singing the song in schools and community gatherings, visiting national parks and enjoying the outdoors. It is also a time to care for local nature, from planting to litter clean-ups.

Evaluate Your Life Day on 19 October is an informal day for stopping to take stock of how your life is going. Rather than marking an event, it matters as a pause in the busy last stretch of the year, a chance to look honestly at your goals, habits and relationships. People mark it by setting aside quiet time, often with a notebook, going through areas like health, work, money, friendships and learning, and writing down one or two changes worth making.

National Basketball Day on November 6 marks the birthday of James Naismith, born in 1861 in Ontario, Canada. As a physical education teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts, he invented basketball in 1891 as an indoor winter game, using two peach baskets nailed to a balcony. People celebrate with pickup games, free-throw contests and by watching a game with friends.

National Ladies Learning Code Day on November 6 comes from Ladies Learning Code, a Canadian nonprofit founded in Toronto in 2011 and now known as Canada Learning Code. It runs beginner-friendly workshops in programming and digital skills for women, girls and other groups underrepresented in technology. On the day, volunteers and mentors across Canada host free or low-cost sessions where participants write their first lines of code.

International Civil Aviation Day on December 7 marks the signing of the Convention on International Civil Aviation in Chicago in 1944, which created the International Civil Aviation Organization. The convention set the shared rules that let aircraft from almost every country fly safely through each other's skies. The day was recognised by the UN General Assembly in 1996 and highlights air safety, sustainable aviation and the role of flight in connecting the world.

Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day on December 7 remembers the more than 2,400 people killed in the 1941 attack on Hawaii. Ceremonies are held across the country, survivors are reunited, and the flag flies at half mast until sunset. At the memorial itself, the names of the lost are still read aloud.

Computer Science Education Week is held each December around December 9, the birthday of the computing pioneer Grace Hopper, born in 1906. Since 2013 it has been home to the Hour of Code, organised by the nonprofit Code.org, in which millions of students around the world try a one-hour coding activity. The week encourages schools to treat computer science as a basic skill and to welcome girls and students from all backgrounds into it.

The National Day of the Horse on December 13 was established by the US Congress in 2004 to recognise the role horses have played in American life. Horses pulled ploughs and wagons, carried settlers and soldiers, and still work on ranches today, while also starring in sport, recreation and therapy programmes. The day encourages people to visit a stable, support horse rescues and learn about caring for these animals.

slogans.en: They carried us, we owe them care.

descriptions.en: St Lucia Day on December 13 honours Lucia of Syracuse, a young Christian martyred in Sicily around the year 304, whose name comes from the Latin word for light. In Sweden, Norway and Finland it falls in the darkest weeks of the year, and under the old Julian calendar it coincided with the winter solstice. Girls in white gowns with red sashes, one wearing a crown of candles, lead processions singing the song Santa Lucia, and families eat saffron buns called lussekatter.

Green Monday is the second Monday of December, one of the busiest online shopping days of the year in the United States. The term was coined in 2007 by eBay, and the green refers to money being spent, not to the environment. It is often the last day shoppers can order gifts with standard shipping and still expect them before Christmas, so stores push one more round of discounts.

Halcyon Days on December 14 recall an ancient Greek myth about Alcyone, who was turned into a kingfisher, the halcyon bird. According to the story, the gods calmed the winds for seven days before and seven days after the winter solstice so that she could nest on the sea. The phrase halcyon days came to mean a time of calm and happiness, and the day is a reminder to enjoy a quiet moment in the middle of winter.

Sustainable Entrepreneurship Day on December 14 puts the spotlight on businesses that measure their success by their effect on people and the planet, not only by profit. These companies design products that last, cut waste and emissions, treat workers and suppliers fairly, and find business opportunities in solving environmental and social problems. The day encourages founders, investors and customers to support that kind of business and to ask harder questions of the rest.

Bill of Rights Day on December 15 marks the ratification in 1791 of the first ten amendments to the US Constitution, known as the Bill of Rights. They protect freedoms such as speech, religion, the press and assembly, the right to a fair trial, and protection from unreasonable searches. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proclaimed the first Bill of Rights Day in 1941, on its 150th anniversary, and schools and libraries mark it with readings and debates on how these rights apply today.

National Heroes and Heroines Day on December 19 is a public holiday in Anguilla, a small British Overseas Territory in the Caribbean. It honours the people who shaped the island's history, especially the leaders of the Anguilla Revolution of 1967, when islanders rejected rule from neighbouring St Kitts and eventually won a separate status under Britain. Ceremonies, school assemblies and community events recall their courage and the island's long road to self-government.

National Mathematics Day in India on December 22 honours Srinivasa Ramanujan, born on that date in 1887 in Tamil Nadu. Largely self-taught, he sent his results to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy in 1913, was invited to England, and in a short life produced thousands of results in number theory and infinite series that mathematicians still study. The day was declared in 2012, the 125th anniversary of his birth, and schools and universities mark it with competitions, lectures and maths fairs.

Forefathers' Day on December 22 commemorates the landing of the Pilgrims at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in December 1620. The Old Colony Club of Plymouth first marked it in 1769, and an error when converting the date from the old Julian calendar fixed the celebration on the 22nd rather than the 21st. In Plymouth the club still marks the day with a dawn procession, a cannon salute and a traditional dinner that includes succotash.

International Cello Day on December 29 celebrates the cello on the birthday of the Catalan cellist Pablo Casals, born in 1876. Casals rediscovered Bach's six Cello Suites, which had been largely forgotten, and his recordings made them part of every cellist's life; he was also a lifelong campaigner for peace. Cellists mark the day with concerts, online performances and lessons, and listeners are invited to hear the instrument live.

National Boss's Day began in 1958, when Patricia Bays Haroski registered it with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in honour of her father, who was also her boss; she chose October 16, his birthday. It is a day for employees to thank the managers who support, mentor and stand up for their teams. When the date falls on a weekend, offices mark it on the nearest working day. A card signed by the whole team, a shared lunch or simply a sincere thank-you is the usual way to celebrate.

slogans.en: Great teams start with a great boss.

descriptions.en: Administrative Professionals Day falls on the Wednesday of the last full week of April in the United States. It began in 1952 as National Secretaries Week and took its current name in 2000, as office roles grew far beyond typing and taking dictation. The day honours the assistants, secretaries, receptionists and office managers whose organisation and quiet problem-solving keep every workplace running. Colleagues and managers mark it with thank-you cards, flowers, a team lunch or a little time off.

slogans.en: The office runs on their organization.

descriptions.en: International Sloth Day draws attention to the slow-moving sloths of Central and South America. It was started in 2010 by the AIUNAU Foundation, a Colombian group that rescues and rehabilitates these animals. Sloths are threatened by deforestation, power lines, roads and the illegal pet trade. On the day, zoos, sanctuaries and conservation groups share facts about sloths, raise money for rescue work and remind people that a sloth belongs in the forest, not in a selfie.

slogans.en: Slow down. They need us to speed up.

descriptions.en: World Immunization Week, led by the World Health Organization every year from 24 to 30 April, highlights how vaccines protect people of all ages from diseases such as measles, polio and diphtheria. Vaccination prevents millions of deaths every year, yet many children still miss out on basic vaccines. During the week, health ministries, clinics and aid groups run vaccination drives and information campaigns, urging families to keep up with their shots and calling for every child and adult to be reached.

World Chagas Disease Day raises awareness of a parasitic illness that affects millions of people, most of whom do not know they are infected. The date recalls 14 April 1909, when Brazilian physician Carlos Chagas diagnosed the first patient, and the World Health Assembly made it an official day in 2019. Spread mainly by triatomine bugs, the disease can quietly damage the heart for years, so health groups use the day to push for early testing and treatment.

slogans.en: Know it, test for it, treat it.

descriptions.en: World Neglected Tropical Diseases Day on January 30 was recognised by the World Health Assembly in 2021 and recalls the London Declaration on Neglected Tropical Diseases, signed on that date in 2012. Around twenty diseases, among them leprosy, dengue, sleeping sickness, river blindness and trachoma, affect more than a billion people, mostly in the poorest communities with little access to clean water and health care. Most are preventable and treatable, and on the day landmarks around the world are lit up while health groups campaign for the funding and medicines needed to end them.

World Hand Hygiene Day, on 5 May, is the World Health Organization's yearly SAVE LIVES: Clean Your Hands campaign, run since 2009. The date stands for the five fingers on each hand. Its message is simple: clean hands at the right moments, before touching a patient, before a procedure, after contact with body fluids, stop infections from passing from person to person. Hospitals and clinics mark it with training, posters and handwashing checks, and the same habit protects families at home.

World Hypertension Day, held on 17 May, draws attention to high blood pressure, one of the most common health problems in the world. The World Hypertension League launched the day in 2005 and has held it on 17 May since 2006. Because high blood pressure often causes no symptoms while raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease, the day urges everyone to have their blood pressure measured and know their numbers. Clinics and pharmacies offer free checks, and doctors share simple advice on salt, exercise and regular follow-up.

slogans.en: Measure your blood pressure. Know your numbers.

descriptions.en: Africa Day on 25 May marks the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963, when leaders of newly independent African states came together; the African Union replaced it in 2002. Across the continent and its diaspora it celebrates African unity, independence and culture, and each year the African Union sets a theme. People mark it with concerts, festivals, traditional dress, food and debates on Africa's future, and some countries make it a public holiday.

Extra Mile Day on November 1 celebrates people who give more than is asked of them, at work, in their goals and for their community. It was started in 2009 by author Shawn Anderson, whose Extra Mile America campaign has since been joined by hundreds of US cities that proclaim the day each year. People mark it by volunteering, finishing a task they have put off, or thanking someone who went beyond the call.

Be the Impact Day on November 2 encourages people to turn good intentions into something real for their community. The idea is that change does not need to wait for leaders or large budgets: a single act of help can start it. People mark the day by volunteering, supporting a local cause or doing one concrete thing for a neighbour.

One Health Day on November 3 promotes the idea that the health of people, animals and the environment is closely linked. It was launched in 2016 by three organisations, the One Health Commission, the One Health Platform and the One Health Initiative. Many new diseases jump from animals to humans, so the day brings together doctors, vets and environmental scientists for talks, student events and joint projects.

Movember turns November into a month of moustaches grown for men's health. It began in Melbourne, Australia, in 2003, when a group of friends dared each other to bring back the moustache and then tied the idea to raising money for prostate cancer. The Movember Foundation now funds work on prostate cancer, testicular cancer, mental health and suicide prevention, and participants grow a moustache, move, or host events to raise donations.

National Stress Awareness Day was set up by Carole Spiers of the International Stress Management Association to make stress something people notice, name and manage. Held on the first Wednesday of November, it asks workplaces and families to look at the pressures people carry — and at simple tools such as journaling, breathing and clear boundaries that take the strain off. The day grew out of a global stress crisis that costs lives as well as productivity.

slogans.en: Notice it. Name it. Tame it.

descriptions.en: Use Your Common Sense Day on November 4 is a reminder that the most useful wisdom is often the plainest. Common sense means stopping to think before acting, learning from experience and choosing the sensible option over the clever one. People mark the day by tackling a problem with a simple, practical fix, or by passing on a piece of down-to-earth advice that served them well.

National Men Make Dinner Day, on the first Thursday of November, invites men who rarely cook to take over the kitchen for one evening. The idea is to share the work of feeding a household and to discover that following a recipe is less daunting than it looks. Men mark the day by planning a meal, shopping for it, cooking it from start to finish and, ideally, doing the washing up too.

slogans.en: Sharpen the knife, take the apron.

descriptions.en: National Mate Day celebrates yerba mate, the herbal drink that Argentina shares with Paraguay, Uruguay and Brazil. Brought to the country by Guaraní and Jesuit missionaries in the 16th century, it is now drunk from a gourd with a metal straw at nearly every table, at every hour of the day. The 30 November holiday says thank you to a plant, a people and a way of sharing time.

Stomach Cancer Awareness Day brings a quiet disease into the light on 30 November. Gastric cancer can grow for years behind symptoms that look ordinary — bloating, nausea, stomach pain — and is often found late. The day asks people to listen to those signals, to know the risk factors, and to talk to a doctor early, when treatment is far simpler.

Cyber Monday is the Monday after Thanksgiving, when the American holiday shopping rush moves from stores to screens. The term was coined in 2005 by Shop.org, part of the National Retail Federation, after retailers noticed a spike in online sales as people returned to work and their faster office internet connections. It has since become one of the biggest online shopping days of the year worldwide, and a good day to watch for fake shops and too-good-to-be-true offers.

Cities for Life Day, organised by the Community of Sant'Egidio, gathers cities around the world on 30 November to speak out against the death penalty. Municipalities light their landmarks, hold public readings and ask for a world without executions, turning a legal question into a shared human one. More than two hundred cities have joined the call over the years.

Secondhand Sunday, created by the resale platform Poshmark, falls on the Sunday after Thanksgiving and makes a case for second-hand clothes and home goods. Resale keeps garments in use for years instead of months, cuts the demand for new production and makes good finds normal rather than odd. On the day, sellers across the platform put their best pre-owned pieces up for grabs.

Red Planet Day on November 28 marks the launch of NASA's Mariner 4 in 1964, the first spacecraft to fly past Mars successfully. In July 1965 it sent back the first close-up pictures of another planet, showing a cratered, dry surface rather than the canals and vegetation some had imagined. Mars gets its red colour from iron oxide dust, and the day is a chance to follow today's rovers and orbiters or look for the planet in the night sky.

Fur-Free Friday falls on the last Friday of November, the same day as Black Friday, and asks people to rethink fur. On the day, campaigners protest outside fur shops and the retailers who still stock pelts, while animal-welfare groups offer the alternative: faux fur, second-hand coats and a wardrobe that needs no trapped animal at all. Millions of animals are killed every year for the trade.

National Book Week is a week in late November given over to reading. Books take you anywhere without leaving your seat, and studies keep finding that a few minutes inside a story lower stress and sharpen the mind. The week is a chance to pick up the novel that has been waiting on the shelf, to read aloud to children, and to remember that a good book is still the cheapest holiday you can take.

National Play Day with Dad, created by the National Fatherhood Initiative, is set aside for play on 25 November. The day is a reminder that a board game, a football in the park or a cardboard castle in the living room does more for a child than any screen — and that fathers who play with their children build the kind of confidence and closeness that lasts. It is a day for the two of them, and for the grown-ups to remember how it feels to be a kid.

National Brand Day, started by Brand Camp USA, falls on the fourth Monday of November and belongs to the people who build brands. A good name, a logo and a voice can turn a small workshop into a household word, and the day puts the spotlight on the designers, founders and marketers behind it. It is also a moment to thank the customers who make a brand worth having.

Road Safety Week, started by the charity Brake, takes place in the third week of November and turns a daily risk into a shared responsibility. Schools teach children how to cross a road, drivers are asked to put the phone away, and everybody is asked to wear a seatbelt and keep to the speed limit. The week remembers the people who died on the road and asks what each of us can do so it happens less often.

BOTOX Cosmetic Day is a marketing day held on November 20 in the United States around one of the world's best-known injectable cosmetic treatments. Clinics run special offers, loyalty rewards and prize draws, and many patients book appointments weeks in advance. Beyond the promotions, it is a reminder to choose a qualified medical professional and to ask about risks and realistic results before any cosmetic procedure.

Children in Need is the BBC's annual charity appeal for disadvantaged children and young people in the UK, broadcast as a telethon on a Friday in November since 1980. Its mascot, Pudsey Bear, wears a spotted bandana over one eye, and schools, offices and towns raise money with bake sales, sponsored challenges and dress-up days. The money funds local projects that help children facing poverty, illness, disability, neglect or caring for a family member.

World Pancreatic Cancer Day falls on the third Thursday of November and speaks about a cancer that is usually found late. Almost half a million people are diagnosed with it every year worldwide, and the survival rate is low because the symptoms — weight loss, back pain, yellow skin — only appear once the disease has spread. The day funds research, supports patients and pushes for earlier diagnosis.

Women's Entrepreneurship Day on November 19 was founded by Wendy Diamond and first celebrated at the United Nations in 2014. It honours women who build businesses of their own, from market stalls and clinics to factories and software companies, creating jobs and solving problems in their communities. The day also highlights the gap that remains in funding and support for women founders, and is marked with mentoring events, pitch sessions and awards.

slogans.en: Build it, own it, grow it.

descriptions.en: Discovery of Puerto Rico Day on 19 November marks the 1493 landing of Columbus in the Caribbean, the first European contact with the island. The name Puerto Rico comes from the rich port of San Juan de Puerto Rico, and the island kept its own Taíno name, Borinquén, in its people's memory. The day is a chance to look at the island's history — and its living culture of music, food and colour.

slogans.en: An island with its own story.

descriptions.en: Use Less Stuff Day, held on the third Thursday of November, pushes back against the newest gadget that nobody asked for. The idea is simple: buy less, borrow more, repair what you have and let go of the rest. Less stuff means less waste, less spending and more room in the house, and the day asks people to clear one drawer or one cupboard as a start.

National Camp Day on 19 November belongs to the children who will spend their summer in a tent. Camps teach swimming, riding, climbing and how to light a fire safely, but they also teach the quieter things — sleeping outside, cooking for a group and making a friend you did not know last month. The day points families to the camps near them and to the sliding-scale fees that make them possible.

International Journalist Day honours the reporters, photographers and editors who keep the public informed. They cover wars, corruption, disasters and elections, often in places where few others will go, and every year some of them are jailed, threatened or killed for their work. The day remembers those who died doing the job and invites readers to support independent journalism, whether by subscribing, sharing reliable reporting or defending press freedom.

Transgender Awareness Week covers the seven days before the Transgender Day of Remembrance, from 13 to 19 November. It is a week to look at the needs and rights of transgender people, who deserve to be treated with dignity, and to ask the practical questions: safe bathrooms, accessible health care, names that are respected. Awareness is the step before the changes that matter.

slogans.en: Every name, every pronoun, every day.

descriptions.en: Geography Awareness Week, promoted by the National Geographic Society, runs in the third week of November and asks how well we know the place we live in. It is a week of map reading, field trips and talks about how rivers, borders and weather shape a life. Knowing your own geography is not schoolwork for its own sake — it is what lets you read a map, follow a river and understand where your food comes from.

slogans.en: Know the ground you stand on.

descriptions.en: Housing Day on 18 November puts a roof on the scale of a single day. Around the world, hundreds of thousands of people have no home at all, and most of them are one missed payment or one broken lease away from losing the one they have. The day asks for affordable housing, honours the shelters and volunteers that keep people safe, and reminds everyone what a warm, safe door actually means.

Occult Day on 18 November opens the door on the mysterious half of the calendar — the part of the world that deals in astrology, tarot, alchemy and old magic. For one day the candles are lit, the crystals laid out and the old books opened, and people everywhere pause to look at the shadow side of spirituality. It is a day of curiosity, kept light and kept safe.

National Baklava Day on 17 November belongs to the pastry of thin leaves, honey, nuts and syrup that stretches across Greece, Turkey and Cyprus. Baklava is the dessert that took the long route west — from Ottoman kitchens to the Balkans and then to Europe — and every family has its own version: walnut or pistachio, syrup or honey, rolled or layered. The day is a good excuse to bake one and argue about the filling.

names.en: Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day

descriptions.en: Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day, marked in the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 17 November, remembers the student demonstrations of 1989. Half a million people filled the streets of Prague and Bratislava, and within weeks the communist rule that had lasted four decades was over. The day remembers the courage of ordinary people and asks what a democracy owes them today.

National Homemade Bread Day on 17 November is for the smell of a real oven and hands covered in flour. Sliced bread is convenient, but a loaf you mix, prove and bake yourself tastes of yeast and time, and the ritual is worth the washing up. The day is an invitation to start a sourdough starter, borrow a bread machine, and find out what your kitchen smells like on a cold afternoon.

Icelandic Language Day on 16 November celebrates a language that kept its shape while its neighbours changed. While English, French and the other European languages shuffled through centuries of grammar, Icelandic barely moved: the sagas were written in it, and the words for horse, ship and volcano are still the ones the first settlers used. Started by Björn Bjarnason, the day is about the quiet strength of keeping a language alive.

slogans.en: A language that refused to change.

names.en: World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims

descriptions.en: The World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims on 16 November exists because the numbers on the roads are still enormous: more than a million people die in traffic accidents every year. The day gathers families, friends and communities to remember the ones taken too soon, and to turn statistics into names. Beyond the mourning, it is a call for safer streets, safer speeds and sober driving.

The Night of Hekate, also called Hecate's Night, is celebrated on 16 November, the eve of the ancient festival of the goddess of crossroads, thresholds and magic. Hecate's night has three faces — the maiden, the mother and the crone — and she was worshipped at the gates and at the edges of things. Modern pagans light fires, walk the boundaries between worlds and ask her for safe passage through the dark.

National Recycling Day, known as America Recycles Day, on 15 November is about making one habit stick. Recycling is easy for a week and hard for a lifetime, so the day asks offices, schools and households to do it properly every day: separate the paper, the plastic and the glass, and put them in the right bin. The National Recycling Coalition uses it to push for the markets and rules that make recycling worth doing.

National Save the Eagles Day on January 10 celebrates one of the great conservation success stories in the United States. The bald eagle, the national bird, had fallen to only a few hundred nesting pairs in the lower 48 states by the 1960s, largely because the pesticide DDT thinned its eggshells. After DDT was banned in 1972 and the bird was protected by law, numbers recovered so well that it was removed from the endangered species list in 2007, and the day encourages people to keep protecting eagles and their habitats.

slogans.en: Give wild eagles room to fly.

names.en: National Cut Your Energy Costs Day

descriptions.en: National Cut Your Energy Costs Day on January 10 arrives in the middle of winter, when heating bills are often at their highest. It encourages households to find where their energy goes and waste less of it, through steps such as sealing draughts around doors and windows, switching to LED bulbs, lowering the thermostat a degree or two and unplugging devices on standby. Saving energy cuts bills and emissions at the same time, and many utilities offer free home energy checks.

League of Nations Day on January 10 marks the day in 1920 when the Covenant of the League of Nations came into force, together with the Treaty of Versailles that ended the First World War. Based in Geneva, the League was the first permanent organisation created to keep peace between nations through talks, arbitration and collective security. It failed to stop the aggression that led to the Second World War, but its ideas and agencies shaped the United Nations, which replaced it in 1946.

National Milk Day on January 11 marks the date in 1878 when milk was first delivered to customers in sterilised glass bottles in the United States, a big step for hygiene at a time when milk sold from open cans often spread disease. Pasteurisation and refrigeration later made milk much safer, and for decades the milkman's doorstep delivery was part of daily life. The day celebrates dairy farmers and the simple glass of milk, and is a good moment to learn where the milk in your fridge comes from.

slogans.en: From the farm to the glass.

descriptions.en: National Human Trafficking Awareness Day on January 11 was established in the United States by a Senate resolution in 2007, and January is also National Slavery and Human Trafficking Prevention Month. Trafficking traps people in forced labour, domestic servitude and sexual exploitation, often through debt, deception or threats, and victims can be found in farms, factories, homes and online. The Department of Homeland Security's Blue Campaign asks people to wear blue on the day and learn the signs, and to report suspicions to a hotline.

Plough Monday, the first Monday after Epiphany, traditionally marked the return to work in the fields after the Christmas season in England. Farm labourers dragged a decorated plough from house to house, sometimes in costume, asking for money, food or drink, and threatening in jest to plough up the doorstep of anyone who refused. The custom included plough plays and Molly dancing, and it has been revived in parts of England, especially East Anglia, with blessings of the plough in churches.

slogans.en: Back to the fields, back to work.

descriptions.en: National Gluten-Free Day on January 11 raises awareness of what it means to live without gluten, the protein found in wheat, barley and rye. For people with coeliac disease, an autoimmune condition affecting about one in a hundred people, even small amounts of gluten damage the small intestine, so cross-contamination in kitchens matters as much as ingredients. The day encourages restaurants and hosts to label food clearly and offer safe options, and invites everyone to try naturally gluten-free foods such as rice, corn, potatoes and buckwheat.

slogans.en: Cook for everyone at the table.

descriptions.en: Thank You Day on January 11 is a reminder to thank the people who make life easier, from a teacher or a colleague to the bus driver and the person who serves your coffee. Psychologists find that expressing gratitude improves wellbeing and strengthens relationships, for the person saying it as much as for the one hearing it. The day is a good moment to write the thank-you notes left over from the holidays or to send one unexpected message of appreciation.

National Youth Day in India on January 12 marks the birthday of Swami Vivekananda, born in Kolkata in 1863, the monk and thinker who introduced Hindu philosophy to the West at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. The government declared the day in 1984, seeing in his call for strength, service and self-confidence a message for young people. Schools and colleges mark it with speeches, essay and debate competitions, sports, yoga and community service.

National Pharmacist Day on January 12 thanks the pharmacists who make sure medicines are used safely. Beyond filling prescriptions, they check for dangerous drug interactions, give vaccinations, advise on minor ailments and are often the most accessible health professional in a community, with no appointment needed. The day is a chance to thank your local pharmacist and to ask them the questions about your medicines you never had time to raise with your doctor.

slogans.en: Thank the people who know your meds.

descriptions.en: Work Harder Day is a nudge to stop putting things off and give your best effort to the task you have been avoiding. The point is not longer hours or burning out, but more focus: finishing what you start, learning a new skill properly and going a step beyond good enough. In the second week of January, when new-year resolutions start to wobble, it is a good moment to pick one goal and push it forward.

Korean American Day on January 13 marks the arrival in Honolulu in 1903 of the first group of Korean immigrants to the United States, about one hundred people who came to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations. It was first proclaimed in 2003, on the centennial, and has been recognised by Congress. The day celebrates the contributions of more than two million Korean Americans to the country's business, arts, science, food and public life, with festivals, exhibitions and community events.

slogans.en: A new home, a lasting culture.

descriptions.en: National Take the Stairs Day, held in January, encourages people to skip the lift and climb the stairs. Stair climbing is a short, intense workout that raises the heart rate, strengthens the legs and burns more energy than walking on flat ground, all without a gym membership. The American Lung Association promotes the day alongside its Fight for Air Climb events, in which people race up skyscraper stairwells to raise money for lung health.

slogans.en: Skip the lift, climb the flight.

descriptions.en: National French Bulldog Day celebrates the small, bat-eared dogs that have become one of the most popular breeds in the world. Despite the name, the breed was shaped in 19th-century France from small bulldogs brought by English lace-makers, and Frenchies are known for their playful, affectionate personalities. Their flat faces can cause serious breathing, spine and heat problems, so the day is also a reminder to choose responsible breeders or rescues and to keep them cool and fit.

Survakari are the children and young people who perform survakane, a Bulgarian New Year custom of tapping relatives and neighbours on the back with a survachka, a cornel branch decorated with popcorn, dried fruit, coloured thread and coins. As they tap, they recite blessings for health, a rich harvest and a happy year, and are rewarded with treats or money. The custom is kept on New Year's Day, or in some regions on Vasilitsa, the old New Year in mid-January, and the cornel is chosen because it is the first tree to bloom in spring.

slogans.en: Knock on the door, wish the year well.

descriptions.en: Kolyady, or Koliada, is the winter carolling season of the Eastern Slavs, kept in Ukraine, Belarus and among Ukrainian and Belarusian communities abroad. Groups of young people, often carrying a star and dressed as goats, kings or other characters, go from house to house singing koliadky and shchedrivky, carols wishing the household health and a good harvest. The songs mix Christmas themes with much older pre-Christian midwinter rites, and hosts reward the carollers with sweets, food or money.

slogans.en: Sing the winter solstice into every home.

descriptions.en: National Organize Your Home Day in January is a push to finally tackle the clutter that builds up over the holidays and the year before. Clearing a drawer, a wardrobe or a garage can make a home easier to live in and, according to many people, lighter to think in. The day suggests working one space at a time, donating or recycling what you no longer use, and setting up simple systems so things have a place to go.

slogans.en: Clear the space, clear your head.

descriptions.en: International Kite Day on January 14 grew out of Uttarayan, the kite festival of Gujarat in India, held at Makar Sankranti when the sun begins its northward journey. Across Ahmedabad and other cities, people spend the whole day on rooftops flying kites and trying to cut each other's strings, and the city hosts an International Kite Festival with flyers from many countries. Kite traditions also thrive from China, where kites were invented, to Afghanistan, Brazil and Japan.

The Washing of Bonfim, Lavagem do Bonfim, is held in Salvador, Bahia, on the second Thursday of January. Hundreds of thousands of people follow a procession of about eight kilometres to the Church of Nosso Senhor do Bonfim, led by baianas in white lace dresses carrying vases of scented water, which they pour over the church steps. The ritual blends Catholic devotion with Candomblé, in which the Lord of Bonfim is associated with the orixá Oxalá, and is part of Brazil's recognised cultural heritage.

slogans.en: Clean the steps, wash the soul.

descriptions.en: World Logic Day on January 14 was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019, at the initiative of the logician Jean-Yves Béziau, with the support of the International Council for Philosophy and Human Sciences. The date honours two great logicians: Kurt Gödel, who died on January 14, 1978, and Alfred Tarski, born on January 14, 1901. Logic underpins mathematics, computer science and clear argument, and the day is marked with lectures, debates and puzzles around the world.

Old New Year on January 14 is New Year's Day according to the Julian calendar, which runs thirteen days behind the Gregorian calendar. It is still celebrated in Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and other countries where the Orthodox Church kept the old calendar. It is a quieter second New Year: families gather for another festive dinner, the Christmas tree stays up a little longer, and in Serbia people meet in town squares at midnight for concerts and fireworks.

names.en: National Healthy Weight, Healthy Look Day

descriptions.en: Healthy Weight, Healthy Look Day, held in January, encourages people to focus on habits rather than the number on the scale. Crash diets and punishing workouts rarely last, while steady changes such as more vegetables and whole foods, regular movement, enough sleep and less stress tend to stick. The day is a reminder that a healthy body comes in many shapes, and that feeling good in your own skin matters as much as how you look.

slogans.en: Feel good, not just look good.

descriptions.en: Magh Bihu, also called Bhogali Bihu, is the harvest festival of Assam in northeast India, celebrated in mid-January when the granaries are full. On the night before, called Uruka, families and friends build temporary huts called bhelaghar from bamboo and straw and share a great feast. At dawn they burn the meji, a tall bonfire, offering prayers for the year ahead, and the days are filled with rice cakes called pitha, traditional games and buffalo fights in some areas.

Wikipedia Day on January 15 marks the launch of Wikipedia in 2001 by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger, as a free encyclopedia that anyone could edit. It has grown into one of the most visited websites in the world, with more than 60 million articles in over 300 languages, written by volunteers and run by the nonprofit Wikimedia Foundation. Communities mark the day with edit-a-thons, meetups and campaigns to fill gaps in coverage, such as articles about women, local history and smaller languages.

Guru Gobind Singh Jayanti celebrates the birth of the tenth Sikh Guru, born in Patna in 1666, and its date follows the lunar calendar, usually falling in December or January. In 1699 he founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, giving it the five articles of faith, and before his death in 1708 he declared the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, to be the eternal Guru. Sikhs mark the day with prayers and hymn singing at gurdwaras, processions called nagar kirtan, and langar, the free community kitchen open to all.

National Classy Day celebrates class as a way of behaving rather than a matter of money or fashion. It honours qualities such as good manners, humility, grace under pressure, respect for others and keeping your word, often summed up by figures like Audrey Hepburn, whose birthday falls in May. The day invites people to dress up a little if they like, but above all to treat everyone, from the waiter to the boss, with the same courtesy.

slogans.en: Class is how you treat people.

descriptions.en: Artist as Outlaw Day celebrates artists who have broken rules, challenged power and paid a price for their work. Painters, writers and musicians have long used art as protest, from Goya's images of war to banned books and songs that became anthems of resistance. The day asks what art can do in a world that resists change, and invites people to discover an artist who risked something to say what they believed.

National Cheese Lovers Day on January 20 celebrates one of the oldest prepared foods, made for perhaps 7,000 years or more. There are well over a thousand varieties, from fresh cheeses like feta and mozzarella to aged ones like Parmigiano Reggiano, Comté and Turkish kaşar, and each depends on the milk, the bacteria and moulds, and the time it is left to mature. The day is a reason to try a new cheese, build a cheese board or cook a fondue with friends.

National Coffee Break Day defends the short pause in the working day, ideally with a warm cup and a colleague. The coffee break became an American workplace habit in the mid-20th century, and studies suggest that brief breaks away from the screen restore attention and reduce fatigue. The day is a reminder to actually stop for ten or fifteen minutes, step away from the desk and talk about something other than work.

slogans.en: Take the break, not just the coffee.

names.en: International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction

descriptions.en: The United Nations General Assembly declared 13 October the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the day argues that disasters cannot be avoided but that their damage can be cut. Households make a family disaster plan, keep an emergency bag packed, train for the unexpected and learn the early warnings, while institutions cooperate on the risks they share. In Türkiye this work runs under AFAD, the Presidency of Disaster and Emergency Management.

slogans.en: Prepared for disasters, ready for less damage.

descriptions.en: 12 November was declared Disaster Preparedness Day after the earthquake that struck Düzce in 1999. Being ready for disasters, taking precautions and learning what to do when one happens save lives. The work runs under AFAD, Türkiye's disaster and emergency authority, and covers training, drills and early warning for earthquakes, floods, landslides and fires.

slogans.en: Be ready, and you save lives.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Peaceful Coexistence on January 28 is one of the newest observances proclaimed by the UN General Assembly. It calls on people and nations to live side by side in peace despite differences of culture, religion, language and opinion. Schools, faith groups and civic organisations mark it with dialogue between communities, shared meals and projects that bring neighbours from different backgrounds together.

slogans.en: Different, side by side, in peace.

descriptions.en: The International Day of Human Fraternity on February 4 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2020 and first observed in 2021. The date recalls February 4, 2019, when Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar, Ahmed el-Tayeb, signed the Document on Human Fraternity for World Peace and Living Together in Abu Dhabi. The day promotes dialogue, tolerance and mutual respect between people of different faiths and cultures, and is marked with interfaith meetings, lectures and the Zayed Award for Human Fraternity.

names.en: International Day of Zero Tolerance to Female Genital Mutilation

descriptions.en: The International Day of Zero Tolerance for Female Genital Mutilation on February 6 has been recognised by the UN General Assembly since 2012, building on a call first made by African women's groups in 2003. Female genital mutilation covers procedures that injure or remove a girl's external genitals for non-medical reasons; more than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone it, mostly in parts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia. The day supports survivors and the communities, health workers and religious leaders working to end the practice, which causes lifelong pain and health risks and is recognised as a violation of human rights.

slogans.en: Every girl deserves to grow up whole.

descriptions.en: World Pulses Day on 10 February celebrates lentils, chickpeas, beans and peas. The United Nations proclaimed it in 2018, building on the International Year of Pulses in 2016, and the Food and Agriculture Organization leads it each year. Pulses are cheap, rich in protein and fibre, and they enrich the soil by fixing nitrogen, which makes them important for both health and farming. People mark the day with recipes, cooking events and talks on food security.

names.en: International Day of the Arabian Leopard

descriptions.en: The International Day of the Arabian Leopard, held on 10 February, was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 2023. It draws attention to the Arabian leopard, the smallest leopard subspecies, which is critically endangered and survives only in small, scattered populations in the mountains of the Arabian Peninsula. Conservation groups, zoos and schools use the day to talk about habitat protection, breeding programmes and living alongside wildlife.

slogans.en: Fewer than 200 left. Let them stay.

names.en: International Day for the Prevention of Violent Extremism as and when Conducive to Terrorism

descriptions.en: On 12 February the United Nations marks the International Day for the Prevention of Violent Extremism as and when Conducive to Terrorism. The General Assembly set the day aside to stress that extremism is best stopped before it takes root, by tackling the exclusion, injustice and lack of opportunity that can draw people, especially the young, towards violence. Governments, schools and community groups use it to share what works, from education and dialogue to giving young people a real voice.

Global Tourism Resilience Day falls on 17 February. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2023 to help tourism prepare for, cope with and recover from shocks such as pandemics, natural disasters, conflicts and climate change. Millions of people, many in small island and developing countries, depend on travel for their livelihoods, and the COVID-19 pandemic showed how fast that income can vanish. Governments and businesses use the day to share plans that keep tourism safe and sustainable.

World Seagrass Day, held on 1 March, was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 2022 to raise awareness of underwater seagrass meadows. These flowering plants shelter young fish and other sea life, help keep coastal waters clear, protect shorelines from erosion and lock away large amounts of carbon in the seabed. Yet meadows are being lost to pollution, coastal development and damage from boats. Scientists, divers and coastal communities mark the day with clean-ups, talks and campaigns to protect and restore them.

names.en: International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness

descriptions.en: The International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness, on 5 March, reminds people how reducing weapons keeps them safer and frees money for health, schools and development. The UN General Assembly set up the day in 2022, choosing the date on which the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons came into force in 1970. It is marked with UN events, youth programmes, talks and educational campaigns about nuclear and conventional arms.

The International Day of Women Judges, on 10 March, honours the women who serve on the bench and calls for them to be fairly represented at every level of the judiciary. The UN General Assembly created the day in 2021, and it was first marked in 2022. Courts that reflect the societies they serve earn more trust, yet in many countries women are still rare in senior judicial posts. The day is marked with conferences, talks and stories of women judges, past and present.

slogans.en: Justice is better when it looks like us.

names.en: Week of Solidarity with the Peoples Struggling against Racism and Racial Discrimination

descriptions.en: The Week of Solidarity with the Peoples Struggling against Racism and Racial Discrimination runs from 21 to 27 March each year. Set by the United Nations, it begins on the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination and stretches that single day into a full week of attention. Its message is that racism is not someone else's problem: standing beside those who face it is a shared duty. Schools, community groups and human rights organisations use the week for talks, exhibitions and campaigns against prejudice.

names.en: International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination is held every year on 21 March. On that day in 1960, police opened fire on a peaceful protest against apartheid pass laws in Sharpeville, South Africa, killing 69 people. The United Nations proclaimed the day in 1966 so that the massacre would never be forgotten and to call for an end to racial discrimination everywhere. Governments, schools and civil society groups mark it with remembrance events, education campaigns and calls for equal rights.

slogans.en: Equal in dignity, equal in rights.

names.en: International Day for the Right to the Truth concerning Gross Human Rights Violations and for the Dignity of Victims

descriptions.en: This UN day affirms the right of victims of serious human rights abuses, and of their families, to know what happened and who was responsible. It is held on 24 March, the date Archbishop Óscar Romero of El Salvador was shot dead in 1980 while celebrating Mass, after years of speaking out for the poor and against violence. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2010. It is marked with memorial events, testimonies and calls for justice, honouring those who defend human rights at great personal risk.

slogans.en: Truth is the first step to justice.

names.en: International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade

descriptions.en: On 25 March the UN remembers the more than 15 million men, women and children who were forcibly taken from Africa during some four centuries of the transatlantic slave trade. The General Assembly established the day in 2007, two hundred years after Britain abolished its slave trade. It honours those who suffered and died, and the resistance of enslaved people. Events, exhibitions and school programmes also call attention to racism and prejudice that still trace back to slavery.

names.en: International Day of Solidarity with Detained and Missing Staff Members
