descriptions.en: On 25 March the United Nations stands with staff members, peacekeepers and journalists who have been detained, abducted or gone missing while working for others. The date marks the anniversary of the 1985 abduction of Alec Collett, a journalist working for the UN agency for Palestine refugees, who was later killed. UN offices around the world hold vigils and moments of silence. The day renews calls for the release of those still held and for the safety of everyone serving in dangerous places.

The International Day of Zero Waste promotes a world where we waste less by reducing, reusing and recycling, so fewer resources end up in landfills and oceans. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2022 on a resolution led by Türkiye, inspired by Türkiye's own Zero Waste movement, and it was first marked on 30 March 2023. Governments, cities, schools and businesses use it to launch recycling campaigns, cut single-use plastics and show how small daily habits add up.

names.en: International Day for Mine Awareness and Assistance in Mine Action

descriptions.en: The International Day for Mine Awareness and Assistance in Mine Action is marked on 4 April. The United Nations General Assembly declared it in 2005 to draw attention to landmines and other explosive remnants of war, which go on killing and maiming people, many of them children, long after the fighting has stopped. The day supports the work of clearing contaminated land, teaching communities to recognise the danger and helping survivors rebuild their lives. Exhibitions, talks and fundraising campaigns are held around the world.

The International Day of Conscience is marked on 5 April. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed it in 2019, and it was first observed in 2020. It invites people to listen to their conscience and to act with love and respect toward others, helping to build a culture of peace in their families and communities. Schools, faith groups and civic organisations mark it with talks, dialogues and small acts of kindness that show how everyday choices shape a fairer world.

names.en: International Day of Sport for Development and Peace

descriptions.en: The International Day of Sport for Development and Peace is marked on 6 April, the date the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens in 1896. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed it in 2013 to recognise the power of sport to bring people together, promote health and education, and build bridges across divides. Schools, clubs and communities mark the day with friendly matches, fun runs and open training sessions, often bringing together people who might not otherwise meet.

slogans.en: One game, one team, one world.

names.en: International Day of Reflection on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda

descriptions.en: On 7 April the world remembers the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, which began on this day in 1994. In about 100 days, an estimated 800,000 to more than a million people were killed, most of them Tutsi, along with moderate Hutu and others who opposed the killing. The United Nations marks the day to honour the victims and to reflect on how genocide can be prevented. In Rwanda it opens Kwibuka, a period of national mourning, and people around the world gather for vigils, candle lighting and moments of silence.

International Wellness Day on 15 April is a reminder that health is more than the absence of illness. It promotes physical, mental and social wellbeing as the foundation of a good life and of healthy communities. People mark it by taking time for a walk, rest or a healthy meal, checking in on friends and family, and by workplaces and schools sharing simple habits that help everyone feel better day to day.

names.en: International Day of Greening the Planet

descriptions.en: The International Day of Greening the Planet is marked on April 22, alongside Earth Day. It calls on people, cities and governments to plant trees, restore damaged land and bring more green space into towns and cities. Forests and healthy soils store carbon, cool the air, hold back deserts and give shelter to wildlife, so greening the planet helps fight both climate change and desertification. People mark the day by joining tree-planting drives, starting community gardens and caring for parks and green corners near home.

International Girls in ICT Day is held on the fourth Thursday of April and is led by the International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for digital technologies. It has been celebrated since 2011 to encourage girls and young women to study and build careers in information and communication technology, a field where women are still under-represented. Schools, universities and tech companies mark the day with coding workshops, office visits, mentoring sessions and talks by women working in technology, showing girls that the digital future is theirs to shape.

English Language Day is one of six days the United Nations sets aside for its official languages, each meant to celebrate multilingualism and cultural diversity. It falls on 23 April, the date traditionally given as both the birthday and the death date of William Shakespeare, the language's best-known writer. UN offices, schools and language clubs mark it with readings, quizzes and talks on how English grew from a local tongue into a language spoken around the world.

slogans.en: A language that connects the world.

descriptions.en: Spanish Language Day is one of six days the United Nations dedicates to its official languages, celebrating multilingualism and cultural diversity. It is held on 23 April, a date tied to Miguel de Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote, who died in April 1616. Spanish is spoken by hundreds of millions of people across Spain and the Americas, and the day is marked with readings, film screenings, exhibitions and events about the language and its literature.

names.en: International Day of Multilateralism and Diplomacy for Peace

descriptions.en: The International Day of Multilateralism and Diplomacy for Peace, proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2018, is observed on 24 April. It celebrates countries working together through the United Nations and other shared institutions, and peaceful negotiation as the best way to settle disputes and tackle problems no nation can solve alone, from conflict to climate change. The day is marked with debates, lectures and events that remind people why dialogue and cooperation matter.

International Delegate's Day honours the people who represent their countries at the United Nations and in diplomacy more widely. The date recalls 25 April 1945, when delegates from 50 nations gathered in San Francisco for the conference that drafted the UN Charter. The UN General Assembly set the day aside in 2019. It is marked with events at UN offices and missions, and with a nod to the patient, often unseen work of negotiating between nations.

On 26 April 1986 a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine, the worst nuclear accident in history. Radiation spread across Europe, Belarus was hit especially hard, and the nearby town of Pripyat was evacuated and never resettled. The UN General Assembly made 26 April a day of remembrance in 2016. People hold vigils and lay flowers for the victims and the emergency workers, and recall the communities still living with the disaster's effects.

names.en: World Day for Safety and Health at Work

descriptions.en: The World Day for Safety and Health at Work, held every 28 April, is the International Labour Organization's day for preventing accidents and illness on the job. The ILO has marked it since 2003, building on the Workers' Memorial Day that trade unions hold on the same date for those killed or injured at work. By ILO estimates, close to three million people still die each year from work-related accidents and diseases. Workplaces run safety drills and training, and unions and employers pick up the ILO's yearly theme.

names.en: International Day in Memory of the Victims of Earthquakes

descriptions.en: The International Day in Memory of the Victims of Earthquakes, on 29 April, remembers everyone who has lost their life to an earthquake. It also reminds us that much of that loss can be prevented through sturdier buildings, careful planning and people who know what to do when the ground shakes. Communities hold moments of silence and memorial gatherings for the victims. Schools, rescue teams and local authorities use the day for drills and preparedness campaigns.

World Portuguese Language Day on 5 May celebrates Portuguese, spoken by more than 250 million people on four continents, from Brazil and Portugal to Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde and Timor-Leste. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries had already marked the date for years before UNESCO proclaimed it a world day in 2019, honouring the language's role in literature, music and the shared history of its speakers. Schools, embassies and cultural institutes hold readings, concerts, film screenings and talks, and many people take the day to discover writers such as Camões, Fernando Pessoa or Machado de Assis.

names.en: Time of Remembrance and Reconciliation for Those Who Lost Their Lives During the Second World War

descriptions.en: The Time of Remembrance and Reconciliation is held on 8 and 9 May, the anniversary of the end of the Second World War in Europe in 1945. The UN General Assembly set these days aside in 2004 to honour the tens of millions of soldiers and civilians who lost their lives in the war. Countries may mark either or both dates in their own way. Alongside remembrance, the days call on nations to learn from the war, work for reconciliation and protect peace.

The International Day of Argania falls on 10 May and celebrates the argan tree, which grows wild almost only in southwestern Morocco. The United Nations proclaimed the day in 2021. Hardy and deep-rooted, the argan tree holds the soil against the desert and supports rural communities, especially the women's cooperatives that crack the nuts by hand and press them into argan oil, used in cooking and cosmetics. The day is marked with events on protecting argan forests and the traditional knowledge built around them.

The International Day of Plant Health falls on 12 May and reminds us that healthy plants are the base of our food and of life on Earth. The United Nations proclaimed it following the International Year of Plant Health in 2020, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) leads it. FAO estimates that pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of food crops each year. The day promotes safe trade in plants, careful pest control and simple habits, like not carrying plants or seeds across borders without checks.

names.en: International Day of Living Together in Peace

descriptions.en: The International Day of Living Together in Peace falls on 16 May and asks people to live side by side in unity, whatever their differences. The UN General Assembly declared the day in 2017 as a way to promote tolerance, reconciliation and mutual respect. It invites communities, schools and governments to listen to one another and to see diversity as a strength. People mark it with interfaith meetings, neighbourhood gatherings, school projects and talks on dialogue and inclusion.

The International Day of Light, held each year on 16 May, celebrates light and the science behind it. UNESCO chose the date because on 16 May 1960 the physicist Theodore Maiman operated the first working laser. The day highlights how light-based technologies shape medicine, communications, energy, education and art. Universities, museums and science groups mark it with public talks, hands-on experiments, light shows and open lab days.

World Fair Play Day, on 19 May, celebrates honesty, respect and integrity in sport, both on and off the field. The United Nations proclaimed the day, and it was first marked in 2025. Fair play means playing by the rules, respecting opponents and officials, and winning or losing with grace. Clubs, schools and sports federations mark it with matches, talks and awards that honour sporting gestures, reminding everyone that how you play matters as much as the result.

names.en: World Day for Cultural Diversity for Dialogue and Development

descriptions.en: The World Day for Cultural Diversity for Dialogue and Development, on 21 May, celebrates the richness of the world's cultures and their role in building understanding between people. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2002, following UNESCO's Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity adopted in 2001. Its message is that diversity is a source of creativity and a driver of development, not a cause of division. People mark it by sharing food, music and stories from other cultures, visiting exhibitions and learning a few words of a new language.

names.en: International Day to End Obstetric Fistula

descriptions.en: The International Day to End Obstetric Fistula on 23 May focuses on a childbirth injury caused by prolonged, obstructed labour without timely medical help. Fistula leaves women with chronic incontinence and often with stigma and isolation, yet it is preventable and in most cases can be repaired by surgery. The UN, led by its population fund UNFPA, uses the day to push for skilled birth care, emergency obstetric services and free repair surgery.

The International Day of the Markhor on 24 May celebrates a wild goat with long corkscrew horns that lives in the mountains of Central and South Asia and is Pakistan's national animal. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2024, recognising how community-led conservation helped markhor numbers recover after years of decline. It is marked with talks, school events and campaigns about mountain wildlife and the local communities that protect it.

names.en: Week of Solidarity with the Peoples of Non-Self-Governing Territories

descriptions.en: From 25 to 31 May, the United Nations holds a week of solidarity with the peoples of the Non-Self-Governing Territories. These are the 17 places still on the UN's decolonization list, among them Western Sahara, New Caledonia and Gibraltar. The week was set by the UN General Assembly to support their right to decide their own future. It is marked with UN statements, discussions and events that raise awareness of these often-forgotten peoples.

The International Day of Potato on 30 May celebrates one of the world's most important food crops. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2023, and the Food and Agriculture Organization leads the observance. The potato was first domesticated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago and now feeds over a billion people. The day is marked with talks on food security, farmer support and cooking events that show off its many varieties.

names.en: International Day of Innocent Children Victims of Aggression

descriptions.en: The International Day of Innocent Children Victims of Aggression, on 4 June, recognises the suffering of children caught up in war and armed conflict. The UN General Assembly established it in 1982, initially in response to the many children killed and wounded in the war in Lebanon. Today it highlights grave violations against children such as killing and maiming, recruitment as soldiers, abduction and attacks on schools and hospitals. Agencies and campaigners use the day to call for children to be protected in every conflict.

slogans.en: No child should pay for war.

names.en: International Day for the Fight against Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated Fishing

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Fight against Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated Fishing is observed on 5 June. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2017, choosing the date on which the Port State Measures Agreement, the first binding international treaty aimed at this kind of fishing, entered into force in 2016. Illegal fishing empties the seas, harms marine ecosystems and undercuts the honest fishers and coastal communities who depend on them. Governments, the FAO and conservation groups use the day to push for better monitoring, traceable seafood and closed ports for illegal catches.

names.en: International Day for Dialogue among Civilizations

descriptions.en: The International Day for Dialogue among Civilizations is observed every 10 June. The United Nations General Assembly established it in 2024 to promote respect, understanding and exchange between the world's cultures and to protect the shared heritage of humanity. Its message is that differences in faith, language and tradition are a source of richness rather than conflict. The day is marked with conferences, cultural events and educational programmes that bring people of different backgrounds together.

The International Day of Family Remittances, on 16 June, honours migrant workers who send part of their earnings to relatives back home. First promoted by the UN's International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), it was recognised by the UN General Assembly in 2018. These transfers pay for food, school fees and medical care in millions of households, so the day is used to call for cheaper, safer ways to send money and to thank the people who make them.

slogans.en: Sent with love, from far away.

descriptions.en: Sustainable Gastronomy Day, on 18 June, celebrates food that is good for people, communities and the planet. The UN General Assembly established it in 2016, and FAO and UNESCO help promote it. The idea is simple: cooking with local, seasonal ingredients protects biodiversity, keeps culinary traditions alive and supports the farmers and fishers who grow our food, so chefs, schools and families mark the day by cooking regional dishes and wasting less.

names.en: International Day for Countering Hate Speech

descriptions.en: The International Day for Countering Hate Speech, on 18 June, stands against words that attack people for their religion, ethnicity, nationality, gender or other identity. The UN General Assembly created it in 2021, and it was first observed in 2022. Hate speech online and offline can fuel discrimination and even violence, so the day encourages schools, media and social platforms to promote respect, teach people to spot hateful content and stand up for those targeted.

names.en: International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict, on 19 June, stands with survivors of rape and sexual abuse used as weapons of war. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2015, choosing the date on which the Security Council adopted Resolution 1820 in 2008, which condemned sexual violence as a tactic of war. The day honours survivors and the people who support them, and calls for justice, care and an end to impunity for these crimes.

names.en: International Day of the Celebration of the Solstice

descriptions.en: The International Day of the Celebration of the Solstice, on 21 June, recognises the solstices and equinoxes and the place they hold in cultures around the world. Proclaimed by the UN General Assembly, it falls on the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere and the shortest in the Southern. For thousands of years these turning points of the sun have guided farming calendars, religious festivals and monuments aligned with the sunrise. People mark the day by watching the sun rise or set, gathering at ancient sites and joining midsummer or midwinter festivals.

slogans.en: The sun stands still, we celebrate.

descriptions.en: United Nations Public Service Day on June 23 honours the people whose everyday work keeps communities running: teachers, nurses, clerks, firefighters, police officers and countless other public servants. The UN General Assembly designated the day in 2002 to highlight the value of public service and encourage young people to choose it as a career. On this day the UN presents its Public Service Awards to outstanding institutions, and many governments thank their staff with ceremonies and open days.

names.en: United Nations International Day in Support of Victims of Torture

descriptions.en: The United Nations International Day in Support of Victims of Torture, on June 26, stands with survivors and restates that torture is forbidden everywhere and in all circumstances. The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 1997, choosing the date on which the UN Convention against Torture entered into force in 1987. Human rights groups, rehabilitation centres and governments mark it with events, campaigns and calls for accountability, and the UN Voluntary Fund for Victims of Torture highlights the medical, psychological and legal help survivors need to rebuild their lives.

The International Day of Deafblindness is held on 27 June, the birthday of Helen Keller, the American author and activist who lost both her sight and hearing as a small child. Deafblindness is a distinct disability, not simply blindness plus deafness, and people living with it often rely on touch-based communication, interpreters and specialised support. Organisations and families use the day to share stories, teach tactile sign language and call for services that let deafblind people learn, work and take full part in society.

International Asteroid Day falls on 30 June, the anniversary of the 1908 Tunguska event, when an object from space exploded over Siberia and flattened millions of trees across a remote forest. The United Nations proclaimed the day in 2016 to raise public awareness of asteroid impacts and of the work to detect and track near-Earth objects. Observatories, planetariums and space agencies mark it with talks, live streams, stargazing nights and school activities.

The International Day of Parliamentarism is marked on 30 June, the date the Inter-Parliamentary Union was founded in 1889. The United Nations established the day in 2018 to celebrate parliaments as the place where citizens' voices are turned into laws and where governments are held to account. Parliaments around the world mark it with open days, debates and youth sessions, and use it to look at how they can become more inclusive and transparent.

World Rural Development Day turns attention to the countryside, home to a large share of the world's people and to the farmers, herders and fishers who grow much of its food. Many rural communities still struggle with poor roads, distant schools and clinics, unreliable power and internet, and young people leaving for the cities. The day is marked with talks, campaigns and local events that call for better services, fair incomes and opportunities that let rural life thrive.

World Kiswahili Language Day, held on 7 July, celebrates one of Africa's most widely spoken languages, used by more than 200 million people across East and Central Africa. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2021, making Kiswahili the first African language to have its own UN day. The date recalls 7 July 1954, when Julius Nyerere's party in Tanganyika adopted Kiswahili as the language that would unite the independence struggle. It is marked with poetry, music, lectures and events that celebrate the language as a bridge between peoples.

names.en: International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica

descriptions.en: On 11 July the world remembers the genocide at Srebrenica, where more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces in July 1995, in the worst atrocity on European soil since the Second World War. The UN General Assembly established the international day in 2024 to honour the victims, support the survivors and counter denial. Each year thousands gather at the Srebrenica-Potočari Memorial, where newly identified victims are laid to rest. Many also join the peace march that retraces the route of those who tried to flee through the forests.

World Horse Day, on 11 July, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2025 to honour one of humanity's oldest companions. Since horses were domesticated on the Eurasian steppes thousands of years ago, they have pulled ploughs, carried travellers and goods, linked distant cultures and shaped the history of whole peoples. Today they still work on farms, take part in sport and therapy, and remain central to many traditions. The day is a chance to celebrate horses and to call for their good care and welfare.

slogans.en: Six thousand years side by side.

names.en: International Day of Combating Sand and Dust Storms

descriptions.en: The International Day of Combating Sand and Dust Storms is observed on 12 July, a date the UN General Assembly set in 2023. These storms lift huge clouds of dust from dry lands and can carry them across continents, harming people's health, damaging crops and disrupting flights and roads in more than 150 countries. Their effects are made worse by land degradation, drought and poor land management. The day calls for better early warning, sustainable land and water use, and cooperation between countries, since dust knows no borders.

The International Day of Hope is observed on 12 July, a date the UN General Assembly adopted in 2024. It recognises hope as a universal human aspiration and a force that helps people and societies get through crises, rebuild and work towards peace and sustainable development. The day encourages governments, communities and individuals to nurture hope through education, solidarity and action, especially for those facing war, poverty or disaster. People mark it by sharing stories of resilience and by doing something concrete that gives others reason to look ahead.

slogans.en: Hope is a choice we make together.

descriptions.en: The International Day for Judicial Well-being, on 25 July, was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2025. It recognises that judges and court staff carry heavy caseloads, isolation and distressing material, and that this strain can affect the quality of justice. A judiciary that is healthy and supported is better able to stay fair and independent, so courts and judicial associations use the day for workshops, peer support and talks about workload and mental health.

World Breastfeeding Week runs from 1 to 7 August and promotes breastfeeding as one of the best ways to protect the health of babies and mothers. It was launched in 1992 by the World Alliance for Breastfeeding Action to mark the 1990 Innocenti Declaration, and today it is supported by WHO and UNICEF. Breast milk gives infants the nutrients and antibodies they need, and WHO recommends breastfeeding alone for the first six months. During the week, hospitals, health workers and community groups hold talks, support circles and campaigns calling for paid leave, space to breastfeed at work and practical help for mothers.

names.en: International Day of Awareness of the Special Development Needs and Challenges of Landlocked Developing Countries

descriptions.en: This United Nations day, first observed on 6 August 2025, draws attention to the 32 developing countries that have no coastline, from Bolivia and Paraguay to Mongolia, Nepal and Ethiopia. Without their own ports, these countries depend on their neighbours' roads, railways and harbours, so their goods travel further, wait longer at borders and cost more to trade. Governments, UN agencies and researchers use the day to push for better transport links, simpler border crossings and fairer access to world markets.

World Steelpan Day, on August 11, celebrates the steelpan, the tuned percussion instrument born in Trinidad and Tobago in the twentieth century from discarded oil drums. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the day in 2023, recognising the steelpan as a gift from the Caribbean to the world's music. It is marked with concerts, steel band performances and workshops, especially in Trinidad and Tobago, where the steelpan is the national instrument.

names.en: International Day Commemorating the Victims of Acts of Violence Based on Religion or Belief

descriptions.en: Every 22 August the United Nations remembers people who have been attacked, persecuted or killed because of their religion or belief. The General Assembly created the day in 2019 after a series of deadly attacks on worshippers in mosques, churches, synagogues and temples. It affirms that everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the right to hold no religion at all. Faith communities hold joint prayers and vigils, and many use the day to build friendships across different beliefs.

slogans.en: Free to believe, safe to live.

names.en: International Day for the Remembrance of the Slave Trade and Its Abolition

descriptions.en: UNESCO marks 23 August in memory of the night of 22 to 23 August 1791, when enslaved people in Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, rose up against their masters. The revolt led to Haiti's independence and became a turning point in the fight to end the transatlantic slave trade. The day remembers the millions of Africans who were captured, shipped across the ocean and forced to work, and honours those who resisted. Museums, schools and memorial sites hold readings, exhibitions and ceremonies, and many use the day to reflect on the racism that slavery left behind.

names.en: International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances

descriptions.en: The International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances is observed on 30 August. An enforced disappearance happens when people are detained or abducted by state agents, or with the state's consent, and their fate is then hidden from their families. The UN General Assembly established the day in 2010, after adopting an international convention against the practice. It honours the disappeared and the families who keep searching for them, and human rights groups hold vigils and campaigns for truth and justice.

names.en: International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence

descriptions.en: The International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence was adopted by the UN in 2026 for 31 August. Artificial intelligence now shapes how people work, learn, communicate and receive public services. The day calls for AI systems that are safe, transparent and respectful of human rights, and for their benefits to reach every country rather than a few. Governments, researchers, companies and schools mark it with discussions on responsible AI, digital literacy and fair access to the technology.

names.en: International Day of the World's Indigenous Women and Girls

descriptions.en: The International Day of the World's Indigenous Women and Girls on September 5 honours Indigenous women as keepers of language, knowledge, culture and land. The date was first chosen in 1983 by Indigenous organisations meeting in Tiwanaku, Bolivia, in memory of Bartolina Sisa, an Aymara leader of an uprising against Spanish colonial rule who was executed on 5 September 1782. Communities mark it with gatherings, marches and talks that celebrate Indigenous women's leadership and call out the discrimination and violence they still face.

The International Day of Police Cooperation, on 7 September, highlights how police forces work together across borders against crimes such as terrorism, trafficking and cybercrime. The date recalls the founding of the International Criminal Police Commission in Vienna in 1923, the body that grew into today's INTERPOL, and the day is now observed by the United Nations. Police services and international organisations mark it by honouring officers' work and stressing how sharing information between countries helps keep communities safe.

slogans.en: Crime has no borders, neither does cooperation.

descriptions.en: World Duchenne Awareness Day, on 7 September, raises awareness of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a rare genetic disease that gradually weakens the muscles and mostly affects boys. Signs usually appear in early childhood, and over time the condition affects walking, breathing and the heart. Patient organisations around the world started the day to make Duchenne better known, and families, doctors and researchers use it to share their stories, call for earlier diagnosis and better care, and support research into new treatments.

names.en: International Day to Protect Education from Attack

descriptions.en: The International Day to Protect Education from Attack falls on 9 September. The UN General Assembly created it in 2020, at a time when schools, students and teachers in war zones were being bombed, occupied by armed groups or threatened for simply showing up to class. UNESCO and UNICEF lead the day, calling on governments to keep schools safe and to let children keep learning even in conflict. Schools and charities mark it with talks, campaigns and appeals for support.

names.en: United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation

descriptions.en: The United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation, on 12 September, celebrates how developing countries share knowledge, technology and trade with one another. The date recalls 12 September 1978, when the Buenos Aires Plan of Action on cooperation among developing countries was adopted. Rather than relying only on aid from richer nations, countries of the Global South learn from each other's experience in farming, health, education and infrastructure. UN agencies and governments mark the day with forums, partnership announcements and stories of shared projects.

names.en: International Day of Science, Technology and Innovation for the South

descriptions.en: The International Day of Science, Technology and Innovation for the South falls on 16 September. The UN General Assembly adopted it in 2023 to support research and innovation in developing countries and to narrow the technology gap between the global North and South. It highlights cooperation among countries of the South as they share knowledge, train scientists and build technology together. Universities, research bodies and governments mark it with conferences, talks and initiatives that bring science closer to everyday development needs.

The International Day for Interventional Cardiology falls on 16 September, the anniversary of the first coronary balloon angioplasty, performed by Andreas Grüntzig in Zurich in 1977. Using a thin catheter threaded through an artery, he widened a narrowed heart artery without open-heart surgery, and the technique, later refined with stents, now helps countless patients around the world. The day promotes fair access to these procedures, especially rapid treatment for heart attacks. Hospitals and heart societies mark it with awareness campaigns and talks.

slogans.en: A tiny tube, a saved life.

descriptions.en: World Maritime Day is observed on the last Thursday of September under the lead of the International Maritime Organization, the UN agency for shipping. It draws attention to the ships and crews that carry most of the world's trade by volume, from food and fuel to the goods on our shelves. Each year the IMO sets a theme, often on safety at sea, cleaner ships or the welfare of seafarers, and ports, maritime schools and shipping companies hold events around it.

names.en: International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, on 26 September, recalls one of the United Nations' oldest goals: a world free of nuclear weapons, a subject of the General Assembly's very first resolution in 1946. The UN established the day in 2013, and it was first observed in 2014. Around 12,000 nuclear warheads still exist today. Governments, campaigners and survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki use the day for talks, petitions and events calling for disarmament.

slogans.en: A world free of nuclear weapons.

names.en: International Day for Universal Access to Information

descriptions.en: The International Day for Universal Access to Information on September 28 champions everyone's right to seek, receive and share information. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2015, and the UN General Assembly adopted it in 2019. Access to public records, a free press and an open internet help people hold governments to account, make informed choices and take part in public life. Governments, libraries, journalists and civil society mark it with debates, reports on freedom-of-information laws and events on digital access.

names.en: International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste

descriptions.en: The International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste on September 29 draws attention to the huge amount of food that never gets eaten while millions of people go hungry. The UN General Assembly designated the day in 2019, and it is led by the FAO and the UN Environment Programme. Food is lost on farms, in storage and in transport, and wasted in shops, restaurants and homes, along with the water, land and energy used to produce it. People mark the day by planning meals, using leftovers, buying imperfect produce and supporting food banks.

World Cotton Day, on 7 October, celebrates cotton, the natural fibre in much of what we wear and a living for millions of farming families. It began in 2019 at the World Trade Organization, at the request of four West African cotton producers: Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali. In 2021 the UN General Assembly made it an official international day. It is marked with talks on fair prices, sustainable growing and the place of cotton in developing economies, and with a fresh look at the cotton shirt in your wardrobe.

The International Day of Rural Women, on 15 October, honours the women who farm, fish, herd and keep households running in the countryside. The United Nations set it up in 2007, placing it on the eve of World Food Day, because rural women grow a large share of the world's food yet often have less access to land, credit, training and services than men. The day is marked with talks, local markets, campaigns and stories that put these women's work in the spotlight.

Disarmament Week runs from 24 to 30 October, starting on United Nations Day. The UN General Assembly called for it in 1978, at its first special session devoted to disarmament, to keep public attention on the dangers of the arms race. During the week, governments, schools and peace groups hold talks, exhibitions and events on nuclear weapons, the arms trade and small arms, and on how money spent on weapons could serve development instead.

World Development Information Day draws attention to development challenges such as poverty, hunger and inequality, and to the role information plays in tackling them. The United Nations General Assembly created it in 1972, and it was first held in 1973. It falls on 24 October, United Nations Day, which is also the date in 1970 when the UN adopted its strategy for the Second Development Decade. Schools, libraries and UN offices use the day to share data, stories and ideas that help people understand and take part in development.

names.en: Global Media and Information Literacy Week

descriptions.en: Global Media and Information Literacy Week runs from 24 to 31 October and is led by UNESCO. Media and information literacy means being able to find, question, judge and share information wisely, whether it comes from the news, social media or AI tools. In a world full of misinformation, these skills help people make informed choices and take part in public life. Schools, libraries, journalists and youth groups mark the week with workshops, fact-checking exercises and conferences.

World Day for Audiovisual Heritage on 27 October draws attention to films, sound recordings and radio and television broadcasts as records of our shared history. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2005, and the date recalls its 1980 recommendation on safeguarding moving images. These materials are fragile: film decays, tapes wear out and formats become unreadable, so whole archives can vanish without care and funding. Archives, libraries and cinemas mark the day with screenings, restored footage and open days.

slogans.en: Save the sounds and images of our past.

names.en: International Day of Care and Support

descriptions.en: The International Day of Care and Support, on October 29, recognises the work of looking after children, older people, the sick and people with disabilities. The UN General Assembly established it in 2023, noting that most of this work is unpaid and falls mainly on women and girls, while paid care workers are often poorly paid and undervalued. The day is marked with campaigns, reports and policy debates that call for decent pay for care workers, shared responsibility at home and public services that support carers.

names.en: International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists

descriptions.en: The International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2013. Its date recalls the killing of two French journalists, Ghislaine Dupont and Claude Verlon, in Mali on November 2 of that year. UNESCO, which leads the day, reports that in most killings of journalists no one is ever convicted, and it uses the day to press governments to investigate and prosecute.

slogans.en: Truth should not cost a life.

names.en: International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict

descriptions.en: The International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict was declared by the UN General Assembly in 2001 and is observed on November 6. Wars poison rivers and wells, burn forests and oil fields, and leave mines and debris in farmland, damage that harms people long after the fighting ends. The day calls for protecting nature in conflict and for treating environmental recovery as part of building peace.

names.en: International Week of Science and Peace

descriptions.en: The International Week of Science and Peace is held each year in the week that includes November 11. It was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1988, during the final years of the Cold War, to encourage scientists to work across borders for peaceful ends. Universities, research centres and schools mark it with lectures, open days and joint projects on themes such as disarmament, health and climate.

names.en: International Day for the Prevention of and Fight against All Forms of Transnational Organized Crime

descriptions.en: The International Day for the Prevention of and Fight against All Forms of Transnational Organized Crime was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2024. It falls on November 15, the anniversary of the adoption in 2000 of the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, known as the Palermo Convention. The day draws attention to human trafficking, migrant smuggling, the drug and arms trades and money laundering, and to the cooperation between countries needed to stop them.

names.en: International Day of the Mediterranean Diet

descriptions.en: The International Day of the Mediterranean Diet is a UN observance on November 16, the anniversary of the diet's inscription on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010. The listing recognises more than a way of eating: the skills, knowledge and rituals around farming, fishing, cooking and sharing food in countries around the Mediterranean. The day celebrates olive oil, vegetables, legumes, grains, fish and long meals eaten together, a pattern linked to better heart health.

slogans.en: Olive oil, sunshine and shared tables.

names.en: World Day for the Prevention of and Healing from Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Violence

descriptions.en: The World Day for the Prevention of and Healing from Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Violence was established by the UN General Assembly in 2022 and is marked on November 18. It aims to bring the subject out of silence, so that children learn they can speak up and adults learn to recognise the signs. The day also stresses support for survivors on the long path to healing and the need to hold abusers to account.

World Conjoined Twins Day on November 24 was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2024. Conjoined twins are very rare, occurring in roughly one in every 50,000 to 200,000 births, and many need complex surgery and lifelong specialist care. The day raises awareness of the condition, highlights advances in surgery and care, and calls for support and access to treatment for affected families wherever they live.

World Sustainable Transport Day on November 26 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2023 and first observed that year. Transport carries people to work, school and hospitals and goods to markets, but it is also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution and road deaths. The day promotes safe, affordable and low-carbon options such as public transport, rail, cycling and walking, and better access for rural and poorer communities.

names.en: International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage

descriptions.en: The International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage is a UN observance on November 27. Around 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year, often ending their schooling and exposing them to early pregnancy, poverty and violence. The day calls for laws that set 18 as the minimum age, for keeping girls in school and for support for girls and young women already affected.

names.en: International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People

descriptions.en: The International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People on November 29 was designated by the UN General Assembly in 1977. The date recalls November 29, 1947, when the Assembly adopted Resolution 181 on the partition of Palestine. The day reaffirms support for the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including self-determination, independence and the right of refugees to return, and is marked with meetings at the UN and events around the world.

names.en: Day of Remembrance for all Victims of Chemical Warfare

descriptions.en: The Day of Remembrance for All Victims of Chemical Warfare is observed on November 30, a date set in 2015 by the states that are party to the Chemical Weapons Convention. It honours those killed and injured by chemical weapons, from the gas attacks of the First World War to later attacks on soldiers and civilians. The Convention, in force since 1997, bans these weapons entirely, and the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, which oversees it, marks the day with ceremonies in The Hague.

The International Day of Banks on December 4 was established by the UN General Assembly in 2019 and first observed in 2020. It recognises the role of multilateral and international development banks in financing schools, hospitals, roads, clean energy and other projects that countries could not pay for alone. The day is also used to discuss how finance can support the Sustainable Development Goals and help poorer countries cope with debt and climate change.

names.en: International Day Against Unilateral Coercive Measures

descriptions.en: The International Day against Unilateral Coercive Measures on December 4 was established by the UN General Assembly in 2024. It draws attention to the effects of sanctions imposed by one country or group of countries outside the UN framework, which supporters of the day say can restrict access to food, medicine, fuel and finance. The day calls for exemptions and safeguards so that ordinary people do not bear the cost of disputes between governments.

The International Day of Neutrality on December 12 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2017. The date recalls December 12, 1995, when the UN recognised Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality, and the day highlights the role neutral states can play in peace. Neutral countries such as Switzerland have long hosted peace talks and humanitarian work, and the day promotes preventive diplomacy and dialogue as ways to stop conflicts before they start.

International Universal Health Coverage Day on December 12 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2017. The date recalls a UN resolution of December 12, 2012, calling on countries to make sure everyone can get the health care they need without being pushed into poverty to pay for it. Around half the world's people still lack access to essential health services, and the day is used to campaign for stronger primary care, fair financing and health workers where they are needed most.

names.en: International Day against Colonialism in All its Forms and Manifestations

descriptions.en: The International Day against Colonialism in All its Forms and Manifestations is marked on December 14, a UN observance adopted in 2025. The date recalls December 14, 1960, when the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, which helped speed the independence of dozens of nations in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean. The day remembers the harm colonial rule caused and calls attention to the territories that are still not self-governing.

slogans.en: Every people decides its own future.

descriptions.en: World Turkic Language Family Day on December 15 was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2025. The date marks December 15, 1893, when the Danish linguist Vilhelm Thomsen announced that he had deciphered the Orkhon inscriptions, 8th-century Old Turkic texts carved on stone monuments in Mongolia. Turkic languages, among them Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Turkmen, Uyghur and Tatar, are spoken by more than 200 million people from the Balkans to Siberia.

names.en: International Day of Recognition for Women Searchers of Missing Persons

descriptions.en: The International Day of Recognition for Women Searchers of Missing Persons on December 19 is a UN observance honouring the mothers, sisters, wives and daughters who search for loved ones who have disappeared. In countries such as Mexico, Colombia and Argentina, many of these women dig through fields, visit morgues and confront officials on their own, often facing threats and violence. The day calls for their protection, for governments to take up the search, and for justice for the missing and their families.

The International Day against Cybercrime on December 24 marks the anniversary of the adoption, in 2024, of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime, the first global treaty on the subject. Online fraud, ransomware, identity theft and the abuse of children online cross borders easily, so investigating them depends on cooperation between countries. The day raises awareness of how to stay safe online, from strong passwords and two-factor authentication to recognising scams, which often spike during the holiday season.

names.en: World Day for African and Afrodescendant Culture

descriptions.en: The World Day for African and Afrodescendant Culture on January 24 was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019. The date marks the adoption in 2006 of the African Union's Charter for African Cultural Renaissance, which promotes African cultures as a source of identity, development and unity. The day celebrates the music, languages, art, literature and traditions of Africa and of the African diaspora around the world, and the role of culture in sustainable development.

names.en: International Day of Women in Multilateralism

descriptions.en: The International Day of Women in Multilateralism on January 25 was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2024. It recognises the women who lead and shape international organisations, diplomacy and peace negotiations, while women remain under-represented among ambassadors, heads of agencies and negotiators. The UN and member states mark the day with panels, campaigns and calls for equal representation at every level of international decision-making.

names.en: World Engineering Day for Sustainable Development

descriptions.en: World Engineering Day for Sustainable Development, on 4 March, celebrates engineers and the part they play in building a fairer, greener world. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2019 at the proposal of the World Federation of Engineering Organizations, and it was first observed in 2020. Universities, engineering societies and schools mark it with talks, exhibitions and student projects on clean energy, safe water, resilient cities and other solutions for a sustainable future.

The International Day for Digital Learning on March 19 celebrates learning with digital technology and asks how it can reach everyone. Computers, the internet and online courses can open up education to people far from any classroom, yet many learners around the world still lack a device, a reliable connection or the skills to use them. The day is a chance to think about how technology can support teachers and students without leaving anyone behind. Schools, universities and education groups mark it with talks, online events and projects that share good ways of teaching and learning with digital tools.

names.en: International Day for Small Island Developing States

descriptions.en: This day draws attention to small island developing states, the island nations scattered across the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. They have contributed very little to climate change, yet they are among the first to feel it, through rising seas, stronger storms and the loss of land, fresh water and cultural heritage. Their small economies often depend on fishing and tourism, so every disaster hits them harder. The day is marked with talks, exhibitions and campaigns that share island voices and call for climate action.

African World Heritage Day, held on 5 May, celebrates the continent's cultural and natural World Heritage sites, from the ancient city of Timbuktu to the plains of the Serengeti. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2015 and it has been marked since 2016, to raise awareness of Africa's heritage and of the threats many of its sites face, from conflict and poaching to climate change and uncontrolled development. Museums, schools and heritage groups hold talks, exhibitions and site visits, and encourage young Africans to learn about and protect these places.

World Metrology Day, on 20 May, celebrates the science of measurement that quietly underpins trade, medicine, technology and everyday life. The date marks the signing of the Metre Convention in Paris on 20 May 1875, when nations first agreed on a shared international system of measurement. The International Bureau of Weights and Measures and the International Organization of Legal Metrology mark the day together with a new theme each year. Laboratories and standards institutes hold open days, talks and school activities about why accurate measurement matters.

names.en: International Day for Underwater Cultural Heritage

descriptions.en: The International Day for Underwater Cultural Heritage draws attention to shipwrecks, sunken cities and other traces of the past that lie beneath seas, lakes and rivers. These sites are fragile and easily damaged by looting, trawling and careless diving, which is why UNESCO adopted a convention in 2001 to protect them. Türkiye has some of the richest of all: the Uluburun wreck off Kaş is a Bronze Age ship more than 3,000 years old, and its cargo can be seen in Bodrum's Museum of Underwater Archaeology. Museums, divers and archaeologists mark the day with talks, exhibitions and dives.

names.en: International Day for Caves and Karst

descriptions.en: The International Day for Caves and Karst, on 13 September, celebrates caves and the karst landscapes carved by water dissolving limestone and similar rock. These landscapes hide underground rivers and aquifers that supply drinking water to millions of people, and caves shelter rare animals and preserve traces of early human life. Türkiye is especially rich in them, from Damlataş Cave in Alanya to Karain Cave near Antalya, where people lived in the Stone Age. The day is marked with cave visits, talks and calls to keep groundwater clean.

The International Day of University Sport, held on 20 September, celebrates student athletes and the place of sport in university life. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2015, and it is promoted around the world by FISU, the International University Sports Federation, which also organises the World University Games. Universities mark it with open training sessions, friendly matches, fun runs and talks on how sport supports health, learning and friendship on campus.

International Geodiversity Day, on 6 October, celebrates the variety of rocks, minerals, fossils, landforms and soils that shape our planet and support all life on it. UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2021, and it was first celebrated in 2022 to raise awareness of the value of this natural heritage. Geologists, geoparks, museums and schools mark it with field trips, guided walks and talks, inviting people to discover landscapes such as Cappadocia's fairy chimneys with fresh eyes.

names.en: International Day of the Intangible Cultural Heritage

descriptions.en: This day celebrates intangible cultural heritage: the living traditions people carry rather than build, such as music, crafts, festivals, storytelling and cuisine. It falls on 17 October, the anniversary of UNESCO's 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, which led to lists of traditions worth protecting. Türkiye's entries include Turkish coffee, ebru marbling and the Mevlevi Sema ceremony. Museums, schools and communities mark it with performances, workshops and masters passing their skills to younger people.

slogans.en: Heritage you can hear, taste and dance.

descriptions.en: World Coding Day, on October 29, celebrates programming as a basic skill for understanding the modern world. Code runs the phones, cars, hospitals and banks we rely on every day, and learning how it works helps people move from simply using technology to shaping it. Schools, libraries and coding clubs mark the day with beginner lessons, puzzles and small projects, especially aimed at children and young people trying it for the first time.

slogans.en: Write the future, line by line.

descriptions.en: The International Day for Biosphere Reserves on November 3 was proclaimed by UNESCO and first celebrated in 2022. Biosphere reserves are areas where people live and work alongside protected nature, testing ways to balance conservation with farming, tourism and local livelihoods. There are now more than 750 of them in over 130 countries, and the day is marked with guided walks, school visits and local events in the reserves.

The World Day of Romani Language on November 5 celebrates Romani, spoken by millions of Roma across Europe and the Americas. Romani descends from languages of northern India and arrived in Europe around a thousand years ago, absorbing words from every country along the way. The day, now recognised by UNESCO, is marked with readings, music, language classes and efforts to bring Romani into schools and media.

names.en: International Day against Violence and Bullying at School, including Cyberbullying

descriptions.en: The International Day against Violence and Bullying at School, including Cyberbullying, was established by UNESCO's member states in 2019 and is held on the first Thursday of November. UNESCO estimates that almost one in three students worldwide is bullied by peers at least once a month, and much of it now happens online. Schools mark the day with lessons on respect, campaigns that teach bystanders to speak up, and clear ways for pupils to report abuse.

names.en: International Day against Illicit Trafficking in Cultural Property

descriptions.en: The International Day against Illicit Trafficking in Cultural Property was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019 and is marked on November 14, the anniversary of UNESCO's 1970 Convention on the subject. Looting of archaeological sites and the smuggling of antiquities rob communities of their history and can fund armed groups. Countries use the day to showcase returned treasures; Türkiye has recovered thousands of artefacts, including the upper half of the Weary Herakles statue, returned from Boston in 2011.

The International Day of Islamic Art was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019 and is celebrated on November 18. It honours more than fourteen centuries of art from Spain to Indonesia, including calligraphy, geometric tile work, carpets, metalwork, book illumination and architecture such as the Alhambra and the great mosques of Istanbul. Museums and cultural centres mark it with exhibitions, workshops in calligraphy and tile painting, and talks on the shared heritage of the Islamic world.

World Olive Tree Day on November 26 was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019 to honour a tree that has shaped Mediterranean life for thousands of years. The olive branch is an ancient symbol of peace, and the tree's oil, wood and fruit have fed and supported communities from Spain to Türkiye and the Levant. Some olive trees are more than a thousand years old, and the day is marked with harvest festivals, oil tastings and planting events, including in the groves of Türkiye's Aegean coast.

slogans.en: A tree of peace and plenty.

names.en: International Day of Engagement in Science for Sustainable Development

descriptions.en: The International Day for Science Engagement on November 27 was proclaimed by UNESCO to bring science closer to the public. It encourages people to take part in research rather than just read about it, through citizen science projects such as counting birds, mapping plants or classifying galaxies online. Universities, museums and research institutes mark the day with open labs, public talks and invitations to join projects that rely on volunteers.

World Futures Day on December 2 is a UNESCO observance that encourages people to think about the future in a more open way. Rather than predicting a single outcome, futures thinking explores many possible futures and asks which ones we want and how to get there. Schools, cities and organisations use the day for workshops and conversations that turn that foresight into better decisions today.

names.en: 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence

descriptions.en: The 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence run each year from November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, to December 10, Human Rights Day. The campaign was launched in 1991 by activists at the Center for Women's Global Leadership and is now backed by the UN through its UNiTE campaign, which turns landmarks orange. About one in three women worldwide experiences physical or sexual violence in her lifetime, and the campaign calls for prevention, support for survivors and accountability.

International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week takes place each October, led by the World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme. Lead is a toxic metal still found in some paints, pipes, toys, cosmetics and ceramics. It harms children's developing brains for life, and no level of exposure is known to be safe. During the week, health agencies and campaigners push for laws banning lead paint, test homes and schools, and show families how to reduce their exposure.

World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day on November 17 marks the launch, on that date in 2020, of the WHO strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem. Cervical cancer is almost entirely caused by the human papillomavirus and is one of the most preventable cancers, yet it still kills hundreds of thousands of women a year. The strategy's 90-70-90 targets call for vaccinating girls against HPV, screening women regularly and treating those diagnosed, and the day is marked with awareness drives and screening campaigns.

names.en: European and World Day against the Death Penalty

descriptions.en: The European and World Day against the Death Penalty, on 10 October, calls for capital punishment to be abolished everywhere. The World Day was launched in 2003 by the World Coalition Against the Death Penalty, and the Council of Europe and the European Union declared the European Day on the same date in 2007. Each year has a theme, such as the risk of executing the innocent or the conditions on death row. Human rights groups mark it with campaigns, debates and petitions to countries that still carry out executions.

slogans.en: Life is a right, not a sentence.

descriptions.en: European Heritage Days open the doors of castles, churches, workshops, archives and private houses that are usually closed or charge for entry, mostly free of charge. The idea began in France in 1984 and has been run jointly by the Council of Europe and the European Union since 1999, now spanning around 50 countries. Most events fall on September weekends, with guided tours, craft demonstrations, concerts and walks that invite people to discover the history on their own doorstep.

World NGO Day, held on 27 February, honours non-governmental organisations and the people who work and volunteer for them. NGOs reach where governments and markets often do not, defending human rights, delivering aid in emergencies, supporting health and education and protecting the environment. The day is a chance to recognise that work, learn how these groups operate and see how ordinary people can take part. Many people mark it by volunteering, donating or simply thanking a local organisation whose work they value.

slogans.en: Thank the people who show up.

descriptions.en: The Day of International Criminal Justice is held on 17 July, the anniversary of the adoption of the Rome Statute in 1998. That treaty created the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the first permanent court able to try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The day is a reminder that the gravest crimes should not go unpunished, and it is marked with conferences, statements and campaigns supporting victims and the rule of law.

slogans.en: No one is above the law.

descriptions.en: Earthquake Week is held in Türkiye every year from 1 to 7 March. Türkiye lies on some of the world's most active fault lines, and the week aims to build an everyday culture of earthquake preparedness. Schools, AFAD and local authorities run drills and lessons on the drop, cover and hold on routine, securing furniture, family emergency plans and packing an emergency bag. Many people use the week to check their own homes and talk through with their families what to do when the ground shakes.

Civil Defence Day is marked in Türkiye on 28 February to draw attention to protecting people and property in wartime, natural disasters, fires and other emergencies. Civil defence was long run by its own national organisation, and since 2009 the work has been coordinated by AFAD, Türkiye's disaster and emergency management authority. The day reminds everyone that preparedness starts at home and in the neighbourhood. Schools, public offices and workplaces mark it with drills, evacuation exercises and talks on first aid and emergency planning.

At 3:02 in the morning on 17 August 1999, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake centred near Gölcük struck the Marmara region, killing more than 17,000 people in Kocaeli, Sakarya, Yalova, Istanbul and nearby provinces. It remains one of the deadliest disasters in modern Turkish history and changed how the country thinks about building safety. Each year Türkiye remembers the victims with ceremonies and moments of silence at 3:02, and renews its call for earthquake-resistant homes and disaster preparedness.

names.en: African Day of Peace and Reconciliation

descriptions.en: The African Day of Peace and Reconciliation on January 31 is marked by the African Union to honour efforts to end conflicts and heal divided societies across the continent. Many African countries have lived through civil wars and political violence, and the experience of truth commissions, peace agreements and community reconciliation has shown that lasting peace needs justice and dialogue as well as an end to fighting. The day fits the African Union's wider goal of silencing the guns on the continent, and it is marked with dialogues, commemorations and events that bring former rivals and young people together.

slogans.en: Silence the guns, heal the land.

descriptions.en: The African Day of School Feeding is marked on 1 March by the African Union, which adopted it in 2016. It promotes school meal programmes, which help keep children in the classroom, improve their nutrition and concentration, and give families one less worry. When the food is bought from nearby farms, these programmes also support local agriculture and economies. Governments, schools and aid partners use the day to share progress, celebrate local meal programmes and call for more children to be reached.

slogans.en: A full plate, an open mind.

names.en: Africa Environment and Wangari Maathai Day

descriptions.en: On 3 March the African Union marks Africa Environment Day together with Wangari Maathai Day, joining care for the continent's land with the memory of one of its great defenders. Maathai, a Kenyan biologist, founded the Green Belt Movement, which helped rural women plant tens of millions of trees, and in 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. The day is marked with tree planting, clean-ups and talks on forests, water and soil across Africa.

slogans.en: Plant a tree, grow a future.

names.en: Day of the Battle of Cuito Cuanavale

descriptions.en: This day remembers the Battle of Cuito Cuanavale, fought in southern Angola in 1987 and 1988 between Angolan and Cuban forces on one side and South African troops and their UNITA allies on the other. The long siege ended in stalemate, but it pushed South Africa to the negotiating table, and the agreements that followed opened the way to Namibia's independence in 1990. Across southern Africa it is remembered as a turning point in the struggle against apartheid, with commemorations, wreath-laying and talks on liberation history.

Africa Border Day on 7 June is an African Union observance that promotes peace, integration and cooperation across the continent's borders. Most of Africa's borders were drawn by colonial powers, often cutting across communities, and disputes over them have fuelled conflict. The AU uses the day to encourage peaceful settlement of border questions, joint development of border regions and freer movement of people and goods. Governments and border communities mark it with meetings, cultural events and cross-border projects.

The Day of the African Child, on 16 June, remembers the students of Soweto, South Africa, who marched in 1976 against inferior education under apartheid and were met with police gunfire. The Organisation of African Unity, today's African Union, established the day in 1991 to honour them. Each year it carries a theme on children's rights, and governments, schools and charities across Africa use it to push for better education, health and protection for every child.

slogans.en: Every African child deserves a future.

descriptions.en: The Day of Africa's Scientific Renaissance, held by the African Union on 30 June, honours African scientists, engineers and inventors. It stresses that science, technology and innovation are central to the continent's development, from health and farming to energy and digital services. Universities, research centres and schools mark it with science fairs, lectures and prizes, and use it to encourage young Africans, especially girls, to choose scientific careers.

African Integration Day celebrates the long-held dream of a more united Africa, with goods, people and ideas moving freely across its borders. The African Union links the date to the African Continental Free Trade Area, whose operational phase was launched at an AU summit in Niamey, Niger, in July 2019, creating one of the world's largest free trade areas by number of countries. The day is marked with conferences, trade fairs, cultural events and debates on how closer ties can bring jobs and growth.

African Anti-Corruption Day is observed on 11 July, the anniversary of the African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption, adopted in Maputo in 2003. Corruption drains public money away from schools, hospitals and roads, and weakens trust between citizens and the state. The day calls for transparent, accountable governance across the continent. Governments, civil society groups and young people mark it with debates, campaigns and reports on what has been done and what still needs to change.

names.en: Africa Day of Seas and Oceans

descriptions.en: The Africa Day of Seas and Oceans, held on 25 July, is promoted by the African Union. It draws attention to the waters around a continent where dozens of countries have a coastline and millions of people live from fishing, ports and shipping. The day stresses protecting marine life and building a sustainable blue economy, and it is marked with conferences, coastal clean-ups and school activities about the sea.

African Women's Day on July 31 marks the founding of the Pan-African Women's Organization in 1962, which brought together women from across the continent during the struggle for independence. The day honours the part African women played in liberation movements and the role they continue to play in their families, economies and societies. It is marked across Africa with conferences, community events and campaigns on women's rights, education, health and leadership.

names.en: Africa Day of Decentralisation and Local Development

descriptions.en: The Africa Day of Decentralisation and Local Development, held by the African Union on 10 August, champions the idea that many decisions are best made close to the people they affect. It promotes elected local councils, a fair sharing of money and powers between national and local government, and citizens' say in how their towns and villages are run. The AU has a charter devoted to these values, which member states are encouraged to ratify. Mayors, local authorities and civil society mark the day with forums, public debates and reviews of how well services such as water, roads and clinics reach communities.

names.en: Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Day

descriptions.en: Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Day, set by the African Union for 10 August, calls for every birth, marriage, divorce and death on the continent to be officially recorded. A birth certificate is often the first proof of a person's legal identity, opening the door to school, health care, inheritance and the vote, yet many African children are still never registered. Reliable records also give governments the population data they need to plan services. Ministries, statistics offices and civil society use the day to run registration drives and push for systems that reach every village.

slogans.en: Every birth counts, every person counts.

descriptions.en: African Traditional Medicine Day has been marked on 31 August since 2003, an initiative of African health ministers through the World Health Organization's regional office for Africa. Across the continent, many people rely on traditional healers and herbal remedies for their everyday health care. The day recognises this knowledge and calls for traditional medicine to be researched, regulated and safely brought into national health systems. Health ministries, universities and healers' associations hold conferences, exhibitions and public talks.

Africa-CARICOM Day, on 7 September, celebrates the bond between Africa and the Caribbean Community, two regions joined by shared history, culture and the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade. The day was declared at the first Africa-CARICOM summit in 2021, where leaders pledged to deepen cooperation between the two regions in trade, investment and other fields. It is marked with diplomatic meetings, cultural programmes and conversations that bring Africans, Caribbean people and their diasporas closer together.

African Union Day, on 9 September, recalls the Sirte Declaration of 1999, when African leaders meeting in Libya called for a new union to replace the Organisation of African Unity. The African Union was launched in Durban in 2002 and today brings together 55 member states to promote peace, integration and development across the continent. The day is marked with flag-raisings, speeches, cultural events and debates about Africa's future.

African Human Rights Day is marked on 21 October, the day in 1986 when the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights entered into force. The charter was adopted in 1981 by the Organisation of African Unity and protects both individual rights and the collective rights of peoples. It is overseen by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. Governments, rights groups and schools across the continent use the day to discuss freedoms, justice and the work still to be done.

names.en: Africa Food Security and Nutrition Day

descriptions.en: Africa Food Security and Nutrition Day, on October 30, is observed by the African Union to keep hunger and malnutrition high on the continent's agenda. Millions of Africans still lack enough nutritious food, and poor nutrition in early childhood can hold back health, schooling and earnings for a lifetime. Governments, farmers' groups and aid organisations use the day to share progress and call for stronger local farming, fairer trade within Africa and better nutrition programmes for mothers and children.

slogans.en: Grow more, waste less, feed all.

descriptions.en: African Youth Day is held on November 1 by the African Union to celebrate the young people who make up the majority of the continent's population. The date recalls the African Youth Charter, adopted in 2006, which sets out young people's rights to education, work and a voice in public life. Across Africa it is marked with youth forums, volunteering, cultural events and debates on jobs and leadership.

slogans.en: The youngest continent, the brightest future.

descriptions.en: African Statistics Day has been marked on November 18 since 1990, when it was adopted by African ministers responsible for planning and statistics. Reliable figures on population, health, jobs and prices are what governments need to plan schools, clinics, roads and budgets, yet many countries still lack them. The day is used by national statistics offices, universities and the African Union to promote better data collection, census work and public trust in official numbers.

Africa Telecommunications and ICT Day on December 7 is marked by the African Union to celebrate the role of telecommunications and digital technology in the continent's development. Africa leapfrogged landlines with mobile phones, and services such as mobile money have changed how millions of people save, pay and run businesses. The day highlights the work still needed on affordable broadband, digital skills and connecting rural communities.

The Day of African Sport on December 14 is marked by the African Union to celebrate the role of sport on the continent. Africa has produced legendary distance runners from Ethiopia and Kenya, football stars who play in the world's biggest leagues, and champions in boxing, athletics and basketball. The day highlights sport as a way to promote health, peace and opportunity for young people, and calls for investment in facilities and grassroots programmes.

slogans.en: Run with the spirit of Africa.
