descriptions.en: March is Red Cross Month in the United States, a tradition that began in 1943 when President Franklin D. Roosevelt proclaimed the first one during the Second World War. Every president since has renewed the proclamation. The month honours the volunteers, blood donors and disaster responders of the American Red Cross, who help families after fires, floods and storms and support members of the armed forces. People mark it by giving blood, volunteering, learning first aid or donating to support the organisation's work.

Memorial Day, observed on the last Monday of May, honours the men and women who died while serving in the United States armed forces. It began after the Civil War as Decoration Day, when families laid flowers on soldiers' graves, and became a federal holiday in 1971. Americans visit cemeteries and memorials, fly the flag at half-staff until noon, and pause for the National Moment of Remembrance at 3 p.m.

slogans.en: Remember the ones who gave everything.

descriptions.en: Flag Day on June 14 marks the day in 1777 when the Second Continental Congress adopted the Stars and Stripes as the flag of the United States. President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed the first national observance in 1916, and Congress made the day permanent in 1949. Homes, schools and public buildings fly the flag, and the week around it is National Flag Week.

slogans.en: Thirteen stripes, fifty stars, one story.

descriptions.en: Columbus Day, on the second Monday of October, marks Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas on October 12, 1492. First celebrated by Italian American communities in the 19th century, it became a federal holiday in 1937 and remains a day of pride in Italian American heritage. Parades such as New York's Columbus Day Parade fill the streets, while many places also observe Indigenous Peoples' Day on the same date.

slogans.en: Honour the voyage and the heritage it carries.

descriptions.en: Armed Forces Day, held on the third Saturday of May, thanks everyone serving in the US Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Space Force and Coast Guard. President Harry Truman created it in 1949 to replace the separate days each branch once kept, after the services were unified under the Department of Defense. Bases open their gates for tours, air shows and parades, and the whole of May is National Military Appreciation Month.

slogans.en: One day to thank all who serve.

descriptions.en: National Grandparents Day falls on the first Sunday after Labor Day and celebrates the love, wisdom and stories grandparents pass on. West Virginia homemaker Marian McQuade campaigned for it, and President Jimmy Carter signed it into law in 1978. Families visit, call or write to their grandparents, and the day's official flower is the forget-me-not.

Peace Officers Memorial Day on May 15 honours the federal, state and local law enforcement officers killed or disabled in the line of duty. President John F. Kennedy signed the law creating it in 1962, and flags across the United States fly at half-staff from sunrise to sunset. Thousands gather at the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial in Washington, D.C., where the names of fallen officers are read aloud.

slogans.en: Their watch has ended; our gratitude has not.

descriptions.en: Police Week is the calendar week that contains May 15, Peace Officers Memorial Day, and recognises the service of law enforcement officers across the United States. Congress established it in 1962 alongside the memorial day, and it has grown into a gathering that brings tens of thousands of officers and families to Washington, D.C. A candlelight vigil at the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial adds the names of officers who died in the past year.

slogans.en: Standing together for those who protect us.

descriptions.en: National Maritime Day on May 22 honours the merchant mariners who carry America's trade and, in wartime, its troops and supplies. The date recalls the SS Savannah, which set out from Savannah, Georgia, on May 22, 1819, on the first transatlantic voyage made partly under steam power. Congress created the day in 1933, and ports and ships mark it with wreath-laying ceremonies and by sounding their whistles.

slogans.en: Fair winds to those who keep the seas moving.

descriptions.en: The National Day of Prayer, held on the first Thursday of May, invites Americans of all faiths to pray or reflect for the nation. Congress created it in 1952, and a 1988 law fixed the date and requires the President to proclaim it each year. Gatherings take place at the Capitol, in city halls, churches, synagogues and mosques, and in homes across the country.

Religious Freedom Day on January 16 marks the 1786 adoption of Thomas Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom by the Virginia General Assembly. The statute became a model for the First Amendment's protection of the free exercise of religion and the separation of church and state. Presidents have proclaimed the day every year since 1993, and schools use it to teach students about freedom of conscience.

slogans.en: Free to believe, free to differ.

names.en: Gold Star Mother's and Family's Day

descriptions.en: Gold Star Mother's and Family's Day, on the last Sunday of September, honours the families of service members who died in the line of duty. The gold star comes from the service flags families hung in their windows during World War I, when a blue star was replaced with a gold one after a loss. Congress created the day in 1936, and communities hold ceremonies, lay wreaths and fly the flag in their honour.

National POW/MIA Recognition Day, on the third Friday of September, honours Americans who were held as prisoners of war and those still missing in action. More than 81,000 US service members remain unaccounted for from World War II to the present, and the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency still works to bring them home. The black POW/MIA flag flies over the White House, the Capitol and military installations, and ceremonies close with the pledge "You are not forgotten."

names.en: National Former Prisoner of War Recognition Day

descriptions.en: National Former Prisoner of War Recognition Day on April 9 honours the Americans who endured captivity while serving their country. The date recalls April 9, 1942, when US and Filipino troops on the Bataan Peninsula surrendered and thousands were forced onto the Bataan Death March. Veterans' groups and communities use the day to thank surviving former prisoners of war and to remember those who never returned.

National Agriculture Day, held each March, celebrates the farmers and ranchers who grow the food, fibre and fuel the United States depends on. The Agriculture Council of America has organised it since 1973, and the President proclaims it every year. Schools, farms and the US Department of Agriculture host events that show where food comes from and how a single American farm today feeds well over a hundred people.

General Pulaski Memorial Day on October 11 honours Casimir Pulaski, the Polish nobleman who fought for American independence and is remembered as the father of the American cavalry. He covered George Washington's retreat at the Battle of Brandywine in 1777 and was mortally wounded leading a charge at the Siege of Savannah in 1779. The day celebrates Polish American heritage, and New York's Pulaski Day Parade on Fifth Avenue is one of its biggest events.

Leif Erikson Day on October 9 honours the Norse explorer who reached North America around the year 1000, nearly five centuries before Columbus. Erikson, born in Iceland, landed at a place the sagas call Vinland, and the Norse site found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms such voyages. The date marks the arrival of the ship Restauration in New York in 1825, which began organised Norwegian immigration, and Nordic American communities celebrate with festivals and flags.

slogans.en: Sail beyond the edge of the map.

names.en: U.S. Hostage and Wrongful Detainee Day

descriptions.en: U.S. Hostage and Wrongful Detainee Day on March 9 stands with Americans held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad and with the families waiting for them. The date recalls Robert Levinson, a retired FBI agent who disappeared in Iran on March 9, 2007, and Congress made the day official in 2023 together with a national hostage and wrongful detainee flag. The flag is raised in Washington, D.C., and families gather to keep their loved ones' names in public view.

slogans.en: Until every one of them is home.

names.en: National Physical Fitness and Sports Month

descriptions.en: National Physical Fitness and Sports Month fills May with a call to get moving, whether through team sports, a daily walk or a new workout. Presidents have proclaimed it every year since 1983, and it is led by the President's Council on Sports, Fitness and Nutrition, which traces back to the youth fitness council President Eisenhower created in 1956. US guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults and an hour a day for children, and schools, gyms and parks run events to help people get there.

Women's History Month turns March into a celebration of the women whose work, courage and ideas shaped history, often without the credit they deserved. It grew from a 1978 Women's History Week in Sonoma County, California, which President Jimmy Carter made national in 1980, and Congress expanded it to the whole month in 1987. The United Kingdom and Australia also mark it in March, with exhibitions, talks and school lessons about women from suffragists to scientists.

Jewish American Heritage Month celebrates in May the contributions Jewish Americans have made to the United States since the first Jewish community arrived in New Amsterdam in 1654. President George W. Bush first proclaimed it in 2006, after Congress passed resolutions supporting it, and every president since has renewed it. Museums, libraries and communities mark it with exhibitions, talks and events about Jewish history, arts and culture in America.

slogans.en: Stories that helped build a nation.

descriptions.en: Irish-American Heritage Month celebrates in March the millions of Americans with Irish roots and the long history of Irish immigration to the United States. Congress designated the month in 1991, and it surrounds St. Patrick's Day on March 17, when cities from Boston to Chicago turn green. Today more than 30 million Americans claim Irish ancestry, and the month brings parades, céilí dances, music and talks about the Great Famine migration that reshaped American cities.

National Foster Care Month in May recognises the foster parents, relatives, social workers and mentors who care for children who cannot live safely with their own families. More than 300,000 children are in foster care in the United States on any given day, and many wait years for a permanent home. Proclaimed by presidents since 1988, the month encourages people to become foster parents, volunteer as court-appointed advocates, or support the families who open their homes.

slogans.en: Every child deserves a place to belong.

descriptions.en: National Adoption Month in November raises awareness of the children and teenagers in US foster care who are waiting for permanent families. It grew out of a state Adoption Week in Massachusetts in 1976 and was expanded to the whole month in 1995. Many courts hold National Adoption Day on the Saturday before Thanksgiving, finalising hundreds of adoptions in a single day of celebrations.

slogans.en: Every child deserves a forever family.

descriptions.en: Mental Health Awareness Month in May works to break the silence around mental illness and help people find support early. Mental Health America started the observance in 1949, and today about one in five American adults lives with a mental health condition in any given year. People wear green ribbons, share their stories and learn about resources such as the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which anyone in the US can call or text.

slogans.en: It's okay to not be okay.

descriptions.en: American Heart Month in February raises awareness of heart disease, the leading cause of death in the United States for both men and women. President Lyndon B. Johnson issued the first proclamation in 1964, and Congress has asked every president since to renew it. The first Friday of February is National Wear Red Day, and the month encourages blood pressure checks, CPR training and heart-healthy habits.

slogans.en: Love your heart, it loves you back.

descriptions.en: National Donate Life Month in April encourages Americans to register as organ, eye and tissue donors and honours those who have given the gift of life. More than 100,000 people in the United States are waiting for an organ transplant, and a single donor can save up to eight lives. Hospitals raise flags, families share donor stories, and Blue and Green Day invites everyone to wear the colours of the Donate Life movement.

National Child Abuse Prevention Month in April calls on families, neighbours and communities to help keep children safe from abuse and neglect. It has been proclaimed every year since 1983, and its symbol is the blue pinwheel, which stands for the happy childhood every child deserves. Communities plant pinwheel gardens, share parenting resources and remind adults that reporting a concern can change a child's life.

slogans.en: Every child deserves a safe childhood.

names.en: Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month

descriptions.en: Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month in April works to prevent sexual violence and to support survivors across the United States. Advocates began organising events in the 1980s, the month was first observed nationally in 2001, and presidents have proclaimed it every year since 2009. Its colour is teal, and on Denim Day people wear jeans to challenge the myth that what a victim wears invites assault.

National Ocean Month in June celebrates the seas that surround the United States and the jobs, food and climate balance they support. America's exclusive economic zone covers about 3.4 million square nautical miles, more ocean than the country has land, and its coasts hold marine sanctuaries from the Florida Keys to Hawaii. The month joins World Ocean Day on June 8 with beach clean-ups, aquarium events and science programmes that invite people to protect the ocean.

slogans.en: Protect the blue that sustains us.

descriptions.en: National Homeownership Month in June highlights the role a home of one's own plays in building family stability and wealth. The observance began as National Homeownership Day in 1995 and was expanded to the whole of June in 2002. Lenders, housing counsellors and the Department of Housing and Urban Development use the month to help first-time buyers understand mortgages, down payments and the path to owning a home.

National Small Business Week, held each spring, celebrates the entrepreneurs and small firms that employ nearly half of America's private-sector workers. Presidents have proclaimed it every year since 1963, and the US Small Business Administration hosts awards and events for owners across the country. It is a week to shop local, leave a review for a favourite shop, and thank the people who keep main streets alive.

National Hurricane Preparedness Week, held in early May, helps families get ready before the Atlantic hurricane season begins on June 1. The National Weather Service uses the week to explain storm surge, flooding and wind risks, which reach far inland as well as along the coast. People are urged to know their evacuation zone, build an emergency kit, and check their insurance before a storm is on the way.

National Park Week each April invites everyone to explore America's national parks, from Yellowstone, the world's first national park, to historic sites in the heart of cities. The National Park Service cares for more than 400 sites that welcome over 300 million visits a year. Entrance is free at every park on the week's opening day, and rangers lead walks, junior ranger programmes and volunteer projects throughout.

National Volunteer Week in April thanks the millions of Americans who give their time to food banks, schools, shelters, hospitals and disaster relief. President Richard Nixon established it in 1974, and every president since has proclaimed it. Around one in four Americans volunteers through an organisation each year, and the week invites more people to find a cause and lend a hand.

National Crime Victims' Rights Week each April honours victims and survivors of crime and the advocates who stand beside them. President Ronald Reagan first proclaimed it in 1981, at a time when victims had few rights in the justice system. Communities hold candlelight vigils, rallies and memorial walks, and the Justice Department's Office for Victims of Crime honours people who have advanced victims' rights.

slogans.en: Every victim deserves to be heard.

descriptions.en: National Poison Prevention Week, held in the third full week of March, teaches families how to prevent poisonings at home, where most of them happen. Congress established it in 1961, and President John F. Kennedy issued its first proclamation in 1962. Poison control centres answer about two million calls a year on the free Poison Help line, 1-800-222-1222, and the week reminds people to lock up medicines and cleaning products, especially where young children live.

slogans.en: Lock it up, look it up.

descriptions.en: National Consumer Protection Week, held in early March, helps people spot scams, protect their personal information and know their rights as buyers. The Federal Trade Commission has led it since 1999 with partners across government and the non-profit world. Americans reported losing more than 12 billion dollars to fraud in 2024, so the week shares free advice on impostor calls, online shopping and identity theft.

slogans.en: Know the scam, keep your money.

descriptions.en: World Trade Week, held each May, celebrates the role international trade plays in American jobs, farms and factories. Presidents have proclaimed it every year for decades, and chambers of commerce and the Department of Commerce use the week to help small firms start exporting. Ports, trade councils and universities host export workshops, trade fairs and talks about how goods travel the world.

Captive Nations Week, held in the third week of July, stands with people living under authoritarian and communist rule and their right to freedom and self-determination. Congress created it in 1959, during the Cold War, and every president since Dwight D. Eisenhower has proclaimed it. Diaspora communities from Eastern Europe, Asia, Cuba and beyond hold rallies and remembrance events, keeping the stories of political prisoners in view.

slogans.en: Freedom is not a gift; it is a right.
